It is the responsibility of the project engineer to request that the above equipment be added to a Preventative Maintenance plan. Thereafter, it is the responsibility of the appropriate Industry Source 01 CHP personnel (i.e. maintenance & reliability coordinator) to ensure that the required testing is completed.

2.33.3 Hoses that are intended for permanent use shall be assigned appropriate SP numbers and/or equipment numbers.

## SECTION 3: COMPONENT LIMITATIONS

### 3.1 General

Piping materials selection shall be in accordance with Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205, including additional components limitations listed in the General Notes of that standard.

### 3.2 Size Prohibitions

Piping smaller than 1/2" and pipe sizes 1-1/4" (except in plumbing systems), 2-1/2", 3-1/2", 4-1/2", 5", and 7" shall not be used. If equipment is furnished with connections in the above sizes, the transition to a Standard pipe size shall be made as close as possible to the equipment.

### 3.3 Pipe Caps

Threaded or socket weld pipe caps shall not be used, unless use of a round solid pipe plug or other piping alternative is not possible. For cases where the designer believes there is no alternative except use of a threaded or socket weld pipe cap, provide justification to and obtain approval from the Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer before proceeding.

### 3.4 Welded Austenitic Stainless Steel

Austenitic (300 series) stainless steel materials which will be welded during fabrication shall be dual grade (such as 316/316L) or low carbon grade (such as 316L), except for seal oil and lube

oil piping in section 2.18, or unless otherwise approved by the Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer. Dual grade material should normally be specified since it fully meets the requirements of both grades and provides the combined benefits of both grades. Low carbon grade provides better resistance to carbide precipitation and intergranular corrosion of welds and heat affected zones. The dual grade then combines the better corrosion resistance with the higher mechanical properties of the standard grade material.

## SECTION 4: PIPING JOINTS

### 4.1 Acceptable Joint Types

4.1.1 For piping 1-1/2" and smaller handling hydrocarbons, toxic, or hazardous fluids, typically socket weld fittings will be used, except where full penetration welds are required for special conditions as specified in 4.1.5 for reciprocating compressors, or as specified in 4.3.2 for severe thermal gradients or thermal cycling, or as specified in Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205 pipe classes. With approval of the Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer, threaded fittings may be allowed in place of socket weld fittings where the piping requires frequent disassembly or where flanges are impractical, such as fuel gas and fuel oil burner manifolds, pump gland plates, and similar applications. Socket welds shall be in accordance with drawing LA-000-0100-0200-018.

4.1.2 Pipe, fittings, flanges and valves may be threaded in sizes 1-1/2" and smaller for air and water service within the temperature-pressure limitations of Class 150 ASME B16.5 flanges. Threaded piping shall not be used underground unless approved by the Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer.

4.1.3 Threaded pipe and fittings may be used downstream of 1-1/2" and smaller block valves (the last valve in the case of double blocks) which bleed, vent, or drain to atmosphere.

4.1.4 Pipe, fittings, flanges and valves shall be in accordance with Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205. Except as previously permitted in this section, steel and alloy piping components in line classes with ASME B16.5 Class 150 or higher flanges shall be joined as follows:

a) Nominal Pipe Size 2" and Larger - Piping components shall be butt welded or flanged, except as described in Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205 General Notes section 9.2.2 for special circumstances for 2" size only.

b) Nominal Pipe Size 1-1/2" and Smaller - Piping components will normally be socket welded, except where flanged valves or flanged joints are needed at flanged equipment connections, blinding locations, or similar situations. Socket welds may be upgraded to butt welds where needed for special situations.

4.1.5 At reciprocating compressors in hydrocarbon, flammable, toxic, hazardous, sour, or corrosive services, all NPS 2 and smaller piping vents and piping branch connections for new or redesigned trim piping systems shall be full penetration welds or weld neck flanges. This is for the purpose of preventing high cycle fatigue failures at joints in small piping. Trim piping can be in any service and includes but is not limited to piping connections, instrument connections, vent/drain connections, lube oil connections, vents to flare, and similar items connecting to the following compressor system components:

a) Suction liquid knock-out vessels.

b) Suction piping within 50 pipe diameters of compressor.

c) Compressor.

d) Interstage piping within 50 pipe diameters of compressor.

e) Intercoolers and associated separators.

f) Aftercoolers.

g) Pulsation suppression devices.

h) Discharge piping within 50 pipe diameters of compressor.

4.1.6 For all piping systems containing H₂S streams with greater than 1000 ppm by volume for vapor stream or 1000 ppm by weight for liquid stream, joints are required to be welded. For vent, drain, and instrument branch connections or other branch connections to services which do not contain more than 1000 ppm H₂S, welded joints are also required at least up through the first block valve.

## 4.2 Branch Connections

4.2.1 Branch connections shall be in accordance with Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205, including the applicable branch connection charts referenced in the pipe classes.

4.2.2 Branch connections shall have adequate length to prevent valves and instruments from being covered by insulation.

4.2.3 Stub-in or stub-on branch connections shall not be used without prior written approval by the Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer, except for thermowell connections using LWN flanges as shown on drawing LA-000-0100-0200-019.

4.2.4 Branch connections shall not be made by threading directly into the wall of the run pipe. Half couplings are not permissible for use as branch connections.

4.2.5 Hot tap connections, defined as the installation of a branch connection by welding and drilling on piping in service, shall be done in accordance with Industry Source 01 CHP Safety and Health Policy 1620 Welding and Inspection in Service and Hot Tapping.

4.2.6 All integrally reinforced branch connection fittings (such as pipets and weldolets) shall be attached to the run pipe by a full penetration groove weld and a finish cover fillet weld as specified in ASME B31.3 or B31.1 as applicable, and as shown on drawing LA-000-0100-0200-019.

## 4.3 Flanges

4.3.1 Flanges are to be manufactured in accordance with ASME B16.5 and the various Standards listed in ASME B31.3 or B31.1 for sizes up to and including 24". Flanges above 24" shall be in accordance with ASME B16.47 Series B (previously API 605), except ASME B16.47 Series A (previously MSS SP-44) flanges may be used where necessary to connect to existing piping or equipment. Since Series A and B flanges are incompatible with each other, designers must verify dimensions of existing flanges for mating to new flanges.

4.3.2 Socket weld and threaded flanges are not recommended for services above 500°F if several thermal gradients or thermal cycling are involved.

4.3.3 Slip-on flanges shall not be used in any flammable, hydrogen, or steam services, or any service above 500°F operating temperature. Slip-on flanges shall not be used where severe bending stresses are likely to be present, or where there is vibration or cyclic temperature conditions. Slip-on reducing flanges are allowed for steam jacketed piping in Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205 line classes CAY and CXY.

4.3.4 Loose or optional-type flanges and lap joint flanges are not permitted.

## 4.4 Flange Bolting

4.4.1 Flange bolting shall meet the requirements of ASME B31.3 along with the following additional criteria:

4.4.1.1 Carbon steel bolts are only allowed where Code requires them to be used with cast iron flanges, and shall be machine bolts conforming to ASTM A307 Grade B. Carbon steel stud bolts are not permitted.

4.4.1.2 Stud bolts shall be threaded full length and shall be furnished with heavy hexagon pattern nuts. Thread fit shall be Class 2A-2B. Unless otherwise

approved by the Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer, bolting shall be Coarse Thread Series for nominal sizes 1" and smaller, and 8-Pitch Thread Series for all larger sizes.

4.4.1.3 The unthreaded points on the ends of stud bolts shall be either flat and chamfered, or rounded.

4.4.1.4 Bolting exposed to the process fluid shall be of a material at least as corrosion resistant as the flange material.

4.4.2 Unless otherwise approved by Industry Source 01 CHP, the design temperature for the bolts shall be at least the maximum allowable working temperature of the piping with no credit taken for cooling.

4.4.3 Flange bolting materials shall be as follows unless otherwise approved by Industry Source 01 CHP:

> **Table - Design Conditions Fluid Temperature / Type Bolt / ASTM Specification** - see [XLSX](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-01/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-01_p0029_tbl01_flange-bolting-materials.xlsx) and [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-01/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-01_p0029_tbl01_flange-bolting-materials.png)

| Design Conditions Fluid Temperature | Type Bolt | ASTM Specification | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | | **Bolts** | **Nuts** |
| -150°F to -21°F | Alloy Stud Bolts | A320 Gr. L7 | A194 Gr. 7 |
| -20°F to 450°F | Carbon Steel Bolts* | A307 Gr. B* | A307* |
| -20°F to 750°F | Alloy Stud Bolts | A193 Gr. B7 | A194 Gr. 2H |
| 751°F to 1100°F | Alloy Stud Bolts | A193 Gr. B16 | A194 Gr. 7 |
| Above 1100°F | ** | ** | ** |

\* The use of carbon steel machine bolts is limited to use with cast iron flanges, where required by Code. Machine bolts or cap screws shall not be used with steel flanges.

\*\* Flange bolting materials for piping design temperatures above 1100°F shall be determined by the design engineer for the specific line class specification. ASME B31.3 listings for bolt materials in this temperature range are very limited, and typically have additional use restrictions as specified in the referenced notes in the code. Use of unlisted materials may be necessary as allowed by B31.3 paragraph 323.1.2. For example, see bolting in Industry Source 07 Piping Material Specification 3SC0501.

4.4.4 Flanged joint assembly, stud bolt lengths, and bolt tensioning shall be in accordance with Industry Source 01 CHP STP 50. The types of flanged joints and gaskets which require bolt torquing are also specified in STP 50, along with bolting procedures and torque values.

4.4.5 For flanged joints where the bolts are specified to be tightened with a torque tool, install sets of two lubricated hardened washers under each nut at only one end of the studs, on the side of the joint where the torque tool will be applied. The hardened washers shall be as specified in STP 50. Stud bolt lengths shall be increased to accommodate the thickness of the two washers. Washer thicknesses will vary based on stud diameter.

4.4.6 Bolting shall be assembled with a thread lubricant as specified in STP 50. The lubricant shall be applied to the threads, washers, and metal-contacting faces of the nuts.

4.4.7 For flanged joint situations where the stud bolt tables in STP 50 are not applicable, the length of stud bolts shall be designed for two threads to protrude through the full face nuts at each end. In accordance with ASTM A193, stud lengths are measured from first thread to first thread, and do not include the unthreaded points on the ends. The specified stud length may be rounded to the next higher commercial length, as long as the maximum thread protrusion criteria is not exceeded.

4.4.8 The acceptance criteria for installed stud bolts is a minimum protrusion of one full thread through the nuts, and a maximum protrusion of four threads. Stud bolts shall be installed centered in the flange joint with nearly equal lengths protruding at both ends. Longer studs with additional thread protrusion is allowed where bolt tensioning is specified or approved by the Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer.

4.4.9 Bolt tensioning is not a normal practice at Industry Source 01 CHP and shall not be specified unless approved by the Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer. If bolt tensioning is approved by Industry Source 01 CHP, longer studs shall be specified as required for the specific bolt tensioning tools to be used, along with hardened washers with a minimum 35 Rockwell C hardness.

**4.5 Orifice Flanges**

4.5.1 Orifice flanges shall be specified and installed without jacking bolts/screws to prevent interference during installation which may inadvertently hinder proper bolt-up and gasket seating. Orifice flanges shall be specified per the applicable piping class in Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205. Separation of flanges for installation of orifices can be performed with separate wedging tools.

## SECTION 5: FLANGE FACINGS AND GASKETS

**5.1 Flange Facing**

5.1.1 Flange facings shall be in accordance with dimensions established in ASME B16.5 or ASME B16.47 as applicable. Raised face flanges are preferred for new installations. Do not use ring joint flanges for new work unless approved by Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer, except when needed for mating to existing flanges.

5.1.2 The raised portion of raised face steel or alloy flanges shall be removed if the flanges are to mate with flat faced flanges of cast iron, FRP, or other low strength materials susceptible to break under bending stress.

5.1.3 Flange facings and gaskets shall be in accordance with the appropriate service class in Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205.

**5.2 Sheet Gaskets**

Sheet gaskets shall be full faced when fitted to flat faced flanged valves and equipment. It is common for cast iron, fiberglass, and plastic flanges to be flat faced.

## SECTION 6: BENDS

**6.1 Bends**

Bends may be used when economical; however, minimum bend radius shall be six pipe diameters. Fittings manufactured by the Induction Bending Process are not allowed without specific approval from Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineering.

## SECTION 7: VALVES – GENERAL

**7.1 Valve Standards and Service Definition**

7.1.1 Where no specific applicable design Standard exists, the design of all pressure containing components shall conform to the requirements of ASME B31.3 and ASME B16.34.

7.1.2 Valves shall be supplied per the applicable line class in Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205. When a line class provides the option of flanged or buttweld valves, flanged valves shall be supplied unless otherwise approved by Industry Source 01 CHP.

> **Note:** Flanged valves are advantageous for the purposes of blinding or maintenance/replacement. Buttweld valves provide less risk of leakage, but in most cases the benefit will be considered less than the inherent difficulties with maintenance/replacement.

7.1.3 When valves other than those specified in the individual service classes are required, they shall be indicated on the P&ID as specialty valves, with Specialty Item Numbers (SP#) assigned by the Document Control Group.

## 7.2 Site Re-Hydrotesting (Third Party)

Site re-hydrotesting of valves is not required if the valves have been procured per Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205 or the Industry Source 01 R&M Approved Manufacturers List (AML). Re-hydrotesting of valves procured through normal channels is optional and may be performed at the discretion of the Industry Source 01 CHP Engineer/Project Team. Critical valves and valves purchased outside of the approved lists above should be considered for local re-testing.

## SECTION 8: REQUIREMENTS FOR SPECIFIC VALVE TYPES

### 8.1 Butterfly Valves

8.1.1 Butterfly valves shall conform to Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205 and Industry Source 01 CHP STP 204.

8.1.2 Due to their short service life compared to gate valves, butterfly valves require specific Industry Source 01 CHP approval for each application. High performance designs are preferred.

8.1.3 Triple offset butterfly valves shall be installed per the manufacturer's instructions with the valve oriented to have the higher pressure on the shaft side of the disc when in the closed position. Triple offset butterfly valves are designed to be leak tight in both directions at the rated pressure and temperature of the valve, however best sealing performance will be achieved when pressure acts on the shaft side of the disc. Piping designers shall indicate the correct orientation of the valves on the piping design drawings.

### 8.2 Ball Valves

8.2.1 Ball valves shall conform to Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205 and Industry Source 01 CHP STP 203. Ball valves shall be designed to be fire safe and shall be certified to comply with the latest edition of API 607 or other equivalent fire test approved by the Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer.

### 8.3 Check Valves

8.3.1 Check valves shall be sized appropriately for the flow conditions, to assure that the valve will not operate in the nearly closed position and will not experience excessive wear due to disc chatter. It is not acceptable to use a check valve matched to the pipe size without reviewing the manufacturer's sizing criteria.

### 8.4 Globe Valves

8.4.1 Globe valves shall conform to Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205 and Industry Source 01 CHP STP 206. Globe valves are normally suitable for throttling when the disc is at least 20 % open; otherwise flow-induced vibration may result, leading to valve damage. For this reason, valve sizing is important to assure that the valve is not too large for its intended flow conditions. Typically, a bypass valve is too large if it is the same NPS as the control valve it bypasses. For bypass valve applications with high differential pressure or critical services, a standard globe valve may not be suitable. An engineered control valve design should be considered in such applications. The globe valve sizing should be reviewed by the Industry Source 01 CHP Instrument Engineer and Fixed Equipment Engineer during project design. If an engineered control valve design is selected, an upstream isolation block valve should be installed since control valves have an inherent seat leakage rate. The leak rate should be carefully considered in this application.

## SECTION 9: INSTRUMENT PIPING

### 9.1 Scope

It is the intent of this section to supplement Industry Source 01 CHP STP 314.

### 9.2 Definitions

9.2.1 The terms "close coupled" and "remote mounted" used in conjunction with the installation of differential pressure transmitters signifies that the orifice taps have line class valves which are not an integral part of the three valve manifold.

9.2.2 Close coupled further signifies that the transmitter is line mounted with short impulse lines that connect the line class valves with the three valve manifold. Remote mounted signifies the transmitter is located at grade, or similar far removed location relative to the orifice isolation valves.

9.2.3 For typical sketches of close coupled, and remote mounted transmitters see API RP 551, Process Measurement Instrumentation, Section 3.

9.2.4 The term "service condition" as used in the following Sections shall refer to a Piping Class utilized within the design parameters stated, for a specific service (such as steam or hydrogen). See Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205.

## 9.3 Design Considerations

9.3.1 Control valves shall be located near their respective instrument indicators. If this is not feasible, remote indicators shall be provided. Control valve manifolds and bypasses shall be designed in accordance with drawings LA-000-0100-0200-030, LA-000-0100-0200-031, LA-000-0100-0200-032, and LA-000-0100-0200-033.

9.3.2 All regulating, throttling, or control valves shall be accessible for hand operation. When a local indicator, which responds to the operation of the valve is provided, it shall be observable from the operating position at the valve.

9.3.3 Where a high pressure drop condition exists across a control valve, sonic flow with high noise levels may be expected. When this situation exists, the piping should be designed to lessen vibration and noise.

9.3.4 Instruments mounted in shop fabricated control panels or racks need no field piping. Complete prefabrication of piping and electrical wiring is generally done by the control panel fabricator. If the control panel or rack is fabricated in the field, Industry Source 01 CHP STP 314 applies.

9.3.5 Piping materials shall be in accordance with Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205.

9.3.6 Piping design and the layout for field instruments shall be in accordance with Industry Source 01 CHP STP 314.

9.3.7 Industry Source 01 CHP philosophy towards special instruments, such as on-stream analyzers, is to incorporate the vendor recommended piping configuration into the specified service condition. This should be accomplished by the design Contractor requesting a specification defining the scope and objectives of the system to candidate vendors. Their response is then evaluated by the Contractor and submitted to Industry Source 01 CHP for approval.

## 9.4 Temperature

9.4.1 Nozzle length for thermowells shall be in accordance with drawings LA-000-0100-0200-027 and LA-000-0100-0200-028, and Industry Source 01 CHP STP 205.

9.4.2 Unless otherwise approved by Industry Source 01 CHP, thermowell nozzles shall be 2" flanged.

## 9.5 Pressure

9.5.1 Pipe nozzles for pressure sensors shall be 3/4" minimum.

9.5.2 Vessel connections shall be in accordance with Industry Source 01 CHP STP 40.

9.5.3 Remote mounted gauges shall be provided with a block valve at the process line and a block valve located at the gauge if required by the distance. The piping configuration from the block valve to the gauge valve shall be determined by the service conditions of the process line.

## 9.6 Differential Pressure

### 9.6.1
Orifice flanges shall be provided with 1/2" minimum size pipe nipple, socket welded to the orifice tap and directly connected to a socket weld x threaded gate valve, welded on the process side.

### 9.6.2
Remote mounted and close coupled transmitters shall be provided with a three valve manifold that is flanged directly to the instrument.

## 9.7 Instrument Air Piping

Instrument air piping shall be sized for twice the maximum design flow rate, with a maximum pressure drop of 5 psi. The design shall also comply with the requirements for utility air piping in paragraph 2.32.

## 9.8 Level Instruments

### 9.8.1
Level instruments shall be designed per drawing LA-000-0100-0200-029.

### 9.8.2
Gauge glass installations shall be per Industry Source 01 CHP STP 308.

### 9.8.3
The Contractor shall issue a typical installation drawing in accordance with Industry Source 01 CHP STP 308. This drawing shall depict the number of sections, the piping configuration, the material of construction, and the service condition.

## SECTION 10: FLEXIBILITY (STRESS) ANALYSIS OF PIPING SYSTEMS

### 10.1 General

In general, a flexibility analysis shall be performed for new piping systems and modifications to existing systems by a "qualified designer", as defined in Section 301.1 of ASME B31.3. The analysis may be informal, or formal, at the discretion of the qualified designer and in accordance with ASME B31.3 sections 319.4.1 and 319.4.2 respectively. Formal analysis includes simplified, approximate, and comprehensive methods. The applicable method to be used shall be determined by the qualified designer.

It is essential that the analysis consider the full extent of the piping "system", defined as the assembly of piping and equipment between at least two adjacent "logical" anchor points (where displacements are known or can be defined).

Primary stresses (pressure and other sustained loads such as weight) and secondary stresses (thermal expansion - stress range from the design minimum to design maximum temperatures) must be within code allowances.

All lines shall be designed and supported to provide adequate flexibility to handle thermal expansion from ambient temperature fluctuations, and all known operating conditions and expected transients.

ETP GP 42-10 Section 319 may also be used for guidance, but is non-mandatory.

Design life shall be part of the analysis where any node in the piping system is in the creep range for the material (normally temperatures above 850 F).

### 10.2 Critical Lines

As a minimum requirement, a formal flexibility analysis shall be performed for all critical lines as defined in this paragraph. Critical lines include all piping systems with conditions shown on the right side of the curve in Figure 1, and all piping systems regardless of pipe size or design temperature which meet any of the following criteria:

a) Piping connected to rotating equipment such as pumps, turbines, compressors, and blowers, or subject to slug flow, water hammer or shock loading.

b) Process and steam lines connected to air coolers, fired heaters, and steam boilers.

- c) Major suction and fill lines connected to storage tanks
- d) Piping connected to other equipment with special loading limitations
- e) Piping subjected to severe pressure or thermal cyclic loading (such as coke drum piping)
- f) Relief lines connected to discharge of PSVs and rupture discs if reaction forces are significant
- g) Branch lines connected to headers that are subject to significant movement
- h) All piping potentially subject to auto refrigeration and/or thermal shock (such as flare headers or LPG lines)

  **Note:** Ensure sufficient flexibility to allow for thermal contraction without exceeding stresses to where brittle fracture may occur.

- i) All piping requiring expansion bellows, spring hangers or proprietary support mechanisms.

![Figure 1](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-01/figures/01-overall-piping-design-standards-01_p0034_fig01_figure-1-nominal-pipe-diameter-vs-design.png)

## 10.3 Analysis Proposal

When applicable, early in the design phase of a project the engineering contractor shall develop a list of lines proposed for formal flexibility analysis in accordance with this document. The proposed list shall be submitted to Industry Source 01 CHP for review and approval.

## 10.4 Information Required for Analysis

The following information is typically required to perform a flexibility analysis of piping systems:

a) Complete isometric drawing (or equivalent collection of 3D model plus 2D drawings) of the proposed piping, up to "logical" anchor points (where displacement is known or can be defined) including:

- All dimensions
- Pipe size, schedule, line class, corrosion allowance, design temperature and coincident pressure
- Insulation type and thickness

- All pipe supports

b) Certified drawings of pumps, turbines, and similar equipment which are part of the piping system. If certified drawings are not available, approximate dimensions and allowable nozzle loads are required.

c) Weights and dimensions of any special in-line equipment (including control valves)

d) List of lines not designed for flooded conditions and/or not designed for hydrotest (both require separate Industry Source 01 approval). Specify gravity of contents (liquid, vapor and/or two-phase).

e) Any special limitations which may exist (such as nozzle loading constraints, expected tank settling, highly cyclic loading)

*Note: For modification to existing systems, it is important to know of any unusual corrosion, erosion, and/or material degradation (such as embrittlement).*

## SECTION 11: PIPE LINE NUMBER REQUEST/SUBMITTAL FORM

### 11.1 Requirements

The Industry Source 01 CHP Pipe Line Number Request/Submittal Form shall be filled in and submitted to the Industry Source 01 CHP Document Control Department for new pipe lines in the refinery. The form is available in Documentum. The form includes the design and operating data for each line number. A separate row on the form shall be filled in for each line size, therefore there may be multiple rows for a specific line number. The line numbers will be assigned by Industry Source 01 CHP. All applicable fields in the form shall be filled in. Notes on the form will provide explanations for what is expected for some of the data fields.

## SECTION 12: DEAD LEG DESIGN CRITERIA

### 12.1 Definition

Dead legs may be defined as areas, segments or sections of piping systems with little or no flow where fluids can become stagnant. Dead legs produce potential corrosion, fluid quality and bacterial problems and, therefore, should be eliminated or minimized whenever possible. Dead legs are particularly detrimental in water or wet fluid systems as they provide sites for the accumulation of water and water wet solids, aggravating the problems outlined above.

### 12.2 Corrosion

Corrosion rates in dead legs can be significantly higher than that measured in free flowing segments of the system because 1) they collect water and solids, causing concentration cell corrosion and 2) they are difficult, if not impossible to protect in chemically inhibited systems as the stagnant condition prevents the chemical from circulating to the pipe walls. Failures often occur in dead legs in systems that show low corrosion rates at monitoring locations in the free flowing stream.

### 12.3 Design Criteria

During the 3D CAD review of piping, special attention shall be given to minimizing dead legs. The ideal piping system would be a single pipe from point A to point B with no branches or side connections. Since this is seldom possible, the following guidelines should be followed to minimize potential dead leg problems.

#### 12.3.1 Future Connections

Piping branches for future tie-ins should be made up fitting to fitting without nipples or other extensions. When possible, such connections should be at the top of a horizontal pipe rather than at the bottom. Top connections in gassy or oily waters will fill with gas or oil, minimizing the dead leg effect.

#### 12.3.2 End of Header

When possible, headers should end with an elbow rather than a tee. When a header is designed for future expansion (or ended in a blind flange) the flange connection should be located at the last branch and not at the end of an extended pipe.

#### 12.3.3 Pipe Support

When a piping system changes direction and the elbow is short of a pipe support, the pipe should not be extended to the pipe support. Rather, there should be an elbow with a welded dummy to provide support for the pipe. However use of dummy supports shall also be minimized, where other piping design options are available.

#### 12.3.4 Bypass or Recirculation Line

Piping should be made up fitting to fitting with valve installed as close to main line as possible. Also, bypass connections should be oriented (top or side rather than bottom) to minimize solids and water accumulation.

#### 12.3.5 Drain Headers

Drain headers on dirty vessels should be provided with valves for flushing header after vessel cleaning.

#### 12.3.6 Hot Vacuum Residual Lines (Vacuum Bottoms/Coker Feed)

This section applies to carbon steel and chrome alloy (<17% chrome) pipe lines in Vacuum Residual service operating above 450°F with branch line flow rates less than 1 ft/sec. For branch connections that meet these conditions, the piping shall be designed to avoid thermally induced flow and the potential to trap corrosive vapor in the dead leg. The three piping arrangements listed below are acceptable designs. Branch distance requirements listed in the three design options are measured from the outside of the main line. If other design options are necessary, approval by the Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer is required.

a) A branch connection that comes off the bottom of the main line, must drop vertically down a minimum of 5 pipe diameters before any change in direction to a horizontal or upward path.

b) A branch connection that comes horizontally off the side of the main line shall slope downward a minimum 1/16" per foot away from the main line, and run for a minimum distance of 150 pipe diameters with no pockets where vapor can collect. Within this minimum distance, downward or horizontal turns are acceptable if the minimum slope is maintained. If the horizontal branch line turns down vertically for a minimum distance of 5 pipe diameters, the 150 pipe diameter distance specified above is no longer required.

c) A branch connection that comes vertically off the top of the main line shall have a normally closed block valve installed within a maximum straight distance of 4 pipe diameters measured to the valve joint.

#### 12.3.7 Nitrogen Connections

Close attention to detail shall be given to nitrogen connections to process lines, such as the inlet to a hydrotreating reactor. Tie-ins to the process lines shall be made to the top of horizontal lines or to the side of vertical lines. The piping shall be self-draining with no pockets where water can collect. Piping shall be designed fitting to fitting with the block valve installed as close to the process line as possible, but without creating a pocket at either side of the block valve when in the closed position. This is intended to prevent collection of hydrotest water, which if left undiscovered can result in a freeze induced leak.

## 12.4 Alternative Action

If dead legs cannot be avoided, alternate methods approved by the Industry Source 01 CHP Reliability Engineer and Corrosion Engineer shall be utilized to mitigate the risk of dead leg problems. Some potential alternate methods are upgrading the piping materials, applying internal protective coatings, or adding circulating lines with inhibitors.

## SECTION 13: INJECTION AND MIXING POINTS

### 13.1 General

Effective and reliable service from injection piping and quills depends on numerous factors. Failures at injection and mixing points may create high risk situations. Alternate designs need to be carefully and thoroughly evaluated by all applicable parties, including, but not limited to, Operations, Process Engineering, Corrosion Engineering, and Reliability Engineering.

All new and replacement injection and process mixing points shall comply with the requirements of NACE SP0114, with the exception that any requirements in Sections 13.2 through 13.3 below supersede the NACE requirements.

### 13.2 Design Criteria

#### 13.2.1 Orientation

Injection and mixing points shall be designed for concurrent flow (pointing downstream, parallel with bulk flow). Countercurrent (against the flow) and crossflow (through or across the flow) injection designs are rarely the correct designs and are not allowed without an approved Standard Deviation Request. Concurrent designs should consider the proximity to the downstream piping components, such as elbows, for erosion concerns. See NACE SP0114 for this and other concurrent flow design considerations.

Injection piping and quills, either retractable or fixed, shall be designed so that there is only one obvious way of installing the quill, with respect to the direction of the bulk flow into which they are being inserted. The design shall indicate with an arrow which direction the bulk flow is going, accompanied by the text "FLOW," and the discharge opening of the quill or nozzle shall inject in the same direction. Also, a secondary indication of direction shall be shown, such as a global coordinate like "NORTH," or with some other positive indicator like the downstream equipment number, etc.

The quill shall be designed so that there is physically only one way of installing it to achieve the above concurrent flow, or, shall have matching alignment tabs on the quill flange and mating piping flange that clearly indicate they should fit together to ensure correct flow direction. If alignment tabs are used, they should also be shown on the downstream side of the flanges. See Directional Detail Drawing LA-000-0100-0419-001 for an example of alignment tabs and detail that must accompany any quill.

#### 13.2.2 Documentation Requirements

If the quill or injection piping is retractable, the manufacturer's detail drawing should be stored in Equipment and Vendor Files, in Documentum, or as a Industry Source 01 piping detail drawing. Any new quill that is installed shall have a reference on the P&ID to the drawing containing these details.

Injection quills shall be assigned a 3200 series Location number and a GP number, per the Location Codes, Class, and Subclass tables in the Equipment Number Request form in Documentum.

### 13.3 Lifecycle Requirements

Injection and mixing points have increased inspection requirements and shortened intervals, which are already defined by Inspection Practices. Whenever a quill is pulled for inspection, it should be inspected for mechanical integrity (fatigue cracks, corrosion, obvious signs of packing glands leaks, etc.). When an injection or mixing point is added, deleted, or modified, the Inspection department shall be notified.

## 1. PURPOSE AND SCOPE

1.1. This standard provides recommendations for the layout of plot areas, equipment, pipe racks, piping, platforms, roads, other miscellaneous items for onshore process plants and facilities, upstream surface facilities, etc., i.e., all assets within the boundary fence of on-shore oil and gas production facilities, oil refineries, gas plants, chemical plants and supply/marketing installations.

1.2. Layout includes equipment location, access and egress for personnel safety, access for operations and maintenance, access for fire fighting, and provisions for operational housekeeping and constructability.

1.3. Additional or different access or spacing may be required because of local codes or regulatory requirements, process conditions, special hazards, environmental requirements, etc.

1.4. This standard shall be used for new facilities as well as for maintenance revamps, or expansions of existing facilities.

1.5. Where there are different requirements within this standard or with referenced Publications, Codes, and Standards, the more stringent criteria shall be applied.

## 2. RESPONSIBILITIES

### 2.1. Director Of Engineering

2.1.1. Responsible for approving and implementing this standard.

### 2.2. Subject Matter Expert

2.2.1. Responsible to revise and update this Standard.

### 2.3. Project Engineering Manager

2.3.1. Responsible to ensure this standard is properly implemented when adopted for a project.

### 2.4. Project Discipline Engineer

2.4.1. Responsible to ensure the requirements of this standard are incorporated in the course of a project design.

## 4. DEFINITIONS AND ACRONYMS

4.1. The "**Owner**" - means Industry Source 10

4.2. The "**Buyer**" - means Industry Source 10 or its agent designated for that project

4.3. "**Owner's Engineer**" - means a registered, professional engineer employed directly by Industry Source 10 responsible for the technical integrity of the project.

4.4. "**Owner's Inspector**" - means the person authorized by Industry Source 10 for inspection.

4.5. The "**Contractor**" – is the party which carries out all or part of the design, engineering, procurement, construction, commissioning or management of a project, or operation or maintenance of a facility. The Owner may undertake all or part of the duties of the Contractor.

4.6. The "**Supplier**" - means the entity, manufacturer, fabricator, vendor, or contractor that supplies the material or services.

4.7. "**Local Authorities**" - means the governmental regulatory authority controlling laws, codes, rules, or regulations for the design, fabrication and testing of industrial piping in the Province of Alberta.

4.8. "**P&ID**" - means Process and Instrumentation Diagram.

4.9. "**ISO**" - means Piping Isometric Drawing.

4.10. "**NPS**" - means Nominal Pipe Size in inches.

4.11. **Small Bore Piping** - Piping in sizes NPS 2 and smaller.

4.12. **Constructability** – Optimum use of construction knowledge and experience in planning, design/engineering, procurement, and field operations to achieve overall project objectives.

4.13. **Offsites** – Equipment grouped outside a process unit battery limits (e.g., tanks, loading/unloading facilities, cooling towers, flares etc.).

4.14. **Upstream Facilities** – Upstream facilities for oil and gas wellsites and gathering systems.

4.15. The word **shall** indicates a requirement.

4.16. "**Process Unit**" is defined as an assembly of sequence related equipment and process control valves functioning as, or within, an identifiable system which performs a specific function of a process within a process plant, and bounded by battery limits. Battery limits are as shown on the plot plan.

4.17. "**Main Operating Areas**" are defined as areas at grade or levels above or below grade, where plant personnel are present continuously or are scheduled for presence at least once every shift while the plant is operating.

4.18. "**Auxiliary Service Areas**" are defined as all other plant areas and levels above or below grade.

4.19. "**Equipment**" is defined in the equipment list and includes such items as vessels, heat exchangers, furnaces and pumps.

4.20. **"Plant Areas"** are defined as a grouping of process unit equipment performing a predetermined process operation as defined by the enclosing battery limit lines. Plant area battery limits are shown on the Plot Plan.

4.21. **"Lethal Service"** as it applies to Industry Source 10 Major Projects, is defined in Major Projects Engineering Standard "Lethal Service" PEG-GS-0036

## 5. STANDARD

### 5.1. General

#### 5.1.1. Units

5.1.1.1. SI (International System) units of measure are shown in parentheses following the Imperial Units where applicable.

#### 5.1.2. Other Requirements

5.1.2.1. Separate specifications cover the requirements for sewer and drainage systems. Special requirements shall apply to fire protection, heating, ventilating, air and water systems serving buildings rather than plant or process areas and shall conform to applicable plumbing, heating, and ventilating, or refrigeration codes. The appropriate Codes and Industry Source 10 Specifications shall be used for those services.

### 5.2. Codes and Standards

#### 5.2.1. Local Codes

5.2.1.1. Where provincial, state, or federal codes take precedence over CSA standards, ANSI or ASME codes, such codes shall govern.

#### 5.2.2. Boiler Code Piping

5.2.2.1. Section I, Power boilers, of the ASME Boiler and pressure Vessel Code, latest edition, applies to certain portions of steam, feedwater, and blow-off piping associated with boilers and steam generating equipment, as defined by that code. Such piping shall be designed in accordance with rules for that piping as stipulated in ASME B31.1.

5.2.2.2. The preferred documents to show the limits of the piping governed by the boiler Code are the Piping and Instrument Diagrams (P&IDs). They shall indicate which codes or requirements, other than ASME B31.1, apply to various parts of the piping systems.

#### 5.2.3. Refinery and Chemical Plant Code Piping

5.2.3.1. The ASME Code for Pressure Piping, ASME B31.3, Process Piping, latest edition, generally applies to all other piping within property limits of the plant. Exceptions as stated in paragraph 5.1.2 shall be identified on the P&IDs, and shall be identified on each ISO. For slurry piping, the requirements of ASME B31.11 shall be met.

### 5.3. Design Conditions

#### 5.3.1. Operating Conditions

5.3.1.1. Normal design conditions of pressure and temperature shall be the most severe conditions expected to coexist under usual long-time operating conditions. These usual operations shall include all pressure and/or temperature increases caused by throttling, blocking, bypassing, or any other manipulation likely to be used for operation and control.

- 5.3.1.2. Usual operating conditions do not include more severe temporary conditions, such as Pressure Tests, and those incidental to start-up, shutdown, abnormal operation, or steam-out. (The steam-out and other temperature conditions higher than the normal design temperature shall be used for thermal expansion calculations).

- 5.3.1.3. The allowances for occasional variations in temperature and pressure, as specified in ASME B31.3, paragraph 302.2.4, shall NOT be used without prior approval of the Owner's Engineer. When approved, the variations shall be identified in the Line Designation Tables.

### 5.3.2. Design Temperature

- 5.3.2.1. The design temperature, as stated in the Line Designation Table, shall be the most severe sustained fluid temperature, subject to conditions of Paragraph 5.3.1 above. Design temperature of internally-insulated or un-insulated components may be the metal temperature rather than the fluid temperature.

- 5.3.2.2. The design temperature for steam tracing piping shall be the fluid temperature or,

  a) 300°F (149°C) for 50 psig (344 kPag) tracing steam.

  b) 400°F (204°C) for 150 psig (1034 kPag) tracing steam.

- 5.3.2.3. The design temperature for electrically heat traced piping shall be based on the fluid temperature. The LDT and each Isometric Drawing shall specify the "Maintenance Temperature" of at least 20°F (11°C) above the solidification temperature of the fluid shall be specified. For design of the electric heat tracing system, refer to Industry Source 10 Standard 0521, latest edition.

- 5.3.2.4. The design temperature for piping with a fluid operating temperature below minus 20°F (-29°C) shall be the normal fluid operating temperature. In addition, design shall be suitable for pressure at 100°F (38°C).

- 5.3.2.5. Piping design temperature should generally be the same (or higher) than that of the major equipment item from which the contents of the line flow. If flow can come from more than one source, the most stringent coincident conditions shall be the guiding criteria.

### 5.3.3. Design Pressures

- 5.3.3.1. Except for Boiler Code Piping (ASME Section I) the design pressure shall be the most severe condition of internal or external fluid pressure, subject to conditions of Paragraph 5.3.1 above. The design pressure for Boiler Code Piping shall be established in accordance with the Code for Power Piping ASME B31.1.

- 5.3.3.2. Minimum positive design pressure shall be 25 psig (170 kPag).

- 5.3.3.3. Design pressure for unrelieved piping systems subject to pump discharge pressure shall be pump shut-off discharge pressure, where pump shut-off discharge pressure is pump differential pressure at shut-off or stalling conditions plus maximum suction pressure and discharge static head.

5.3.3.4. Design pressure for relieved piping systems shall be the safety valve set pressure plus the static head below the relief valve adjusted for allowances per design criteria of ASME B31.3.

5.3.3.5. Design pressure for piping systems operating under vacuum shall be full vacuum, and shall be stated in the Line Designation Table.

5.3.3.6. For piping systems protected by relief valves, the relief valve set pressure shall be equal to the design pressure minus the static head below the relief valve.

5.3.3.7. Design pressures shall be as stated in the Line Designation Table.

## 5.4. Materials

### 5.4.1. Piping Material Specifications

#### 5.4.1.1.

Std. 0202, Piping Materials Specification, or the Piping materials Specification of the particular business unit, includes individual Pipe Class Tables. The specification shows in detail pipe, valve, flange, fitting, bolting, gasket, branch connection and other specific material requirements for various classes of fluid, temperature and pressure services.

#### 5.4.1.2. Material Specifications within Skid or Vendor Packages

a) Although every attempt shall be made to utilize Industry Source 10 Materials Specifications, the practice of vendors designing skid packages based on their own sound engineering practices utilizing materials, end preps, fabrication, installation, testing, etc does occur.

b) Where piping used in Skid or Vendor Packages is designed to standards other than Industry Source 10 standards, the design shall be subject to review and approval by Owner's Engineer prior to fabrication or supply as part of the design evaluation process. It shall be understood that in these cases, the equipment/skid manufacturers assume all responsibility for design, material selection, procurement, fabrication, inspection, quality, registration, and performance of their finished product.

c) Industry Source 10 Piping Material Specifications have been developed and shall be used for the safe design of interconnecting piping between equipment, skid packages and other components within Industry Source 10 Operations' units.

### 5.4.2. Corrosion Allowances

#### 5.4.2.1.

Corrosion allowances shown in the Piping Material Specifications are minimum for the respective services.

### 5.4.3. Wall Thickness and Requirement

#### 5.4.3.1.

Unless specified otherwise in the Industry Source 10 Piping Material Specification, pipe wall design thickness shall be calculated in accordance with the applicable codes. Refer to section 5.2.

### 5.4.4. Junction of Different Services

5.4.4.1. Where two services of different classifications join, the more severe service shall govern through the first isolation valve or other means provided to separate the two services.

5.4.5. Dissimilar Welds

5.4.5.1. All pressure retaining dissimilar welds are to be logged and called out on Piping Isometric Drawings.

5.4.6. Flanges

5.4.6.1. The use of flanges in piping shall be limited to connections at flanged equipment and valves, and under the following conditions;

a) Where frequent dismantling of equipment is required.

b) Where piping lined with non-metals or non-metallic piping cannot be bonded or otherwise joined except by flanges.

c) To provide clearance for dismantling of equipment such as compressors or reactor heads.

d) For maintenance such as cleaning, decoding, installing blanks, or slurry service.

e) For hydrotesting, plant start-up sequencing or safety purposes.

5.4.6.2. Flanges shall be installed as close as practicable to the equipment for make or break connections.

5.4.6.3. When bolting a cast iron flange to a steel flange, or other non-ferrous flange, both flanges shall be flat faced, with a full face gasket at the joint.

5.4.6.4. Bolt holes shall straddle natural centerlines. Bolt holes which do not straddle the centerline of flanged valves or fittings shall be noted on the piping drawings.

5.4.6.5. For orifice flanges the minimum rating is Class 300. Orifice tap nipples shall be XXS.

5.4.6.6. Class 300 flanges shall be used in Class 150 systems as required to match instrument and rotating equipment flanges.

5.4.6.7. Slip-on flanges shall be used only in Class 150 systems with normal operating temperature less than 250°F (120°C). Slip-on flanges shall not be used in Special Services (see Section 5.28).

5.4.6.8. For pressure safety valves and relief valves, where dynamic loading analysis shows piping connecting to the valve is subject to excessive dynamic stresses, the safety valve body and connected pipe flange shall be analyzed to ensure flange sealing integrity. In some cases it may be necessary to increase the flange class ratings on the valve inlet side.

5.4.6.9. For flanges up to and including NPS 24, all flanges shall comply with ASME B16.5.

5.4.6.10. For flanges of NPS 26 to 60, ASME B16.47 Series A is preferred. ASME B16.47 Series B (previously API 605) shall be used where required to match existing flanges, with prior approval by the Owner's Engineer.

5.4.6.11. For flanges larger than NPS 60, all flanges shall be designed to the appropriate code.

5.4.6.12. All changes to flanges shall comply with the appropriate ASME code.

5.4.7. Compact Pipe Joints

5.4.7.1. Compact pipe joints, such as Grayloc, OTECO, or equal, in Class 900, 1500, 2500 and above may be utilized in lieu of ANSI weld neck flanges for certain piping systems. Since the compact joints are smaller and lighter, they can be used where size and weight are important, such as on offshore platforms or in vibratory service around reciprocating compressors. The compact joints also prevent spray-type gasket leaks in acid or similar services.

5.4.8. Bends and Elbows

5.4.8.1. Changes in direction of welded piping systems shall be made with long radius welding ells.

5.4.8.2. Pipe bends with a minimum radius of five pipe diameters are also acceptable, where design permits. A greater bend radius may be required because of material, nominal pipe size or nominal wall thickness.

5.4.8.3. Bends shall be in accordance with ASME B31.3, except that no buckling is permitted. Creased or corrugated bends shall not be permitted.

5.4.8.4. Short radius welding ells are permissible only where required by space limitations.

5.4.8.5. Cold bending of NPS 2 and smaller carbon steel pipe, with a minimum bend radius of 5D is acceptable.

5.4.8.6. Hot or cold bending carbon steel pipe NPS 3 and larger and all sizes of alloy steel process piping require prior approval of the Owner's Engineer.

5.4.9. Pipe Bending

5.4.9.1. All bending procedures shall be reviewed and approved by the Owner's Engineer. Risks related to in-service corrosion, erosion or cracking shall be considered as part of this review. Consideration shall also be made of the effects of the heating time and temperature on the mechanical properties of hot induction bends and this may require the production of test bends.

5.4.9.2. When ordering pipe bends the applicable jurisdiction (e.g., ABSA) shall be contacted to determine whether bend designs must be registered (e.g., as a fitting). If registration is required, it shall be the responsibility of the bending contractor in cooperation with the requisitioning organization.

5.4.9.3. Pipe bending shapes have a capability to both hot and cold bend piping to several bend radii from 1.5 to 6 pipe diameters. ASME B31.3 section 332 contains criteria for bending which cover the general requirements including heat treatment. These requirements are general but comprehensive for all piping covered by the code. However, they do not cover service specific or economic considerations. The thickness schedule of a given pipe spool may have to be increased in order to meet minimum wall thickness requirements in the bent (thinned) portion of the spool.

5.4.9.4. In addition to the Code requirements mentioned above, hot bending shall be in accordance with the International Tube and Pipe Association Standard TPA-IBS-98. A written procedure is required.

5.4.9.5. In addition to the Code requirements mentioned above, cold bending shall be in accordance with International Tube and Pipe Association Standard TPA-CBS-98. A written procedure is required.

5.4.9.6. Carbon and Low Alloy Steel

a) Pipe bending in accordance with ASME B31.3 is acceptable where design permits with the exceptions/cautions listed below:

   i. Hardness's after bending shall not exceed limits specified in relevant Industry Source 10 or industry standards such as Industry Source 10 0903, 0202, NACE MR0103 or NACE MR0175

   ii. Carbon steel piping for service temperatures of less than -20°F (-29°C) (Charpy impact tested) generally is not a candidate for bending without special precautions and additional testing.

5.4.9.7. 300 Series Stainless Steels

a) Cold bending of 300 series stainless steel is acceptable where there is no risk of stress corrosion cracking. Where there is a risk of stress corrosion cracking, cold bending followed by solution annealing is acceptable. Prior to hot bending of 300 series stainless steel the fabricator shall show, by qualification tests including a 400x micrograph and ASTM A 262 Test Practices A and E, that the base material will not be damaged during bending.

5.4.9.8. Other Materials

a) A qualified materials/fabrication/piping engineer shall be consulted for advice concerning bending of materials not covered in this Standard.

5.4.9.9. Bending shops/fabricators shall be involved at the piping design stage and suitable specifications agreed on so that understanding is reached on all pertinent design and fabrication requirements and issues.

5.4.9.10. Bends shall be used to change direction when:

a) The bend radius required is not standard for factory made fittings.

b) Flow requirements dictate their use.

5.4.9.11. Miter bends shall be used for lines NPS 26 and larger in Category "D" fluids, if cost effective when compared with pipe bends or factory made buttwelding fittings. Miter bends shall be in accordance with the requirements and limitations of ANSI/ASME B31.3. Exceptions require written approval by the Owner's Engineer.

5.4.10. Reducers

5.4.10.1. In welded piping systems, reducers shall normally be used for line size reductions. Reducing flanges are acceptable only when used as entry connections etc, for

services where pressure drop or turbulence is not a consideration. Eccentric reducers shall be installed belly up to maintain level pipe bottoms on horizontal runs, except in horizontal suction lines to pumps in non slurry service shall have the belly turned down.

5.4.11. Blanks

5.4.11.1. Flanged joints shall be provided for the insertion of paddle blanks at process connections to vessels. This location will permit personnel to safely enter the purged vessel during shutdown. Locations shall be such as to permit insertion of the paddle blanks as close to the vessels as practical from permanent platforms, walkways or grade.

5.4.11.2. All hydrocarbon or other flammable or toxic service to or from process units shall be flanged for blinding or blanking during shutdowns. Such flanges shall be inside the process unit limits and accessible from grade, platforms, or walkways.

5.4.11.3. Spectacle blanks, blanks or spacers shall be used in all lines that require operational blanking not limited to shut-down periods.

5.4.11.4. Spectacle blanks, blanks, and spacers shall be made of materials according to the specified business unit piping material specification. Test blinds shall not be used as service blanks.

5.4.11.5. Nozzles over NPS 12 on towers where blanks are installed shall be equipped with lifting points above the nozzle.

5.4.11.6. Spectacle blanks, blanks, and spacers shall be specified in accordance with ASME Standard B16.48 latest edition.

5.4.12. Bolting and Threading Lubricant

5.4.12.1. A suitable thread compound shall be applied to all flange bolts just before installation.

5.4.12.2. "Grafoil" and "Teflon" tape or a thread compound shall be used on threaded joints for services under 400°F (204°C). Threaded joints in instrument air service shall be made up using "Teflon" dispersion sealant. Threaded joints upstream of PSV inlets shall be made up with "Teflon" (under 400°F (204°C)) or Grafoil dispersant sealants (over 400°F (204°C))

5.4.12.3. Thread compounds or tapes shall not be used on joints which are to be seal welded.

5.4.12.4. Lubricating compounds containing copper are NOT allowed.

5.4.13. Seal Welding

5.4.13.1. Where seal welding is required, the joints shall be made up without application of thread lubricant and threads shall be thoroughly cleaned of all grease and oil. Welds on threaded fittings shall be the same size as for socket fittings and shall cover the exposed threads completely.

5.4.13.2. Seal welding is required as follows:

- a) All services subject to vibration and pulsation, such as process piping at reciprocating pumps and compressors. For auxiliary piping requirements, see the appropriate API Standard 610 for rotating equipment.

- b) Hydrocarbon service

- c) Through first block valve on pressure vessels and exchangers.

- d) All services in which a single exposure to a very small quantity of a toxic fluid, caused by leakage, can produce serious, irreversible harm to persons.

- e) Steam and condensate services above 60 psig (414 kPag).

- f) Upstream side of only first block valve for instrumentation, such as pressure gauges and orifice taps, and in piping connected to an open (atmospheric) system, such as a vent, drain, sample connection and hose station, all when, required by the services listed in this paragraph.

- g) All hydrogen-rich [hydrogen partial pressure of 75 psia (517 kPa) or greater] services..

- h) Hydrostatic test plugs on systems where threaded connections are permitted and which will be covered with insulation.

- i) Vacuum service piping.

- j) Between connections to columns, vessels, tanks, and exchangers in hydrocarbon service and the first valve.

- k) Orifice flange taps in those systems where socket welding small bore piping is specified.

- l) Unvalved, plugged hydrostatic test vents in systems where socket welding small bore piping is specified.

**5.4.13.3.** The following items shall never be seal welded:

- a) Screwed thermowells

- b) Union nuts

- c) Screwed ends of instrumentation devices.

- d) Lines in pipe classes such as galvanized (any pressure class rating) or air, water, nitrogen services in Class 150 piping systems.

**5.4.13.4.** Only the pipe ends of threaded unions shall be seal welded where seal welding is required by paragraph 5.4.13.2 of this standard.

**5.4.13.5.** Flanged thermowells shall be used in any service where threaded connections must be seal welded.

**5.4.14.** Bleed Rings.

5.4.14.1. Bleed rings shall be limited to maximum ASME Class 600 flange rating and shall be installed to ensure proper centering. Wherever possible, preference is to utilize pipe spool and drain for positive isolation.

5.4.14.2. Bleed rings shall be installed in locations where installation of a standard drain valve is not practical such as:

- a) A control valve immediately between two reducing fittings where drilling and installing a drain directly onto a reducer is not practical.
- b) A positive isolation configuration where there is no room for a pipe spool between two block valves for a bleed installation, except for a bleed ring.
- c) A location where vents or drains are required at flanged connections with space constraints.

5.4.14.3. Bleed ring mating face surface finish shall match the mating flange surface finish per the applicable piping material specification.

5.4.14.4. Bleed rings shall not be used in services where gusseting is required.

5.4.15. Flexible Hoses

5.4.15.1. The use of flexible hoses in any fixed or permanent piping system where the hose is utilised to compensate for large thermal movements in the hard piping to which it is connected is not recommended. The use of hoses in any new installation requires approval of the Owner.

5.4.16. Expansion joints.

5.4.16.1. Limited use of slide or bellows-type expansion joints is permitted when all other practical means of controlling thermal expansion or displacements have been considered. They shall be used when limitations in space and/or pressure drop do not permit any other practical solution. The use of expansion joints shall be reviewed and approved by the Owner's Engineer.

5.4.16.2. Only packless expansion joints shall be utilized if required in flammable service.

5.4.16.3. Expansion joints shall adequately satisfy the following design conditions:

- a) Axial deflections
- b) Transverse deflection
- c) Angular rotation
- d) Design pressure-temperature of the system
- e) Test pressure (not necessarily the same as the system test pressure)

5.4.16.4. The expansion joint shall be installed in such a manner that the system in which it is installed shall not impose any damaging forces on the joint in the shutdown condition.

5.4.16.5. Systems in which expansion joints are installed shall be controlled by suitable anchors, guides, supports, or stops, to avoid deflecting the joints beyond their designed limits (see Standards of the Expansion Joints Manufacturers Association).

5.4.16.6. Unless otherwise specified by supplementary design data, the material selection for the flexible elements and all external attachments, such as lugs, rods, etc., shall be as recommended by the expansion joint manufacturer. The material for the other components shall be in accordance with the piping material specification of the line in which it is to be installed.

5.4.16.7. To avoid chloride stress corrosion cracking of expansion joints subject to metal temperatures in excess of 175°F (79°C), and to increase low cycle fatigue life, Alloy 625 shall normally be used in lieu of 300 series stainless steels. The suitability of Alloy 625 for the intended service shall be reviewed and approved by the Owner's Engineer.

5.4.17. Bolts

5.4.17.1. All bolting materials shall be as listed the Piping Material Specification (of the relevant business unit) line classes.

5.4.18. Gaskets

5.4.18.1. All gaskets shall be in accordance with the applicable line class in the Piping Material Specification of the relevant business unit.

5.4.19. Bolt and Stud Tensioning

5.4.19.1. Bolt and stud tensioning shall be executed in all new and retro-fit piping installations and shall comply with applicable business unit or project specific procedures such as Industry Source 10 Procedure No. 03-00004-SE-2A-00-2.4.4-12 Industry Source 11 Project bolt and stud tensioning.

5.4.19.2. Where the use of hydraulic bolt tensioning equipment is required, designers shall ensure there is sufficient space around flanges for access.

5.4.20. Compression Type Couplings

5.4.20.1. Compression type couplings that utilize elastomeric sealing elements (such as Dresser™ brand) may be installed in tank farm piping to compensate for differential settlement subject to Owner's Engineer approval.

5.4.21. Tubing

5.4.21.1. Tubing used for sample lines shall be cold drawn and solution annealed 316L seamless stainless steel to ASTM A269, connected with 316 SS compression fittings.

5.4.21.2. For tubing requirements associated with instrumentation see Standard 401-P1.

5.4.21.3. For tubing requirements associated with steam tracing see Standard 209.

5.4.21.4. For tubing requirements associated with jumpovers on jacketed piping systems see Standard 209.

5.4.21.5. Manufacturer's recommended practice for installation shall be followed with particular care taken against over tightening of compression fittings.

5.4.21.6. The use of tubing in vibrating service installations shall be carefully considered.

5.4.21.7. Freeze protection shall be applied where necessary.

## 5.5. Line Sizing

5.5.1. Piping shall be sized for design rated flow conditions. Provision for future increased capacity shall be made only when specifically required.

5.5.2. Pipe Size Limitations

5.5.2.1. NPS ¾, 1-¼, 2-½, 3-½, 5, 7, 22, 26, 28, 32, 34, 38, 40, 44, 48, 52, 56, and 58 pipe sizes shall not normally be used, except where required to connect to equipment or where necessary in fire sprinkler systems to obtain proper hydraulic balance. Conversion to standard piping shall be as near the equipment as possible.

5.5.2.2. Minimum nominal pipe size run shall be NPS ¾, except for connections to equipment, instrument services, steam tracing, and auxiliary services such as pump cooling.

5.5.2.3. The minimum header size in pipe racks for process and utility piping shall be NPS 2, unless intermediate supports are available.

5.5.2.4. Small branch lines which span across a rack shall be increased to NPS 2 due to span limitations if no intermediate support steel is available.

## 5.6. Valving

5.6.1. Valves

5.6.1.1. Operating and block valves shall be provided consistent with good design and operating practice. The design shall include valving and or blanking provisions for the safe isolation of piping and equipment for maintenance and inspection purposes as per, but not limited to, the Safety Regulations of the relevant Occupational Health and Safety Act applicable to the local jurisdiction. All other applicable regulatory design and safety codes also apply. There shall be no exceptions without specific written approval from the Owner's Engineer.

5.6.1.2. For valve specifications, see relevant business unit specifications.

5.6.1.3. Whenever more than one (alternative) valve type or tag numbers are listed in a line class, it is the designer's responsibility to verify that the selected valves are optimum for the application, locations, and the pressure-temperature ranges of the operating conditions.

5.6.1.4. Many Valve tags have alternate and/or multiple suffixes. It is the designer's responsibility to ensure that the correct suffix(es) are included in the bill of material. For valve tag and suffix designations see relevant Industry Source 10 business unit valve specifications.

5.6.1.5. Valve requirements shall be shown on piping and instrument diagrams as follows:

a) All operating and block valves.

b) All vent and drain valves required for operation.

c) Valves required for start-up, shutdown, and testing, purging, rundown and auxiliary systems, such as corrosion probes.

5.6.1.6. Block valves shall be provided at all NPS 2 and smaller connections at equipment.

5.6.1.7. Valves shall be provided for instrument connections, high point vents and low point drains for hydro-testing and/or purging and draining.

5.6.1.8. Valves with extended bonnets for cryogenic service, [below -176°F (-80°C)] shall be installed with stems vertically up, or with a maximum incline of 45° from the vertical.

5.6.1.9. The use of extended length bolt connections such as used with wafer style valves, bleed rings, spacer rings or blanks shall be minimized for fire prevention. Refer to Standard 0060 for further details. At locations where extended length bolts (or studs) are exposed between flanges the stud bolts and flanges shall be protected from possible flame impingement in case of a fire, by a metal shield as shown in Industry Source 10 Std. Dwg. DD00-L-1099-1.

## 5.6.2. Positive Isolation

5.6.2.1. For examples of positive isolation, refer to Industry Source 10 Standard drawings DD00-L-1073-1, DD00-L-1073-2 and DD00-L-1073-3. However, final requirements for all isolation (owner protection, equipment, unit/battery/perimeter limits) shall be analyzed, discussed, and decided upon by Industry Source 10 process and operating personnel and subject to Owner's Engineer's approval. Isolation requirements shall meet applicable OH&S/OSHA requirements as a minimum. All isolation requirements shall be identified on the Piping and Instrument Diagrams (P&ID's).

5.6.2.2. Positive Isolation shall consist of a double block valve complete with bleed or a valve and blank arrangement with a bleed valve installed between the two to ensure the closed valve is not passing. Where blanks are used for Positive Isolation, the arrangement shall be such that the blank remains in place when removable spools are separated. For confined space entry suitable blanks or blinds shall be used at equipment nozzles to achieve positive isolation.

5.6.2.3. For isolation/root valves for instrument isolation at Oil Sands, refer to drawing DD00-L-1-1.

5.6.2.4. In hydrocarbon service, toxic or hazardous service, where a blind flange is bolted to a block valve, in sizes NPS 3 and above, whether the block valve be a vent, drain, or future connection, the blind flange shall be fitted with a NPS ¾" vent valve in accordance with Industry Source 10 Std Dwg. GD00-L-1076-1.

## 5.6.3. Valve Sizing

5.6.3.1. Where system flow and pressure characteristics permit, and arrangement economically justifies, valves shall be smaller than line size.

5.6.3.2. See Industry Source 10 Engineering Standard Drawing DD00-L-1054-1/DD00-L-1054-2 for control valve manifold arrangements and block and bypass valve sizes.

5.6.3.3. Where practical, valving at equipment connections smaller than line size shall be the same size as the equipment connection. For non-standard size equipment connections, the valve size shall be increased to the next standard pipe size. For situations where a smaller valve size will adversely affect pressure drop, valve size may be equal to line size.

5.6.4. Valve Type and Size Identification

5.6.4.1. The valve type shall be identified on the P&IDs. The valve size shall also be identified if it is not the same as the line size.

5.6.4.2. Gate valves shall not be used as throttling valves for flow control. Globe valves shall not be used for isolation purposes.

5.6.5. Valve Locations and Access

5.6.5.1. For valve installations see Industry Source 10 Engineering Standard Drawing GD00-L-1055-1.

5.6.5.2. Branch line block valves from pipe rack headers shall be located as close as possible to the edge of the pipe rack for accessibility. All block valves shall be accessible/operable as per Table 1 below and Paragraphs 5.6.5.3, 5.6.5.4, and 5.6.5.5. Block valves on steam branches shall be installed in a horizontal pipe run.

> **Table - Table 1, Valve Accessibility Table** - see [XLSX](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-02/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-02_p0024_tbl01_valve-accessibility-table.xlsx) and [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-02/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-02_p0024_tbl01_valve-accessibility-table.png)

**Table 1, Valve Accessibility Table**

| TYPE OF VALVE | Grade | Fixed Platform | Rolling Platform or Scaffold | Fixed Ladder | Portable Ladder |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **TYPE OF ACCESS REQUIRED** | | | | | |
| Operating Valves (1) | Yes | Yes | No | No | No |
| Operating Valves, Small (1,3) | Yes | Yes | No | Yes | No |
| Non-operating Valves (2) | * | * | Yes | No | No |
| Non-operating Valves, Small (2,3) | * | * | Yes | * | Yes |
| Instrument Valves | (See Paragraph 5.13.1.1 - Instrument Access) | | | | |

1. Operating valves are valves that are essential for plant operation.
2. Non-operating valves are valves that are not essential for plant operation.
3. Small valves are defined as valves that can be easily operated with one hand and are normally NPS 2 and smaller.
   \* — To be used if available.

5.6.5.3. For safe access in case of leakage, all caustic, acid, and toxic services shall have at least one isolation valve located no higher than 4'-6" (1370 mm) above grade, and shall also be provided with a protective shield.

5.6.5.4. Operating valves with bottom of handwheel over 6'-6" (1980 mm) above actual grade or platform shall be chain operated. Chain must not hang in a walkway or access

area and shall terminate approx. 3'-0" (915 mm) above grade or platform. Chain operators shall not be used for screwed valves or any valve NPS 1½ and smaller.

5.6.5.5. Extension stems shall also be used to facilitate valve operation, with prior approval of the Owner's Engineer.

5.6.5.6. For valves at heights 5'-5" (1650 mm) to 6'-6" (1980 mm), add a one foot (305 mm) high step for access. Where the step is required to be installed on a platform or catwalk, it shall have a guardrail 3'-0" (915 mm) minimum in height from the surface of the step.

5.6.5.7. Battery limit valves and spectacle blanks shall be provided as indicated on P&IDs and provided with permanent access platforms. If battery limit valves require access using supplied breathing air respirators, stair access is required. Pressure release bleeders/vents/drains as required shall be provided on both sides of blanking locations.

5.6.6. Chain operators

5.6.6.1. The preferred chain operator type is the direct mount (adaptor) type. These are safer than clamp on types which can pose a hazard if bolts come loose. If clamp on types are used, double nuts and safety cables shall be installed as safeguards.

5.6.7. Line Vents and Drains

5.6.7.1. Line vents and drains fall into two categories, operating and non-operating.

5.6.7.2. Operating Vents and Drains for equipment and piping shall be valved, capped or flanged and are shown on the piping and instrument diagrams.

5.6.7.3. Non operating vents and drains shall be plugged, capped or flanged.

5.6.7.4. Drain connections from piping in services involving abrasive fluids or materials which are of high viscosity when cold shall be NPS 1 minimum size.

5.6.7.5. In services where drain valves can become plugged due to sediment or congealing fluids, provisions shall be made to permit rodding out of the drain.

5.6.7.6. Drains emptying into open hubs shall terminate 2" (50 mm) above the top of the drain hub, and the discharge shall be visible from the location of the drain valve.

5.6.7.7. Operating drains and vents are not recommended in services where the hydrogen partial pressure is greater than 75 psia (517 kPa) and these shall require Owner's Engineer approval.

## 5.7. Plant Layout and Arrangement

5.7.1. General

5.7.1.1. The primary consideration in arrangement of units and equipment shall be to provide an economical plant, safe and easy to operate and maintain. The arrangement shall favour compactness and integrated disposition of units and equipment. Space shall be provided around equipment for convenient operation and required access and

mobility for construction and maintenance. Within the units, space for future needs shall be provided only where specifically designated.

5.7.1.2. This standard shall be used for the development of plans, electronic models, and working drawings for process units and facilities. The intent is for this standard to be coordinated with the overall site and offsites layout for geotechnical, grading, zoning, building codes, life safety, fire codes, and insurer's requirements such as G.E. GAP 2.5.2.

5.7.1.3. To facilitate space planning, a plot plan showing desired accessways, clear maintenance areas, flare and/or blowdown facilities, and spacing of major equipment items shall be prepared using this standard as a guide. The plot plan shall be drawn to scale and be dimensioned to indicate location and spacing requirements for main piping runs, main electrical equipment areas, etc., to the extent necessary to show that there is ample spacing of major equipment to permit installation of all necessary facilities without crowding or infringing on the recommended clear spacing requirements. Provisions for future expansion shall also be shown when approved by Owner.

5.7.1.4. Plant equipment shall be located far enough from public areas and thoroughfares to minimize risk to or from the public. Obtain and apply local zoning and building regulations for specific setback, type of facilities permitted, and type of construction allowed.

5.7.1.5. The process unit shall be integrated within a common plant site such that an independent operating and shutdown requirement for maintenance of other process units is not affected. Facilities shall be provided for the isolation of a process unit when independent operation and shutdown is required for maintenance of that process unit. Emergency isolation capability shall also be considered.

5.7.1.6. Plant and equipment layout shall ensure that a safe means of egress is provided for personnel evacuation and access for emergency vehicles in the event of an emergency. Egress routes shall be continuous (not necessarily in a straight line), unobstructed, marked and lighted. Consideration shall be given to design leak scenarios in developing egress routes.
