5.13.1.2. Maintenance access is required to all instruments but can be by portable ladder from grade or by platform.

5.13.1.3. All level instruments shall be accessible from grade, platform or ladder. Their location shall be consistent with function and with convenience of plant operation.

5.13.1.4. Where strong backs are provided for external level instruments, their minimum pipe size will be NPS 3, STD. WT for carbon and low alloy steels and NPS 3, SCH 80S for S.S. Block valves shall be provided at the vessel connections.

5.13.2. Control Valve Manifolds

5.13.2.1. For preferred types and arrangements see Standard Drawings DD00-L-1054-1/DD00-L-1054-2.

5.13.2.2. Control valves shall be located at grade or on conveniently accessible platforms. Their locations shall be consistent with their function and with convenience of plant

operation. In general, they shall be located in sight of instruments or indicators showing variables they control.

5.13.2.3. Control valves in flashing service shall be located near the end of the piping, to minimize flow induced vibration, erosion and cavitation problems. Also, the downstream block valve shall be the same size as the downstream line.

5.13.2.4. Where high pressure drop conditions exist across control valves, sonic harmonics along with extreme noise levels can be expected. Piping subjected to these conditions must be carefully analyzed and designed to ensure that its size and configuration downstream of the valve prevents excessive vibration and noise.

5.13.2.5. The location of control valves shall be planned for accessibility and removal. Clearance shall be provided in the piping arrangement to permit removal of the plug and valve superstructure without removing the valve body from the piping.

5.13.2.6. When practical, lines shall be routed to group control valves at grade or at an operating platform; otherwise. Access platforms shall be provided. An effort shall be made to locate all upstream or downstream instrument devices for control valves, other than level devices, at the control valve location.

5.13.2.7. Normally, block and bypass valves shall be installed around all control valves, unless they have been omitted (dependant on process operating conditions) during the detailed P&ID review. Control valves without block and bypass valves shall be supplied with a manual handwheel.

5.13.2.8. When required, the size of block and bypass valves shall be as follows:

- a) Where the header is NPS 2 or smaller, a globe type bypass valve the same size as the header shall be used.
- b) Where the header is NPS 3 or larger, a globe type bypass valve one size smaller than the header shall be used. Where globe valves of this size are not available in the piping material specification, gate valves may be used.
- c) Block valves shall be at least one size larger than the control valve, but not larger than the header.

5.13.2.9. Bypass valves installed around a pressure reducing valve shall not have a greater capacity than the reducing valve. A pressure gage shall be installed on the low pressure side of and immediately adjacent to the pressure reducing valve.

5.13.2.10. Where a flanged control valve smaller than line size is used, flush bottom eccentric reducers shall be used adjacent to the control valve flanges to prevent trapping liquids or vapours in the line. Frangeless control valves shall require installation of a control valve size spool to allow removal of the bolts.

5.13.2.11. Control valve stations for steam to pumps, turbines or other critical types of equipment shall be located at operating levels. The control valve shall be installed in such a manner to prevent the collection of sediment and scale at the valve inlet. A NPS 1¼ blowdown valve shall be provided at the lowest point of the inlet steam line,

5.13.2.12. NPS ¾ (minimum) gate valves, for draining and/or release of pressure, shall be provided at the low points in the piping on both sides of the control valve and the adjacent block valves. These drain/depressurising valves shall be installed on the underside of the line and shall point downward. Round head pipe plugs shall be inserted in the open ends of the valves, or where the drain valves are flanged due to line class requirements, the blind flange shall be equipped with a 4" long nipple and cap.

5.13.2.13. By-pass valves in steam control sets shall be located at the top horizontal portion of the by-pass line in order to avoid a build up of condensate.

5.13.3. Level Instruments

5.13.3.1. For Level Instrument installation details, refer to Industry Source 10 Standard 0401-P1.

5.13.4. Orifice Runs

5.13.4.1. Horizontal meter-runs are preferred. Determine the length of each meter run in accordance with Industry Source 10 OSG Standard 0401-P1. Sufficient clearance shall be provided at orifice flanges for installation of instrument piping and seal pots where they are required. Refer to Standard Drawing GD00-L-1049-1 and GD00-L-1049-2.

5.13.4.2. Orifice flanges shall be equipped with jack screws.

5.13.5. Thermowell Connections

5.13.5.1. Threaded thermowells are permitted only in services where threaded fittings are acceptable in the Pipe Class Table.

5.13.5.2. Except where listed in the Pipe Class Table as NPS 1½ for Energy Services, flanged thermowell nozzles shall be pipets, NPS 2 x 6" long with wall thickness per Pipe Class and Class 300 flange minimum. If butt welds are used, the root pass must be ground smooth.

5.13.5.3. On NPS 4 lines, thermowells shall be installed on elbows per Standard Drawing GD00-L-1035-1.

5.13.5.4. Lines NPS 3 and smaller shall be increased to NPS 4 at the thermowell elbow. Straight line increases require prior approval from Instrument and Process Engineering.

5.13.5.5. Thermowell nozzles on clad or weld overlayed pipe shall be sized to account for the reduction of internal diameter due to the cladding or weld overlay.

## 5.14. Pressure Relief Systems

5.14.1. Safety and relief valves shall be provided, sized and installed in compliance with the applicable boiler, pressure vessel and piping codes.

5.14.2. Piping

5.14.2.1. The size of the inlet line shall not be less than the size of the relief valve inlet.

5.14.2.2. The length of the inlet piping shall be as short as practical to avoid excessive pressure drop in the line.

5.14.2.3. Full inlet line class requirements shall be used up to and including the isolation valve downstream of the PSV for pilot operated PSVs.

5.14.3. Discharge to Atmosphere

5.14.3.1. For water service discharge to paving or suitable drain. For thermal relief valves, the valve can be located on the pipe centerline with the discharge pointing downwards.

5.14.3.2. Small reliefs, protecting blocked-in process piping or equipment against fluid thermal expansion shall discharge to a suitable drain or closed blowdown system. See 5.10.3.4 for additional requirements.

5.14.3.3. Relief valves discharging to into a closed blowdown system shall be elevated to provide self draining of discharge side into the blowdown system. Relief valves discharging vapour to atmosphere must be provided with a pipe stack ending at least 10'-0" (3050 mm) above any platform within a 25'-0" (7625 mm) radius. A NPS ½" weep hole (or as sized on P&ID) shall be provided at the bottom of the stack to prevent liquid accumulation. If the stack is insulated, weep hole shall be provided with a nipple to clear the insulation. If the weep hole would discharge to a platform, a NPS ¾" sockolet and NPS ¾" line shall be provided to a safe location. EHT and insulation shall be used on this weep hole drain if there is a possibility of freezing.

5.14.3.4. Vent valves shall be provided between the inlet block valve and the PSV, and between the PSV and the outlet block valve. See Industry Source 10 Std. drawing DD00-L-1073-3.

5.14.4. Piping to Closed System

5.14.4.1. Any pressure relief valve discharging to a closed system shall be installed so that the discharge piping slopes away from the relief valve, into the header. If this is not possible, a NPS ¾ valved drain line shall be installed from the lowest point in the discharge piping to a safe area.

5.14.4.2. Blowdown headers shall be installed so that the piping slopes into the blowdown drum. Where this is not practical, the low points in the header shall be steam traced and insulated, and a NPS ¾ valved drain line shall be provided.

5.14.4.3. The bonnet vent of a relief valve with bellows shall NOT be piped to the discharge line, but be piped to atmosphere if safe or a closed reservoir at atmospheric pressure. The line shall be freeze protected.

5.14.4.4. Thermal relief valves on blocked-in sections of storage tank piping shall discharge back to the non-blocked-in tank piping, tank, or disposal system.

5.14.5. Block Valves

5.14.5.1. Where a block valve is installed to permit removal of a relief valve during unit operation it shall be located immediately below the relief valve, and be car-sealed or locked open.

[Industry Source 10 logo]

# Corporate Technical Standard

Department: **PROJECT SERVICES** | Number: **0201**
Subject: **Piping Design and Plant Layout** | Revision: **9**

5.14.5.2. Where a pressure relief valve discharges into a header and an outlet block valve is installed, this valve shall be car-sealed or locked open.

5.14.5.3. Any block valve shall be full port gate or plug type.

5.14.5.4. Any valve mounted in a horizontal pipe run shall be orientated with the valve stem at or below the horizontal centerline to avoid line blockage in the event that the gate breaks away from the stem.

5.14.5.5. Where a relief valve is fitted with block valves and a by-pass valve, the by-pass valve shall be mounted in a horizontal leg and shall drain into the relief valve outlet line.

5.14.6. Location

5.14.6.1. Access to pressure relief valves shall be in accordance with Table 3.

5.14.6.2. Relief valves may be located on the piping instead of on the equipment and shall be located at the lowest possible elevation that may be economically justified. This shall be reviewed and approved by the Process System and Instrumentation Engineers.

## 5.15. Underground Piping

5.15.1. General

5.15.1.1. Underground piping refers to process and utility lines below grade. Lines shall be laid along the side of roads and outside of tank walls. Lines shall not be routed under foundations. See Industry Source 10 STD. 1516 Construction of Underground Utilities.

5.15.1.2. All underground steel pipes and sleeves must be coated and wrapped. This includes pipe to be installed in casings. See Industry Source 10 STD. 0216.

5.15.1.3. Burial depth for lines susceptible to freezing shall provide a minimum cover from top of pipe to finished grade at least equal to the frost line. The frost line shall be considered:

- a) 10'-0" (3050 mm) for Ft. McMurray
- b) 4'-0" (1220 mm) for Sarnia.
- c) 3'-0" (915mm) for Denver.

The use of alternative designs to prevent freezing shall require Owner's Engineer approval.

5.15.1.4. Additional depth and/or casings may be required for mechanical protection. Depth of fire protection lines must be per NFPA 24.

5.15.1.5. For lines not susceptible to freezing, burial depth is for mechanical protection only, not necessarily below the frost line. Minimum burial depth shall be 4'-0" (1220 mm).

5.15.1.6. Buried steel lines shall be provided with a 6 in (150 mm) minimum protective covering of sand on sides, bottom and top with the balance of the trench filled to grade with earth backfill.

5.15.1.7. Lines with operating temperatures 160°F (71°C) and above shall not be buried without written permission of the Owner's representative.

5.15.1.8. Underground lines beyond the unit area limits shall be NPS 3 minimum pipe size except for sanitary water and chemical lines.

5.15.1.9. Elevation of underground lines shall be given to the outside bottom (OB) of pipe or to the invert or inside bottom (IB) of sewer lines.

5.15.1.10. Non-insulated pipes going through casings must be installed with commercially available casing insulators which will support the pipe and isolate it electrically from the casing.

5.15.1.11. Refer to Standard Drawing GD00-L-1050-1 for requirements for lines running through dykes.

5.15.1.12. There shall be no direct burial of flanges, non-seal welded threaded connections, or other mechanical connections which have the possibility of leakage.

5.15.1.13. Where underground metallic piping is cathodically protected, insulation kits shall be provided at all flanged joints where the underground piping is connected to above ground piping.

5.15.1.14. The need for cathodic protection shall be assessed as part of the design and prior to construction of underground piping systems.

5.15.1.15. Minimum clearance for sewer lines shall be 2'-0" (610 mm) between outside diameter of the pipe. Clearance between underground lines shall be 12" (305 mm) minimum except cooling water lines shall have 18" (460 mm) clearance where heat transfer is probable. Local building codes must be followed for clearance.

5.15.2. Road Crossings

5.15.2.1. Piping below city, county, provincial or refinery roads shall run in sleeves, tunnels or culverts and shall conform to local, provincial or state regulations. The design of such crossings shall be submitted to the appropriate regulatory authority for approval before installation is started. For typical configuration of insulated and uninsulated lines see Standard Drawing GD00-L-1050-1.

5.15.2.2. Road crossings shall normally be at 90° to the road, never less than 45°.

## 5.16. Tank Field Piping

5.16.1. Tank field piping requires special restraints and allowances for large non-thermal movements. The special restraints are due to dike penetrations and the non-thermal movements due to possible tank settlement.

5.16.2. Dike penetrations may be in open sleeves, sleeves sealed with the lines welded to one end with steel collars and with the lines buried.

5.16.3. Lines connected to tanks subject to settlement cannot be supported rigidly from grade near the tank. When the settlement is large, the lines must be supported from the tank itself, or

on resilient supports such as springs. Tank nozzle rotations or deflections due to Industry Source 08 bowing require consideration in supporting lines connected to the tank.

5.16.4. See Industry Source 10 STD. 1521 Design of Tank Pads and Dykes.

## 5.17. Stress Analysis

5.17.1. The purpose of this Section is to establish guidelines and procedures that must be followed in order to provide a uniform approach to piping stress analysis, starting with stress critical lines, and ending with field inspection after installation and start-up. Stress analysis is done mostly for thermal expansion or contraction, but also included are lines where weight or fluid dynamics causes excessive stresses.

5.17.2. Stress Critical Lines

5.17.2.1. The following minimum criteria shall be used for selecting lines to be stress analyzed, and for which stress sketches shall be produced.

a) Lines of NPS 3 and 4 with design temperature above 500°F (260°C).

b) Lines of NPS 6 and larger with design temperature above 250°F (121°C).

c) All lines with design temperature below minus 20°F (-29°C).

d) Non-ferrous lines with design temperature above 212°F (100°C).

e) Non-metallic lines with design temperature above 122°F (50°C).

f) All lines with very long horizontal or vertical straight runs that have lower design temperature limits than stated in paragraphs a) thru e) above. Lines which require assessment shall be determined by the Piping Stress Engineer.

g) All lines NPS 24 and larger.

h) Lines with wall thickness less than schedule 10/10s or greater than extra strong.

i) All lines subject to any mechanical, fluid, or 2-phase flow induced impact, vibration, or dynamic loads.

j) All PRV inlet and discharge piping to ensure adequate supporting and restraint for all moments, forces, shock loads, and stresses on the valve body, the connection flanges, the piping, and the supporting structure.

k) All pump, compressor and turbine piping, excluding instrument or auxiliary piping.

l) All fired heater, steam generator, Industry Source 08 and tube exchanger with bellows, and air cooler piping, excluding instrument, fuel gas or auxiliary piping.

m) Piping connected to vessels, tanks or equipment subject to different settlement (or upheaval), or to thermal expansion.

n) Lines containing expansion joints, or quick disconnect couplings.

o) Lines with special non-standard fittings or supports that locally reduce the strength.

- p) All jacketed lines.

- q) Lines that although not in themselves stress critical, tie into stress critical lines and have a significant impact on stress or flexibility.

- r) Lines connected to equipment or non-ferrous material, or equipment with brittle lining.

- s) Lines connected to equipment for which the manufacturer has specified low loadings.

- t) Any line that the Owner or the Designer designates as stress critical.

- u) Buried lines with a design temperature above 160°F (71°C).

- v) All lines in severe cyclic service as defined by B31.3 section 300.2.

5.17.2.2. The person(s) responsible for piping design and stress analysis shall be notified immediately when any changes that affect the design conditions are made to stress critical lines.

## 5.17.3. Stress Sketches and Analysis

### 5.17.3.1.

To ensure an efficient stress analysis the following information must be shown on the stress sketch:

- a) Branch points complete with line number.

- b) Co-ordinates and elevation of at least one reference point to assist in locating on orthographics.

- c) Critical clearances from piping and equipment.

- d) Design/upset and operating pressures and temperature.

- e) Dimensions +/- 2" (+/- 50 mm) where possible. Dimensions shall be shown from support to support, support to branch or fitting to fitting.

- f) Direction of flow

- g) Insulation type and thickness.

- h) Line numbers.

- i) Line sizes.

- j) Location and size of reducers.

- k) Location and type of all proposed pipe supports.

- l) Location of fixed end of horizontal vessels and heat exchangers.

- m) Location of nozzle centre lines relative to fixed points or anchors for horizontal vessels and bottom tangent lines for vertical vessels.

- n) Location of structural steel.

- o) Location of wall or roof penetrations.
- p) Nature of flowing commodity (vapour, liquid, 2-phase).
- q) North Arrow.
- r) Pipe schedule.
- s) Piping class and specification breaks.
- t) Piping materials.
- u) Routing type.
- v) Unusual or special conditions such as lethal service, cyclic operation, etc. These shall be found as notes on the P&IDs or Piping or Stress shall be advised separately by Projects, Process or Start-up Engineers.
- w) Nozzle number for each vessel or heat exchanger connection.
- x) Extent of gusseting required (see section 5.12.9).

5.17.3.2. The piping stress analysis shall comply with the applicable Code for the service and location.

5.17.3.3. The piping stress analysis shall be done with a computer program, manual calculation, or with reference to pre-calculated tables of U-shape and L-leg configurations. The method used shall be recorded on the stress sketch.

5.17.3.4. Depending on the complexity of the project, and to avoid major relocation of equipment or rerouting of pipes during the detail design, preliminary stress sketches followed by preliminary stress analysis shall be made. This preliminary work may be done while some of the items listed in paragraph 5.17.3.1 are "assumed", and when required shall include alternate locations and routing.

5.17.3.5. The results of the piping stress analysis shall be marked-up on the stress sketches and shall include:

- a) Nozzle loadings on equipment.
- b) Loads on anchors and stops.
- c) Loads of over 1000 lb (454 kg) and movements of over 1" (25 mm) on solid pipe supports.
- d) All loads and movements on spring hangers.

5.17.3.6. It is the stress analyst's responsibility to ensure that pipe loadings on equipment comply with industrial standards, or are accepted by the equipment manufacturer.

5.17.3.7. If the mark-ups on a stress sketch include re-routes or relocation of supports, spring hangers, anchors, or stops, it is the Piping Designer's responsibility to include them in the final design. If that is not possible then alternatives must be developed and re-calculated.

5.17.3.8. Before the piping drawings are issued for construction the person(s) responsible for stress analysis and Piping Design shall double-check the construction drawings to ensure that all stress recommendations and requirements have been incorporated.

5.17.4. Field Work

5.17.4.1. Before any changes are made during fabrication or installations, the person(s) responsible for stress analysis and piping design shall be notified and shall decide whether those changes affect the piping stresses. Their agreement is required before the changes can be made.

5.17.4.2. Near the end of construction the stress analyst or his designate shall make site visits to ensure that the piping systems are properly installed. Particularly important are:

a) Spaces for thermal expansion and contraction

b) Expansion joints including their tie-rod and supports

c) Spring hangers including their "cold and empty" loading

5.17.5. Documentation and Records

5.17.5.1. The Document Control System shall have cross-references between the line number, the Stress Sketch(es), and the piping stress analysis calculations, Including the alternate sketches and analysis.

5.17.5.2. At the completion of the project the final versions of the stress sketch(es), and the piping stress analysis calculations, including any changes made during construction or start-up, shall be submitted to the Owner's Records Department.

## 5.18. Injection Points and Process Mix Points

5.18.1. Injection points are locations where chemicals or process additives are introduced into a process stream. Special attention is required in designing the point of injection of corrosion inhibitors, neutralizers, process antifoulants, antifoam, desalter demulsifiers, oxygen scavengers, caustic, and water washes to mitigate the potential for erosion, corrosion, fatigue or other mechanical damage and to also ensure proper mixing occurs.

5.18.2. The design the injection system shall consider the purpose, location and method of injection as well as materials selection for the injection device (quill/nozzle), injection delivery system and piping or equipment into which the material is being injected. High alloy materials are normally required.

5.18.3. Injection quills/nozzles shall be designed to be removable for inspection and/or cleaning. The need for in-service removal of injection quills shall be identified if required.

5.18.4. Mix points, where the joining of two or more process streams of differing composition and/or temperature takes place require attention to design. Risks such as cyclic service (due to thermal cycling or flow induced vibration for example), differential thermal stress, localized erosion, localized corrosion, environmental cracking, and mechanical loads shall be addressed in the design.

5.18.5. Injection points and process mix points shall be located to allow sufficient time for mixing, contacting, reactions, etc. to occur prior to flow disruptions in the process line which could lead to localized erosion or corrosion. The design shall ensure risks associated with of impingement erosion or erosion-corrosion are minimised.

## 5.19. Cleaning of Piping Systems

5.19.1. Cleaning of piping systems shall comply with Industry Source 10 Std. No. 0215 Standard for Chemical Cleaning of Piping Systems.

5.19.2. The following piping systems shall be specified for special cleaning by either mechanical or chemical methods, prior to be placed in service:

- a) Oxygen service piping
- b) Lube oil and seal oil piping.
- c) Compressor suction piping
- d) Steam turbine inlet piping
- e) Boiler feedwater systems, downstream of De-aerators
- f) Other process sensitive systems (to be determined by Process Engineering)

5.19.3. All cleaning procedures shall be approved by the Owner before cleaning is carried out.

## 5.20. Internally Coated Piping

5.20.1. Internally coated piping shall comply with the requirements of Industry Source 10 Std. No. 0216 Standard for Underground Piping External and Internal Coatings.

5.20.2. Internally coated piping shall be no smaller than NPS 2.

5.20.3. Root passes of butwelds performed in a fabrication shop shall be specified as GMAW or GTAW process to facilitate an internally smooth surface. Coating will be stopped 7 inches (180 mm) back from any field welds which will be left bare after field welding.

5.20.4. Piping spools shall contain no more than one elbow so that reasonable access for coating application can be maintained.

5.20.5. Piping spools shall be small enough to fit in the applicator's curing oven if specified.

## 5.21. Piping in Vibrating Service

5.21.1. To limit piping vibration, anchors and supports for piping in vibration service shall be selected in accordance with recommendations of an acoustic and mechanical resonance study.

5.21.2. Piping subject to vibration whether insulated or un-insulated shall be anchored and guided by means of heavy duty pipe clamps specially designed for this type of service.

5.21.3. "Welded on Tee" shaped beam cut shoe supports are not permitted in the section of piping deemed to be in vibrating service.

[Industry Source 10 logo]

# Corporate Technical Standard

**Department:** PROJECT SERVICES **Number:** 0201

**Subject:** **Piping Design and Plant Layout** **Revision:** 9

5.21.4. Designs with fillet or corner welds shall be minimized. If corner welds are unavoidable, instructional notes will be placed on the fabrication/isometric drawings to minimize stress concentrators in the finished fabricated product. Partial penetration welds or reinforcing pads are not permitted. Buttwelding components shall be lined up accurately and root pass of welds shall be ground smooth wherever possible. GTAW shall be used for the root pass if it is not possible to grind the root smooth. Welding shall comply with Industry Source 10 Std. 0903. Piping fabrication and Installation shall comply with Industry Source 10 Std. 0204.

5.21.5. All gaskets in vibrating service shall be spiral-wound type.

## 5.22. Foam System Piping

5.22.1. Refer to Industry Source 10 Standard 0060 for foam system piping requirements.

## 5.23. Galvanized Piping

5.23.1. Galvanized piping in sizes NPS ½ up to NPS 2 shall be constructed from pre-galvanized threaded pipe and fittings in accordance with the relevant pipe class.

5.23.2. Galvanizing piping NPS 3 to NPS 8 of welded construction shall be made from pre-fabricated pipe spools in accordance with the relevant pipe class. These spools shall be flanged and shall be restricted to shapes and dimensions that permit hot dip galvanizing after fabrication. The maximum size of these spools is limited to the size of the fabricators galvanizing bath and by the shipping envelope for spools.

## 5.24. Oil Mist Systems

5.24.1. Oil mist generators shall be located to minimize pipe runs to the pumps. i.e. in the centre of a group of pumps.

5.24.2. Oil mist distribution header, normally NPS 2, and equipment drop piping, normally NPS ¾ shall be galvanized and threaded pipe and fittings.

5.24.3. Oil mist header installation shall comply with the following:

5.24.3.1. Wherever possible the oil mist header shall be installed so that the entire system slopes and drains towards the oil mist console.

5.24.3.2. The oil mist header shall be sloped a minimum of 1 inch per 20 feet (25 mm in 6 m).

5.24.3.3. Oil mist header piping shall be installed without low spots or pockets. Sags and low spots in the header pipe collect oil, which restricts or may completely block oil mist flow to downstream equipment.

5.24.3.4. Oil mist distribution header shall have no valves of any type.

5.24.3.5. Continuous sections or joints of pipe will be joined using threaded pipe tees. Couplings are not to be used. The tees will be installed with one outlet pointing up. A galvanized pipe plug will be installed in the upward port.

5.24.3.6. Branch headers shall be at least the same pipe size as the header from which it originates.

5.24.3.7. Branch headers will connect to the top of the header from which it originates. Wherever possible, branch headers will be sloped toward the main oil mist header so that oil drains back to the oil mist console.

5.24.4. Equipment drop piping installation shall comply with the following:

5.24.4.1. Equipment drop piping will be connected to the top of the main oil mist header.

5.24.4.2. Equipment drop piping will be sloped toward the oil mist header from which it originates up to the first section of pipe that extends vertically down. From thereafter, all drop piping will sloped toward the equipment being serviced. Drop piping will have the same slope as the oil mist header.

5.24.4.3. Equipment drop piping shall not exceed 35 feet (10.6 m) in length.

5.24.4.4. Drop piping shall be located so that it:

- a) Terminates no less than 2 feet (600 mm) nor more than 6 feet (1.8 m) above the equipment to be serviced.
- b) Is located off centre so that equipment can be serviced without the need to remove the oil mist drop piping.
- c) Does not impeded access to the equipment.
- d) Does not interfere with installation or removal of the equipment.

5.24.5. Drop piping shall be anchored to permanent structures or piping not normally removed for maintenance.

5.24.5.1. Drop piping shall not be branched.

5.24.5.2. Drop piping shall terminate with a manifold block. Mist manifolds shall include:

- a) A self closing valve for draining oil that collects at the end of the drop piping. Valve will be such that it cannot vibrate open.
- b) Tapped connections for installation of reclassifiers.
- c) A site viewing glass to reveal oil that collects in the bottom of the drop, and to allow viewing of mist flow when the drain valve is opened.
- d) If specified, a drain line shall be installed from the mist manifold drain outlet connection to the oil collection container. Drain tubing shall be 3/8 inch OD.

5.24.6. Oil mist distribution header, branch header and equipment drop piping shall be supported to limit sagging to a maximum deflection of 1/8 of the pipe ID.

## 5.25. OWS & CHD Systems

5.25.1. See Industry Source 10 Std. 1517 Design of Clean Water, Industrial and Chemical Sewer Systems and Culverts, or relevant business unit Standard.

## 5.26. Hot Taps

[Industry Source 10 logo]

# Corporate Technical Standard

Department: **PROJECT SERVICES** | Number: **0201**
Subject: **Piping Design and Plant Layout** | Revision: **9**

5.26.1. Hot Taps shall comply with Industry Source 10 Std. 0220 Hot Tap Design and Installation Requirements, or relevant business unit Standard.

## 5.27. Pipeline PIG Launchers/Receivers

5.27.1. Pipelines, and pig launchers/receivers shall comply with Industry Source 10 Std. 0222 Pipelines (CSA Z662)

## 5.28. Special Services

5.28.1. Sulphuric Acid Service

- 5.28.1.1. Threaded or socket welding connections are prohibited for carbon steel piping in sulphuric acid service.
- 5.28.1.2. Butt-weld connections shall be used for all pipe sizes.
- 5.28.1.3. All flanged connections shall have polyethylene safety covers with snap type fasteners.
- 5.28.1.4. Copper or copper-bearing alloys are not be permitted in this service.
- 5.28.1.5. For material classes, see relevant business unit Piping Material Specifications.

5.28.2. Chlorine Service

- 5.28.2.1. Chlorine shall be treated as a very toxic substance.
- 5.28.2.2. A minimum of schedule 80 seamless pipe of minimum size NPS ½ shall be used to ensure rigidity and for protection against mechanical damage resulting in possible leaks.
- 5.28.2.3. Piping arrangements shall be as simple as possible, with a minimum of welded or flanged connections. For pipe of NPS 4 and smaller, pipe bending shall be applied rather than using elbows. Cold bending is not permitted unless the finished bend is stress relieved.
- 5.28.2.4. Horizontal pipes shall be self draining with a slope of at least 1:100.
- 5.28.2.5. The number of field welds shall be minimized.
- 5.28.2.6. Socket welding is not permitted. All piping shall have butt-welded joints, except for NPS ½ vents, drains, and instrument connections which are to be threaded and seal welded.
- 5.28.2.7. For material classes, see relevant business unit Piping material Specifications.

5.28.3. Hydrogen Fluoride (HF) Service

- 5.28.3.1. HF shall be treated as a very toxic substance.
- 5.28.3.2. Expansion bellows shall not be used.

5.28.3.3. All connections shall be welded or flanged; however flanged connections shall be reduced to the least number possible to avoid leakages.

5.28.3.4. All pipe flanges valve flanges and valve bonnet flanges shall be painted with one coat of HF-detecting paint and shall not be insulated.

5.28.3.5. All valves and instruments shall be located at an elevation of maximum 3 feet 3 inches (1 m) above the working floor for safe easy handling during operation and maintenance.

5.28.3.6. All HF piping shall be installed above grade and shall be self draining (minimum slope of 1:100) to equipment or low point drains.

5.28.3.7. Process piping shall not be smaller than NPS 1. Vents and drains shall not be smaller than NPS ¾. Pipe and fittings shall be threaded in sizes NPS 1 and smaller.

5.28.3.8. All threaded connections shall be made up with PTFE tape only. Threaded connections shall not be seal-welded.

5.28.3.9. Socket welded fittings are not permitted.

5.28.3.10. Drains and vents shall be connected to a closed system.

5.28.3.11. All control valves in HF service shall be installed with block valves and a by-pass globe valve and shall have flush connection on both sides of the control valve.

5.28.3.12. Level indicators shall be of the magnetic type. Gauge glasses are not permitted.

5.28.3.13. For material classes, see relevant business unit Piping material Specifications.

5.28.4. Sodium Hydroxide (Caustic Soda) Service

5.28.4.1. Steam connections shall be provided on caustic piping for line cleaning and blowdown purposes.

5.28.4.2. All attachment welds to piping shall be done prior to PWHT. PWHT requirements shall be determined in accordance with NACE SP0403.

5.28.4.3. Hot spots due to direct wall to wall contact with steam or electric tracing shall be avoided by fitting spacers (ceramic, glass fibre, or filled phenolic resin).

5.28.4.4. All drawings for the fabrication of carbon steel piping for this service shall be clearly marked "SODIUM HYDROXIDE SERVICE".

5.28.4.5. Where heat loss through pipe supports could result in process solution freezing, clamp type supports shall be used with thermally insulating strips (e.g., glass-fibre material) shall be fitted between the pipes and supports.

5.28.4.6. For material classes, see relevant business unit Piping Material Specifications.

5.28.5. Gaseous Oxygen Service

5.28.5.1. Oxygen piping systems shall be kept as simple as possible, with the smallest possible number of valves, fittings, branches, and nozzles. See CGA Pamphlet G-

4.4 Industrial Practices for Gaseous Oxygen Transmission and Distribution Piping Systems.

5.28.5.2. Oxygen piping shall be located as far as possible from other piping. Pipes containing flammable fluid, gas or steam shall not be installed within 3 feet 3 inches (1 m) distance of oxygen piping. The free space may be utilized for lines carrying water, nitrogen or other non-flammable fluids at ambient temperature. At points where the above requirements cannot be fulfilled, the Owner shall be asked whether any additional preventative or corrective measures are required.

5.28.5.3. Oxygen pipes shall be located on the outermost position in pipe racks.

5.28.5.4. Installation of oxygen pipes through tunnels or (covered or uncovered) trenches shall be avoided. If unavoidable, flanged connections or valves shall not be used (except for low point drain connections) and the tunnel or trench shall not contain lines carrying flammable fluids or gases. Oxygen piping shall not support other pipes.

5.28.5.5. Underground oxygen piping installed outside process or hazardous areas, shall be clearly identified above ground and kept separate from electrical cables and other piping.

5.28.5.6. The underground piping shall have external corrosion protection.

5.28.5.7. Expansion bellows shall not be used.

5.28.5.8. In carbon steel and stainless steel piping systems, branches shall be made with equal tees, reducing tees or swept outlets. In nickel-based alloy piping systems, branches shall also be made with equal tees, reducing tees or swept outlets, but branch outlets (weldolets) and branch fittings (nipples) are permitted.

5.28.5.9. Changes in diameter shall be minimized. Where changes in diameter are unavoidable, they shall be accomplished in steps of one nominal size at a time, and the distance between successive diameter changes shall be at least 3 feet 3 inches (1 m).

5.28.5.10. Dead ends in piping shall be avoided.

5.28.5.11. To assist in removal of the degreasing agent after cleaning, low points in equipment and piping, except underground piping, shall have drain connections with a valve but closed by a blind flange. Underground piping shall not be provided with drains for this purpose.

5.28.5.12. Above ground oxygen piping shall be grounded.

5.28.5.13. Connections for purging and venting shall be situated such that purging and venting of the system can only be done in the normal direction of the oxygen flow.

5.28.5.14. Where an oxygen line enters the plot of a process unit or a hazardous area, a block valve shall be installed. This valve will normally only be used in emergency situations and shall be operated from behind a fire shield, or remotely from one or more suitable locations.

5.28.5.15. Insulating flanges of cathodically protected oxygen lines shall only be fitted in a vertical section of line in order to avoid the deposition of particulate matter that might bridge the insulation. Insulating flanges shall be protected against internal sparking caused by elevated electrical potential differences across the insulation and stray currents, induction or otherwise. Polarization cells of sufficient rating shall always be installed across insulating joints or flanges.

5.28.5.16. Vent lines shall be fabricated from stainless steel, and be vertical and straight in configuration. The end of the vent line shall terminate in a tee, with a length of pipe welded on each end of the tee equal to D/2 in length.

5.28.5.17. Gaskets shall be carefully sized to prevent any protrusion beyond the free inner surface of the pipe.

5.28.5.18. A pipe section made from material suitable for high velocities shall be installed downstream of throttling valves. All block valves must only be operated in the fully open or fully closed position.

5.28.5.19. Careful attention to cleaning of oxygen system piping, valves etc, throughout fabrication, transport, installation, and commissioning is of paramount importance. Cleaning procedures shall be in accordance with CGA Pamphlet G-4.1 as a minimum.

5.28.5.20. For piping materials selection and line classes, see the relevant business unit Piping Material Specifications.

5.28.6. Amine Service

5.28.6.1. All rich amine systems shall be treated as sour service applications.

5.28.6.2. All welds in carbon steel piping shall be PWHT including external attachment welds.

5.28.6.3. Copper or copper-based alloys shall not be used in amine service.

5.28.6.4. For piping material selection and classes, see relevant business unit Piping material Specification.

5.28.7. Hydrogen Peroxide Service

5.28.7.1. Dead ends shall be avoided in hydrogen peroxide piping.

5.28.7.2. Piping shall be vented to prevent an over pressure as a result of hydrogen peroxide decomposition.

5.28.7.3. All piping components shall undergo a passivation process in accordance with ASTM A380 (latest revision) as applicable for austenitic stainless steels or such alternative vendor recommended process that shall be approved by the Owner.

5.28.7.4. Spray shields shall be installed at all flanged joints.

5.28.7.5. Vents and drains shall use flanged gate valves

5.28.7.6. Instrument connections shall use threaded ball valves.

5.28.7.7. Ball valve cavities shall be vented to prevent entrapment of peroxide fluid in the open or closed position.

5.28.7.8. Equal or reducing tees shall be used for branch connections.

5.28.7.9. For piping material selection and classes, see relevant business unit Piping material Specification.

5.28.8. Hydrochloric Acid Service

5.28.8.1. PTFE lined piping system shall be utilized for hydrochloric acid service.

5.28.8.2. PTFE lined pipe spools shall be fitted with a vent hole in the pipe. For insulated lines, the vent hole shall be extended to take it outside the insulation.

5.28.8.3. Gaskets are required only for connection to equipment or unlined components.

5.28.8.4. For vents, drains, and instrument connections use flanged ball valves.

5.28.8.5. Spray shields shall be fitted to all flanged joints.

5.28.8.6. Refer to manufacturer's recommendation for bolt torquing requirements.

5.28.8.7. Double check valves shall be installed upstream of dilution tee's on both the acid and the dilution water piping.

5.28.8.8. For piping material selection and classes, see relevant business unit Piping Material Specification.

5.28.9. Slurry Piping

5.28.9.1. For Oil Sands Extraction see business unit Standard ETS0011A which describes the basis for design, fabrication and installation of slurry pipeline systems.

## 6. IMPLEMENTATION

6.1. It shall be the responsibility of the applicable Project Engineering Manager to ensure that the requirements of this standard are implemented on projects where this standard is adopted.

Interpretation and guidance shall be provided by the applicable Peer Review Network member for the business unit or the applicable Industry Source 10 Project or Discipline Engineer for a project. The Subject Matter Expert responsible for this technical standard shall be consulted by the applicable Project or Discipline Engineer for any interpretation of the requirements within this standard.

## 1.0 GENERAL

### 1.1 Scope

This specification describes the basis for the overall design of process and utility piping and shall apply to all piping systems and parts of such systems.

### 1.2 Intent

The intent of this specification is to provide for a complete package in accordance with standard practice. This is a general specification, and therefore subject to variations in materials, design and construction, provided that the requirements of standard practice are met. Prior approval shall be obtained from the Owner before making any change to these specifications.

### 1.3 Conflicting Requirements

Should a conflict arise between this specification and other specifications or government regulations, the Vendor shall contact the Owner and a decision reached in writing before any work is done.

### 1.4 Vendor Responsibility

The Vendor shall be responsible for conformance to governing codes, Owner's specifications, drawings, legal and contractual requirements. In the event of on compliance with the foregoing, the Owner may correct any deficiencies, and the cost of such repairs shall be charged to the Vendor.

## 2.0 CODE REQUIREMENTS

### 2.1 Codes and Standards

Minimum piping requirements are to be equal to or shall exceed requirements of latest editions of the following applicable codes. Any mandatory federal, provincial or local codes in effect at the project site are to be complied with:

- Local pressure piping regulating authority
- ABSA, Alberta Boilers Safety Association
- API 520, Design and Installation of Pressure-Relieving Systems
- API 521, Guide for Pressure-Relieving and Depressurizing Systems
- ASME, B31.3, Chemical Plant & Petroleum Refinery Piping
- ASME, Section IX, Welding & Brazing Requirements
- CSA Z662, Oil & Gas Pipeline Systems
- Department of Labour, Boilers Branch for the applicable province
- OHSA, Occupational Health and Safety Act
- Regulations of the applicable province and Canada

[Industry Source 06 logo]

## 3.0 DESIGN CONDITIONS

### 3.1 Operating Conditions

3.1.1 Normal design conditions of pressure and temperature shall be the most severe conditions expected to co-exist under long-time operating conditions. These usual operations include all manipulation and control functions such as throttling, blocking and bypassing likely to be used for operation and control.

3.1.2 Usual operating conditions do not include more severe temporary conditions, such as those incidental to start-up, shutdown, steam-out or abnormal operations. Temporary conditions govern as design conditions only when there is clear evidence they definitely exceed time and severity limits in paragraph 302.2.4 of Refinery Piping Code, ANSI B31.3.

### 3.2 Design Temperature

3.2.1 Design temperature is the most severe sustained fluid temperature, subject to conditions of Section 3.1 above. Design temperature of internally insulated or non-insulated components may be the metal temperature rather than the fluid temperature.

3.2.2 Design temperature for steam traced piping shall be the fluid temperature or 10° C below saturation temperature of tracing steam, whichever is greater.

3.2.3 Design temperature for piping with a fluid operating temperature below -29° C, shall be the minimum fluid operating temperature. In addition, design shall be suitable for design pressure at 38° C.

### 3.3 Design Pressure

3.3.1 Design pressure shall be the most severe condition of internal or external fluid pressure, subject to conditions of Section 3.1 above.

3.3.2 Minimum positive design pressure shall normally be 175 kPA.

3.3.3 Design pressure for unrelieved piping systems subject to pump discharge pressure, shall be pump differential pressure at shutoff of stalling conditions, plus normal pump suction pressure and hydrostatic head.

3.3.4 Design pressure for piping systems operating under vacuum shall be full vacuum. Exception may be taken where suitable protection against vacuum failure is provided.

3.3.5 For piping systems protected by relief valves, the relief valve set pressure shall be equal to the design pressure minus the hydrostatic head below the relief valve.

### 3.4 Other Conditions

3.4.1 Allowable stress values apply to total loads imposed on piping materials. Design shall provide for all loading significantly affecting pipe material stresses. See sections 301.4 through 301.7 of Refinery Piping Code for loadings in addition to fluid pressure, which may affect piping stresses.

## 4.0 LINE SIZING

### 4.1 General

[Industry Source 06 logo]

Industry Source 06 Doc 5000
Piping Design

4.1.1   Piping shall be sized for normal operating conditions. Provision for future increased capacity shall be made only when specifically required.

4.1.2   Each line shall be sized individually in accordance with good engineering practice and economical service. The following velocity and pressure values shall be used as a guide for line sizing. Consideration shall also be given to length of line, working pressure, availability of pressure drop, vapour pressure of fluid, required pump NPSH and any other considerations of significance. In instances where normal operations requires a large pressure drop between the terminals of line, the line shall be sized to take an appreciable amount of the drop rather than through a valve.

**4.2 Velocities**

Velocities in lines shall not exceed the following:

4.2.1

Light hydrocarbons and water:

Pump discharge    1.5 - 2.5 m/s    (5-8 fps)
Pump suction      0.9 m/s          (3 fps)
Gravity flow      0.76 m/s         (2.5 fps)

4.2.2

Gases:

100 psig              18-24 m/s    (60-80 fps)
200 psig              15-18 m/s    (50-60 fps)
300 psig              12-15 m/s    (40-50 fps)
500 psig              9-12 m/s     (30-40 fps)
1000 psig             3-6 m/s      (10-20 fps)
Compressor suction    15 m/s       (50 fps)
Compressor discharge  18 m/s       (60 fps)

4.2.3

Steam:

0 - 30 psig (saturated)            30 m/s    (100 fps)
30 - 150 psig (saturated or superheated)  50 m/s    (167 fps)
150 psig and up (superheated)       75 m/s    (250 fps)

In corrosive service line velocities shall be reduced to 80% or less of the maximum.

## 4.3 Pressure Drop Requirements

4.3.1 Pressure drop shall not exceed the following for Pump Suction and Discharge Lines:

> **Table - Pump Suction and Discharge pressure drop limits** - see [XLSX](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-03/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-03_p0005_tbl01_pump-suction-discharge-pressure-drop.xlsx) and [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-03/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-03_p0005_tbl01_pump-suction-discharge-pressure-drop.png)

| | **Pump Suction** | **Pump Discharge** |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| Water, amine, caustic and hydrocarbon liquids more than 28°C below boiling point. | 11.3 kPA/100m (0.5 psi/100') | 22.6 kPA/100m (1 psi/100') |
| Water, amine, caustic and hydrocarbon liquids less than 28°C below boiling point. | 2.26 kPA/100m (0.1 psi/100') | 22.6 kPA/100m (1 psi/100') |

NPSH considerations shall govern selection of pipe size on pump suctions; however, pressure drop shall not exceed maximum set out above. On plunger pumps size shall also account for acceleration head loss.

4.3.2 For reboiler vapour and liquid gas individual attention shall be given to each case considering the hydraulics for the system and operating levels resulting from the design pressure drops.

4.3.3 Size of compressor suction and discharge piping shall be determined in accordance with compressor manufacturer's recommendation. Pressure drops shall not exceed the following:

> **Table - Suction and Discharge Piping and Headers pressure drop limits** - see [XLSX](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-03/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-03_p0005_tbl02_suction-discharge-piping-headers-pressur.xlsx) and [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-03/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-03_p0005_tbl02_suction-discharge-piping-headers-pressur.png)

**Suction and Discharge Piping**

| | **kPA/100m** | **(PSI/100')** |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| 10 psig and under | 2.8 | 0.125 |
| 11 to 50 psig | 5.7 | 0.25 |
| over 50 psig | 22.6 | 1.0 |

**Headers**

| | **kPA/100m** | **(PSI/100')** |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| 75 psig and under | 11.3 | 0.5 |
| over 75 psig | 22.6 | 1.0 |

4.3.4 Piping in flare systems shall be adequately sized to prevent over pressuring of equipment in case of an operational failure. Flare header shall be designed for largest vapour load caused by a single failure or full ESD blowdown capacity - greater shall apply.

4.3.5 For other lines, pressure drops shall not exceed the following:

| | **kPA/100m** | **(PSI/100')** |
| :--- | :---: | :---: |
| Steam - above 50 psig | 22.6 kPA/100m | (1.0 psi/100') |
| - below 50 psig | 11.3 kPA/100m | (0.5 psi/100') |
| Flashing steam condensate return | 11.3 kPA/100m | (0.5 psi/100') |
| Cooling water | 22.6 kPA/100m | (1.0 psi/100') |
| Hydrocarbon vapours | 11.3 kPA/100m | (0.5 psi/100') |
| Hydrocarbon liquids | 22.6 kPA/100m | (1.0 psi/100') |
| Hot oil and condenser effluents | 45.2 kPA/100m | (2.0 psi/100') |

### 4.4 Other Limitations

4.4.1 NPS 3/8, 1-1/4, 2-1/2, 3-1/2, 5, and 7 pipe sizes shall not be used, except where required to connect to equipment. Conversion to standard piping shall be as near the equipment as possible.

4.4.2 Minimum pipe size run shall be NPS 3/4, except for connections to equipment or instrument services.

4.4.3 In pipeway runs the minimum size for process and utility piping shall be NPS 2 or as otherwise governed by length of span.

4.4.4 All piping size NPS 2 and larger shall be flanged/butt-welded unless otherwise specified.

4.4.5 In threaded piping, swage nipples shall be used for change in pipe size. Bushings are not permitted.

## 5.0 EQUIPMENT PIPING

### 5.1 Compressor Piping

5.1.1 Large centrifugal compressors may be elevated sufficiently for piping and auxiliaries to be located below main operating platforms. Smaller compressors shall be grade mounted with piping and auxiliaries arranged for convenient access and maintenance.

5.1.2 Particular consideration shall be given to design of piping subject to vibration from dynamic loading associated with reciprocating compressors. Volume bottles shall be provided as required at the suctions and discharges. Suction and discharge lines shall be securely clamped. Small piping around compressors and on the same supports as suction and discharge lines shall be well braced to reduce vibration. Reciprocating compressor suction and discharge piping shall be run on substantial supports near grade if at all possible.

5.1.3 The piping drawings shall show the limits of compressor suction piping where special internal cleaning is required. Temporary screens or strainers shall be provided.

5.1.4 Removable spool pieces shall be provided at compressors where needed to permit maintenance without major piping disassembly.

## 6.0 PRESSURE RELIEF SYSTEMS

### 6.1 General

6.1.1 A schedule showing the location, type, marking size, flange rating, orifice identification, area and setting pressure of all pressure relief devices on each unit shall be supplied to Owner. This shall also include the type of fluid, gravity or molecular weight, maximum operating inlet pressure and temperature and relieving capacity as well as the presence of any corrosive agent.

6.1.2 Consideration shall be given to providing pressure relief devices between block valves where thermal expansion due to ambient temperature changes or steam tracing may cause damage.

[Industry Source 06 logo]

6.1.3  A pressure relief device shall be placed on the low-pressure side of pressure reducing valves where the piping and/or equipment in the low-pressure side are not suitable for the conditions which exist on the high-pressure side.

6.1.4  Compliance with Owner's General Specification GS 4.0 Instrumentation is required.

## 6.2 Piping

6.2.1  The size of the inlet line shall not be less than the size of the relief valve inlet. The size of the outlet line shall not be less than the size of the relief valve outlet.

6.2.2  The length of the inlet piping shall be kept to a minimum.

6.2.3  At maximum flow, the pressure drop due to entrance losses and pipe friction shall not exceed three percent of the set pressure of any valve.

## 6.3 Discharge to Atmosphere

6.3.1  A pressure relief valve discharging vapours to atmosphere shall be provided with outlet piping as follows:

6.3.1.1  For hydrocarbons, shall be vented a minimum of two metres above building peak. Regardless of height or conditions the riser shall be at least 15 m horizontally from any furnace.

6.3.1.2  For steam, to atmosphere at a safe location.

6.3.1.3  A pressure relief valve in liquid service and discharging to atmosphere shall do so at a visible safe place.

## 6.4 Piping to Closed System

6.4.1  Any pressure relief valve discharging to a closed system shall be installed so that the discharge piping slopes into the header.

6.4.2  Blowdown headers shall be installed so that the piping slopes into the blowdown drum. Where this is not practical, the low points in the header shall be traced and insulated, and a NPS 3/4 valved drain tie shall be provided.

6.4.3  The bonnet vent of a relief valve with bellows shall be piped to the discharge line.

## 6.5 Block Valves

6.5.1  Where a block valve is installed to permit removal of a relief valve during unit operation it shall be located immediately below the relief valve, and be car-sealed open.

6.5.2  Where a pressure relief valve discharges into a header and an outlet block valve is installed, this valve shall be car-sealed open.

6.5.3  Car-sealed open valves shall be numbered on the engineering flow plans and a list of numbers and locations shall be supplied to Owner.

6.5.4  Block valves at relief valves and in blowdown lines shall be positioned so that the block valve remains open if any component of the valve accidentally fails.

6.5.5  Any block valve in the relief path shall have a full port and shall have a clear path from inlet to

outlet (i.e. ball or gate). It shall have a means of readily identifying valve position (i.e. handle, position indicators, etc.).

6.5.6 An NPS 3/4 bleeder valve shall be provided between any block and pressure relief valve.

6.5.7 The size of the inlet valve shall not be less than the size of the relief valve inlet. The size of the outlet valve shall not be less than the size of the relief valve outlet.

**6.6 Location**

6.6.1 Relief valves may be located on the piping instead of on the equipment and shall be located at the lowest possible elevation that may be economically justified.

## 7.0 FLEXIBILITY

### 7.1 General

Piping shall be designed with sufficient flexibility to absorb stress due to the following:

7.1.1 Line expansion or contraction as a result of operating or ambient conditions.

7.1.2 Expansion or contraction of connected equipment.

7.1.3 Settlement of equipment or tankage.

### 7.2 Design

7.2.1 Stresses due to thermal expansion or contraction shall be analyzed by the methods in ANSI B31.3 or ANSI B31.1 as applicable.

7.2.2 Piping shall normally be laid out to provide sufficient flexibility without the use of expansion loops or joints.

7.2.3 Anchors and guides shall be provided where necessary to minimize the movement of lines across supports.

### 7.3 Provision for Expansion

Where the layout does not provide sufficient flexibility the following may be used:

7.3.1 Expansion loops with guides and anchors.

7.3.2 Cold springing.

7.3.3 Expansion joints with guides and anchors, when approved by Owner.

7.3.4 Spring loaded supports or hangers where rigid supports restrict line movement or cause over stressing of the line.

## 8.0 PIPE SUPPORTS

### 8.1 Design

8.1.1 Supports shall normally be designed to transmit all piping loads directly to foundations.

8.1.2 Loadings to be considered in design calculations include:

- Weight of pipe and insulation
- Weight of the line contents based on water
- Wind loading
- Lateral loading due to movement of lines on supports, guides and anchors
- Vibrations due to pulsations from reciprocating pumps, compressors and possible line surges.

8.1.3 The material for pipe supports shall be structural steel or reinforced concrete, unless otherwise approved in writing by Owner.

## 8.2 Requirements

8.2.1 Supports shall be located so that the force transmitted to connections on machinery such as pumps, compressors, turbines, etc. does not exceed that allowed by the machinery manufacturer. The design of such supports shall be detailed and not left for field improvisation.

8.2.2 Supports shall be located to minimize the load transmitted to connections of equipment such as vessels, exchangers, etc.

8.2.3 Piping to equipment requiring removal for maintenance, including control valve assemblies shall be supported so that temporary supports are not required during removal.

## 8.3 Shoes and Guides

8.3.1 Shoes shall be installed on insulated pipe at supports.

8.3.2 Non-insulated lines shall rest directly on the supports but shoes shall be provided on lines subject to excessive or continuous movement.

8.3.3 Guides shall be installed on supports to restrict lateral movement.

## 8.4 Spring Supports and Hangers

8.4.1 Spring supports may be either variable or constant load type provided that overstressing of line or nozzles is not produced.

8.4.2 Variable sprint hangers and supports shall be provided with a scale showing the range of working load and a means of adjustment.

8.4.3 Constant support spring hangers shall be provided with the calibrated load clearly indicated, a scale showing the range of movement and an accurate means of adjustment.

8.4.4 All spring supports and support shall be adjusted in the field outer unit start-up and in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions.

# 9.0 PIPING FOR INSTRUMENTS

9.1 Unless otherwise approved by Owner, control valves shall be located high enough to permit valve stem removal, but not higher than 900 mm above grade or a platform.

9.2 Where vaporization occurs in control valves, they shall be placed as close as practical to the

destination of the stream.

9.3 Control valve by-pass piping shall provide sufficient clearance for the removal of the control valve from the loop.

9.4 All control valves shall be provided with block, and by-pass valves rated for the same design pressure as the upstream piping.

9.5 By-pass valves shall be designed for a capacity at least equal to the capacity of the control valve.

9.6 Flanged end reducers or spools shall be used between flanged control valves and block valves. The length of the reducers or spools shall be sufficient to permit removal of bolts, and the installation of drain or vent connections.

9.7 Valved NPS 1 drains shall be provided upstream of control valves.

9.8 All control valves in socket weld piping shall be flanged.

9.9 The only devices which may be mounted on control valves shall be valve positioners, volume boosters, lock-up relays and pressure controllers. These devices shall be installed so as to be easily accessible for servicing. The devices shall not be so mounted when vibration may cause malfunction.

9.10 Orifice flanges shall be located adjacent to walkways, platforms, or structures and shall be installed in horizontal pipe runs, wherever possible. Orifice flanges shall have socket weld taps except where screwed connections are specifically permitted in Owner's Specification GS 2.3 Line Class Detail.

9.11 Instrument air distribution headers shall be NPS 2 minimum. A block valve shall be provided for each take-off connection from these headers.

9.12 All gauge glasses and instruments in process services shall be provided with NPS 1/2 minimum drain connections, piped to their respective closed drain systems. They shall be supplied complete with isolation valves in addition to the gauge cocks.

## 10.0 THERMAL TRACING

10.1 All equipment, piping and instrumentation which may be subject to freezing shall be heat traced per Owner's General Specification Industry Source 06 Doc 5005 Winterization.

## 11.0 SAMPLE CONNECTIONS

### 11.1 Requirements

**11.1.1** When specified, double valved sample connections (using a NPS 3/4 main block valve and a NPS 1/2 bar stock needle valve for regulation) shall be provided as required to permit full evaluation without disconnecting piping or instruments during plant performance tests. Every line containing a process flow meter shall be provided with a sample connection. Liquid sample connections shall be taken off the side of the pipe.

## 12.0 SOUR SERVICE REQUIREMENTS

Piping in sour service shall be designed per Owner's General Specification Sour Service, Industry Source 06 Doc 5001 Piping Material Service Index and Industry Source 06 Doc 5002 Piping Material Line Class Detail. Design for critical sour service is outside the scope of this specification.

### 12.1 Threaded Piping and Instrument Connections

**12.2.1** Threaded connections shall be classified according to the following definitions, and use of threaded connections shall comply with Table 12-2:

- (a) Primary threaded connections are connections made directly to a process stream, without capability for isolation from the process by means of upstream flanged, socket welded, or socket welded by screwed block valves connected directly to the process by welds, flanges, or welded fittings.

- (b) Secondary threaded connections are connections with capability for isolation from the process by means of upstream flanged, socket welded, or socket welded by screwed block valves connected directly to the process by welds, flanges, or welded fittings.

**12.2.2** When threaded connections are used for sour service, the following conditions apply:

- (a) Pipe diameter shall be less than NPS 2.

- (b) Pipe thickness shall be Schedule 80 minimum.

- (c) Threading shall be only be accomplished by a cutting operation. Rolled threads shall not be used without the written concurrence of the Owner engineer. If rolled threads are considered, a suitable heat treatment shall be applied after thread rolling, so that the microhardness at all thread roots is below 248 HV₁₀₀. Microhardness test data shall be supplied to support any request for use of rolled threads.

- (d) Connections shall be located away from areas where liquid water may accumulate.

- (e) Requirements of applicable codes, standards and specifications shall be satisfied.

# PURPOSE AND USE OF Industry Source 07

In an effort to minimize the cost of process industry facilities, this Practice has been prepared from the technical requirements in the existing standards of major industrial users, contractors, or standards organizations. By harmonizing these technical requirements into a single set of Practices, administrative, application, and engineering costs to both the purchaser and the manufacturer should be reduced. While this Practice is expected to incorporate the majority of requirements of most users, individual applications may involve requirements that will be appended to and take precedence over this Practice. Determinations concerning fitness for purpose and particular matters or application of the Practice to particular project or engineering situations should not be made solely on information contained in these materials. The use of trade names from time to time should not be viewed as an expression of preference but rather recognized as normal usage in the trade. Other brands having the same specifications are equally correct and may be substituted for those named. All Practices or guidelines are intended to be consistent with applicable laws and regulations including OSHA requirements. To the extent these Practices or guidelines should conflict with OSHA or other applicable laws or regulations, such laws or regulations must be followed. Consult an appropriate professional before applying or acting on any material contained in or suggested by the Practice.

This Practice is subject to revision at any time.

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Purpose

This Practice provides requirements for designing metallic piping systems to *ASME B31.3, Process Piping* (hereinafter referred to as the *Code*).

### 1.2 Scope

This Practice provides requirements for piping systems arrangement, design conditions, components, and joints. This Practice shall be used in conjunction with the *Code*.

The requirements of this Practice are more stringent than the *Code* for the purpose of standardization and not because the *Code* is considered unsafe.

Piping systems designed in accordance with other piping codes are not included in this Practice.

## 2. References

Applicable parts of the following Practices, industry codes and standards, and references shall be considered an integral part of this Practice. The edition in effect on the date of contract award shall be used, except as otherwise noted. Short titles will be used herein where appropriate.
