# 3. Requirements

## 3.1 General

3.1.1 Piping systems shall be in accordance with this Practice and with all applicable federal, state, and local laws.

3.1.2 New piping systems within the scope of this Practice shall be in accordance with the *Code*.

3.1.3 Alterations to existing piping systems shall be in accordance with *API 570*. Changes in service or in design conditions shall be considered alterations.

3.1.4 Items that are normally fabricated from piping components (e.g., strainers and devices that serve such purposes as mixing, separating, snubbing, distributing, and metering or controlling flow), if identified by the owner as specialty piping (SP) items, shall be designed in accordance with this Practice unless otherwise specified by the owner. Piping components such as pulsation dampeners, surge bottles, condensate collection pots, and like components may be furnished as piping, as permitted by ASME Section VIII, U-1.

3.1.5 Design of piping at machinery shall be in accordance with *Industry Source 07 REH686* and *NEMA SM-23*, as applicable.

3.1.6 All piping shall be identified by the owner as Category D, Category M, high pressure, or normal fluid services as defined in the *Code*. "Severe cyclic conditions" in accordance with the *Code* shall also be identified by the owner.

## 3.2 Design Conditions

3.2.1 The internal and external design pressure and temperature of piping shall be determined by considering the following conditions:

a. Normal operations

b. Start-up operations, including any start-up procedure, operation, routing, etc.

c. Shutdown operations, including shutdown procedures, operations, pumpout, etc.

d. Switching operations, including any cyclic regeneration, spare pump switching, coke drum switching, etc.

e. Regeneration procedures

f. Equipment bypassing

g. Turndown operations

h. Pump shutoff (deadhead) pressure

i. Any control valve in a fully opened or closed position

j. Any block valve in a fully opened or closed position, except for locked or car-sealed valves

k. Blocked exits

l. Equipment trip or shutdown

m. Upset conditions

n. Maintenance, repair, or neutralization procedures

o. On-stream or purging operations

p. Steamout or purging operations

q. Solar temperature effects

r. Heat-tracing effects

3.2.2 The design minimum temperature shall be determined by considering the following:

a. Normal conditions

b. Expected autorefrigeration effects, including emergency depressurizing.

*Comment:* The design minimum temperature shall be the coincidental temperature where the pressure reaches 25% of the design pressure.

c. One-day-mean low temperature in accordance with *API 650*, Figure 4.2

## 3.3 Design Practices

### 3.3.1 Basic Layout

Piping layout shall be in accordance with *Industry Source 07 Doc 00003*.

### 3.3.2 Piping

#### 3.3.2.1. Underground Piping

1. Except for the following services, piping should be located above grade:

   a. Firewater supply systems

   b. Cased road and tank dike crossings

   c. Lines in concrete trenches

   d. Oil-free compressed air lines

   e. Lines with secondary containment and a leak-detection method

   f. Other lines as designated by the owner

2. All below-grade piping, including piping in trenches, shall be protected from external corrosion.

3. Buried steel piping in hazardous materials service shall be externally coated and cathodically protected.

4. The minimum cover over buried process piping shall be 18 inches (46 cm) in paved or unpaved areas and 30 inches (76 cm) under paved roads except under a reinforced concrete slab or other protective cover approved by the owner.

5. Sewers may be covered by this Practice if specified by the owner.

#### 3.3.2.2 Block Valve Bypasses

1. If required, a block valve bypass shall be shown on the applicable Piping & Instrument Diagrams (P&ID).

2. Bypasses shall be integral with the valve or installed in the piping immediately adjacent to the valve.

### 3.3.2.3 Dead Legs

1. A dead leg is a pipe section connected to a flowing stream where the pipe section is not self-draining and is not normally flowing.
2. Piping layouts in all services shall be designed to eliminate the presence of dead legs.
3. If dead legs cannot be avoided, either corrosion resistant materials or an approved coating system shall be used for the dead leg section.
4. Live dummy legs shall not be permitted.

### 3.3.2.4 Vibration

1. In locations where potentially severe vibration can occur, small piping branches (i.e., NPS 2 and smaller) shall be adequately designed to minimize its effects.
2. The following examples are acceptable practices/configurations for minimizing the effects of vibration on small piping branches, depending on the severity of the vibration:
   a. Brace all nipples (with reinforcing pads if required).
   b. Where bracing cannot be effectively provided, install schedule 160 nipples with reinforcing pads.
   c. Use an *API 602* integrally reinforced extended body (IREB) valve.
   d. Brace all configurations that have a nipple between the welding boss and the root valve.

3.3.2.5 Blind flanges shall be used as end closures on flanged ends and valves, unless end caps are clearly required by design necessity.

3.3.2.6 Except for standard spectacle plates and blinds, flanged connections with long-exposed bolts for sandwiched components (e.g., wafer type valves) should not be used in fire hazardous areas unless the bolting is protected by a fire-resistant shield.

### 3.3.2.7 Jackscrews

1. Jackscrews shall be used to facilitate flange separation for maintenance. Joint assemblies that often require frequent separation include orifice plates, spectacle plates, spacers, screens, and dropout spools.
2. Piping layout shall be designed such that flanges can be separated without excessive force.
3. Jackscrews shall be accessible from both sides of the pipe.
4. For orifice flanges, jackscrews shall be installed at three- and nine-o'clock positions.
5. If flange separators are provided, jackscrews shall not be required.

### 3.3.3 Isolation (Block) Valves

3.3.3.1 Block valves shall be provided at vessel and storage tank nozzles as follows:

a. In piping at all nozzles below the maximum operating liquid level of storage tanks

b. In a liquid draw-off line of a vessel containing 10,000 pounds (4,550 kg) or more of a flammable liquid at the maximum operating liquid level if the line does not contain a block valve located within 30 feet (9 m) in a horizontal direction from the vessel

3.3.3.2 Block valves shall be provided for piping crossing the plant limits and operating unit limits as required for the planned operation, isolation, and maintenance of the plant as directed by the owner.

3.3.3.3 If positive isolation is required or cross-contamination cannot be tolerated, one of the following shall be used:

a. Blanks

b. Two block valves with a bleeder valve between them

c. A double-seated valve (e.g., expanding gate or plug, trunnion-mounted ball, through conduit slab gate, etc.) with body bleeder

d. Removable spool

3.3.3.4 Valving of operating vent, drain, and sample connections shall have one block valve as a minimum. Additional block valves shall be provided as specified by owner.

*Comment:* Operating vent, drain, or sample connections are used regularly when the source equipment or piping is in service and/or pressurized.

3.3.3.5 Equipment that may be removed from service during unit operation shall be furnished with single block valves with provisions for blinding or blanking.

#### 3.3.3.6 Small Piping Root Valves

1. For all process services, branches NPS 2 and smaller shall have a root valve located as close as feasible to the run.

2. The root valve shall be no farther than three times the branch diameter (except for insulated lines) measured from the far end of the boss to the near end of the valve.

3. Unions shall not be installed in the pipe section between the main pipe run and the root valve.

3.3.3.7 Flangeless valves shall not be used as the first block valve against storage tanks or vessels containing hydrocarbons or hazardous materials.

3.3.3.8 See *Crane Technical Publication 410* for information on sizing valves.

### 3.3.4 Control Valve Manifolds

3.3.4.1 If specified, control valves shall be installed with a valved bypass and a block valve on each side of the control valve.

3.3.4.2 As a minimum, block and bypass valves shall be provided in the control valve manifolds for the following cases:

a. If loss of control function for a service could adversely affect plant operations as determined by the owner

b. If shutdown of a service cannot be tolerated (e.g., fuel lines to furnaces or boilers, steam reducing stations [main headers], etc.)

c. If the absence of blocks and bypass valves would inhibit start-up efforts for a service as determined by the owner

#### 3.3.4.3 Bleed Valves

1. Bleed valves shall be provided for each control valve manifold.

2. One bleed valve shall be located between the upstream block valve and the control valve.

3. If specified by owner, an additional bleed valve on the downstream side of the control valve shall be provided.

### 3.3.5 Vents, Drains, and Sample Outlets

3.3.5.1 Valved vent and drain connections shall be provided on all equipment that is not self-venting or self-draining. Connections shall be located on equipment, if practical, but may be located in connecting piping if there are no blocks between the vent or drain connections and the equipment.

3.3.5.2 Vent connections shall be provided for trapped high points of piping and shall be in accordance with one of the following configurations:

a. Valved if required for operational purposes or removal of process fluid

b. Plugged (valve omitted) if required for hydrostatic test purposes

3.3.5.3 Drain connections shall be provided for the low points of all lines located above grade and shall be in accordance with one of the following configurations:

a. Valved if required for operational purposes or removal of process fluid

b. Plugged (valve omitted) if required for hydrostatic test purposes

3.3.5.4 Unless otherwise specified, vent, drain, and sample outlet connections shall be NPS 3/4 minimum.

3.3.5.5 For services of fluids with suspended solids or of high viscosity materials, all piping connections shall be NPS 1 minimum.

3.3.5.6 Unless otherwise specified, operating vent and drain connections shall be designed to drain liquid from equipment and piping in 2 hours or less.

*Comment:* Operating vents and drain lines are used regularly when the source equipment or piping is in service and/or pressurized.

3.3.5.7 Hydrocarbon vapors or mixtures of hydrocarbon vapors and other vapors (e.g., steam) may be discharged to the atmosphere contingent on adequate safety and environmental considerations.

3.3.5.8 All vents and drains open to the atmosphere shall be provided with plugs or blind flanges.

3.3.5.9 Cooling shall be considered for sample outlets in piping or equipment operating at 140°F (60°C) or greater. One cooler may be used for multiple sample outlets.

3.3.5.10 Unless otherwise specified, for horizontal piping, sample connections shall be located at the side of the pipe for liquids and at the top of the pipe for gases.

3.3.5.11 If practical, discharge from drains emptying into open hubs (e.g., drain cups or sumps) shall be visible from the location of the drain valve.

3.3.5.12 If releasing controlled materials, operating vents and drain lines shall discharge into a closed system as specified by owner.

## 3.3.6 Check Valves

3.3.6.1 Unless otherwise specified, check valves shall be provided in discharge piping of centrifugal pumps.

3.3.6.2 Check valves shall be used where utility or chemical injection lines are permanently tied into process lines or equipment.

3.3.6.3 A check valve shall not be used as a substitute for a block valve for flow isolation purposes.

3.3.6.4 Check valves in vertical piping shall be installed for upward flow only and shall be installed with a drain connection immediately above the check valve.

3.3.6.5 If a lower pressure rated system flows into a higher pressure rated system, a check valve shall be installed in the lower pressure connection and the higher pressure rating shall extend to include the check valve.

3.3.6.6 If a sudden loss of pressure in a higher pressure system could lead to undesirable contamination from a lower pressure system, a check valve shall be considered for the higher pressure system.

3.3.6.7 Except for check valves in intermittent service or check valves in skid-mounted systems, for piping NPS 3 and greater, a turbulence-free minimum distance of five pipe diameters upstream and two pipe

diameters downstream of every check valve should be maintained. Pipefittings (e.g., elbows, reducers, tees, etc.) or flow-restricting devices (e.g., orifices, control valves, etc.) should not be installed in these zones.

3.3.6.8 See *Crane Technical Publication 410* for information on sizing check valves.

## 3.3.7 Blanks (Blinds)

3.3.7.1 The piping layout shall provide for the insertion of line blanks for flanged equipment isolation for maintenance, inspection, testing, and alternative operation.

3.3.7.2 If piping flexibility and equipment arrangement do not permit the insertion of temporary maintenance blanks at convenient flanging, permanent line blanks shall be provided in accordance with the following:

a. At piping connections at equipment that can be physically entered

b. At plant limits in process, utility, and auxiliary (e.g., fuel oil, fuel gas) piping connected to other piping outside plant limits that can be in use during shutdown of the plant

3.3.7.3 Figure-8 type blinds shall not be greater than 100 pounds (45 kg) or NPS 12. Figure-8 type blinds within these limits are shown in Table 1:

> **Table - Table 1 – Maximum Figure-8 Blind Sizes** - see [XLSX](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-04/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-04_p0011_tbl01_table-1-maximum-figure-8-blind-sizes.xlsx) and [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-04/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-04_p0011_tbl01_table-1-maximum-figure-8-blind-sizes.png)

| Class | Max. Figure-8 Size (NPS) |
| :--- | :---: |
| 150 and 300 | 12 |
| 600 and 900 | 8 |
| 1500 and 2500 | 6 |

3.3.7.4 Circular blanks or spacers shall be provided for blind sizes greater than the limits of Section 3.3.7.3.

3.3.7.5 Circular blanks or spacers shall be used in place of figure-8 type blinds for cold-insulated piping less than 70°F (21°C).

3.3.7.6 Commercially available blinding systems in accordance with the *Code* shall be permitted.

3.3.7.7 See *ASME B16.48* for guidance for the use of blanks in piping systems.

## 3.3.8 Strainers and Filters

3.3.8.1 If strainers are not furnished as part of the equipment, strainers in the piping shall be considered for the protection of the following equipment:

a. Mechanical equipment in accordance with *Industry Source 07 REIE686*

b. Steam traps and steam jet ejectors in steam inlet lines

c. Burners in main fuel oil supply piping

d. Upstream of low noise design control valves

3.3.8.2 If filters are not furnished as part of the equipment, filters shall be provided in the piping for the protection of the following equipment:

a. Air supply piping for Industry Source 07 Doc umatically actuated equipment

b. Air piping upstream of air dryers

c. Open-air intakes for blowers, compressors, or engines

3.3.8.3 Providing permanent strainers with plugged connections for the installation of differential pressure measurement across the strainer shall be considered.

3.3.8.4 Installation of spacer rings may be required after temporary strainers are removed.

## 3.3.9 Utility Piping Connections to Process Equipment

3.3.9.1 Firewater systems shall not be connected to process equipment except by using a temporary connection when the equipment is not in operation and not under pressure.

3.3.9.2 Except for air or steam, permanent connections shall not be made to process equipment operating above 212°F (100°C).

3.3.9.3 Water or steam shall not be permanently connected to equipment that operates below 32°F (0°C).

3.3.9.4 Permanent connections without a break tank shall not be made except if the required service is continuous or frequent (at least twice per week) or is needed for emergencies.

3.3.9.5 If air is injected as a reaction agent, all of the following shall be required:

a. The hydrocarbon/air mixtures shall not be permitted to enter the flammable range unless otherwise required by the process

b. Instrumentation shall be provided to shut off the airflow if the process flow fails

c. A restriction orifice shall be provided

3.3.9.6 For all components of permanent connections, the pressure/temperature rating shall be suitable for either the process or the utility service, whichever is more severe.

3.3.9.7 For temporary connections, the pressure/temperature rating of the process side shall extend to the hose or breakaway spool.

3.3.9.8 If the process fluid requires internal lining or material other than that used in the utility system, the lining or the material shall extend from and include the check valve on the process side.

3.3.9.9 Valves with bodies of gray cast iron, ductile iron, or low melting point alloys (e.g., brass or bronze) shall not be used in a permanent connection including the utility side.

3.3.9.10 The material selection of the valve bodies and trim in a permanent connection shall be suitable for both the process and the utility fluid.

3.3.9.11 Operator access shall be provided to the block valves on either side and to the blind or breakaway spool of the connection.

3.3.9.12 Chain-operated valves shall not be permitted.

## 3.4 Hot Tapping

Hot tapping shall be in accordance with *API 2201* and *OSHA 29 CFR 1910.147*.

## 3.5 Piping Components

### 3.5.1 General

3.5.1.1 Recommended piping components are shown in the Industry Source 07 Piping Material Specifications. Other piping components and constructions that are in accordance with the *Code*, although not mentioned in the Industry Source 07 Piping Material Specifications are permitted.

3.5.1.2 Minimum pipe size shall be NPS 3/4, except for the following applications:

- a. Category D fluid service
- b. Individual instrument leads
- c. Pump and compressor auxiliary piping
- d. Steam tracing
- e. Reduction at instruments or other equipment provided with smaller than NPS 3/4 connections

3.5.1.3 Pipe sizes NPS 1-1/4, NPS 2-1/2, NPS 3-1/2, and NPS 5 shall not be used, except for connections to equipment requiring these sizes and in jacketed pipe systems. In such cases, the transition to standard sizes shall be made as soon as practical.

3.5.1.4 Pipe sizes and schedules shown in the Industry Source 07 Piping Material Specifications are in accordance with *ASME B36.10M* and *ASME B36.19M*.

### 3.5.2 Pipe

3.5.2.1 Nominal wall thickness for carbon and low-alloy steel piping joined by welding in new construction shall be, as a minimum, in accordance with the following requirements:

- a. Utility (Category D) fluid services
  - (1) For NPS 1/2 – 2: Not normally welded
  - (2) For NPS 3 – 6: Standard

- (3) For NPS 8 – 32: 0.250 inch (6.4 mm)
- (4) For NPS 34 and greater: Diameter/135

    b. Normal and Category M fluid services

    - (1) For NPS 1/2 – 1-1/2: Extra strong
    - (2) For NPS 2 – 6: Standard
    - (3) For NPS 8 – 32: 0.250 inch (6.4 mm)
    - (4) For NPS 34 and greater: Diameter/135

3.5.2.2 Nominal wall thickness for nonferrous alloy and stainless steel (> 13% Cr) piping joined by welding in new construction shall be, as a minimum, in accordance with the following requirements:

    a. For NPS 1/2 – 3/4: Schedule 40S
    b. For NPS 1 and greater: Schedule 10S

## 3.5.3 Joints and Fittings

3.5.3.1 Unless otherwise specified, piping joints shall be of welded construction. Flanges, unions, and threaded connections shall be used minimally, except in Category D fluid services.

3.5.3.2 Butt-welded fittings shall be used for pipe greater than NPS 1-1/2, except as required at equipment or control valve connections.

3.5.3.3 Butt-welded or socket-welded fittings shall be used for pipe sizes not covered in Section 3.5.3.2, except as follows:

    a. Threaded fittings may be used downstream of a welded or flanged block valve to instruments, at equipment connections, and for terminal vent and drain connections.
    b. Threaded fittings may be used for Category D fluid services.

3.5.3.4 Socket-welded and threaded constructions should be avoided in services if corrosion is accelerated in crevices.

3.5.3.5 For lube oil and seal oil lines, only butt-welded or flanged joints shall be used between filters and equipment in accordance with *API 614*.

3.5.3.6 Butt-welded piping systems shall have long radius elbows. Short radius elbows may be used only if required because of space limitations.

3.5.3.7 Flush bushings, close nipples, locknuts, street elbows, and street tees shall not be permitted.

## 3.5.4 Branch Connections

3.5.4.1 Unless otherwise specified, branch connections shall be at a 90-degree intersection to the run pipe centerline.

3.5.4.2 Unless otherwise approved by the owner, a welded branch connection shall not be designed with an intersecting angle of less than 45 degrees.

### 3.5.4.3 NPS 2 and Less

1. If the branch is the same size as the header, a straight tee shall be used.

2. For headers NPS 2 and less, one of the following configurations shall be used if the branch size is less than the header size:

   a. Reducing tees

   b. Straight tee with butt-welding reducer

   c. Swage nipple

3. For headers NPS 3 and greater, branch connections shall be provided with integrally reinforced branch connection fittings.

4. Integrally reinforced extended body (IREB) valves in accordance with *API 602* may be used for valved piping connections (e.g., pressure gauges, vents, and drains).

### 3.5.4.4 NPS 3 and Greater

1. Branch connections shall be of all welded construction (e.g., unreinforced fabricated tees, reinforced fabricated tees, reducing tees, and forged integrally reinforced welded fittings).

2. If the branch is the same size as the header, a straight tee shall be used.

3. Branch connections for piping at reciprocating equipment shall be welding tees or forged integrally reinforced weld fittings.

### 3.5.4.5 Weep Holes

1. Weep holes of 1/4-inch (6-mm) diameter shall be provided in reinforcing pads for branch connections, in wear pads, and in support reinforcing pads if the pads cover welds that are not pipe manufacturing seam welds.

2. Weep holes shall also be provided to vent gases on piping that requires heat treatment after fabrication, or in special cases where hydrogen buildup could occur.

3. Weep holes shall be packed with heavy grease.

3.5.4.6 Branch tables in the Industry Source 07 Piping Material Specifications provide reinforcing pads designed for full area replacement.

3.5.4.7 Branch tables in the Industry Source 07 Piping Material Specifications are minimum requirements. Other equal or better configurations may be selected to suit a particular project need.

### 3.5.5 Valves

#### 3.5.5.1 General

1. Ball, butterfly, and plug valves shall have gear operators in accordance with the Industry Source 07 Piping Material Specifications.
2. Block valves and bypass valves at control valve manifolds, equipment, and pressure-reducing stations shall be of the higher pressure rating.
3. For soft-seated valves, pressure-temperature ratings for the same class valve may vary between manufacturers and may be lower than the ratings shown in Industry Source 07 Piping Material Specifications.
4. Screwed bonnet and screwed body valves shall not be used in any hydrocarbon or hazardous material services unless the bonnets/bodies are seal-welded.
5. Union bonnet valves shall not be used in any hydrocarbon or hazardous material services.

#### 3.5.5.2 Gate Valves

Gear operators are recommended for wedge gate valves for the pressure ratings and sizes shown in Table 2.

> **Table - Table 2 – Gear Operator Applications for Gate Valves** - see [XLSX](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-04/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-04_p0016_tbl01_gear-operator-applications-gate-valves.xlsx) and [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-04/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-04_p0016_tbl01_gear-operator-applications-gate-valves.png)

#### 3.5.5.3 Check Valves

1. Dual- and single-plate wafer check and swing check valves shall not be used in reciprocating pump and compressor suction and discharge services or similar pulsating services.
2. In parallel pump or compressor systems, check valves installed at the discharge of pumps or compressors should be of a nonslam internal-spring-assisted type. Swing check valves should not be used in this service.
3. For parallel pump systems with individual pump discharge piping of NPS 20 and greater, a hydraulic analysis shall be conducted to verify that the selected check valves have the correct dynamic response to prevent slamming and limit pressure surge to an acceptable level. The analysis shall include consideration of the "worst case" operating mode scenario.

## 3.5.6 Flanges

3.5.6.1 Flanges NPS 24 and less shall be in accordance with *ASME B16.5* for the listed materials.

3.5.6.2 Unless otherwise specified, steel flanges larger than NPS 24 shall be in accordance with *ASME B16.47*, Series B.

3.5.6.3 The use of flanges in piping shall be minimized. Flanges shall be typically used in the following applications:

a. At flanged equipment

b. At valves

c. At blanks

d. In removable sections of pipe

e. Where frequent dismantling of piping is required

f. Where piping lined with nonmetals or nonmetallic piping cannot be bonded or otherwise joined

g. To provide for erection requirements

h. To allow for modifications in areas where welding is not permitted

i. To provide clearance for dismantling of equipment (e.g., compressors, reactor heads, etc.)

j. For maintenance cleaning, decoking, or slurry service

3.5.6.4 Slip-on flanges may be used in piping NPS 24 maximum for Classes 300 and less at design temperatures 800°F (430°C) or less.

3.5.6.5 Lap joint flanges may be used in piping for Classes 300 and less at design temperatures 500°F (260°C) and less.

3.5.6.6 Except for proprietary flanges, flange facing shall normally be raised-face for Classes 150 through 2500.

3.5.6.7 Flat-faced flanges with full-faced gaskets shall be used for connecting piping to flat-faced flanged valves and equipment manufactured from nonductive materials.

3.5.6.8 Flange facing finish for cast iron, ductile iron, and bronze shall be in accordance with *MSS SP-6*.

3.5.6.9 Flange facing finish for steel, nickel alloy, and other alloys shall be in accordance with *ASME B16.5*.

3.5.6.10 Orifice flanges shall be in accordance with *ASME B16.36*.

3.5.6.11 Blind flanges shall not be drilled for connections (e.g., drain, vent) unless a stress calculation in accordance with *ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code*, Section VIII, Appendix 2, shows that the flanges shall not be overstressed.

3.5.6.12 For pipe of minimum wall thickness, the bore of welding neck flanges shall not be greater than the inside diameter of the attached pipe, and shall be in accordance with *ASME B16.25* tolerances.

3.5.6.13 Except as stated in Section 3.5.6.14, the design thickness of the flange hub at the welding end of flanges with a specified minimum yield strength (SMYS) less than that of the attached pipe shall be at a minimum equal to the pipe wall thickness multiplied by the pipe-to-flange ratio of the SMYS if the SMYS ratio is from 1.0 to 1.5. See *ASME B16.5*, Figure 14.

3.5.6.14 The bore of welding neck flanges of the lower SMYS may be equal to the inside diameter of the attached pipe of the higher SMYS, if calculations in accordance with *ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code*, Section VIII, Appendix 2, show that the flanged joint shall not be overstressed.

### 3.5.7 Gaskets

Gasket selection shall be in accordance with the individual Industry Source 07 Piping Material Specification.

### 3.5.8 Bolting

Bolting selection shall be in accordance with the individual Industry Source 07 Piping Material Specification.

## 3.6 Piping Flexibility

Piping flexibility analyses shall be in accordance with *Industry Source 07 Doc 00004*.

## 3.7 Piping Support

Piping supports shall be in accordance with *Industry Source 07 Doc 00001*.

## 3.8 Specific Piping Systems

### 3.8.1 Instrument Air

3.8.1.1 Instrument air systems shall be in accordance with *Industry Source 07 PCCIA001*.

3.8.1.2 Instrument air branch lines shall be taken from the top of the header.

3.8.1.3 Block valves shall be provided for branch connections less than NPS 2 and shall be located at the header.

3.8.1.4 The main instrument air header size should be NPS 1-1/2, as a minimum.

3.8.1.5 The instrument air supply to an individual user should be NPS 1/2, as a minimum.

### 3.8.2 Plant Air

3.8.2.1 Plant air branch lines shall be taken from the top of the header.

3.8.2.2 Block valves shall be provided for branch connections less than NPS 2 and shall be located both at the header and at the equipment.

### 3.8.3 Cooling Water

3.8.3.1 Block valves for every branch from cooling water supply and return headers shall be located either at the header or at the equipment being served.

3.8.3.2 Block valves shall not be provided in return lines operating at or below atmospheric pressure unless needed for equipment or system isolation.

3.8.3.3 If heat exchangers are provided with process isolation valves for inspection and cleaning during plant operation, block valves shall be provided in the cooling water inlet and outlet piping. In freezing climates, an antifreeze bypass from the inlet to the outlet or other means to prevent freezing shall be provided.

3.8.3.4 All aboveground cooling water supply and return branch lines shall be connected to the top of the headers.

### 3.8.4 Utility Water

3.8.4.1 Utility water branch lines shall be taken from the top of the header.

3.8.4.2 Block valves shall be provided for branch connections less than NPS 2 and shall be located both at the header and at the equipment.

### 3.8.5 Potable Water

3.8.5.1 Potable water shall not be connected to any other system unless isolated in accordance with state and local requirements.

3.8.5.2 Connections to the potable water system shall be in accordance with applicable ordinances and approved by the owner.

### 3.8.6 Steam and Steam Condensate Removal

#### 3.8.6.1 Steam Headers

1. Steam headers shall run level or shall pitch downward in the direction of steam flow.

2. A vertical rise required in the direction of steam flow shall be designed with a vertical leg equipped with a drip leg at the low point.

### 3.8.6.2 Steam Branch Lines

1. Steam branch lines shall be connected to the top of the headers.

2. Branch lines shall run level or pitch downward in the direction of the steam flow.

3. A vertical rise required in the direction of steam flow, downstream of the connection to the steam header, shall be designed with a vertical leg equipped with a drip leg at the low point.

4. Block valves shall be provided in the branch lines from the steam headers located at and above the elevation of the steam header and installed in such a manner that no pocket is formed where condensate may collect.

3.8.6.3 Steam tracing shall be in accordance with *Industry Source 07 Doc 0035*.

3.8.6.4 Steam traps discharging into the atmosphere shall be provided with upstream block valves.

3.8.6.5 Steam traps discharging to a condensate collection system shall be provided with both upstream and downstream block valves.

3.8.6.6 Condensate from vacuum steam systems shall be re-evaporated into the system by means of a condensate flash pot or removed by eductors, pumping traps, or other suitable means.

3.8.6.7 All steam traps shall be provided with an internal strainer or a strainer located upstream of the trap. The strainer shall be equipped with a blowdown valve piped to a safe location.

3.8.6.8 A steam separator or other means of condensate removal (e.g., pumping trap) shall be provided in the steam piping to each group of steam turbines operating on saturated steam and also to each group of steam-driven reciprocating compressors and other water-sensitive equipment.

3.8.6.9 A minimum of one steam trap shall be provided for each steam separator, header drip leg, branch drip leg, and low point where condensate may collect.

3.8.6.10 Each steam trap shall be sized and specified to operate at all anticipated pressures and condensate loads for the installed location.

3.8.6.11 Steam traps shall be sized and specified to discharge noncondensable gases at the maximum rates required to purge the steam system of these gases.

3.8.6.12 Staged large and small steam traps may be required to handle large flows of condensate from start-up and small flows of condensate from normal operations.

3.8.6.13 Steam-trap discharge and other condensate lines shall be consolidated into headers and returned to the condensate collection system.

3.8.6.14 Condensate discharge to the waste system may be made only if a condensate collection system is not economically feasible or if condensate is contaminated.

3.8.6.15 Drip legs equipped with steam traps shall be installed at the bottom of steam headers at the following locations:

a. Dead ends of steam headers and branch lines

b. Low points

c. Upstream of risers and vertical legs

d. Upstream of expansion joints and raised expansion loops

e. Upstream of block, reducing, and control valves

f. Intervals of approximately 150 feet (45 m) in straight, horizontal steam lines (i.e., without natural drainage points), but not greater than 300 feet (90 m)

3.8.6.16 Provisions shall be made to protect steam and condensate lines from freezing where freezing conditions are encountered. Freeze protection shall include provisions for operating locations and shutdown conditions.

### 3.8.7 Utility Stations

3.8.7.1 The following equipment shall have utility stations:

a. Pump and compressor areas shall have permanent utility stations as follows:

(1) Stations shall have steam, water, air, and nitrogen outlets as required for anticipated needs.

(2) Station spacing shall be such that equipment can be covered with 50-foot (15-m) hose lengths.

b. Columns and vessels shall have steam, water, air, and nitrogen, as required for anticipated needs.

c. Exchangers and furnaces shall be provided with steam, water, air, and nitrogen connections as required for anticipated needs. The locations of the connections shall be as specified by the owner.

3.8.7.2 Each utility take-off connection for steam, water, air, and nitrogen shall be located at the top of the horizontal main header or auxiliary header.

3.8.7.3 Root valves shall be provided for each utility take-off connection from a main header or auxiliary header that cannot be taken out of service without shutting down a complete processing unit or operating facility.

3.8.7.4 Each utility line shall be provided with an isolation valve just upstream of the specified hose connector at the termination.

3.8.7.5 Pressure bleed-off valves shall be provided for each utility line in accordance with the owner's requirements.

3.8.7.6 Each utility line shall have a service nameplate indicating the service.

3.8.7.7 The utility pipe and the ends of hoses provided with the station shall be color-coded.

3.8.7.8 Color-coding and type of connectors shall be in accordance with the owner's location standard.

3.8.7.9 Hose connections, where applicable, shall be positioned approximately 4 feet (1.2 m) above finished plant grade or above platform of multilevel equipment. The piping shall be securely bolted to a supporting structure.

3.8.7.10 If an overhead system for water or steam is used in a freezing climate, either an additional block valve shall be provide at the header or other measures shall be taken to ensure that the piping is protected against freezing.

3.8.7.11 Hose connections to nitrogen systems shall have special fittings to provide positive segregation from the air system.

3.8.7.12 The nitrogen system shall have a check valve at each connection and at each utility station to prevent the introduction of air or hydrocarbons into the nitrogen system.

3.8.7.13 Other requirements for utility stations shall be provided in accordance with the owner's location standard.

### 3.8.8 Burner Fuel Piping

3.8.8.1 Burner fuel piping shall be in accordance with the following requirements:

- a. Piping for fuel oil with viscosity greater than 20 centistokes shall be arranged for continuous circulation of the oil through the headers.

- b. Fuel gas supply piping shall be arranged to produce equal distribution of flow and to permit condensate drainage, unless dry gas is assured.

3.8.8.2 If a safety shutdown valve is required in fuel piping at furnaces or fired heaters, the valve shall have remote and local shutoff capability and shall be located in close proximity (i.e., within 50 feet [15 meters]) to the equipment.

3.8.8.3 An emergency shutoff valve in fuel piping at furnaces or fired heaters shall be provided at a safe distance (i.e., minimum of 50 feet [15 meters]) from the equipment.

### 3.8.9 Heat Transfer Fluid Piping

3.8.9.1 The use of flanged and threaded connections should be minimized. Welded construction should be used wherever possible.

3.8.9.2 Any connection that is expected to be disassembled shall be provided with an upstream double block-and-bleed valve arrangement to protect personnel.

3.8.9.3 Some heat transfer fluids can freeze at ambient temperatures. If appropriate, heat tracing of the system should be provided to prevent freezing of lines when the system is shutdown.

3.8.9.4 If the piping system is cleaned or flushed using a water solution, the entire system shall be thoroughly dried.

3.8.9.5 Thermal fluids have a high coefficient of thermal expansion. Provisions shall be made to safely absorb the increased volume of thermal fluid at operating temperatures (e.g., an expansion tank).

## 3.9 Fabrication, Assembly, and Erection

Fabrication, assembly, and erection of piping systems shall be in accordance with *Industry Source 07 Doc 00012*, *Industry Source 07 Doc 0001*, *Industry Source 07 Doc 0011*, and *Industry Source 07 Doc 0021*.

# 1 Introduction

This Piping Design Criteria is intended to be site specific for the Industry Source 03 projects on the Industry Source 03 Facility of Alaska. Listed are the minimum requirements for the design, materials, fabrication and testing of In-Plant Piping materials and furnished with packaged equipment. These design guidelines ensure uniformity and consistency of the design by describing the following:

- Piping materials specification
- Piping design and layout requirements
- Piping stress analysis and pipe support requirement
- Definition of design deliverables

## 1.1 Objectives

The purpose of this criteria define the minimum technical requirements for the piping design and layout of process and utility piping system for module piping installation, including the following:

- Plot Areas
- Equipment
- Piping
- Piperacks
- Platforms
- Roads
- Other miscellaneous items

These design criteria does not include the topics of spacing and layout consideration for minimizing losses due to fire.

The plant layout is concerned with the spatial arrangement of the infrastructure and process equipment interconnections within the plant boundaries. The requirement of battery limit beyond the plant boundary is outside the scope of these criteria. If there are local legislative regulations on plant layout in which the site is located, these must be complied with (such as statutory requirements based on local environment and security restrictions).

[Industry Source 03 logo]

## 1.2 Scope

Plant layout shall identify and adopt a layout that is safe and cost effective and which meets the requirements of the process design, safe operation/maintenance, emergency response action and evacuation. The following items shall be used to guide piping engineering design:

- Piping and Instrument Diagram (P&ID's) shall be the basis for piping design and shall show piping schematics, line numbers, process equipment, valve, piping specialties, controls, and instruments. Changes to these diagrams after they are issued for design shall have prior approval from the Company project representative.

- Piping and fittings supplied integrally with vessels, compressors, pumps, and other equipment shall be in accordance with requirement of these criteria concerning limitations on type of piping connection.

- Separation distance for common items of equipment shall be regarded as a maximum for economic layout purposes. Any proposal to increase these separation distances shall be subject to cost benefit analysis.

- Space for probable future equipment shall be designated and located adjacent to related equipment. The allocation of such space should be addressed during the initial project risk assessment in order to identify potential hazards associated with probable future equipment.

- Piping layout shall allow for protection of piping systems, where necessary, to prevent freezing or to prevent difficulties resulting from high viscosities or wax formation.

## 3   Applicable Codes and Standards

This criteria state the Industry Source 03 projects on the Industry Source 03 Facility of Alaska requirements (if available) are to be used in addition to the referenced standards and codes. In the event of an inconsistency, conflict or discrepancy between any of the standards, specifications and regulations the contractor shall follow the most stringent and safest requirement applicable to the project. Any inconsistency critical to the design shall be brought to Company's attention for approval. Items not addressed in these criteria shall comply with the latest issue of all relevant regulatory requirements.

The latest version of the codes and standards listed below are considered a part of these criteria.

# 4   Design Parameters

## 4.1   Applicable Codes

- In-Plant Process and Utility piping shall be built in accordance with ASME B31.3 piping code, except as follows:
- Drill Site/Well Pad manifold piping may be in accordance with ASME B31.4 and /or B31.8 piping codes
- Pumping facility, tank farm, and terminal piping may be in accordance with ASME B31.4.
- Gas Compression facilities may be designed in accordance with ASME B31.9 or B31.8 using a 0.5 design factor.

## 4.2   Severe Cyclic Design

The following piping shall meet the ASME B31.3 requirements for Severe Cyclic Service (including piping built to B31.4 and B31.8).

- Reciprocating compressor or reciprocating pump downstream piping within 100 feet of the equipment discharge flange, or up to the first piping vibration isolation hanger/support - if that distance is shorter.

- Piping that is exposed to conditions meeting the B31.3 definition of severe cyclic conditions.

## 4.3 Design Conditions

All piping designs, including ASME B31.4 and/ or B31.8, shall consider ASME B31.3 Sections 301.4 through 301.10.

Piping systems operating at less than atmospheric pressure shall be designed for 15 psi external pressure.

## 4.4 Corrosion Allowance

A corrosion allowance shall be added to the design wall thickness of carbon and low alloy steel piping. The corrosion allowances specified in the individual line class are nominal. Reduction of the specified corrosion allowance must be approved by the Piping Materials Engineer. Lower allowances shall not be used without the approval of the Company representative.

No corrosion allowance is required where corrosion resistant alloys or internal claddings are specified.

## 4.5 Sour Service

NACE International MR0175 definitions for sour service apply, except process streams with at least 100 ppm H2S shall be considered sour as well. The definition also applies to piping that is not initially in sour service but which is expected to become sour sometime during the life of the piping system. This includes all systems containing production fluids.

For piping in sour service, NACE International MR0175/ISO15156 shall be used to determine appropriate materials for all wetted items.

Hydrogen induced cracking (HIC) resistance shall be considered for pipe and piping components made from rolled plate or strip (e.g., DSAW or HF-ERW).

## 4.6 Nonmetallic Piping

Nonmetallic piping systems shall have a rated burst pressure of no less than three times the system hydrostatic test pressure.

## 4.7 Pipe Sizing

When appropriate, computer models or other analytical techniques will be used to size lines for vapor, liquid and multiphase flow. Size lines to avoid slug flow regions whenever practical.

Consult Process Design Criteria – Industry Source 03 Doc PRCRT-000001 for line sizing and fluid velocity recommendation.

## 4.8 Wall Thickness

The Line Classes list specific wall thickness for each pipe diameter. It is the responsibility of the Piping Material Engineer to verify these dimensions for compliance with the Specification and Code of Construction.

For ASME B31.3, the nominal wall thickness (t) is calculated by factoring the mill tolerance into minimum wall thickness (t_m) including corrosion allowance (i.e., for ASTM A106: t_1 = t_m/0.875, where t_m is the minimum calculated wall plus any corrosion allowance). For ASME B31.4 and B31.8 the mill tolerance is accounted for in the respective design factors used in wall thickness calculations.

## 4.9 Branch Connections

Due to the complexities of design and installation, stub–on pipe branches may be used as branch connections only where the design and fabrication have the specific approval of the Industry Source 03 project representative. Stub-on and stub-in branch connections with full encirclement reinforcement saddles are not allowed without the approval of the Company project representative.

Miter bends shall not be used in hydrocarbon, chemical, erosive or corrosive services.

## 4.10 Supports

Flanged connections at equipment should be capable of accepting maintenance slip blinds.

Dead legs for supporting pipe shall be avoided on all piping. Dummy legs may be provided when pipe runs fall short of supports.

Spring-loaded pipe support elements shall be designed to prevent complete release of piping load in the event of spring failure or misalignment. Hydrostatic load shall be included in design loads. Lines subject to blowdown and impulse loadings shall be identified by the process engineer and the layout and its support shall be designed to avoid high loading and vibration.

## 4.11 Piping Stress Analysis

The In-Plant Piping stress analysis shall be carried out by contractor in compliance with the Industry Source 03 specification. Specific engineering codes, standards and practices shall be applied in the area where the project is developed. This will apply to module piping, in-plant piping and pipelines.

[Industry Source 03 logo]

## 4.12 Electrical Isolation

Flange electrical isolation kits shall be used whenever a galvanic corrosion cell would be created by connecting dissimilar metals, joining flanges like SS to a CS flanges. This mainly used to avoid electrochemical reaction to prevent from galvanic corrosion.

Isolation kits are typically not required in non-electrolyte environment.

## 4.13 Thermowells

Thermowells process connection shall be heavy wall, and typically will be threaded, or flanged type per the applicable piping class specification. The immersion length ("U") shall be defined by instrument engineer for the required minimum insertion depth.

Thermowells shall be constructed from drilled barstock, tapered and the material shall be 316 Stainless Steel (SS) minimum. Refer to Instrumentation Temperature Measurement Specification (Industry Source 03 Doc ICSPE-000008) for thermowells specification and recommendation.

## 4.14 Insulation

Insulation shall be provided for personnel protection on hot surfaces (with a normal operating temperature greater than 140°F) within 3 feet of an established work space of a fixed access area. Protection should extend to a height of 7 feet above platforms and not less than 3 feet beyond handrails.

Outdoors piping other than stainless steel, with continuous operating temperature <300°F, shall be externally coated beneath the insulation to protect from corrosion under insulation. Coating shall be completely extended through the module wall penetration.

When any insulation other than foamed-in-place polyurethane is used on exterior piping, care shall be taken to ensure that the insulation segments and the jacketing are oriented to allow free draining.

# 5 General Design Consideration

## 5.1 Plot Layout

Plot layout shall be an economical design to meet the process and licensors objective reflecting the need for safety to life and property, and allowing adequate access for maintenance, operation and emergency action. To adopt the safest and most effective layout that meets the requirement of process design, the following will be considered:

- Separation distance – It is necessary to define probable maintenance and access needs and the effect of such activities on adjacent equipment.

- Plot drainage – The location of spillage collection areas depends on the likely spillage, volatility of liquid and position of permanent ignition sources and the effect of pool fire on the equipment.

- Special fire risk area – The need for special fire risk areas shall be reviewed to decide if improved equipment design can justify their reduction or elimination.

- Construction consideration – Risk from construction activity should be considered and included in the final risk assessment. Movement of construction equipment and especially operation of cranes and lifting gear near operating units can be a hazard.

- Blast Effect – Consideration should be given to effects of blast where there is a significant risk of unconfined gas/vapor explosion.

## 5.2 Access Ways and In-Plant Roads

Access ways within each unit shall be provided for maintenance and for firefighting from the roads around the plot. The design of road layout shall consider the plant complexity and the type of fire-fighting equipment likely to be utilized during an emergency. Minimum widths for personnel access ways, stairways, elevated walkways, platforms and vehicular access ways shall be considered.

- Routing – Access ways may be run longitudinally under pipe racks, provided that all relevant clearance factors have been considered.

- Access to Platforms – Access to platform shall meet minimum clearance requirement. Platform escape routes shall not be adjacent to each other. Platform escape routes shall not be adjacent to the source of hazard.

## 5.3 Piping

Requirements for process piping system are covered in Plant Piping Design Specification (Industry Source 03 Doc PISPE-000005) that includes information on layout, access, pipe clearances, pipe support, piperacks, valve operation, spades, sample points and battery limit isolation.

# 1 General

## 1.1 Scope

This Specification is intended to assist in the design, materials, fabrication, and testing of in-plant piping and other systems for the Industry Source 03 projects on the Industry Source 03 Facility of Alaska. This specification shall also apply to all piping furnished with packaged equipment.

This specification is not intended to replace progressive architecture or engineering, or impede the constant search for new designs, new materials, or new methods that permit better and more economical piping designs in the future.

No attempt has been made to provide standards to cover every possible combination of service conditions. Hence, where no detailed specifications are available to completely cover the requirements, the designer should be guided by the principle set forth in these general requirements along with his best engineering judgments.

In-plant process and utility piping systems shall be constructed in accordance with the latest edition of In-Plant Piping Design Criteria (Industry Source 03 Doc PICRT-000001). For repair, replacement, or expansion of existing facilities, the use of original construction specifications may be considered.

## 1.2 Sour Service

Any process stream with detectable H2S (or expected to have detectable levels of H2S in the future) should be evaluated for susceptibility to sulfide stress corrosion cracking. This includes all systems containing production fluids. NACE MR0175/ISO 15156 may be useful in determining appropriate materials and procedures for pressure containing components, and other wetted parts based on their potential and consequences of failure that meet the process conditions.

Any system susceptible to sulfide stress corrosion cracking shall be designated as corrosive H2S service if it contains free water such as produced water, liquid hydrocarbons, wet gas, or rich glycols. Corrosion due to H2S can be significant and should be designed for either by materials selection or corrosion control measures, including corrosion allowances. Systems that normally do not contain free water such as dehydrated crude oil, lean glycols, NGL, and dry gas (lift gas, fuel gas, and injection gas) should be evaluated for start-up or upset conditions which can occur and that make these systems susceptible to sulfide stress corrosion cracking.

## 1.3 Applicable Codes and Standards

This specification states requirements in addition to the referenced standards and codes. The precedence applying for the use of codes, standards, specification and regulatory requirements for this project are listed in sections below as follows:

In the event of an inconsistency, conflict or discrepancy between any of the standards, specifications and regulations, the contractor shall follow the most stringent and safest applicable requirement to the project. Any inconsistency critical to the design shall be brought to Company attention for approval.

The contractor shall comply with the latest version of all relevant regulatory requirements. Any updates to the codes and standards during the contract execution (especially related to regulatory permit and safety) shall be immediately brought to Company notice. Wherever applicable, the contractor shall be responsible for getting the design certifications and approvals from recognized certifying bodies.

The design shall be in accordance with the Basis of Design, and/or any deviation subsequently agreed upon, in writing, between the Company and Contractor. The latest versions of the codes and standards listed below are considered as part of these specifications:

## 2 Piping Design Criteria

### 2.1 General Design Considerations

It is the responsibility of the Contractor or other 3rd parties to perform all work in a manner consistent with all applicable codes on health and safety regulations.

P&ID's should be the basis for piping design, and should show piping schematics, line numbers, process requirements, equipment, valves, piping specialties, controls, and instruments. Changes to these diagrams after they are issued for design should have prior approval of the Company.

#### 2.1.1 Severe Cyclic Service

The piping analysis shall consider the effects of pressure cycling, thermal cycling, and other cyclic loading (e.g., displacement, wind sway, vibration etc.). The stress analyst shall determine the number of cycles a piping system shall be designed for.

Severe cyclic conditions occur when the Displacement Stress (or Operating Stress under B31.3 Appendix P) exceeds 80% of the Allowable Stress and the number of cycles (N) exceeds 7000 (equivalent number of full displacement cycles during the expected service life of the piping system). It shall be noted by the stress analyst that per B31.3, if the piping is under severe cyclic conditions, then there are additional Code requirements concerning the piping materials, types of components allowed, construction, examination, and safeguarding.

Any piping within 100 linear feet downstream of reciprocating compressor or reciprocating pump discharges, or to the first piping vibration isolation hanger or support, whichever is less; or any piping,

that will be exposed to process ambient in excess of "Normal Service Conditions", as determined by localized process fatigue factors caused by temperature, pressure, vibration, or other operational transients, shall meet the ASME B31.3 requirements for "Severe Cyclic Service".

## 2.1.2 Temperature Conditions

Usual operating conditions do not include more severe temporary conditions, such as conditions incidental to startup, shutdown, or abnormal operation. Temporary conditions govern as design conditions only when there is clear evidence they definitely exceed time and severity limits in the ANSI B31 codes.

## 2.1.3 Design Temperature

The temperature range used in displacement stress calculations shall generally be from the lower of the minimum ambient temperature and design minimum temperature to the design temperature shown in the Line List. However, consideration shall be given to all possible operating/upset scenarios, especially those producing moment reversal in the piping.

Temperature considerations shall include the Joule-Thomson effect and auto-refrigeration effect upon the rapid depressurization as appropriate.

The maximum design temperature shall be the actual steel temperature expected in service coincident with the load case under consideration to determine the appropriate design stress for the selected material.

The minimum design temperature is used to determine the suitability of the material to resist brittle fracture shall be the lowest steel temperature expected in service.

In cases where the calculated membrane stress can vary with the minimum design temperature (e.g., during depressurization), the various combination of stress and temperature shall be evaluated and agreed with the Company to determine the most severe condition for the purpose of a material selection. The minimum design temperature will normally be -50 °F for low temperature systems and -20 °F for all others.

Both the maximum and minimum design temperatures should be reflected on design documents, such as line list and piping isometrics, to indicate general design requirements. In the case of a deviation from the selected line class limits, this deviation should be noted on the P&ID's.

## 2.1.4 Design Pressure

Minimum positive design pressure will normally be 25 psig. In most cases the line class selected set the design pressure. The design pressure should be reflected on the design documents and drawings such as line list and piping isometrics.

The internal and external design pressure and temperature of piping shall be determined considering the following condition (e.g., normal operation, start-up operation, shut-down operation, pump-out etc.). The maximum differences in pressure between the inside and outside of any piping component shall be considered, including the loss of external or internal pressure.

By requiring the maximum available design pressure to be specified, there will be instances of large differentials between design pressure and operating pressure. In such instances, consideration should be given by using lower than maximum safety and shut-down device set points in order to provide adequate annunciation of operational upsets.

For lower pressure line classes, the design pressure is set equal to the flange limit. For higher pressure line classes, the design pressure may be set as low as the safe operating limit and govern by pipe wall thickness at a pressure less than the flange limit.

For ASME B31.4 and B31.8 piping the full ASME B16.5 100 °F flange limit may be used up to 250 °F. Therefore, when based on the flange limit, the maximum design pressure occurs at design temperature up to 250 °F for B31.4 & B31.8 but it is limited to 100 °F for B31.3. At temperatures above these limits, derating is required due to flange limits in ASME B16.5 and the corresponding design pressure will therefore decrease. When based on metallurgy and pipe wall thickness, derating may also be required due to reduced stress allowable and tensile/yield strengths used in respective design code and wall thickness calculations at elevated temperatures.

In the case where derating is required, both the maximum temperature and derated design pressure should be indicated. In case of a deviation from a selected line class limits, this deviation should be noted on the P&ID's.

Piping downstream of equipment (i.e., exchangers, control valves) shall be designed for the same pressure requirements as that of the inlet piping. This includes piping up to and including the last block valve downstream of the equipment unless an overpressure protecting device is present.

Consider hydrotesting piping at full flange rating for low pressure system. Hydrotest pressure shall always be based on the maximum design pressure.

## 2.1.5 External Pressure Systems

Design pressure for piping systems operating under external pressure shall be 15 psi. Exception may be taken where suitable protection against external pressure failure is provided.

## 2.1.6 Load Affecting Piping Stresses

Allowable stress values apply to total loads imposed on piping materials. All piping design, including ASME B31.4 and B31.8, should provide for all loading significantly affecting pipe material stresses, according to ASME B31.3, Sections 301.4 through 301.10.

### 2.1.7 FRP and HDPE Pipe

The use of HDPE, FRP, or glass reinforced epoxy or polyester material pipe should normally be limited to design pressure conditions of less than 150 psig.

FRP piping systems should have a rated burst pressure of no less than 3 times the system design pressure, and in all cases should be designed to accommodate full vacuum conditions.

HDPE and FRP pipe shall be designed for the specific application in accordance with Manufacturer's specifications.

Normally, FRP and HDPE pipe material should not be used for any service containing hydrocarbon liquids or gases, but the presence of small quantities of hydrocarbons will not necessarily exclude its use, e.g., atmospheric drains, and module sump drains.

FRP hydrotesting should include five cycles at 1.5 times the design pressure.

### 2.1.8 Corrosion Allowance

The design wall thickness should include the corrosion allowance specified in the appropriate line class. In general, a 1/8-inch corrosion allowance should be added to the design wall thickness of carbon and low alloy steel piping in corrosive service and 1/16-inch corrosion allowance in noncorrosive service. No corrosion allowance (0.0 inches) is incorporated where FRP or corrosion resistant alloys, such as stainless steel or duplex stainless steel, is specified.

Generally, crude oil, all waters (i.e., sea, produced, fire, and potable), produced water, produced gas, and utilities such as glycol (process and heating/cooling), and methanol, are considered corrosive. Fuel gas, instrument air, nitrogen, and halon are generally noncorrosive.

### 2.1.9 Sour Service

Sour service is defined as having 100 ppm H₂S, or greater than, 0.05 psia partial pressure of H₂S.

For piping in sour service, threaded joints shall not be used. Root valves shall be socket-welded or flanged on the process side and threaded instrument/sample side. Seal welded threads may not be substituted where socket welded connection are specified.

For piping in sour service, the use of flanges shall be minimized. Whenever feasible, lines with flanges should be arranged so that the flanges are grouped together, thus concentrating these potentials sources of leaks in one location for more effective monitoring and maintenance.

## 2.2 Piping Layout and Clearances

### 2.2.1 General Plant Layout

- Pipes shall be designed with the shortest possible line runs and liquid pockets and the minimum number of fittings, respecting flexibility requirements.

- Piping layout shall ensure that valves are readily accessible, easily operated, and provide proper access to allow maintenance of valves and associated instruments. The design shall enable valves to be removed where hot work is not normally permitted.

- Piping and platforms around columns, where necessary shall leave clear space for lowering equipment to the ground. Space shall be left around equipment and instruments to facilitate maintenance and removal (e.g., tube bundle withdrawal, cleaning, level instrument bridles, etc.).

- Buried piping shall not be used, except when required to provide access (e.g., road crossing), and overhead placement is impractical. Underground lines shall be provided with means for emptying. Where lines need to be drained completely, the piping shall be sloped and be provided with drainage points.

- The pipes shall be designed so as not to block operator access to the equipment, providing the necessary space for maintenance, especially when the equipment or elements have removable parts, such as: columns or pressure vessels with internals, compressors, turbines and pumps, heat exchangers with removable bundles, fired heaters and boilers, basket or cartridge filters, line cleaning accessories.

- Special attention shall be given to locate vent, drain, sample taps and unit limit valve manifolds, so that free circulation roads or open fire equipment will not be categorized as "hazardous areas". Hazardous material shall be released at a safe distance from the drain valve and operator.

## 2.2.2 Floor Clearances

Pipe routing along the floor shall be avoided unless there is no other choice. Piping that is run along a module floor should be arranged so as to prevent a tripping, striking, or safety hazard. Clearance between floor or platform and piping (including the bottoms of flanges) should be 12 inches, but not less than 6 inches. Ramps should be provided over these lines when they run in main aisles or walkways.

Lines crossing each other shall have a minimum clearance of an inch (1") pipe-to-pipe, after allowing for insulation and deflection. Attention shall be given to pipe movement caused by thermal expansion.

## 2.2.3 Penetrating Lines

Lines through floors of elevated structures should be run through sleeves. The sleeves should be sized to permit flanges to pass through, if field welds are impractical. The sleeves should be sized to clear pipe or insulation by a minimum of an inch (1"). Consideration should be given to thermal expansion and/or cold spring when sizing sleeves. Sleeves should project not less than 4 inches above the floor or platform.

Lines penetrating buildings (i.e., module walls) should be provided with flashing to prevent exposure to outside elements. Lines penetrating firewalls should also be provided with flashing for containment.

## 2.2.4 Lines Carrying Category "M" Fluids or Hazardous Chemicals

Lines carrying ASME B31.3 Category "M" fluids or hazardous chemicals should be located with special consideration to avoid spraying personnel in case of leaks. All flanged joints and valves should be provided with plastic indicating type safety shields to avoid injury to personnel.

## 2.2.5 Pipes, Walkways and Obstructions Clearance

Minimum width of passageways (walkways) between pumps, equipment, and any obstruction including piping should be 3 feet. Minimum headroom should be 7 feet, except for hand wheel locations should be 6 feet 6 inches.

Minimum width of platforms should be 3 feet. Minimum clearance around any obstruction on the platform should be 2 feet 6 inches. Minimum headroom on the platform is 7 feet. Maximum vertical distance between platforms should be 30 feet.

![Figure 1: Separation between Pipe Axis](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-06/figures/01-overall-piping-design-standards-06_p0015_fig01_separation-between-pipe-axis.png)

The resultant "A" dimension must be increased with the piping insulation thickness when applicable.

Spacing and routing of piping should be such that expanding lines including insulation (See Figure 1) do not touch an adjacent line, electrical conduits, or structures.

## 2.2.6 Electrical and Instrument Clearance

Adequate space on pipeways should be provided for installation of instrument tubing runs and electrical conduit.

Classified areas shall be considered when locating electrical and process equipment.

Electrical equipment should be protected from possible leakage, which may develop from equipment or piping (i.e., screwed or flanged joints) located above them. Piping shall not be routed through electrical switchgear room.

### 2.2.7 Operation and Maintenance Clearance

Piping systems should be laid out so that all valves, strainers, and instruments can be operated and serviced safely. When possible, valves should be accessible at a platform or grade level.

Control valves and relief valve assemblies shall be accessible from grade or platform, and orifice runs shall be routed at the lowest possible elevation for maintenance. Orifices should be accessible by a portable ladder or fixed access way or platform as per Company request. Senior orifices and relief valve assemblies should be accessible by fixed access way or platform and should be located so that they are accessible by davit or monorail if weight requires.

Instrumentation and equipment that must be observed, adjusted, or regularly serviced during operation should be accessible from a platform, ladder, module floor, or grade. Level instruments over 10 feet from the module floor should be accessible from a permanent platform.

Sample connections should be readily accessible from grade, module floor, or platforms, except that a ladder may be used to gain access to sample connections where samples will be taken infrequently, or not on a normally scheduled basis. Process sampling systems should be designed to minimize personnel exposure to H₂S.

Areas designated for tube pulling, operation, access, maintenance, or future requirements should be kept clear of all piping. Piping should be laid out so that equipment such as control valves, relief valves, start-up strainers, turbine rotors, pump casing and rods, heat exchanger bundles, compressor pistons, etc., can be removed with a minimum amount of dismantling and without providing additional supports. Access to manways and other access openings should not be obstructed. Piping and equipment should be laid out such that dismantling of adjacent piping or equipment is not required to access or to remove a piece of equipment.

### 2.2.8 Vessel Manholes

Vessel manways located more than 14 feet above the module floor should be provided with permanent access platforms.

### 2.2.9 Drainage

Drain outlets, other than those piped directly to sumps, should normally be 12 inches, and in no case less than 6 inches, above the finished floor.

Piping should be suitably free draining to allow the drainage of equipment and the piping itself, whenever possible. All drains periodically blown down, including instrument, piping drains, and drains from major equipment, shall be independently routed to the sump drain valve location.

Drain headers on dirty vessels should be provided with valves for flushing the header after vessel cleaning. Drain systems should be repairable without a production system shutdown. This is

accomplished by installing corrosion resistant valves between the active production system drain points and the drain system piping.

### 2.2.10 Dead Legs

The design of piping systems should minimize dead legs or trapped sections. Where such a section is unavoidable, suitable vent and drain connections should be provided to ensure that residual fluids trapped in valve manifolds or isolated sections of piping can be safely removed. Install piping/tubing to provide corrosion inhibitor circulation to these "dead" areas. The following guidelines should be followed to minimize potential dead leg problems.

- Future Connections - Piping branches for future tie-ins should be made up fitting to fitting without nipples or other extensions. When possible, such connections should be at the top of a horizontal line rather than at the bottom. Top connections in gassy or oily waters will fill with gas or oil, reducing the dead leg effect.

- End of Header - When possible, headers should end with an elbow rather than a tee. When a header is designed for future expansion (i.e., is ended in a blind flange) the flange connection should be located at the last branch and not at the end of an extended pipe.

Pipe Support - When a piping system changes direction and the elbow is short of a pipe support, the pipe should not be extended to the pipe support. Rather, there should be an elbow with a welded dummy to provide support for the pipe.

### 2.2.11 Bypass or Re-Circulation Lines

Piping should be made up fitting to fitting with a valve installed as close to the main line as possible. Bypass connections should be oriented on top or side to minimize solids and water accumulation.

### 2.2.12 Strainers

Flat or coned strainers with 316 SS mesh sized for the service should be provided for pumps and compressors for use during startup. Pressure taps shall be provided for measuring pressure drop at all permanent and temporary strainer. Provisions should be made to remove the strainers after startup. The weight of strainer shall be considered in the design for ease of maintenance.

Permanent strainers in compressor suction line shall be provided with isolation to permit easy removal. Maximum design pressure drops and flow direction shall be indicated by a nameplate permanently attached to the strainer.

Permanent strainers should normally have a steel body incorporating a basket that can be removed without dismantling piping and preferably with a cover closure not requiring the use of a spanner. The mesh size should suit the type of equipment installed. They shall be in accessible position close to the equipment they protect and valve to facilitate cleaning. Duplex strainers should be of the type which

cannot have a cover removed while that side is in service. For permanent strainers or filters, selection of the screening materials shall be based on the specific application and manufacture's recommendations.

Temporary strainers should be fitted in other cases between the suction valve and the equipment and should ensure that the debris is completely removed from the system when the strainer is cleaned, and be cleaned easily without disturbing the main piping. Piping shall be designed to incorporate the strainer, and no pipe springing shall be allowed for retroactive installation. A suitable spacer shall be provided, when specified by Company, for use on removal of the strainer.

## 2.2.13 Tie-In Points

The tie-in points for piping on packaged equipment should be brought to the edge of the skid. Where extending to skid edge is not reasonable or practical, vendor shall consult with the Company for approval of exceptions. All skid piping for connecting to platform or plant piping off the skid should terminate in flanges or unions.

## 2.2.14 PSV Discharge Lines

PSV discharge lines should be self-draining. Pocketing of relief valve discharge lines, blow-down lines, or flare lines shall be avoided. Where this is impractical, a valve drain shall be provided at the low point. Connections to headers should be to the top of the header to prevent accumulation of scale, grit, etc. back onto the PSV.

## 2.2.15 Corrosion Monitoring Coupons

Access for corrosion monitoring coupons should be provided to points in piping systems where erosion and/or corrosion is anticipated (i.e., well flow lines, bends, and production manifolds). Flanged spools should be considered for piping in high erosion and corrosion areas.

## 2.2.16 Quill Type Fittings

Quill type fittings should be used for all chemical injection points.

## 2.2.17 Line Classifications

The piping line classes and associated materials for piping systems will normally be selected based on service descriptions associated with the line classes listed in the Module Piping Material Specification (Industry Source 03 Doc PISPE-000006). In general, this specification provides a division of services into line classes according to pressure, temperature, design code, service conditions, corrosion allowance, and materials of construction. The use of standard line classes facilitates the design process and promotes standardization of materials.

The particular material class used for any given application should be as indicated on the P&IDs. Piping items not covered by Company piping material specifications should be identified with a tag number and called out on the P&IDs and the piping isometrics.

The use of spec breaks can have a considerable economic impact. A slightly more expensive, superior pressure or temperature line class could eliminate the costs of additional safety devices needed to protect a lower classed line.

Changes in line pressure classes should be made at isolation (block) valves. The isolation valves indicated as per P&ID, are normally on the low pressure side of a control, relief, or check valve. The valve and all piping on the high pressure side should be rated for the high pressure line class. If a bypass is furnished, the bypass valve and piping on the high pressure side should be rated for the high pressure.

Piping wall thickness should be determined in accordance with the latest revision of the applicable ASME code. Corrosion allowance should also comply with the appropriate material class. Note that additional wall thickness may be required for structural strength in certain pipe spans.
