## 3.0 DEFINITIONS

**3.1** Contractor – Company or business that agrees to furnish materials or perform specified services at a specified price and/or rate to Owner.

**3.2** First Normally Closed Valve – The first valve that is closed (or intended to be closed) for the majority of the time during the operation of the line. It is opened, for only a brief period of time, a few times during the operational duration of the piping system. Examples of normally closed valves include the following:

- The first block valve off of a piping run intended to segregate piping that is connected to an open (atmospheric) system, such as a vent, drain, sample station, or a hose station.
- The first block valve off of a piping run intended to segregate piping that is used only for start-up, shut-down, decocking, chemical injection, or other intermittent services.

**3.3** Fluid Service – A general term concerning the application of a piping system for a given service, considering the combination of fluid properties, operation conditions, and other factors that establish the basis for design and operation of the piping system.

**3.4** Fluid Service and Service Classification – The design requirements in this REP and other associated piping REPs classify fluid service and service as follows:

**3.4.1** Category D Fluid Service (Non-Flammable, Non-Hazardous): a fluid/material service, as defined in accordance to ASME B31.3, in which all of the following apply:

1. The fluid/material handled is non-flammable, non-toxic, and not damaging to human tissues as defined in paragraph 300.2 of ASME B31.3.
2. The design gauge pressure does not exceed 150 psi.
3. The design temperature is from −20°F through 366°F.

Examples of fluids/materials meeting the above criteria include the following:

- Cooling water.
- Steam condensate < 366°F.
- Storm drains piping.
- Hydraulic fluid.
- Treated waste water.
- Nitrogen.
- Air.
- Non-hazardous chemical additives < 366°F.
- Fire water.
- Drinking water.
- Catalyst, spent catalyst < 366°F.
- Boiler feed water < 366°F.
- Steam < 366°F.
- Plumbing and sewers.

**3.4.2** Non-Flammable, Hazardous Fluid Service – A sub-set of Normal Fluid Service as defined in accordance with ASME B31.3, in which the potential for personnel exposure to a non-flammable fluid/material service is damaging to the human tissues due to the fluid/material's physical and/or chemical properties and/or its pH.

Examples of fluids/materials meeting the above criteria include the following:

- Acids.
- Caustics.
- Hazardous chemical additives (resulting in chemical burns).
- Process water (some residual HCs), stripped sour water.
- Catalyst, spent catalyst ≥ 366°F.
- Boiler feedwater and steam ≥ 366°F.
- Streams with design gauge pressure exceeding 150 psi but less than or equal to the corresponding gauge pressure allowed by the ASME B16.5 Class 1500 rating.

**3.4.3** Flammable and Combustible Fluid Service – A sub-set of Normal Fluid Service as defined in accordance with ASME B31.3, in which the fluid/material is readily ignitable when released to the atmosphere, including flammable liquids; hydrocarbon vapors; and other vapors, gases, or solids. Per NFPA 30, a liquid having a flash point below 100°F and having a vapor pressure not exceeding 40 psia at 100°F is known as a Class I liquid. Class I liquids are subdivided as follows:

- Class IA liquids – liquids with flash points < 73°F and boiling points < 100°F.
- Class IB liquids – liquids with flash points < 73°F and boiling points ≥ 100°F.
- Class IC liquids – liquids with flash points ≥ 73°F but < 100°F.

Per NFPA 30, a combustible liquid is one whose flash point is 100°F or higher, and they are classified as:

- Class II – flash point equal to or greater than 100°F, but less than 140°F.
- Class IIIA – flash point equal to or greater than 140°F, but less than 200°F.
- Class IIIB – flash point equal to or greater than 200°F.

Examples of flammable fluids/materials meeting the above criteria include the following:

- Any flammable and combustible fluids with operating temperatures above their flash points.
- Light hydrocarbons, lighter than 68 degrees API gravity (0.705 specific gravity).
- Flammable services that can auto-refrigerate and lead to brittle fracture.

**3.4.4** Dangerous Fluid Service – A sub-set of Normal Fluid Service as defined in accordance with ASME B31.3, in which the fluid/material is damaging to human tissue due to the fluid/material's chemical properties excluding pH.

Examples of fluids/material meeting the above criteria include materials such as the following:

- Phenol.
- Hydrogen sulfide.
- Chlorine.
- Others contained in a stream at concentrations above those where regulation and local health practice may put limits on personnel exposure.

**3.4.5** Aggressive Environmental Service (AES) – A fluid/material service, as defined in REP 10-2-1 and REP 10-2-2.

**3.4.6** Hydrofluoric Acid (HF) Alkylation Service – A service in which the main purpose is to produce a high-octane gasoline-blending component in presence of HF catalyst under conditions selected to optimize alkylate yield and quality. This document specifically refers to two specific processes: (a) the Industry Source 05 licensed process; (b) the UOP HF licensed process.

**3.4.7** High Pressure Fluid Service – A fluid/material service, as defined in accordance with ASME B31.3, in which the potential for personnel exposure is judged to be significant and in which Owner specifies the use of Chapter IX of ASME B31.3 for piping design and construction (pressure in excess of that allowed by the ASME B16.5 Class 2500 rating); (see also paragraph K300 of ASME B31.3).

**3.4.8** Normal Fluid Service – A fluid/material service, as defined in accordance to ASME B31.3.

**3.4.9** Fatigue/Cyclic Service – A service in which specific piping components or joints operate under conditions that will produce fatigue damage due to cycling condition. Sources of cycling loads on conditions include but are not limited to the following:

1. Pressure cycling.
2. Thermal cycling.
3. Mechanical load cycling not induced by pressure.
4. Loads associated with vibration that may arise from such sources as impact, pressure pulsation, turbulent flow vortices, resonance in compressors, and wind.
5. Any combination of loads described above.

Specific fatigue service design considerations are provided in ASME B31.3.

Examples of piping components operating in fatigue service include the following:

- Reciprocating compressor piping.
- Centrifugal compressor piping.
- High pressure to low pressure let-down valves.
- Relief valve piping operating below 100% of Relief Valve (RV) setting (relief valve chatter).
- Steam traps.
- Know piping circuits of water hammering.
- Drains with components without proper gussets.
- Piping containing two phase flow which induces cyclic stresses.

Other classifications of service are used in other associated piping REPs to classify or define a specific service condition that might affect design, selection, construction, and erection of piping systems.

**3.5** Inspector – A Industry Source 05 appointed engineer or Inspector.

**3.6** Manufacturer – The recipient of a direct or indirect purchase order for materials and/or equipment. In this context, a direct order is one issued to a manufacturer by a contractor or Owner. An indirect order is one issued to a manufacturer by a vendor (recipient of a direct order) for materials, fabricated components, or sub-assemblies.

**3.7** Owner – Industry Source 05.

**3.8** Owner's Engineer – A Industry Source 05 appointed engineer.

**3.9** Piping Service Class – Simplified classification of piping system as established in API 570, based on the risk classification and that is used to establish frequency and extent of inspection. This classification includes four piping service classes, 1 through 4.

[Industry Source 05 logo]

## General Piping Design

**3.10** Piping System – As defined in API 570, an assembly of interconnected piping circuits that are subject to the same set or sets of design conditions and is used to convey, distribute, mix, separate, discharge, meter, control, or snub fluid flows.

**3.11** Purchaser – The party placing a direct purchase order. The purchaser is Owner's designated representative.

**3.12** Small-Bore Piping (SBP) – A piping, as defined in accordance to API 570, that is less than or equal to NPS 2.

## 4.0 GENERAL PIPING DESIGN

### 4.1 General

**4.1.1** Piping shall conform to the requirements of this Practice and ASME B31.3, ASME B31.1, or ASME B31.4, ASME B31.8, NFPA 13, NFPA 24, or NFPA 59A as applicable, except where superseded by more stringent local codes or regulations.

**4.1.2** (\*) This Practice supplements the piping requirements of the applicable ASME piping code. In case of conflict between these Practices and the ASME piping code, the most stringent requirements as determined by Owner's Engineer shall govern.

### 4.2 Design Pressure and Temperature

**4.2.1** The maximum design temperature for each line and its components is the metal temperature that represents the most severe condition along with the coincident pressure that requires the greatest pipe wall thickness and highest flange rating. The metal temperature for piping components shall be determined as follows:

1. For externally insulated piping components, the design metal temperature shall be the maximum design temperature of the contained fluid.

2. For uninsulated (externally) and non-refractory lined (internally) piping components with fluid temperatures 32°F and above, the design metal temperature of the contained fluid, reduced by the percentage shall be as shown in Table 1 of this Practice.

3. For uninsulated (externally) and non-refractory lined (internally) piping components with fluid temperatures less than 32°F, the design metal temperature shall be that of the contained fluid.

4. For lines and internally insulated piping, the design temperature shall be specified or calculated using maximum ambient temperature and zero wind.

**4.2.2** The Minimum Design Temperature (MDT) used in the design shall be the lowest temperature expected in service after considering all of the following:

1. The start-up and shut-down conditions shall be considered when determining the MDT. The MDT may be based on controlled start-up and shut-down procedures that ensure that the MDT and coincident pressure meet the requirements of the ASME piping code. If this alternative is used, the operating manual for the unit shall specifically address these procedures. Typically, the MDT can be set at a temperature where the coincident pressure during the start-up and shut-down conditions is equal to or less than 25% of the design temperature.

2. The MDT may be determined by computation or by measurement from equipment in service under equivalent operating conditions. Consideration shall be given to normal operating conditions, operational upsets, auto-refrigeration, and any other source of potential cooling.

3. If controlled start-up and shut-down procedures are not used (item a.) and the process design conditions do not result in special coding effects (item b.), the MDT shall be set to the lowest expected metal temperature for the site. See the "Isothermal Lines of Lowest One-Day Mean Temperatures" figure in API 650.

4. For piping constructed to ASME B31.3 the MDMT shall be established as the minimum permissible value based upon the selected material specification and furnished thickness based on Table 323.2.2 of ASME B31.3.

5. The MDMT shall be adjusted as applicable to include the restrictions on material toughness per REP 10-2-2.

**4.2.3** The MDT for each line is the lowest metal temperature expected in service. The minimum design metal temperature shall be determined by computation or by measurement from equipment in service under equivalent operating conditions. Consideration shall be given to the lowest expected metal temperature, operational upsets, auto-refrigeration, atmospheric temperature, and any other sources of cooling. The pressure specified at the minimum design metal temperature shall be the design pressure determined in the following paragraphs unless calculations or operating procedures ensure that a lower pressure is coincident with the minimum metal temperature.

**4.2.4** The design pressure for piping components is that pressure that represents the most severe condition along with the coincident temperature that requires the greatest pipe wall thickness and highest flange rating. The design pressure for piping shall be consistent with the design pressure for vessels and equipment to which it is attached, and the following:

**4.2.4.1** Protected by a Pressure Relief (PR) device: The design pressure shall be equal to the set pressure of the PR device protecting the system plus static head and the pressure differential required for flow to the PR device.

**4.2.4.2** Not protected by a PR device: The design pressure for any section of piping not protected by a PR device shall be equal to the maximum pressure that can be developed as a result of control valve failure, pump shut-off, or inadvertent valve closure and static head.

**4.2.5** Variations from design conditions: Variations of short duration in pressure and temperature from the design conditions are permitted by short-time, adjusted, pressure-temperature ratings of piping components in accordance with paragraphs 302.2.4 of ASME B31.3. The short-time design pressure and temperature shall be coexistent values based on variations (more severe than normal design conditions). Such variations may occur during a start-up, shut-down, normal operation of the process such as regeneration and decoking, emergency conditions or a major equipment failure, operating error, etc. Guidelines for establishing these pressures are as follows:

**4.2.5.1** For piping associated with pressure vessels and equipment that are protected by a PR device, the emergency pressure shall be equal to the set pressure of the PR device plus static head and the pressure differential required for flow to the PR device.

[Industry Source 05 logo]

# General Piping Design

**4.2.5.2** For piping not protected by a PR device, the emergency pressure shall be equal to the maximum pressure that can be developed as a result of control valve failure, pump shut-off, or inadvertent valve closure, and static head.

**4.2.5.3** When pump curves are available, the pump shut-in pressure shall be the sum of the pump differential pressure (shut-in) plus normal suction pressure.

**4.2.5.4** When pump curves are not available for determining shut-in pressures, an acceptable estimate of the shut-in pressure shall be the greater of the following:

1. Normal pump suction pressure plus 120% of normal pump differential pressure.
2. Maximum pump suction pressure plus normal pump differential pressure.
3. If shut-in pressures are estimated in accordance with the sub-paragraphs above, they shall be re-evaluated when pump curves are obtained:
   - A lower design pressure than determined from the first sub-paragraph above shall be acceptable if the actual pump supplied has a shut-off differential pressure less than 120% of normal differential pressure.
   - Where the actual pump supplied has a shut-off differential pressure greater than 120% of normal differential pressure, the design pressure, if previously determined from the first sub-paragraph, above shall be corrected.

**4.2.6** (*) Unless otherwise specified by Owner's Engineer, the design pressure for piping components operating at positive pressures only shall be a minimum of 50 psig.

**4.2.7** (*) Unless otherwise specified by Owner's Engineer, the minimum design pressure for piping components operating at vacuum pressure shall be full vacuum (15 psia) and 50 psig internal pressure.

**4.2.8** When designing for external pressure (for example, in jacketed piping), the possible absence of internal pressure in the inner pipe shall be taken into consideration.

**4.2.9** Piping and components between double block valves shall be suitable for the more severe line classification on either side of the double valve installation.

**4.2.10** Piping downstream of such equipment as heat exchangers and control valves shall not be designed for the lower pressure resulting from pressure drop through the equipment if the pressure can increase because of downstream fouling or inadvertent closing of a valve. Valves that are locked or sealed open during operation and closed only for maintenance need not be considered.

**4.2.11** Supplemental design requirements and piping systems in HF service are covered in REP 5-10-1.

## 4.3 Sizing Requirements for Piping

**4.3.1** (*) The design flow quantity for oil, hydrocarbon, gas, and vapor lines shall be the maximum quantity for which the equipment upstream (pumps, vessels, furnaces, etc.) is designed, except that the design capacity of connections between towers and reboilers shall be subject to the approval of Owner's Engineer.

**4.3.2** (*) The design capacities for utility services piping shall be subject to the approval of Owner's Engineer.

**4.3.3** Line sizing criteria for liquids, gases and steam, fluid solids, and mixed phase flow shall be as shown in Table 2, Table 3, Table 4, and Table 5, respectively.

**4.3.4** For two-phase flow, the parameter:

$$\rho_M V_M^2 \leq 10{,}000$$

*With:*

$$\rho_M = \frac{M_T}{\dfrac{M_L}{\rho_L} + \dfrac{M_G}{\rho_G}}$$

$$V_M = \frac{M_T}{3600\,\rho_M A}$$

A = cross sectional area of pipe, ft²

$\rho_M$ = mixture density, lbs/ft³

$\rho_L$ = liquid density, lbs/ft³

$\rho_G$ = vapor density, lbs/ft³

$M_T$ = total mixture flowrate, lbs/hr

$M_L$ = liquid flowrate, lbs/hr

$M_G$ = vapor flowrate, lbs/hr

$V_M$ = mixture velocity, ft/sec

(Note: This erosion velocity equation is taken from API RP 14E, Paragraph 2.5).

**4.3.5** Piping in intermittent service (for example, start-up, pumping-out, bypasses) shall be sized on the basis of available pressure differentials and subject to the line sizing criteria of this Practice.

**4.3.6** Pipe size restrictions on bore and outside diameter shall be as specified in REP 5–2–1.

**4.3.7** Pump suction line sizes shall be determined as follows:

**4.3.7.1** (*) Pump suction lines shall be sized to provide a Net Pump Suction Head Available (NPSHA) not less than the Net Pump Suction Head Required (NPSHR) by the pump selected. NPSHA shall be at the rated pump capacity. The economics of increasing line size versus adjusting vessel elevation shall be considered in providing sufficient Net Positive Suction Head (NPSH). The line shall not be smaller than the pump nozzle and velocity shall not exceed 10 ft/sec. Line velocities higher than 6 ft/sec shall require approval of Owner's Engineer.

**4.3.7.2** The static head used in calculating the available NPSH shall be measured from the bottom tangent line for vertical vessels, or the bottom of horizontal vessels to one of the following:

1. The centerline of a horizontal centrifugal pump or rotary pump.
2. The suction nozzle on a vertical centrifugal pump or reciprocating pump.

**4.3.7.3** The design of storage tank suction lines shall be based on an NPSH taken from the lowest specified liquid level in the tank at which rated pump capacity is required. If vortex-breaking equipment is required, the pressure drop through the equipment shall be considered.

**4.3.7.4** In sizing suction lines for reciprocating pumps, acceleration head shall be considered.

**4.3.8** The pressure drop available for control valves shall be as specified in REP 5-3-17.

**4.3.9** In areas where the level of noise is a concern, the requirements of the *Industry Source 05 Engineering Services Recommended Environmental Guidelines* shall be followed.

## 4.4 Piping Line Lists

**4.4.1** (*) Unless otherwise specified by Owner's Engineer, the Piping Line List (PLL) shall contain the following information for each line:

**4.4.1.1** Line Description:

1. Line number per this Practice, including: the nominal pipe size, unit identifier, line service symbol, line sequence number, Industry Source 05 standard piping class per REP 5-2-3, and insulation code.
2. Pipe thickness (inches) schedule identification and specified corrosion allowance (inches).
3. Origin and termination points.
4. Piping & Instrumentation Drawing (P&ID) drawing number range with contains the referenced line.
5. Service description.

**4.4.1.2** Design Conditions:

1. Design pressure (psi) and temperature (°F).
2. Normal operating pressure (psi) and temperature (°F).
3. Upset pressure (psi) and temperature (°F) per this Practice.
4. Test pressure (psi) (indicate hydrostatic or Industry Source 07 Doc umatic).
5. MDT (°F) and coincident pressure (psi).

**4.4.1.3** Flow Conditions:

1. Fluid phase description: liquid, vapor, mixed or two-phase, or slurry.
2. Velocity (ft/sec) and flow rate (lbs/hr).
3. Density (lbs/ft³).
4. Computed head loss (lbs/in²/100ft).

**4.4.1.4** Additional Notes:

1. Identifier to indicate Steam Traced (ST) or Electrical Traced (ET) lines.
2. Identifier to indicate Hydrostatic (H) or Industry Source 07 Doc umatic (P) pressure test.
3. Identifier to indicate a Stress Relieved (SR) line.
4. Identifier to indicate underground Coated and Wrapped (CW) pipe.

5. Identifier to indicate No Flow (NF) in the line during normal operation.
6. Identifier to indicate whether or not the line will be subject to a piping Stress Analysis (SA).
7. Identifier to indicate whether the fluid contained is a Dangerous Material (DM).
8. Identifier to indicate whether the installed pipe wall thickness has been calculated for the design pressure-temperature (CWT).

*Note: CWT will be used when the actual pipe temperature-pressure rating is less than the Full Flange Rating or 'Calculated' is specified in existing Industry Source 05 Piping System.*

**4.4.2** (*) A typical layout for a piping line list is shown in Table 6. Alternative formats for this table may be used if the alternate table contains the same information and approval is obtained from Owner's Engineer.

**4.4.3** (*) The following information shall be shown on supplemental data sheets; see REP 5-1–3 or on stress isometrics when the format has been reviewed and approved by Owner's Engineer:

**4.4.3.1** Piping metal temperatures used for piping stress analysis (indicate more than one temperature if multiple temperature conditions apply).

**4.4.3.2** Identify the governing condition for piping design, such as maximum or minimum operating temperature; equipment steam-out or line steam-out; line bypassed; regeneration; decoking; steam tracing, tank nozzle rotation; etc.

## 9.0 HOT TAPS AND TIE-INS

### 9.1 Hot Taps

Requirements governing the design, location, inspection, and testing of pressure tap connections (hot taps) on piping, pressure vessels, and tankage are covered in REP 5–7–1.

### 9.2 Tie-Ins

Requirements governing the design and inspection and testing of tie-ins for new piping systems are covered in REP 5–7–2.

## 10.0 PIPING FOR ATMOSPHERIC STORAGE TANKS AND LOW-PRESSURE STORAGE VESSELS

Requirements governing the design, layout, and arrangement of piping connected to atmospheric storage tanks or low-pressure storage vessels are covered in REP 5–6–1.

## 11.0 PIPING AND STRAINERS FOR ROTATING EQUIPMENT

### 11.1 Piping for Rotating Equipment

Requirements governing the design, fabrication, inspection, and testing of the following piping systems are covered in REP 5–6–2.

1. Suction and discharge piping for centrifugal pumps.
2. Centrifugal compressor piping.
3. Reciprocating and positive displacement compressor piping.
4. Steam turbine inlet and exhaust piping.
5. Flushing and drain connections for centrifugal and rotary compressors.
6. Washing systems for steam turbines.

### 11.2 Auxiliary Piping for Rotating Equipment

Design, fabrication, installation, and inspection requirements of auxiliary piping associated with compressors, centrifugal fans, turbines, engines, gears, and pressurized lube and seal oil systems are covered in REP 5–6–2.

### 11.3 Strainers for Rotating and Other Equipment

Requirements governing the design and application of temporary and permanent strainers for the protection of equipment are covered in REP 5–6–5. This basic Practice does not cover metal screen or porous media filters with openings finer than 150 mm.

## 12.0 PIPING FOR FIRED HEATERS

Requirements governing the design, layout, and arrangement of piping systems connected to fired heaters, including fuel gas systems, are covered in REP 5–6–3.

## 13.0 REQUIREMENTS FOR IN-SERVICE PIPING SYSTEMS

### 13.1 Inspection, Repair, Alteration, and Rerating of In-Service Piping Systems

Requirements for inspection, repair, alteration, and rerating of in-service piping systems are covered in REP 5–11–2. This Practice is a supplement to API 570.

### 13.2 Requirements for On-line Leak Repairs

Requirements for performing on-stream repairs leaks in flanges and valve packing are covered in REP 5–11–3. In addition, the on-stream repairs for pipe flanges covered in REP 5–11–3 may be used for pressure vessel nozzle and girth flanges.

### 13.3 Installation of Repair Patches and Sleeves

Requirements governing the design and installation of surface repair patches and sleeves that are fillet welded directly to the pipe, flush insert patches that are butt welded directly to the pipe, and flush insert patches that are butt welded to the pipe are covered in REP 5–11–4. The requirements of REP 5–11–4 apply to damaged areas that are either in-service or out-of-service and are not leaking.

### 13.4 Evaluation and Reuse of In-Service Piping Systems

Requirement covering the evaluation and reuse of in-service piping systems constructed to ASME B31.3 are covered in REP 5–11–2.

## 14.0 PIPING FOR STEAM SYSTEMS

### 14.1 Steam Piping

Requirements governing the design, layout, and arrangement of steam piping systems are covered in REP 5–6–8.

### 14.2 Steam Traps

Requirements for the selection and use of steam traps are covered in REP 5–6–7.

### 14.3 Steam Tracing

Requirements governing the design, layout, and arrangement of steam tracing systems are covered in REP 5–6–8.

[Industry Source 05 logo]

## 15.0 GUIDELINES FOR PRESSURE RELIEF PIPING SYSTEMS

### 15.1 Piping for Pressure Relief Systems

**15.1.1** The design of pressure relief piping systems is covered in REP 3–7–1.

**15.1.2** Additional requirements governing the design, layout, and arrangement of pressure relief piping systems are covered in REP 5–6–4.

### 15.2 Rupture Disk Devices

**15.2.1** General requirements for the use of and design of rupture disk devices are covered in REP 3–7–1.

**15.2.2** Additional design requirements and a specification sheet for rupture disk devices are included in REP 5–3–15.

## 16.0 PIPING FOR INSTRUMENTS

**16.1** General requirements for instrumentation piping systems are covered in REP 12–1–1 and REP 12–2–1.

**16.2** Additional requirements covering the design of instrumentation piping systems are covered in REP 5–6–5.

**16.3** General installation details for instruments and their associated piping systems are shown in REP 12–2–1.

## 17.0 PIPING AND DESIGN OF MANUAL SAMPLING SYSTEMS

Requirements governing the design, layout, and arrangement of piping and manual sampling systems are covered in REP 5–9–1.

## 18.0 DESIGN AND INSTALLATION OF NON-METALLIC PIPE

**18.1** Requirements governing the design and installation of non-metallic pipe are covered in REP 5–9–1.

**18.2** Requirements governing the design and installation of plastic lined metallic pipe are covered in REP 5–9–2.

## 19.0 DESIGN AND INSTALLATION OF CEMENT-LINED PIPE

Requirements governing the design and installation of cement-lined pipe and fittings are covered in REP 5–9–3.

## 20.0 SUPPLEMENTAL REQUIREMENTS FOR PIPING IN HF SERVICE

Supplemental requirements for piping in HF service are covered in REP 5–10–1. The format of this Practice closely follows the Industry Source 05 Specification to facilitate use with existing facilities.

# 1. INTRODUCTION

## 1.1 SCOPE

This Industry Source 08 Doc specifies requirements and gives recommendations for piping systems. It applies to piping for all types of process fluids (including fluidised solids), and all utility fluids. Appendix 10 of this Industry Source 08 Doc specifies additional requirements for specific services.

Piping systems shall be designed, fabricated, erected, inspected and tested in accordance with ASME B31.3 as supplemented by this Industry Source 08 Doc and Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.31-Gen.

Alternatively, piping systems for package refrigeration units may be designed, fabricated, erected, inspected and tested in accordance with ASME B31.5, except that impact test requirements shall be in accordance with Industry Source 08 Doc 30.10.02.31-Gen.

Pipelines are excluded from the scope of this DEP.

This is a revision of the Industry Source 08 Doc of the same number dated September 2002 (subsequently amended by Industry Source 08 Doc Circulars 27/03, 81/03 and 32/04); a summary of the main changes since the last amended edition is given in (1.5).

## 1.2 DISTRIBUTION, INTENDED USE AND REGULATORY CONSIDERATIONS

Unless otherwise authorised by Industry Source 08 GSI or SIEP, the distribution of this Industry Source 08 Doc is confined to companies forming part of the Royal Dutch/Industry Source 08 Group or managed by a Group company and, if necessary, to Contractors and Manufacturers/Suppliers nominated by them.

This Industry Source 08 Doc is intended for use in oil refineries, chemical plants, gas plants, onshore and offshore oil and gas production facilities, loading and unloading terminals, and supply/distribution installations.

When DEPs are applied, a Management of Change (MOC) process should be implemented; this is of particular importance when existing facilities are to be modified.

If national and/or local regulations exist in which some of the requirements may be more stringent than in this Industry Source 08 Doc the Contractor shall determine by careful scrutiny which of the requirements are the more stringent and which combination of requirements will be acceptable as regards safety, environmental, economic and legal aspects. In all cases the Contractor shall inform the Principal of any deviation from the requirements of this Industry Source 08 Doc which is considered to be necessary in order to comply with national and/or local regulations. The Principal may then negotiate with the Authorities concerned with the object of obtaining agreement to follow this Industry Source 08 Doc as closely as possible.

## 1.3 DEFINITIONS AND ABBREVIATIONS

### 1.3.1 General definitions

The **Contractor** is the party which carries out all or part of the design, engineering, procurement, construction, commissioning or management of a project or operation of a facility. The Principal may undertake all or part of the duties of the Contractor.

The **Manufacturer/Supplier** is the party which manufactures or supplies equipment and services to perform the duties specified by the Contractor.

The **Principal** is the party which initiates the project and ultimately pays for its design and construction. The Principal will generally specify the technical requirements. The Principal may also include an agent or consultant, authorised to act for, and on behalf of, the Principal.

The word **shall** indicates a requirement.

The word **should** indicates a recommendation.

### 1.3.2 Specific definitions and abbreviations

**DN** Diameter Nominal. The DN prefix indicates the nominal diameter of a piping system component in millimetres.

**MESC** Materials and Equipment Standards and Code. The MESC codes are contained in the Catalogue Management Tool (CMT) system.

**PEFS** Process Engineering Flow Scheme

**PFS** Process Flow Scheme

**Pipeline** system of pipes and other components used for the transportation of fluids between (but not within) plants. A pipeline extends from pig trap to pig trap (including the pig traps), or, if no pig trap is fitted, to the first isolation valve within the plant boundaries or a more inward valve if so nominated.

NOTE: Pipelines are designed in accordance with codes such as ASME B31.4 and ASME B31.8 and are excluded from the scope of this DEP.

**Piping** assembly of straight and bent pipes, fittings, flanges, gaskets, valves and other components (e.g. expansion joints, swivel joints, strainers, devices for mixing, separating, distributing, metering and flow control). It also includes pipe supporting elements and insulation.

NOTE: Piping does not include supporting structures (such as frames of buildings, stanchions or foundations) or equipment (e.g. heat exchangers, vessels, columns, pumps) or instrument impulse pipes.

**piping class** assembly of piping components, suitable for a defined service and design limits, in a piping system. The piping classes are contained in the following Industry Source 08 Doc binders:
Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.12-Gen. Piping classes developed primarily for oil refineries, chemical plants and gas plants; also suitable for onshore exploration and production facilities.
Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.15-Gen. This binder contains piping classes developed primarily for offshore exploration and production facilities (platform piping).

NOTE: For standardisation and interchangeability, the Principal may decide to use the E&P piping classes also for onshore facilities, depending on the size of the project.

**very toxic** see Industry Source 08 Doc 01.00.01.30-Gen.

## 1.4 CROSS-REFERENCES

## 2. PIPE SIZING

### 2.1 GENERAL

The following pipe sizes shall be used:

DN 15, DN 20, DN 25, DN 40, DN 50, DN 80, DN 100, DN 150, DN 200, DN 250, DN 300, DN 350, DN 400, DN 450, DN 500 and DN 600 in accordance with the following limitations.

- Due to their vulnerability to damage and their limited mechanical strength, sizes DN 15 and DN 20 should not be used for long-run piping.
- Nominal pipe size in pipe tracks shall not be less than DN 50;
- Nominal pipe size in pipe racks shall not be less than DN 40;
- Pipe sizes between those given in the piping classes shall not be used.

For requirements of small bore piping see (3.9).

Unless economically justified otherwise, the range of pipe sizes above DN 600 shall be restricted to the following, in order to avoid the purchase of many different sizes of pipe and fittings:

DN 750, DN 900, DN 1050, DN 1200, DN 1400, DN 1600, DN 1800 and DN 2000.

The pipe numbering system shall be in accordance with Industry Source 08 Doc 31.10.03.10-Gen.

Appendix 8 gives dimensions and properties of pipe up to and including DN 750.

After the basic pipe routes, number of valves, control valves, fittings, etc., have been determined, the anticipated pressure drop for the preliminary pipe sizes shall be checked.

A calculation sheet for pumping data (Industry Source 08 Doc 31.29.01.85-Gen.) shall be prepared for each pump, showing calculations for suction and discharge conditions, static head, static pressure, vapour pressure at pumping temperature and minimum available NPSH (Net Positive Suction Head), including the calculated pressure drop in equipment, pipes, valves, fittings and control valves.

The Principal shall be consulted for piping systems for which the pressure drop calculations are not covered in (2.3).

The pipe sizes shall be listed on data sheet Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.92 Gen. or if more economical a listing in electronic form may be delivered containing the same information.

### 2.2 PRELIMINARY PIPE SIZING

Appendix 1 may be used for preliminary pipe sizing of pump suction and discharge piping.

Appendix 2 gives the flow rates (m³/h) for various velocities (m/s), which may be used for both liquid and gas piping.

The following velocities should be used for preliminary pipe sizing for interconnecting piping:

- water and other liquids: 0.5 To 5 m/s;
- air and other gases: 10 To 20 m/s;
- saturated steam (dry): 15 To 30 m/s;
- superheated steam: 30 To 60 m/s;
- vacuum pipes: 10 To 100 m/s.

The above figures are not applicable to sludge, slurry, erosive fluids or two-phase flow. The Principal shall be consulted for those services.

For sizing of flare and vent systems see Industry Source 08 Doc 80.45.10.10-Gen.

To determine the flow pattern of two-phase flow see Industry Source 08 Doc 31.22.05.11-Gen.

## 2.3 FINAL PIPE SIZING

### 2.3.1 Considerations

The following should be considered in determining a suitable pipe size:

1) The allowable pressure drop.
2) Whether pressure surges could occur in the piping system.
3) Whether erosion could occur in the piping system.
4) Whether the piping system could be subjected to vibrations.
5) Whether solids could settle out from the fluid (e.g. in slurry service).
6) The type of flow pattern of two-phase flow; an intermittent flow pattern shall be avoided.
7) The allowable temperature drop if the fluid is highly viscous.
8) The economic pipe diameter, considering the capital expenditure and operating expenditure of the pumps, compressors and the piping system.
9) Mechanical strength.

The above considerations shall be taken into account both for the design capacity and for conditions such as starting up, shutting down and regeneration.

### 2.3.2 Reynolds number

The Reynolds number indicates whether the product flow is laminar or turbulent. The change from one type of flow to the other occurs at a definite value of the Reynolds number. Laminar flow can be expected in pipes if the Reynolds number is < 2300.

Turbulent flow can be expected when the Reynolds number is > 4000. With Reynolds numbers between 2300 and 4000 the flow can easily switch from one type to the other. This could change the pressure drop by a factor of 3 or more.

Once calculated, the Reynolds number is used in Appendix 3 to determine the friction factor for the different types of pipe (see 2.3.3.2).

The Reynolds number is calculated as follows:

$$\text{Re} = \frac{\rho v d_i}{\eta} \tag{1}$$

in which: Re = Reynolds number (dimensionless)

- ρ = density (kg/m³)
- v = average linear flow velocity (m/s)
- $d_i$ = inside diameter of pipe (m)
- η = dynamic viscosity (Pa.s)

For pipe with a circular cross section, equation (1) can be written as:

$$\text{Re} = \frac{4}{\pi} \cdot \frac{q_m}{d_i \eta} \tag{1a}$$

in which: $q_m$ = mass flow (kg/s)

In terms of kinematic viscosity, equation (1) for Re becomes:

$$\text{Re} = \frac{v d_i}{\upsilon} \tag{2}$$

in which kinematic viscosity $\upsilon = \eta / \rho$ (m²/s)

## 2.3.3 Pressure drop calculations

### 2.3.3.1 General

The formulae for pressure drop calculations given in this section are applicable to fluids whose density and viscosity are constant along the length of the whole pipe, which is normally the case for liquids. Pressure drop due to piping conditions other than straight pipe shall be expressed for calculation purposes as equivalent lengths (L_e) and added to the length of the straight pipe in the system, thus giving the total length (L) to be used in the pressure drop calculations.

For valves and fittings, L_e is given in the table below (in which D = nominal pipe diameter):

> **Table - Equivalent lengths L\_e\(m\) for valves and fittings by type** - see [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0008_tbl01_equivalent-lengths-valves-fittings.png)

| | Type of valve/fitting | | L_e(m) |
|:---|:---|:---|---:|
| | Ball valve | Reduced bore DN 40 and smaller | 65 D |
| | | Reduced bore DN 50 and larger | 45 D |
| | Gate valve | Standard bore | 13 D |
| | | Reduced bore DN 40 and smaller | 65 D |
| Valves (fully open) | | Straight pattern | 340 D |
| | | Y pattern | 160 D |
| | | Angle pattern | 145 D |
| | Check valve | Swing type | 135 D |
| | | Ball or piston type, DN 40 and smaller | 340 D |
| | Plug valve | Regular pattern | 45 D |
| | Butterfly valve | DN 150 and larger | 200 D |
| | Tee-equal | Flow straight through | 20 D |
| | | Flow through side outlet | 65 D |
| Fittings | Elbow | 90°, R = 1 ½ D | 20 D |
| | | 45°, R = 1 ½ D | 16 D |
| | Bend | 90°, R = 4 D | 14 D |
| | | 180°, R = 5 D | 16 D |
| | | 90°, R = 4 D | 14 D |
| | | 180°, R = 5 D | 28 D |
| | Strainer | Pump suction Y-type and bucket type | 250 D |
| Miscel- laneous | Nozzle | Product outlet nozzle vessel/tank | 32 D |
| | | Product inlet nozzle vessel/tank | 64 D |

\* In critical situations the Manufacturer's data shall be obtained.

The pressure drop across control valves shall be determined in consultation with parties responsible for instrumentation. To obtain a reasonable degree of control, the pressure drop across the control valve (at 80% open position) shall be at least 1 bar. However, if the pressure drop across the control valve is too high the installing of a piece of small-bore pipe in front of the control valve in order to reduce the pressure drop across the valve shall be considered.

The pressure drop of in-line instruments, such as vortex or Coriolis flow meters, shall be determined from the Manufacturer's data.

For equipment, the pressure drop shall be taken from the data obtained from the equipment Manufacturer.

### 2.3.3.2 General equation for pressure drop calculation

The pressure drop for a piping system is given by the equation:

$$\Delta p = \lambda \left(\frac{L \rho v^2}{2 d_i}\right) \tag{3}$$

in which: $\Delta p$ = pressure drop (N/m²)

$\lambda$ = friction factor (which depends on the Reynolds number and the roughness factor; *r*, *λ* and *ε* can be found in Appendix 3.

$L$ = total design length (m)

$d_i$ = inside diameter of pipe (m)

$v$ = average linear flow velocity (m/s)

$\rho$ = density (kg/m³)

For pipe having a circular cross section and passing a mass flow $q_m$, equation (3) becomes:

$$\Delta p = 0.81 \frac{\lambda L q_m^2}{\rho d_i^5} \tag{3a}$$

in which: $q_m$ = mass flow (kg/s)

To convert pressure drop from N/m² into metres of liquid, equation (3) can be written as:

$$\Delta h = \lambda \frac{L}{d_i} \frac{v^2}{2g}$$

in which: $g$ = acceleration due to gravity (m/s²)

$\Delta h$ = pressure drop (m liquid)

### 2.3.3.3 Pressure drop for liquids

The formulae given in 2.3.3.2 shall be applied. Appendix 6 gives the pressure drop for carbon steel pipes.

### 2.3.3.4 Pressure drop for gas and vapours

The formulae given in paragraph 2.3.3.2 shall not be applied since the density of the fluid will change due to pressure drop and possible temperature changes. To determine accurately the pressure drop in these cases, pressure drop computer programs should be used.

For applications where an accurate determination of the pressure drop is not required the following guidelines may be applied.

1) If pressure drop is less than 10% of the upstream pressure use ρ (density) and v (average linear flow velocity) based on either the inlet or outlet conditions.
2) If the pressure drop is between 10% and 40% of the upstream pressure use ρ (density) and v (average linear flow velocity) as averages of inlet and outlet conditions.

### 2.3.3.5 Steam pipes

The steam pressure and temperature conditions of Appendix 4 should be used for the economic sizing of steam pipes.

The charts are given for the following steam conditions:

- saturated steam at    3.5 bar and 150 °C;
- saturated steam at    13 bar and 270 °C;
- superheated steam at  18 bar and 350 °C;
- superheated steam at  44 bar and 440 °C.

Steam pipes for conditions not covered in Appendix 4 should be sized in accordance with Appendix 5.

#### 2.3.3.6 Relief valve piping

For sizing of relief valve inlet and discharge piping, see Industry Source 08 Doc 80.45.10.10-Gen.

### 2.3.4 Pressure Surge Calculations

Surge is caused by rapid velocity changes of the fluid, e.g. because of rapid valve closure, pump trip or start. The steep pressure gradients that may occur under some surge conditions and which cannot be avoided by appropriate means (e.g. non-slam check valves) should be evaluated with regard to the effects on the supports and the design pressure of the system.

Pressure surge calculations are relevant to pipes handling incompressible fluids (liquids). The magnitude of the pressure surge is determined by the velocity of the fluid in the pipe and the rate at which this velocity is changed. As a general rule a sudden velocity change of 1 m/s will generate a pressure surge of 10 bar. The effect of a sudden velocity change depends on the length of the pipe and of the closing speed of the end valve.

The designer shall ensure that the occurrence of a pressure surge can be tolerated; if in doubt a surge calculation shall be carried out. As a general rule pressure surges may be ignored if the pipe is shorter than 100 m and the closing time of the end valve is longer than 5 s.

Measures should be taken to avoid cavitation since the collapse of a cavity could generate a high pressure surge. Cavities could occur due to a sudden change in flow rate, which can be caused by a shut down of the supply pump(s) and the closure of the valve at the beginning of the pipe.

The location of the cavity depends on the elevation profile of the pipe and will most likely be directly downstream of the equipment causing the flow reduction (e.g. pump or valve) and at high points in the system.

After a piping system has been checked for surge potential by a full surge analysis and transient analysis the following shall be reported to the Principal for approval:

- selection of surge scenarios and operational conditions;
- final surge pressure analysis;
- selection of the most severe surge;
- selection of representative piping section;
- final static and dynamic stress analysis.

Surge scenarios shall include:

- rapid valve closure with and without pump tripping;
- pump tripping;
- pump start-up;
- pump trip followed by restart.

The study shall cover maximum possible flow rates. Flows in single-pipe operation of multiple pipe systems shall be assessed if pump capacity exceeds the normal pipe capacity.

Surge analysis shall be performed for:

- LNG loading and rundown pipes;
- LPG loading and rundown pipes;
- condensate loading pipes;
- cooling water systems;

- fire water systems:

- loading pipes in general.

### 2.3.5 Two Phase Flow

Extra precautions shall be taken for two phase flow. Particularly if the flow pattern is intermittent (slug or plug flow), the piping system will be subjected to high excitation forces and these flow regimes shall be avoided whenever possible. These flow regimes can be prevented or reduced by proper location of pressure control valves. The graphs in Industry Source 08 Doc 31.22.05.11-Gen. should be used to determine what type of flow pattern will occur, but they are only a rough indication. Furthermore the actual conditions in the plant could largely deviate from the design conditions. This shall be taken into account and in case of doubt the worst case flow pattern shall be taken (3.5).

For two-phase flow in flare pipes see Industry Source 08 Doc 80.45.10.10-Gen.

### 2.3.6 Straight length requirements for flow meters

Straight length requirements for flow meters shall be in accordance with Industry Source 08 Doc 32.31.00.32-Gen.

## 3. PIPING BASICS

3.1 GENERAL

Piping shall be routed so that the optimum piping layout is achieved in terms of process requirements, ergonomics, operation, inspection and maintenance. Having considered these factors, the number of flanges, fittings, valves and welds shall be minimised.

The selection of piping construction materials is covered in the piping classes, which refer to the MESC system to specify the piping components. The following DEPs and MESCs shall apply:

Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.10-Gen., Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.12-Gen., and Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.15-Gen.

MESC Group 74 (line pipe); MESC Group 76 (fittings and flanges); MESC Group 77 (valves); MESC Group 81 (bolting) and MESC Group 85 (gaskets and packing).

In order to have fixed working documents during a project and reference documents during the lifetime of an installation, a specification for piping systems shall be compiled for each project (see Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.21-Gen.). Project modifications to piping classes shall be kept to a minimum.

For the minimum required wall thickness of carbon steel pipes see Appendix 14.

Protective steam heating of piping systems shall comply with Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.30.11-Gen.

Pipe supports shall be in accordance with Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.29-Gen.

Spans of straight pipe shall be in accordance with Appendix 11.

## 3.2 DESIGN CONDITIONS

A piping system shall be designed for the most severe conditions to which it may be subjected. The following may determine the design conditions:

- steaming-out pressure and temperature;
- surge pressure (see 2.3.4);
- pump shut-off pressure;
- static pressure;
- pressure drop;
- vacuum caused by cooling and possible condensing of trapped medium;
- steam/nitrogen purge pressure.

In situations where different design conditions exist in one piping system, different piping classes may be used. These "spec. breaks" shall be located so that the more severe design condition can never occur in the part of the system with the lower piping class. Spec. breaks between piping classes of different materials shall be executed as flanged connections unless otherwise specified by the Principal.

In situations where in-line equipment (e.g. control valves) with a higher ASME rating class than the run pipe is fitted, the connecting flanges shall have the same rating as the in-line equipment and the same wall thickness as the pipe.

If a system operating above 0 °C is connected to a system operating at 0 °C or below, the first 50 D (with a maximum of 10 m) shall be designed to the specifications of the lower temperature system.

ASME B31.3 provides allowances for pressure and temperature variations. Allocating a design pressure below the maximum surge pressure according to these allowances shall be subject to the approval of the Principal and shall only be considered if major cost reductions can be achieved.

If an external pressure can only result from structural failure of equipment, failure of safety devices or other unpredictable events, it shall not be taken in consideration when establishing the design pressure of the piping.

Piping subject to sub-atmospheric pressure shall be designed for full vacuum.

For the definition of various pressure and temperature levels, see Industry Source 08 Doc 01.00.01.30-Gen.

For additional requirements for specific services see Appendix 10.

## 3.3 PIPING ABOVE GROUND LEVEL

Except for the services mentioned under (3.4), piping shall be routed above ground level.

Where practical, piping entering and leaving a plot area or a processing unit shall be grouped together.

Where practical, inside-plot piping shall be routed on overhead pipe racks. These pipe racks usually have a stanchion interval giving a span of around 7 m. If the pipe diameters require closer supports then intermediate beams shall be installed. The smallest allowable pipe size on pipe racks is DN 40.

If the span between the supports is too long for a pipe, the size of that pipe may be increased, instead of additional supports being provided, if this is justified technically and economically (the technical evaluation shall include the possibility of internal corrosion due to the slower flow causing separation of corrosive liquid from the mixture). This decision is subject to the approval of the Principal.

If a pipe rack forms a part of a structure, or is located next to a structure, the stanchions of the pipe rack should be in line with the columns of the structure, to make optimal use of space for incoming and outgoing pipes.

Equipment which is a potential source of fire shall not be located under pipe racks.

Piping with instrument connections shall be routed so that safe access to these connections is ensured; if necessary, platforms or walkways shall be provided (see Industry Source 08 Doc 32.31.00.32-Gen).

Care shall be taken to avoid any possibility of contaminating austenitic stainless steel, duplex stainless steel or high alloy cupronickel steel components with zinc. If hot work is performed on galvanised items situated in the vicinity of these components, they shall be shielded (e.g. with fire blankets) to avoid contamination. For components which are insulated, the cladding is considered to be sufficient protection.

A forked pipe shall be designed and supported so that no excessive loads on equipment may occur when one branch of the pipe is disconnected (e.g. during maintenance operations).

Where multiple nozzles are applied (e.g. on air cooler banks) the connecting piping shall be designed so that small dimensional errors in construction can be accommodated.

Safety relief valve discharge piping shall be designed to withstand the dead loads and the blow-off loads. Blow-off design loads shall take into account the most severe case, such as possible flashing conditions and liquid entrainment in vapour flows.

For requirements of fire water pipes, see Industry Source 08 Doc 80.47.10.30-Gen.

In a pipe rack the heaviest and/or the hottest pipes should be located at the sides of the pipe rack to provide space for expansion loops and to reduce the moments in the beams caused by the weight and thermal expansion of the pipes.

The minimum elevation of the bottom of overhead piping shall be:

6.0 m over railways;
6.0 m over main roads;
4.0 m for crane access;
4.0 m for truck access;
2.7 m for fork-lift truck access;
2.1 m over walkways and platforms.

NOTE: In some situations the lower side of the pipe supports or the supporting steel dictates the minimum elevation of overhead piping.

There shall be a minimum horizontal clearance of 0.75 m for access ways and walkways, and 0.9 m for thoroughfares.

Pipe routings and crossings shall be on different, predetermined elevations.

Complicated crossings should be avoided by not installing pipe rack spurs opposite each other.

## 3.4 PIPING BELOW GROUND LEVEL

### 3.4.1 Buried piping

Buried piping shall be considered for:
- drainage or sewage;
- fire water and other water pipes, for protection against heat or frost;
- large-diameter pipes (e.g. main cooling water ducts) so as not to impede traffic.

Buried piping shall have a minimum cover of soil as shown below:

- fire water pipes (mains) — 0.6 m
- in areas inaccessible to heavy traffic — 0.3 m
- in areas accessible to heavy traffic and at road crossings,
  pipes of DN 600 and smaller — 0.6 m
  pipes over DN 600 — 0.9 m
- pipes crossing beneath railways — 1.0 m
- in areas where only night frost can be expected — 0.6 m
- in areas where daytime freezing can be expected — 0.7 m

The above soil cover depths depend on the outside temperature and the permeability of the soil. In areas where prolonged sub-zero temperatures may occur, the suitability of the above soil cover depths shall be confirmed.

The load on pipes crossing railways and roads should be equalised, e.g. by means of pipe sleeves or a culvert. The pipes shall be kept centrally in the sleeves by distance pieces welded to the pipe or fixed to the sheeting if the pipe is insulated for low-temperature service.

Insulated pipes should not be buried. If this is unavoidable, or if it is desired for life-cycle economic reasons, the insulation material shall be able to withstand the stresses caused by the thermal expansion of the pipe. Special attention shall be paid to avoid corrosion under the insulation and the system shall be designed so that inspection is possible or not needed.

Soil settlement and thermal expansion of the piping shall be taken into account in the design of underground piping.

For buried pipes operating at a temperature of 60 °C or below, there shall be a clear distance of at least 300 mm between the pipe and any electrical or instrument cables.

For buried pipes operating above 60 °C, the pipe shall be insulated to limit the outer surface (cladding) temperature to a maximum of 60 °C and there shall be a clear distance of at least 600 mm between the cladding and any electrical or instrument cables.

For buried pipes which have impressed current cathodic protection, there shall be a clear distance of at least 1 m between the pipe and any parallel-running cables, to prevent stray-current corrosion of the steel wire armouring of those cables.

Piping shall be designed so that the complete system can be flushed and cleaned. (e.g. "dead ends" should be avoided). For vents and drains, see (3.13).

### 3.4.2 Pipe tracks and pipe trenches

Piping outside process units (e.g. piping between process units and storage facilities) should be supported on sleepers, at ground level in pipe tracks or below ground level in pipe trenches. The choice between pipe tracks or pipe trenches is dictated by technical and economic considerations, e.g. the number of road or rail crossings, the ground water level and the length of the required trench. Pipe racks may be used if space at ground level is limited or if the use of culverts or buried piping is uneconomical.

The distance between sleepers in pipe tracks and in pipe trenches shall be based on the maximum allowable span of the majority of pipes in accordance with Appendix 11. Smaller pipes requiring a shorter supporting distance shall be grouped together and be supported on additional supports.

The elevation of the sleepers shall be such that there is access for maintenance and for operation of valves, drains and instrumentation and that pipes and insulation will remain above the highest expected storm water levels.

Flanged connections shall not be installed in trenches, in order to prevent the accumulation of gas and liquid vapours in the trenches.

Concrete trenches in process units shall be adequately drained into a liquid-sealed drainage system and shall be covered with grating.

## 3.5 EXPANSION, CONTRACTION AND SUPPORTING

Piping systems shall be routed, supported, anchored or guided so that thermal expansion/contraction, vibration or movements due to earthquakes and storms will not result in stresses in the piping or in the connected equipment in excess of those permitted by ASME B31.3 and the equipment design code, in order to prevent:

- failure of piping components due to overstress;
- leakage at joints;
- excessive loads and moments on connected equipment, anchor points, flanged connections, etc.

The upper and lower design temperatures (see Industry Source 08 Doc 01.00.01.30-Gen.) and differences in temperature between piping and equipment shall be taken into account for all design cases.

Loops and/or offsets shall be provided in piping systems where improved flexibility is required.

Expansion joints may be installed only where loops or offsets cannot be used (e.g. due to limited space) or will not give sufficient flexibility. Expansion joints shall be used only if the fluid fouling properties cannot make them ineffective. Expansion joints shall be provided with guides and anchors to withstand forces generated by the internal pressure. Where an uneven flow is possible, additional supports and/or anchors should be installed to protect the expansion joints. The stresses, forces and movements on expansion joints shall be within the limits stated by the Manufacturer. Information about expansion joints and about the location of supports in pipes with expansion joints is given in the EJMA standard. Expansion joints shall not be used in very toxic services or in systems where they would be subjected to torsional loads.

Pipes should be supported in groups at a common support elevation.

For pipe supports and a reference to pipe support Standard Drawings see Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.29-Gen.

Since civil design is often done earlier than piping support design, special structural provisions for connecting pipe supports, such as inserts poured in concrete beams or supporting structures, should be made during the civil and mechanical engineering phase and should be located at standard locations.

Identification of standard pipe supports and special pipe supports shall be shown in the 3D-CAD model, on piping plan drawings and on piping isometric drawings.

Supports and supporting structures shall be able to sustain the hydrostatic test load. If this is not economical, temporary supports may be applied. Spring supports shall be blocked, or removed and replaced by temporary supports which are able to sustain the hydrostatic test load.

The use of spring supports, snubbers and sway braces should be avoided. If they are unavoidable they shall be permanently accessible. If this may lead to unacceptable costs the Principal shall be consulted.

The most commonly applied type of spring assembly is the "variable load" unit. If very low variable loads are essential, such as pipes connected to strain sensitive equipment or for critical systems with large movements, "constant load" type units shall be used.

Excitation forces of two-phase flow pipes and flare pipes shall be determined (2.3.5) and a dynamic analysis of the piping system shall be considered. At points where flow conditions change, e.g. where diameter or flow direction change, forces due to two-phase movements shall be analysed and, if necessary, adequate measures shall be taken to hold the pipes in place, without the pipes and the supporting structure being over-stressed by expansion or contraction. Guides near expansion/contraction elements should be of the goal post type. Supports shall be located as close as possible to changes in direction but shall allow adequate flexibility for thermal expansion and settlement of the pipe.

If pipe stress calculations require the approval of national or local authorities they shall be performed by methods approved by those authorities.

Formal computer flexibility analysis shall be made of all critical systems, which include the following:

- pipes DN 500 and larger;
- process pipes DN 80 and larger if connected to rotating equipment;
- pipes connected to air-cooled heat exchangers;
- pipes connected to pulsating equipment;
- pipes to and from boilers and heaters;
- in cases where differential settlement of equipment and/or supports is expected;
- process regeneration pipes;
- pipes where engineered items are required like spring supports, expansion joints, snubbers etc.;
- pipes subject to slug flow or water hammer;
- if required by local regulations;
- pipes for two-phase flow;
- flare pipes DN 100 and larger;
- pipes subjected to relief loads;
- pipes DN 80 and larger in very toxic service operating at temperatures above 200 °C.

## 3.6 PIPING THROUGH WALLS AND CONCRETE FLOORS OF BUILDINGS

Sleeves or holes through walls and floors of buildings and through table tops shall have a size permitting the passage of a flange of the relevant pipe size, or the size of the required insulation, whichever is the larger, to allow the installation of prefabricated piping.

Penetrations through walls and floors shall be sealed with a hydrocarbon-resistant filler after piping installation (e.g. a collar shall be fitted around the pipe) to avoid chimney draught in the case of fire. To prevent liquid dripping onto a lower deck, holes shall be provided with concrete curbs, cast-in extended pipes or other means. Where applicable the fire rating of the wall or floor shall be maintained.

## 3.7 SEISMIC LOADS

If the region is susceptible to earthquakes, the anticipated earthquake loads shall be established.

A piping system in an earthquake region shall have sufficient flexibility to absorb large movements without leading to excessive strain or failure. The following aspects shall be carefully examined and, where necessary, adequate measures shall be taken:

- piping shall be provided with sufficient flexibility between two anchor points, taking into account that the two anchor points may respond in different modes during an earthquake;
- piping offsets, expansion loops, etc. are normally only provided for absorbing thermal movements. Suitable limit stops shall be provided to restrict this movement in the event of a seismic shock;
- supports for branch-off pipes and supports for vital control equipment shall be determined by careful scrutiny;
- instrument lead pipes shall have sufficient flexibility to absorb seismic movements of the columns, pipe rack and/or structures to which the instrumentation pipes are attached;
- piping going through bund walls, building walls and floors shall be provided with sleeves large enough to allow for the anticipated differential movements due to seismic loads. Dampening and sealing material shall be provided where it is required to maintain a liquid tight connection.

In earthquake regions the following pipe supporting aspects require further scrutiny:

- providing additional limit stops for both horizontal and vertical pipes with horizontal thermal displacements, thus preventing further movement in the event of a seismic shock load;
- providing restraints for risers (vertical piping, usually with wind load guides) in the longitudinal pipe direction, thus preventing the pipe jumping in the event of a seismic shock force;
- providing additional guides at column resting supports;
- providing sway braces or sway struts;
- providing snubbers;
- providing jump restraining pipe clamps or clips, thus preventing the pipes from jumping off their support member (especially for horizontal pipes running along pipe racks or pipe tracks in places where no branch-off pipes are holding the pipe in place).

## 3.8 DISTANCE BETWEEN PIPES

The minimum distance between pipes or the insulation of pipes in pipe tracks and trenches and on pipe racks shall be 75 mm.

The minimum distance between a flange and a pipe or the insulation of a pipe in pipe tracks and trenches and on pipe racks shall be 30 mm.

Where required, the distance between pipes shall be increased to allow for movements caused by thermal expansion.

The distance between the insulation of a low-temperature pipe and any other object shall be at least 100 mm.

The distance between pipes shall allow for the turning of a spectacle blind, if present.

## 3.9 SMALL BORE PIPING

Since small bore branches (≤ DN 40) to large bore piping are relatively susceptible to failure, the following points shall be incorporated in the piping design:

- Minimise the number of small bore branches to piping.
- All small bore nozzle welding shall be performed by Gas Tungsten Arc Welding (GTAW) in the prefabrication yard or shop.
- Small bore piping shall be shown in full detail, either on the isometric drawings or on a referenced document.
- Branches shall not be located in removable spools, unless it is impractical to do otherwise.
- Branches shall not be located in high stress areas.
- Branches shall be avoided downstream of high capacity gas pressure reducing systems such as compressor recycle systems, steam desuperheaters, high-rate depressuring valves and safety relief valves. If this is not possible, branches shall be located well away from these sources of vibration. Special attention shall be paid to the bracing of these branches to the run-pipe (see Standard Drawings S 44.030, S 44.031, S 44.032).
- In branches with flanged valves, branch fittings with flanged outlets shall be used wherever possible, in order to reduce the number of welds.

Further information on the avoidance of vibration-induced fatigue can be found in MTD Publication 99/100.

## 3.10 INSTALLATION OF FLANGES

Flanges in piping systems shall be installed only to facilitate maintenance and inspection and where construction or process conditions dictate.

In the event of a flange leak in hydrogen service and services with flammable liquids at or above their auto-ignition temperature, steam shall be used to control fires. The steam has a smothering effect and will limit the overheating of flange bolts. Sufficient steam lances (see Standard drawing S 88.005) with 15 m long electrically-earthed hoses able to reach the flanges shall be provided. Steam ring systems (see Standard drawings S 38.141, S 38.142, S 38.143 and S 38.144) shall be fitted to inaccessible flanges unless it is assessed that a leak would not present a serious hazard (this being subject to the approval of the Principal). In assessing the latter risk, account shall be taken of the normal operating pressure of the process, compliance with the selected piping class, use of bolt tensioning equipment, type of flange connection (end cover, pipe-to-pipe or pipe-to-equipment connection) and size of flanges. Steam rings need not be installed on flange connections smaller than DN 150.

If steam rings are installed, they shall be manually activated. The steam block valves shall be positioned at a safe distance, at least 15 m away from the flange and the related fire hazard. The block valves shall be marked properly to indicate which steam ring they are serving. Steam rings and piping should have 8 mm diameter drain holes at low points.

Flanges shall not be located above roads.

Bolts up to and including 1 in shall comply with UNC standards.

Bolts of 1⅛ in and larger shall have UN threading (8-thread series).

Nuts shall have a height equal to the bolt diameter.

For insulating flanges and isolating joints in cathodically protected piping systems see Industry Source 08 Doc 30.10.73.10-Gen. and Industry Source 08 Doc 30.10.73.31-Gen.

For flange alignment and tolerances, see Appendix 12.

## 3.11 HYDRAULIC BOLT TENSIONING

Hydraulic bolt tensioning shall be used for tightening the bolts of flanged connections of equipment and piping where operating conditions require the stress distribution in the bolts to be properly controlled to obtain a reliable joint. These conditions generally occur at high pressure and elevated temperature in conjunction with a medium which is difficult to seal.

Hydraulic bolt tensioning shall be applied in the following cases:

> **Table - Hydraulic bolt tensioning application cases — SERVICE, ASME RATING CLASSES, BOLT DIAMETER** - see [XLSX](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0025_tbl01_hydraulic-bolt-tensioning-application-ca.xlsx) and [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0025_tbl01_hydraulic-bolt-tensioning-application-ca.png)

| SERVICE | ASME RATING CLASSES | BOLT DIAMETER |
| :---: | :---: | :---: |
| All | All | ≥ 50 mm |
| All | ≥ 1500 | ≥ 38 mm |
| Hydrogen | ≥ 600 | ≥ 38 mm |
| Critical applications (to be agreed between the Contractor and the Principal). | All | ≥ 25 mm |

For bolt-tensioning equipment, see Industry Source 08 Doc 70.08.10.11-Gen.

## 3.12 INSTALLATION OF VALVES

### 3.12.1 General

The number of different types of valves shall be minimised.

All pipes entering and leaving the process unit shall have a block valve and flanges provided to allow for spading (spades or spectacle blinds) at the boundary of the process unit ("battery limit"). The block valves shall be located near each other unless impractical. A drain/vent connection shall be installed as close as possible to the block valves and spades, for draining, venting and testing purposes.

Valves in horizontal pipes shall be positioned with their stem on or above the horizontal, except as follows:

- butterfly valves shall be positioned with the stem horizontal in services where fouling substances could collect in the lower shaft bearing ;
- gate valves should be positioned with the stem horizontal in services where fouling substances could collect in the bottom cavity;
- valves shall be positioned with the stem horizontal in systems where a component failure (e.g. wedge pin) could cause closure of the valve and lead to unsafe situations (e.g. flare systems).

Pipes with water and/or lug type valves may require an extra flanged connection for installing a spade flange or removal of a pipe spool.

For hydrogen-containing services (e.g. hydroprocesses) with ASME rating class 600 and higher, and for other services with ASME rating class 900 and higher, double block valves shall be installed as follows:

- at equipment that needs to be isolated during operation;
- at control valves with bypasses;
- at relief valve inlets;
- at level gauges.

### 3.12.2 Ergonomic aspects of valves

The minimum distance between handwheels and any obstruction shall be 75 mm.

The location of valve handwheels and/or stems shall not obstruct walkways or platforms.

Valves shall not be installed above roads.

Valves should not be located in overhead pipe racks.

Chain-operated valves shall not be used except with prior approval of the Principal for specific applications (these valves are difficult to operate and the chain may cause hazardous situations).

**Critical valves:**

All valves other than those defined below as non-critical or non-operational are considered to be critical. Critical valves shall be permanently accessible for operation and the handwheels shall be positioned as shown in area A of Appendix 9. This applies also to control valves, motor operated valves and check valves because of the need for maintenance access. In situations where the use of Appendix 9 may lead to unacceptably high costs or complicated pipe work, the Principal shall be consulted.

The envelopes shown in Appendix 9 may be used as classified shapes in a 3D-CAD review, see Industry Source 08 Doc 30.10.05.11-Gen.

**Non-critical valves:**

Valves are considered to be non-critical if they satisfy any or all of the following criteria:

- The chance of a failure is small or a failure would not lead to serious consequences;
- Operation frequency is lower than once every six months;

- Quick action is not required.

Permanent access should be provided for non-critical valves. The handwheels shall be positioned in area A or B of Appendix 9 and should be positioned in area A.

**Non-operational valves:**

Non-operational valves are those which are no longer expected to be used. An example of a non-operational valve is a hot-tap valve.

Permanent access should be provided. The handwheels should be positioned in area A or B of Appendix 9.

The possibility and the costs of providing devices to operate these valves shall be taken into account during the design.

In an early design stage the non-critical valves and the non-operational valves shall be explicitly identified on the PFS and PEFS.

## 3.12.3 Selection of gear drives for valves

Gear drives shall be selected in accordance with the applicable valve MESC SPE specifications.

The selection of motorised actuators shall be subject to the approval of the Principal.

## 3.12.4 Control valve installation

Globe control valves shall be installed with their diaphragm actuator stem in the vertical position, with sufficient clearance above the actuator and under the bottom flange to allow the control valve to be dismantled without removing the valve body from the pipe.

There shall be sufficient clearance to lift and remove the valve. Control valves shall be located so that they are accessible for hoisting equipment where needed. Further requirements for control valves are specified in Industry Source 08 Doc 32.36.01.17-Gen.

## 3.12.5 Manifolds for control valves

If required for operational reasons, control valves shall be provided with block valves and a bypass valve, except that a bypass valve shall not be provided in safety shut-off or depressurizing service or in applications where solids suspended in the stream may collect and block the bypass valve.

As the provision of block valves, bypass valves, handwheels, etc. is governed by operational considerations, the PFS and PEFS shall indicate the arrangement required for each application.

The block valves at each side of the control valve shall be of the straight-through type and should be the same size as the control valve, except in the following situations where the block valves should be the same size as the upstream/downstream piping:

- if the additional strength of the larger pipe size is required for proper supporting;
- if the size of the upstream/downstream process piping is DN 50 or smaller.

For typical arrangements of control valve manifolds, see Appendix 13.

The bypass valve shall have a nominal capacity factor at least equal to, but not more than twice, the capacity factor of the control valve. The bypass valve shall be capable of proper throttling. For critical applications, the bypass valve shall be of the same type as the control valve, but with handwheel operation only.

In the following services the bypass pipe shall be designed so that there are no vertical dead ends where liquid can collect:

- fouling process conditions;
- steam;

- hydrocarbons containing water.

Provisions shall be made for draining and/or depressurizing the control valve manifold. At least one drain valve shall be provided just upstream or downstream of the control valve, depending of the physical lay-out. Shut-off valves shall have a drain valve on the downstream side so that the shut-off valve can be leak-tested. More extensive provisions may be required in corrosive or very toxic service.

Start-up strainers shall be provided upstream of control valves with labyrinth-type low-noise trims.

### 3.12.6 Body cavity relief (pressure equalisation) provisions in valves

Double-seated valves that are subjected to temperature changes and consequent expansion of the liquid medium shall be provided with a pressure relief device.

Body cavity over-pressure can occur in:

- valves in steam/condensate systems when condensate is trapped;
- block valves around pumps during warming up prior to operation;
- valves in low temperature systems.

This requirement is to avoid excessive pressure build-up in the cavity of double-seated valves, where the medium (liquid) may be trapped.

Body cavity over-pressurisation (exceeding 33% of the rated pressure at maximum design temperature according to the appropriate class) for soft-seated floating ball valves, operating at temperatures between plus 260 °C and minus 50 °C, shall be prevented by ONE self-relieving seat assembly.

Double metal-seated gate valves or metal-seated floating ball valves shall have a pressure equalising hole drilled in the closure member outside the seat facing area. The pressure equalising hole shall have a diameter of at least 3 mm.

The mechanical loading of spring-energised ball valves (side entry design) and trunnion-mounted ball valves allows the seat to be pushed away from the ball to enable pressure equalisation and for these valves the seats are self-relieving.

In order to avoid leakage through the closure member, the valve body cavity shall be relieved to the high pressure side of the valve when the valve is in closed position. The valve is now single-seated.

Normally the high pressure side is the upstream side of the valve, and in the closed position the closure member will be pressed against the seat at the low pressure side.

In the following situations, the pressure might act on the downstream side of the downstream valves against the normal flow direction when the valves are in closed position:

- block valves upstream and downstream of pumps;
- control valve arrangement with block valves upstream and downstream, and with a bypass;
- block valves upstream and downstream of relief valves.

These valves shall be clearly marked "HP" and these positions shall be shown on the PEFS and piping isometrics.
