#### 8.8.2.3 Valves in steam service

All valves for steam service in ASME rating class 600 and higher shall be of the butt weld end type, except for equipment assembly valves, blow-down valves and instrument isolation valves, which may be flanged.

#### 8.8.2.4 Valves in hydrogen service

Valves for pure hydrogen or fluids containing hydrogen in piping classes 600 and higher should be butt welded except for check valves and instrument isolation valves, which may be flanged.

Valves in hydrogen service require special attention with regard to external leakage, which can be prevented by different methods depending on the required level of tightness and economics (see 8.8.2.7).

#### 8.8.2.5 Valves in low temperature service

Acceptable valve types for low temperature services are specified in BS 6364 and MESC SPE 77/200 and SPE 77/209.

Gate, globe, ball and butterfly valves in low temperature service shall have a vapour space sufficient to maintain the stem packing at a temperature high enough to permit actuation of the valve.

The vapour space of valves in services between 0 °C and minus 50 °C is defined in MESC SPE 77/209.

The vapour space of valves in services below minus 50 °C is defined in MESC SPE 77/200.

NOTE Depending on the valve design, this may require extended valve bonnets.

Systems which operate occasionally below minus 20 °C (e.g. during de-pressuring) and have a lower design temperature between minus 20 °C and minus 50 °C, do not require valves with extended bonnets. Such valves shall not be opened or closed at sub-zero temperatures.

The vapour space is specified so that in flashing services (e.g. LPG or LNG) a gas cap will form under the stuffing box which acts as a thermal barrier and protects the valve against malfunctioning due to freezing. In order to maintain this gas cap, the valve stem shall be positioned with an inclination no more than 30° from vertical.

Valves in no-flow connections (such as vents and pressure gauges) and valves in methanol service, where the trapped gas bubble protects the valve packing from too low temperatures, may be installed at an angle up to 90° from vertical (i.e. they may be installed in vertical pipes).

Drain valves shall be installed with the stem inclined no more than 30° from vertical. The drain connections shall be provided with support/bracing, preferably to the header (see Standard Drawing S 44.032).

#### 8.8.2.6 Valves in very toxic service

Valves in very toxic service require special attention with regard to external leakage, which can be prevented by different methods depending on the required level of tightness, economics and legal requirements (see 8.8.2.7).

#### 8.8.2.7 External leakage prevention

External leakage of valves can be minimized by the use of:

- quarter-turn valves instead of rising stem valves;
- rising stem gate valves and globe valves with a welded bonnet and bellows seals;
- valves with double seats, with or without a sealing/protection medium;
- valves with special stuffing box designs (e.g. live-loaded and special packing materials (cup and cone or wedge rings), as listed in MESC SPE 85/200

#### 8.8.2.8 Valves in ethylene oxide (EO) service

##### 8.8.2.8.1 General

Non-metallic components shall be selected in accordance with the list published by BAM (Bundesanstalt für Material-Forschung).

The gland packing shall be high purity (98%) flexible compressed graphite.

There shall be no sealant injection connections for stem sealing.

The valve geometry shall be designed so that there are no zones that could generate energy or initiate a fire, e.g. high velocities, turbulence and/or uncontrolled temperature elevation by adiabatic compression. All internal conduit surfaces shall be machined smooth.

In the fully open position, the port opening shall be not less than 70% of the nominal bore.

Valves for EO service shall be internally clean and free from moisture, oil and grease.

Valves for EO service shall have a conspicuous label, stating the words "ETHYLENE OXIDE SERVICE".

##### 8.8.2.8.2 Butterfly valves

Triple-eccentric butterfly valves are preferred in EO service due to their short closure time.

##### 8.8.2.8.3 Gate, globe and check valves

Gate and globe valves in EO service shall have a bellows-sealed or special gland packing construction.

Gate, globe and check valves shall have metal body seats. Metal seat rings shall be integral, welded or screwed-in. Screwed-in seats shall be secured against loosening.

Over-pressurization and pressure locking may be caused by EO polymerization and by the entrapment and subsequent heating of liquid in the valve cavity of double-seated valves. To

prevent such over-pressurization, the gate valves shall have a pressure relief feature as specified in (3.12.6).

Valves in nominal sizes DN 40 and smaller shall have a welded bonnet or cover connection with full penetration welds.

For valves with special gland packing constructions in nominal sizes DN 50 and larger, a bolted bonnet connection is allowed in all pressure classes.

#### 8.8.2.8.4 Ball valves

Ball valves used in EO systems shall have a pressure-equalising hole drilled in the ball and shall be fitted with metallic seats.

#### 8.8.2.9 Flow regulation (throttling valves)

The table below summarises the typical duties of various throttling valves:

> **Table - Typical duties of various throttling valves** - see [XLSX](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0079_tbl01_throttling-valves-duties.xlsx) and [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0079_tbl01_throttling-valves-duties.png)

| Valve type | Size range | Duty |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Needle valves | DN 15 to DN 40 | Accurate control |
| Globe valves | DN 15 to DN 200 | General service |
| Diaphragm valves, lined | DN 15 to DN 300 | Low-pressure, corrosive service |
| Butterfly valves, lined | DN 50 and larger | Moderate pressure, corrosive service |
| Choke valves | DN 50 to DN 200 | For high pressure difference and/or erosive service |
| Butterfly valves (high performance) | DN 80 and larger | General service |

Control valves selected for throttling purposes shall not be used for an isolation function. For selection of control valves, see Industry Source 08 Doc 32.36.01.17-Gen.

#### 8.8.2.10 Back-flow prevention (check valves)

The table below summarises the typical selection of check valves:

> **Table - Typical selection of check valves** - see [XLSX](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0079_tbl02_check-valves-selection.xlsx) and [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0079_tbl02_check-valves-selection.png)

| Check valves | Size range | Type |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Check valves | DN 15 to DN 40 | Piston-type, horizontal flow |
|  | DN 50 and larger | Swing type |
|  | DN 50 and larger | Dual-plate type, spring-energized |

Check valves are designed to prevent the reverse flow of liquid or gaseous products. Check valves shall not be relied upon for positive isolation purposes.

Small check valves (DN 15 to DN 40) are normally of the piston-type and shall be used only in horizontal pipes.

Swing-type check valves may be used in horizontal pipes and in vertical pipes when the flow is upwards.

Non-slam, tilting disc and "feather"-type check valves shall be used where unacceptable pressure surges would otherwise be caused.

Non-slam axial flow piston-type check valves are very reliable in clean service and have a low pressure drop. These check valves shall not be used in fouling services due to the close tolerances of the moving parts.

Utility pipes connected to pressurized process equipment or piping shall be equipped with a check valve to prevent process fluids from entering the utility system. The piping class "break" between utility piping and process piping shall be located so that at least two valves (including the check valve) satisfy the process piping class. More stringent safeguarding systems shall be applied if hazardous situations can arise upon failure of such a system.

Check valves which could convey a relief flow (in the forward direction) under fire conditions shall be of a fire-safe type. For fire safe requirements see (8.8.5.2).

Dual-plate check valves have a short face-to-face flange design and are therefore lighter and more compact than swing type check valves. Only dual plate check valves of retainerless design shall be used.

## 8.8.3 Pressure relief valves and depressuring valves

See Industry Source 08 Doc 80.45.10.10-Gen. and Industry Source 08 Doc 80.36.00.30-Gen.

## 8.8.4 Special valve types and their application

Special valves have been developed and proven suitable for process requirements and special services. Care shall be taken to select the correct valves, with a view to the design, materials, fabrication and testing.

Examples of special valves are:

#### 8.8.4.1 Ram-type drain valve

A flush bottom valve (i.e. without a dead nozzle end) with a piston extending upwards, used for viscous or solidifying products, e.g. in reactors and mixing vessels.

#### 8.8.4.2 Flush bottom valve

Drain valve without a dead nozzle end, used on piping or equipment containing viscous products.

#### 8.8.4.3 Plug valves

Plug valves require periodic maintenance by trained staff and therefore their use shall be minimised.

Lubricated plug valves should not be used for general purposes and shall only be used if the product allows the use of a plug lubricant.

Lined or sleeve-type plug valves may be used in pipes containing very toxic substances but not containing scaling deposits or suspended solids.

In high pressure gas systems the use of pressure-balanced (non-lubricated) plug valves may be considered.

Inverted pressure balanced, lubricated plug valves may be used as bypass / equalising and blow down valves in hydrogen and natural gas pipes and as kicker and drain valves of scraper traps.

#### 8.8.4.4 Multi-port valves

Two conventional valves should be used for diverting flow but if this is impractical (e.g. due to space restrictions), multi-port ball valves or multi-port plug valves may be used after approval by the Principal.

#### 8.8.4.5 Iris-type valve with diaphragm closure member

This type of valve may be used for Industry Source 07 Doc umatic or gravity feed of solids and powders.

#### 8.8.4.6 Excess flow valves

Excess flow valves are designed to shut when the flow rate exceeds design flow rates, e.g. in the event of a hose burst. They should not be used in refinery or depot emergency shutdown systems for storage vessels, loading points or multi-product systems, since they are not sufficiently reliable in providing positive shut-off.

#### 8.8.4.7 Rotary star valves

Rotary star valves are designed for solids handling, e.g. dosing of catalyst. These valves are not tight shut-off.

#### 8.8.4.8 Solids sluicing valves

Special through-conduit gate valves may be used for solids sluicing duties (gravity flow).

#### 8.8.4.9 Isolators and dampers

Various valve types (e.g. flap, guillotine, louvre) are available for flue ducts and gas turbine exhausts. These valves are for low pressures and their tightness ranges from 95% to 100%. They are suitable for both shut-off service and regulating service.

### 8.8.5 Special properties of valves

#### 8.8.5.1 Tight Shut-Off (TSO) requirements

Tight shut-off valves shall be marked "TSO" on the PEFS.

Valves are considered TSO if they comply with seat leakage rates A or B according to ISO 5208 and BS 6755-1, or to class V or VI in accordance with IEC 60534-4.

TSO valves are more expensive than valves satisfying standard leakage requirements and shall only be used if standard seat leakage cannot be tolerated.

Control valves shall not be considered TSO because:
- Certain types of control valves (e.g. low noise valves) cannot, as standard, be manufactured to meet TSO requirements.
- Control valves will lose their TSO characteristics quickly after being used in operation.

A practical solution in such cases is to install a normal control valve in combination with a TSO valve.

#### 8.8.5.2 Valves with fire safe design or fire tested design requirements

##### 8.8.5.2.1 General

Fire safe properties of valves are determined by the materials and construction of the valves.

Valves with a fire tested design are those which have successfully passed prototype fire testing.

Fire safe valves are those which are individually capable of passing fire tests.

Valves shall be fire tested and certified in accordance with ISO 10497, BS 6755 part 2 API 607 or API 6FA and are subject to approval by the Principal.

Valves are considered fire safe if, after being engulfed in flames of a certain intensity for a certain period of time:
- the seat leakage of the valve does not exceed a set requirement;
- the external leak rate (e.g. via the valve spindle or valve body joints) remains within specified limits.

##### 8.8.5.2.2 Valves with fire safe design

Valves with a fire safe design shall be certified to API 607, ISO 10497, BS 6755-2 and API 6FA and API 6FB. For requirements for fire safe valves see Industry Source 08 Doc 80.47.10.30-Gen.

NOTE: Standards API 607, API 6FA, BS 6755-2 and ISO 10497 do not address the capabilities of the valve and connections. End connections shall be fire tested in accordance with API 6FB.

If a fire safe metal seated butterfly valve or dual plate check valve is required, valves with (dual) flanged ends or, for the larger sizes, butt welded ends shall be used. Alternatively, wafer lug type or single flanged valves may be considered since their long bolts are not exposed.

##### 8.8.5.2.3 Valves with a fire tested design

Soft seated quarter turn valves shall have a secondary or primary metal sealing arrangement.

The sealing arrangement of these valves shall be capable:

- to withstand a minimum of 6000 cycles of operation
- of passing fire test to API 607 and API 6FB.

#### 8.8.5.2.4 Non fire safe valves

Wafer type valves are not fire safe. The long unprotected bolts will expand in a fire sooner than the flanges and lose their properties, thereby causing leakage and escalation of the fire. Therefore wafer type valves shall not be used in hydrocarbon service.

Lined valves, such as ball, check, diaphragm and butterfly, are not fire safe and shall only be used in systems which contain non-flammable products.

Sleeve-type plug valves may be fire-safe to the outside, but the seat will pass fluid after exposure to high temperatures. Therefore they cannot be classified as fire safe and may only be used in hydrocarbon services (flammable products) if they have successfully passed fire testing.

## 9.8.6 Repair and reconditioning of valves

If economically attractive to do so, valves may be repaired or reconditioned, provided that:

- they are returned as close as possible to the original manufactured condition;
- the guidelines of API RP 621 are taken into account;
- they are equipped with the same components and materials (e.g. gaskets and packing) as the original valves;
- they meet the same specifications as the original valves.

## 9. INSPECTION AND TESTING

### 9.1 SHOP-FABRICATED OR MANUFACTURER-SUPPLIED PIPING

#### 9.1.1 Metallic piping

Shop-fabricated metallic piping shall be inspected and tested in accordance with ASME B31.3 and Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.31-Gen. Metallic piping materials not covered by Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.31-Gen. shall be inspected and tested as specified by the Principal.

If expansion joints are installed in the horizontal position in pipes operating below 0 °C, and if the expansion joints cannot be removed for the hydrostatic test, the pipes may have to be tested Industry Source 07 Doc umatically instead of hydrostatically in order to avoid ice forming in the convolutions of the bellows. See Industry Source 08 Doc 61.10.08.11-Gen. For testing of expansion joints, see also ASME B31.3.

#### 9.1.2 Lined piping

Lined piping shall be inspected and tested in accordance with the Manufacturer's test and inspection procedures, which shall be subject to the approval of the Principal. Industry Source 08 Doc 30.48.00.31-Gen., Industry Source 08 Doc 30.48.30.31-Gen. and Industry Source 08 Doc 30.48.60.10-Gen. shall also apply.

#### 9.1.3 Non-metallic piping

Polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), polyvinylchloride (PVC), glass-fibre reinforced epoxy (GRE) and glass-fibre reinforced polyester (GRP) piping shall be inspected and tested as specified in the relevant DEP, see (8.2.2). Other non-metallic piping shall be inspected and tested in accordance with the Manufacturer's test and inspection procedures, which shall be subject to the approval of the Principal.

### 9.2 FIELD-FABRICATED PIPING

#### 9.2.1 Metallic piping

Field-fabricated metallic piping shall be inspected and tested in accordance with ASME B31.3 and Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.31-Gen. For field inspection prior to commissioning, see Industry Source 08 Doc 61.10.08.11-Gen.

### 9.3 VALVE INSPECTION

Valves shall be inspected when they arrive on site to verify that the following is in accordance with the purchase order:

- number, type, size, bore, ASME rating class and material;
- face-to-face dimension;
- flange-face finish for flanged valves;
- weld preparation for butt welded valves;
- MESC number and die stamp on the flange rim;
- heat number on the body/bonnet;
- nameplate and label with purchase order/indent number, MESC number, item, etc.;
- stem packing material;
- bonnet gasket material;
- arrow for flow direction or marking for cavity relief side, if applicable;
- general condition of the valve (e.g. no parts stained or corroded).

Review of documents should include:

- inspection certificates (e.g. materials of pressure-containing parts, non-destructive examination of body and welds, hydrostatic tests);
- operating/maintenance instructions, if required.

## 10. INSULATION

### 10.1 THERMAL INSULATION

For thermal insulation of piping (including that for personnel protection), see Industry Source 08 Doc 30.46.00.31-Gen.

On top of insulated columns and tanks, and over piping, where applicable, grating should be provided to avoid damage to insulation.

In the following situations flanges shall not be insulated.

- flanges in hydrogen service;
- flanges in systems containing hydrocarbons above their auto-ignition temperature;
- if the 80% rule for bolting has been applied in accordance with ASME B31.3.

#### 10.1.2 **Insulated flanges**

If flanges with a design temperature above 400 °C are insulated, the bolt stress (after relaxation) shall remain within the required seating stress of the applied gasket type.

### 10.2 ACOUSTIC INSULATION

Industry Source 08 Doc 31.46.00.31-Gen. shall apply for acoustic insulation.

## 11. PAINTING AND COATING

Industry Source 08 Doc 30.48.00.31-Gen. shall apply for painting and coating of new piping and Industry Source 08 Doc 70.48.10.10-Gen. shall apply for maintenance painting.

## APPENDIX 1 PRELIMINARY SIZING OF PIPES CONTAINING LIQUID

![Figure 1.1 Flow Rate 0.1 m³/h to 10 m³/h](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/figures/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0093_fig01_figure-1-1-flow-rate-0-1-to-10-m3-h.png)

Select the pipe size for suction and discharge lines within the zones indicated above. If more than any selection is possible, use smaller size for lines up to 100 m length; use larger size for lines over 100 m in length.

The areas for suction and discharge lines have been based on the pressure drop values per 100 m pipe length for water at 20°C as indicated in Appendix 1. The pressure drop in the suction line area is min. 0.034 bar – max. 0.065 bar and in the discharge line area min. 0.144 bar – max. 0.927 bar.

## APPENDIX 3    FRICTION FACTORS AND ROUGHNESS FACTORS FOR FLOW IN PIPES

![Figure 3.1 Friction factors for Reynolds number up to 2x10⁵](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/figures/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0098_fig01_friction-factors-reynolds-number.png)

EXAMPLE:

Determine the friction factor f for 300 carbon steel pipe with Re= 70,000.

1. Start "S" for 200 diameter and project vertically to intersect the "carbon steel/plus" line at "B"
2. From "B" project horizontally and follow the curve for ε/D = 0.0003 to point "C" to intersect the Re = 7 . 10⁴ line at "C"
3. From "C" project horizontally to intersect the "friction factor" line at "D"
4. Read the value of the friction factor = 0.0225

## APPENDIX 10    ADDITIONAL REQUIREMENTS FOR SPECIFIC SERVICES

The following Sections define specific design, fabrication, inspection and testing requirements for specific process services that supplement the requirements of Industry Source 08 Doc 30.10.60.18-Gen. and Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.31-Gen.

### 10.1    SODIUM HYDROXIDE (CAUSTIC SODA) SERVICE

#### 10.1.1    Design

Sodium hydroxide embrittlement is a type of stress corrosion which is strongly influenced by temperature. The temperature the pipe may reach in service shall be established in order to determine the required preventive measures.

The following preventive measures shall be applied (see figure 10.1):

> **Table - Figure 10.1 — Preventive measures for sodium hydroxide service by area and piping class** - see [XLSX](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0117_tbl01_fig-10-1-preventive-measures-sodium-hydr.xlsx) and [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0117_tbl01_fig-10-1-preventive-measures-sodium-hydr.png)

| AREA | | SPECIAL REQUIREMENTS | PIPING CLASS |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | without heat tracing | None | |
| "A" | with heat tracing | PWHT of welds (including attachment welds)<br>PWHT of cold-formed parts (which shall be avoided as far as possible). | For suitable piping class selection see Standard Form Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.84-Gen. |
| "B" | | PWHT of welds (including attachment welds)<br>PWHT of cold-formed parts (which shall be avoided as far as possible). | |
| "C" | | None | |

All attachment welds shall be made before any required PWHT is applied.

For steam tracing, Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.30.11-Gen shall apply.

Hot spots due to direct wall-to-wall contact with steam or electric tracing shall be avoided by fitting spacers (ceramic, glass fibre or filled phenolic resin).

All drawings for the fabrication of carbon steel piping intended for this service shall be clearly marked "SODIUM HYDROXIDE SERVICE".

Pipe supports shall comply with Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.29-Gen. Supports shall not be welded to the pipe. Insulation strips (e.g. glass-fibre material) shall be fitted between pipes and supports.

#### 10.1.2    Fabrication

Gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW) shall be used for piping DN 50 and smaller and for the root pass of larger size piping.

Required PWHT shall be performed in accordance with ASME B31.3. Cooling shall be controlled to a maximum rate of 100°C per hour down to 350°C. The complete PWHT cycle shall be recorded.

#### 10.1.3    Identification

Piping shall be clearly marked after prefabrication, either by painting or by applying adhesive tape, to indicate that it is for sodium hydroxide service and to indicate that PWHT is required for all welds.

The piping class number and the pipe designation shall be painted on each part.

![Figure 10.1 Material selection for sodium hydroxide service](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/figures/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0118_fig01_material-selection-sodium-hydroxide-serv.png)

## 10.2 SULPHURIC ACID SERVICE

### 10.2.1 Design

Piping shall be sized for a nominal velocity of 0.75 m/s in straight sections and designed to avoid sudden changes in flow direction, turbulence and extreme changes in velocity. The use of pipe bends and elbows shall be restricted as far as possible. Pipe bends shall have a radius of at least 5D (where D is the nominal pipe diameter). For the fabrication of sweep-in connections, standard long-radius elbows (DN 80 or larger) shall be used.

Horizontal pipes shall be self-draining, having a slope of at least 1 cm/m.

45° laterals, Y-type or sweep-in junctions shall be used for branches.

Reducers should be avoided. If used, reducers shall be concentric, except in a horizontal pipe where a concentric reducer could inhibit drainage (i.e. where the diameter change is in the direction of drainage), in which case an eccentric reducer (bottom flat) should be used. The reduced bore shall match the connecting bore.

In carbon steel systems where turbulence or unacceptably high velocities cannot be avoided, spool pieces of fully corrosion-resistant unlined material (approved by the materials engineer of the Principal) or carbon steel lined with fully-resistant material (PTFE or polypropylene) shall be used (e.g. piping class x8070 or x8160). The length of such spool pieces shall be at least 20 D.

Flat ring gaskets, with ID dimensions matching the bore of the pipes, shall be used. The OD dimensions shall be in accordance with ASME B16.21. Gasket thickness shall be 1.5 mm.

All drawings for the fabrication of carbon steel piping intended for this service shall be clearly marked "SULPHURIC ACID SERVICE".

### 10.2.2 Fabrication

GTAW shall be used for piping DN 50 and smaller and for the root pass of larger size piping.

Junctions shall be arranged with the branch 'set into' the run pipe. Adequate weld preparation shall be made to ensure full penetration of the welds.

### 10.2.3 Identification

Piping shall be clearly marked after prefabrication, either by painting or by applying adhesive tape, to indicate that it is for sulphuric acid service.

The piping class number and the pipe designation shall be painted on each part.

## 10.3 CHLORINE SERVICE

### 10.3.1 Design

This Section specifies additional requirements for the design, construction and testing of carbon steel piping systems for "dry" chlorine, in either the liquid or gaseous phase, at temperatures between -35°C and +70°C. "Dry" chlorine is defined as containing less than 150 mg/kg of water.

Chlorine shall be treated as a very toxic substance.

Piping class 31271 shall be selected for process piping in dry chlorine service, including vent and relief pipes. Industry Source 08 Doc 30.10.02.31-Gen. shall also apply.

Only Schedule 80 seamless pipe of minimum size DN 20 shall be used to ensure rigidity and for protection against mechanical damage resulting in possible leaks.

Piping arrangements shall be as simple as possible, with a minimum of welded or flanged connections. For pipe of DN 100 and smaller, pipe bending should be applied rather than using elbows.

Horizontal pipes shall be self-draining with a slope of at least 1 cm/m.

Liquid chlorine has a high coefficient of thermal expansion. Due to thermal expansion a pressure rise in a locked system could cause a rupture. Therefore the pipe or pipe section shall have an expansion chamber and a pressure relief valve or rupture disc discharging to a receiver. The expansion chamber capacity shall be at least 20% of the section volume and shall be based on a temperature rise of 27°C above the ambient temperature.

The number of field welds shall be minimised.

### 10.3.2 Fabrication

GTAW shall be used for piping DN 50 and smaller and for the root pass of larger size piping.

All welds shall be inspected in accordance with the "very toxic" category in Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.31-Gen.

### 10.3.3 Testing and preparation for use

Hydrostatic testing shall be carried out before the system is finally cleaned and dried, so test gaskets should be used. Prior to pressure testing, gauges, relief valves and other components which may be damaged should be removed and their openings blocked off.

After the hydrostatic test has been performed, the flange gaskets shall be replaced. Where required, valves shall be removed to enable drying of the system.

All parts of chlorine piping systems shall be cleaned prior to use since chlorine can react violently with oil, grease or other foreign materials. See Industry Source 08 Doc 70.10.80.11-Gen. for cleaning methods.

Before installation, valves shall be tested for seat tightness with clean, dry air at a pressure of at least 10 bar (ga).

The cleaned and dried piping system shall be pressurised with dry air or nitrogen to 10 bar (ga) and tested for leaks by applying soapy water to the outside of joints. Afterwards, chlorine gas should be introduced and the system re-tested for leaks as described below:

The location of a leak in a chlorine-containing system can be detected by the reaction of ammonia vapour with the escaping chlorine, the reaction giving a dense white cloud. The most convenient way is to direct the ammonia vapour at the suspect leak employing a plastic squeeze bottle containing aqueous ammonia. Liquid aqueous ammonia shall not be allowed to come into contact with piping components.

If any repair welding is needed after the system has been filled with chlorine, all system piping shall be thoroughly purged with dry air and checked inside and around the pipe with a gas-test tube to verify the absence of chlorine.

Carbon steel ignites in chlorine at 250 °C. A small flow of air shall be maintained during the welding operation.

### 10.3.4 Identification

Piping shall be clearly marked after prefabrication, either by painting or by applying adhesive tape, to indicate that it is for chlorine service.

The piping class number and the pipe designation shall be painted on each part.

## 10.4 HYDROGEN FLUORIDE SERVICE

This Section addresses materials selection, design, fabrication and testing of piping in hydrogen fluoride (HF) service.

HF shall be treated as a very toxic substance.

### 10.4.1 Design

Fine grain carbon steel piping (piping class 31310) shall be used for:

- Dry liquid and gaseous HF at ambient temperature.
- Mixtures of HF, hydrocarbons (and some water) as they occur in the HF alkylation process used for the production of iso-octane and detergent alkylates:
  - hydrocarbons, with up to 33% HF and traces (up to 15 mg/kg) of water, up to 70 °C
  - hydrocarbons, with up to 4% HF and traces (up to 15 mg/kg) of water, up to 160 °C
  - hydrocarbons, with traces of HF, up to 200 °C

Monel piping (piping class 36080) shall be used for:

- HF, with up to 4% hydrocarbons and 0.5% to 2.0% wt. water, up to 100 °C
- HF, with acid-soluble oil and 0.5% to 2.0% wt. water, up to 145 °C

Expansion bellows shall not be used. All connections shall be welded or flanged; however, flanged connections shall be reduced to the least possible number to avoid leakages.

All flanges shall be painted with one coat of HF-detecting paint and shall not be insulated.

All valves and instruments shall be located at an elevation of maximum 1 metre above the working floor for safe and easy handling during operation and maintenance.

To prevent possible deposition of iron fluoride hampering the operation, the valve types shall be selected as follows:

- Globe valves with Monel trim and soft seats (PTFE) for valves which are normally in the closed position.
- Plug valves with Monel plug and PTFE sleeve for valves which are normally in the open position.

All HF service piping shall be installed above grade and shall be self-draining (minimum slope 1 cm/m) to equipment or low point drains.

Process pipes should be at least DN 25. Drains and vents should be at least DN 20.

Drains and vents shall be connected to a closed system.

All control valves in HF service shall be installed with block valves and a bypass globe valve and shall have a flush connection on both sides of the control valves.

Level indicators shall be of the magnetic type. Gauge glasses shall not be used.

### 10.4.2 Fabrication

All welds shall be PWHT (excluding non-pressure attachment welds). Carbon steel welds shall be PWHT in accordance with ASME B31.3. Monel welds shall be PWHT at a temperature between 560°C and 580°C for 1 hour.

All welds shall be inspected in accordance with the "very toxic" category in Industry Source 08 Doc 31.38.01.31-Gen.

### 10.4.3 Inspection

Piping shall be clearly marked after prefabrication, either by painting or by applying adhesive tape, to indicate that it is for HF service and to indicate that PWHT is required for all welds.

The piping class number and the pipe designation shall be painted on each part.

### 10.4.4 Operation and maintenance

The wearing of protective clothes, gloves, goggles, etc., is particularly critical and it shall be ensured that all safety instructions are strictly observed.

Before flanges of piping in HF service are disconnected, they shall be neutralized by means of ammonia or sodium bicarbonate to prevent HF contact with the skin.

Even if severe corrosion is not experienced, fouling and heavy iron fluoride deposits are often present. Neutralisation of such thick fouling layers is rather difficult and after they have subsequently been removed mechanically, acidic conditions may again be encountered underneath due to insufficient neutralisation. If the acidity is such that it is unsafe to continue work, further neutralisation shall be carried out.

## 10.5 OXYGEN SERVICE

For gaseous oxygen systems, see Industry Source 08 Doc 31.10.11.31-Gen.

## 10.6 "WET H₂S" / "SOUR" SERVICE

This Section governs the selection of piping classes and the selection and testing of carbon steel piping materials in order to mitigate or avoid the effects of aqueous hydrogen charging in "Wet H₂S" or "Sour" process environments (see their definitions below). Types of material damage that can occur as a result of aqueous hydrogen charging include sulphide stress corrosion (SSC) especially in pipe weldments and microstructures, hydrogen blistering, hydrogen induced cracking (HIC) and stress-oriented hydrogen induced cracking (SOHIC).

SSC is the occurrence of brittle fracture under the combined action of stress and H₂S dissolved in water. Hydrogen blistering, HIC and SOHIC are the occurrence of lamellar cracking, often connected or (in the case of HIC and SOHIC) propagating in a stepwise manner. Hydrogen blistering, HIC and SOHIC are most commonly associated with plate or strip product steels and are much less common in seamless pipe or wrought products (although HIC has been experienced in seamless products having a poor microstructure due to incorrect chemistry or heat treatment). Furthermore, in some high pH refinery process streams a form of alkaline stress corrosion cracking (ASCC) may occur. ASCC is normally mitigated by applying PWHT to welds and cold formed products.

### 10.6.1 Definitions of Wet H₂S/Sour Service and Materials Requirements

"Wet H₂S" service is the term commonly used for refinery and gas plant (Industry Source 08 GSI) environments containing water and H₂S (plus other corrosives or contaminants), whereas "Sour" service is the term traditionally used for similar environments in exploration and production (SIEP) services.

However, the chemical composition of the environments is often quite different, and these differences are described in (10.6.2) and (10.6.8).

Although the definitions of these services differ between Industry Source 08 GSI and SIEP, the approach to materials selection and testing has been standardised and is described in the piping classes specifically designated for "Sour" service and in the referenced MESC piping specifications.

In terms of material specifications, SIEP "Sour" service is equivalent to Refinery/Gas Plant "High Sour" service.

### 10.6.2 "Sour" service (E&P applications)

A "Sour" piping class shall be selected to prevent the occurrence of SSC and HIC if:

- Sour conditions, as defined in ISO 15156, prevail; **or**
- In gas-containing systems, the partial pressure of H₂S exceeds 0.0035 bar (abs); **or**
- In liquid containing systems, the concentration of H₂S is higher than that occurring in a liquid equilibrium with a gas containing H₂S at a partial pressure of 0.0035 bar (abs).

**and:**

- the temperature has to be between 0°C and 65°C; **and**
- the pH of the liquid has to be lower than 7; **and**
- an electrolyte (typically an aqueous phase) is normally in contact with the steel.

NOTES: 1. NACE MR0175 is equivalent to ISO 15156.

2 Sour piping classes are identified by the word "Sour" in the title box.

## 10.6.3 "Wet H₂S" service (refinery/gas plant applications)

All carbon steel piping in refineries and gas plants exposed to wet H₂S process streams shall be designed and manufactured to resist the potential cracking mechanisms caused by the generation of free hydrogen in an aqueous corrosion reaction.

In refinery streams containing free water and H₂S, the pH is often around 6 or higher due to the presence of ammonia. Trace quantities of contaminants such as chloride or fluoride may also be present, which form ammonium salts (ammonium chloride and ammonium fluoride). Cyanides also play an important role in refinery streams as they can breakdown iron sulphide scale and possibly cause hydrogen pick-up. In high pH streams containing significant levels of sulphide and carbonate, the pressures shall be taken to prevent carbonate cracking, which is a form of alkaline stress corrosion cracking (ASCC).

Piping classes should be selected according to the potential damage mechanism(s) anticipated or experienced in the service and the severity of the process environment (potential level of hydrogen flux and/or carbonates).

Tables 1A, 1B and 1C should be used to assess the severity of the process environment as applicable to the type of damage mechanism being considered.

NOTE: Tables 1A, 1B and 1C assume that the environment being considered is present during normal operations. Short term upsets should only be considered if the damage mechanism anticipated or experienced is also likely to occur in the short term. If in doubt, the materials engineer of the Principal shall be consulted.

Table 2 summarises the materials selection and PWHT requirements for the potential damage mechanisms in the different severity categories.

### TABLE 1A  SUSCEPTIBILITY TO SSC

If there is no free water likely to be present then the material is **not** considered susceptible to SSC.

If water is likely to be present, the pH is greater than 4.0 and the cyanide level is low, then the following table should be used to estimate the severity category with respect to SSC. Process conditions outside these ranges should be further assessed for hydrogen blistering, HIC and SOHIC severity by means of Table 1B.

> **Table - TABLE 1A SUSCEPTIBILITY TO SSC** - see [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0123_tbl01_table-1a-susceptibility-to-ssc.png)

| 5.5 to 7.5 | (Note 2) | Low | Low | Moderate |
| 7.6 to 7.9 | < 50 | Low | Moderate | High |
| ≥ 8.0 | < 20 | Low | Moderate | High |

2. The level of cyanide has no significance at pH 7.5 and below.

| | **LOW** | **MODERATE** | **HIGH** |
| **MATERIALS AND PWHT REQUIREMENTS** | | | |
| SSC (Table 1A) | Select a normal carbon steel piping class, with no additional requirements | "Moderate sour" service requirements (see Note 2) | "Moderate sour" service requirements (see Note 2) |
| Hydrogen blistering, HIC and SOHIC (Table 1B) | Not Applicable | "Moderate sour" service requirements (see Note 2) | "High Sour" service requirements (see Note 3) |
| Carbonate Cracking (Table 1C) | "Moderate sour" service requirements (see Note 2) | "Moderate sour" service requirements (see Note 2) + PWHT (see Note 4) | "Moderate sour" service requirements (see Note 2) + PWHT (see Note 4) |

NOTES

1. Potential mechanisms are not exclusive, i.e. if there is more than one mechanism active, the materials and PWHT requirements may have to be combined to address the severity of more than one environment. For example, the fractionator overheads in a Fluidized Catalytic Cracking Unit (FCCU) may have a high severity for hydrogen blistering, HIC, SOHIC and carbonate cracking and in such a case the requirements for materials and PWHT shall be combined.

2. For "Moderate Sour" service, the piping classes shall satisfy the following:

   - seamless carbon steel pipe (ASTM A 106 grade B or ASTM A 333 grade 6);
   - seamless carbon steel fittings (ASTM A 234-WPB or ASTM A 420 WPL6);
   - if welded carbon steel pipe and fittings are used they shall be made from HIC-tested plate;
   - valves complying with NACE MR0103;
   - valves with AISI 316 + stellite trim;
   - normal bolting (ASTM A 193 B7 and ASTM A 194-2H); flanges shall not be insulated.

3. For "High Sour" service, the piping classes are identified by the word "Sour" in the title box. These piping classes shall satisfy the following:

   - seamless carbon steel pipe and fittings with low sulphur content (0.010% maximum);
   - if welded carbon steel pipe and fittings are used they shall be made from HIC-tested plate;
   - valves complying with NACE MR0103;
   - valves with AISI 316 + stellite trim;
   - sour bolting (ASTM A 193-B7M and ASTM A 194-2HM).

   Additional mitigation measures, such as injection of polysulphide or inhibitors, may be required; the materials engineer of the Principal shall be consulted.

4. PWHT indicates a requirement for postweld heat treatment of all shop and field piping welds. All welded piping products require PWHT or normalisation of the weld seam during manufacturing.

## APPENDIX 12 FLANGE FACE ALIGNMENT

1. TYPES OF ALIGNMENT

Two types of alignment are recognised:

- **Lateral alignment**, that is the off-set of the aligned flange centrelines, applicable to the complete flange set as well as the relative positioning of bolt holes.
- **Parallelism** of the aligned flange faces, sometimes referred to as angular alignment.

2. SET UP PRIOR TO MEASUREMENT

- The flanges shall be lined up so that the bolts can be inserted without force.
- A gasket and 25 percent of the bolts (with at least four) shall be inserted. The bolts shall be uniformly tightened using manual spanners to take out the free slack, to ensure the real misalignment will be measured.

3. ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA FOR MISALIGNMENT

### 3.1 Lateral alignment

For standard flanges, the free insertion of the bolts is generally sufficient to demonstrate acceptable alignment. Lateral alignment may also be checked by laying a straight edge along the outside diameter of the flange. Measurements should be taken at locations 90° apart around the flange circumference.

The measured lateral misalignment shall not exceed the following values:

> **Table - Maximum lateral misalignment values by DN** - see [XLSX](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0128_tbl01_maximum-lateral-misalignment-by-dn.xlsx) and [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0128_tbl01_maximum-lateral-misalignment-by-dn.png)

| DN | Maximum misalignment |
| :--- | :--- |
| ≤ 100 | 2 mm |
| > 100 | 3 mm |

Bolt holes shall straddle the natural centreline unless specified otherwise. The maximum deviation from the required theoretical bolt hole position, as measured along the bolt circle, shall be 1.5 mm.

### 3.2 Parallelism

Flange face alignment shall be checked by measuring the distance between the mating flanges of the pre-assembled joint. Measurements shall be taken around the circumference at equal distances from the centre line (the outside rim of the flange will normally be the most convenient position).

The difference between the measurements shall not exceed the following values:

(a) ASME B16.5 flanges, all sizes all, all ratings:

2.5 mm/m

Note: This is more stringent than the ASME B31.3 requirement of 5 mm/m but it has been found realistic to achieve these limits with little or no additional manufacturing effort.

(b) ASME B16.47 flanges, all sizes, all ratings:

Table 1 gives these values computed for the flange rim outside diameter.

1.75 mm absolute (regardless of the diameter), measured along the outside diameter of the raised face.

Tables 2 and 3 give these values computed for measurements along the flange rim *outside* diameter.

(c) Flanged pipe spools

The misalignment tolerances given in (a) and (b) above apply to pairs of pre-assembled flanges. For the terminal flange of a pipe spool, the misalignment can only be measured as the deviation from the design plane. Instead of simply halving the allowed tolerance for pre-assembled flanges, allowance should be made for the possibility that the misalignment of an individual flange can be in either direction and the misalignment of its eventual mating flange may compensate. Therefore, a statistical factor is appropriate, so that for the terminal flange of a pipe spool the deviation from the design plane shall not exceed $\frac{M}{2} \sqrt{2}$ (+0.7M), where M is the allowable misalignment for the pre-assembled flanges as given in (a) and (b) above.

(d) Flanged accessories

Accessories are flanged items which are rigid in themselves (e.g. valves, strainers etc.). The individual flange face misalignment from the design plane shall not exceed 2.5 mm/m. Also, the misalignment of the two flange faces shall not exceed 2.5 mm/m.

(e) Face alignment for flange-less components (e.g. wafer type control valves, sandwiched between flanges): Misalignment as per (a) and (b) above.

(f) Nozzle faces on static equipment.

Alignment of nozzle flange face with the indicated plane shall be within 0.5° in any direction.

NOTE: This tolerance is in line with that specified in Industry Source 08 Doc 31.22.10.32-Gen. and Industry Source 08 Doc 31.20.20.31-Gen.

(g) Flanges connecting to rotating equipment (pumps, compressors etc)

The flange face alignment check shall be performed with bolting inserted loosely, and the acceptance criteria shall be as given below:

> **Table - Flange diameter \(DN\) vs Maximum misalignment at OD of flange** - see [source crop](01-overall-piping-design-standards/_assets/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08/tables/01-overall-piping-design-standards-08_p0129_tbl01_flange-diameter-misalignment.png)

| Flange diameter (DN) | Maximum misalignment at OD of flange |
| :--- | :--- |
| < 300 | 0.2 mm |
| 300 to 600 | 0.3 mm |
| ≥ 600 | 0.5 mm |

NOTE: *The above figures are the practical implementation of the tolerances specified in the relevant rotating equipment Industry Source 08 Doc(i.e. 0.05° in all directions).*

## APPENDIX 14    MINIMUM REQUIRED WALL THICKNESS

This Appendix specifies the minimum required wall thickness for API 5L grade B and ASTM A 106 grade B pipe in the following pipe sizes:

DN 25, DN 40, DN 50, DN 80, DN 100, DN 150, DN 200, DN 250, DN 300, DN 350, DN 400, DN 450, DN 500 and DN 600.

**CAUTION:** *THIS APPENDIX SHALL NOT BE USED IF STRESS CORROSION CRACKING IS POSSIBLE DUE TO THE FLUID SERVICE OR THE ENVIRONMENT. THE INCREASED STRESSES DUE TO WALL THINNING COULD EXCEED THE THRESHOLD VALUE AND INITIATE STRESS CORROSION CRACKING.*

Thicknesses below those specified in this Appendix shall not be permitted without further analysis (which may permit localised thinner areas).

The thicknesses specified in this Appendix are not suitable in situations where additional stresses may be expected on the piping system, e.g. stresses caused by thermal expansion, settling or wind loads. In situations where the pipe is directly resting on the supporting structure, unacceptably high stresses and/or deformation may occur in the pipe at the support.

Future corrosion allowance shall be taken into account when deciding to reject or accept pipes using this Appendix.

This minimum required wall thickness is given for different pressure/temperature ratings and are based on the following:

- Material strength and internal pressure calculations in accordance with ASME B31.3. In these calculations a quality factor E = 0.85 has been applied. The wall thicknesses shown in *normal type* font are based on *mechanical strength*. The wall thicknesses shown in ***bold italics*** are based on *internal pressure*.

- Mechanical strength calculations are based on the maximum permitted span as defined in Appendix 11. In order to simulate external forces, an additional load in the middle of the free span has been taken into account. The free span and load used in the calculations is shown below each table.

- Full vacuum to AD Merkblatter B 6.

### 01-overall-piping-design-standards-09

# 100   General Information

**Abstract**

Piping is the bond that holds together any industrial facility, large or small. However, because of its undramatic presence piping is often taken for granted.

In fact, piping operability, ease of maintenance and, moreover, cost and safety are primary concerns. Piping is typically 20 to 25% of total plant cost, and 10% of all fires within the Corporation are related to piping. Good piping design always balances operation, maintenance, and cost. Proper design is as necessary for piping as it is for the equipment it connects.

The *Piping Manual* is a guide for the basic design and construction of piping systems. It focuses on design fundamentals, guidelines for practical installations, and specification and purchase of materials and services. It is applicable to large and small facilities whether used for upstream production, downstream refining, chemical manufacture, offshore production or marketing. Its guidelines encompass the experience of the Corporation's Operating Companies. The manual's broad applicability makes it useful to both engineers and operating personnel.

The *Piping Manual* is concerned only with piping systems in stations and plants. It does not provide design information for pipelines. The manual includes certain topics related to operations and maintenance, but not a comprehensive description of these functions.

## 110 Codes and Industry Practices

The various piping codes (such as ASME/ANSI B31.1 and B31.3 in the United States) contain practices necessary for safe piping systems, but are not intended to be complete specifications for all phases of design. The Company recognizes this fact, and the guidelines and specifications in this manual provide the supplemental requirements normally needed to obtain economical systems for basic fluid services. A few requirements—where experience has shown them to be better choices—are more stringent than code minimums. Engineers responsible for design and construction of piping systems are expected to be familiar with and to comply with the appropriate codes even though some of their provisions may not be specifically included in this manual.

## 111 Piping Code History

The American Standards Association Code for Pressure Piping, ASA B31.1, 1942 through 1955, was for many years a guide for design, fabrication, erection, and testing of industrial piping. Early on, the Company recognized this code as an acceptable basic standard. The Operating Companies and the Engineering Department subsequently developed numerous standards, specifications, and design practices to supplement and extend the Code provisions.

In 1955, the ASA recognized that a single volume of code provisions would no longer meet the growing and divergent needs of industry. It was decided to issue separately bound sections of the ASA Piping Code—each section covering the piping requirements for a major industry. In 1966, the ASA was reorganized as the United States of America Standards Institute (USASI), and in 1969 the name was changed to the American National Standards Institute (ANSI).

Plans for a separate Chemical Industry Process Piping Code (B31.6) were discontinued when by mutual industry agreement both requirements were incorporated into ANSI B31.3. In December 1978, American National Standards Committee B31 was reorganized as the ASME Code for Pressure Piping, B31, Committee under procedures developed by The American Society of Mechanical Engineers and accredited by ANSI. The code designation was also changed to ANSI/ASME B31.

The applicable sections of ASME/ANSI B31 are:

- B31.1 Power Piping
- B31.2 Fuel Gas Piping
- B31.3 Chemical Plant and Petroleum Refinery Piping
- B31.4 Liquid Petroleum Transportation Piping Systems
- B31.5 Refrigeration Piping
- B31.8 Gas Transmission and Distribution Piping Systems
- B31.9 Building Services Piping
- B31.11 Slurry Pipelines
- B31G Manual for Determining the Remaining Strength of Corroded Pipelines: A Supplement to B31, Codes for Pressure Piping

## 112 Code Application

The Corporation Piping Specification (GB135169) and the on-plot specifications discussed in Sections 700 and 800 use ASME/ANSI B31.3 as their principal basis. Producing Department off-plot piping is covered in the *Pipeline Manual*.

The Corporation Piping Specification also includes specifications for two pipe classes for steam boiler external piping to the first block valve that comply with the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section I. This code is discussed in Section 120.

## 120 Government Regulations

Engineers responsible for design and construction of piping in the United States are expected to determine which codes are legally required and if there are any other federal, state, or local regulations governing such construction. The Company requires compliance with the most stringent practice.

In general, piping that conforms with ASME/ANSI B31.3 and the Corporation Piping Specification will meet the legal requirements in North America for refineries, loading terminals, and gas, natural gasoline, bulk, and chemical plants. Similarly, conformance with ASME/ANSI B31.3 and piping specifications cited in Sections 700 and 800 generally assures legal conformance for producing facilities in North America.

All sections of ASME/ANSI B31 have been adopted by most provinces of Canada. Some sections, including B31.3, have also been adopted by some states and localities in the United States; however, it is not a legal requirement in most states.

## 121 OSHA Compliance

In the United States, compliance with the Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSHA) is mandatory. Other countries have similar legislation. For general petroleum industry piping, *the major effect of OSHA is on construction safety and to forbid the use of regular cast iron for flammable or combustible liquids having a flash point below 200°F, or a temperature within 30°F of their flash point. Steel, ductile cast iron or malleable cast iron are required.* The details of OSHA regulations are still changing, and the most recent revision should be reviewed.

OSHA regulations strongly encourage use of the B31 codes by stating that compliance with B31 codes and specific OSHA rules is prima facie evidence of compliance with the basic requirements of OSHA.

## 122 Boiler Piping

Many state and local regulations require piping immediately connected to a boiler or steam generator to conform to ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section I, Power Boilers. The engineer responsible for the design and construction of steam generating facilities should refer to ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section I,

to ASME/ANSI B31.1 Figure 100.1.2, and to local regulations to determine their jurisdictional limits. ASME/ANSI B31.3 specifically covers steam piping beyond the mandatory limits of B31.1 and, unless local regulations require otherwise, is used for such steam piping.

## 123 Pipeline Applications

U.S. Government Code of Federal Regulations, Title 49, Part 192 (49CFR192) and Part 195 (49CFR195), cover interstate oil piping and essentially all gas transportation piping. The minimum design requirements for oil and gas pipelines are defined in 49CFR192 and 49CFR195. However, ASME/ANSI B31.4 and B31.8 provide supplemental design information, and their use is recommended. In case of conflict, the applicable part of 49CFR governs. These requirements are detailed in the *Pipeline Manual*.

## 124 Foreign Applications

For installations outside the United States and Canada, the engineer responsible for piping design and construction should determine if there are national or local regulations pertaining to piping design. For consistency in engineering and fabrication ASME/ANSI B31 is preferred over local rules, unless local rules are more stringent. The ASME/ANSI codes remain good guidelines where no other regulations exist.

# 130 Company Practices

## 131 Corporation Piping Specification

Piping components are designed and fabricated according to current standards and codes established by national bodies such as the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) and the American National Standards Institute (ANSI). The Corporation Piping Specification, developed and used by design groups and operations units within the Company, is based on these standards and codes.

Piping codes prescribe minimum practices necessary for safety. They are not complete specifications. The Corporation Piping Specification adds requirements normally needed to obtain safe and economical piping systems for basic fluid services.

The Corporation Piping Specification (GB135169) was developed for process facilities. The specification covers services encountered in most of the Company's operating facilities.

The Corporation Piping Specification is based on experience, judgment, and economics; use it as a guide for the design of safe and economical piping systems. It is not mandatory. The Specification meets or exceeds ASME/ANSI B31 requirements, and the engineer responsible for design and construction may modify the

recommendations, within the constraints of local legal requirements, when a particular situation warrants it.

The pipe classes included in the Specification cover most low pressure hydrocarbon and utility services. However, they do not include pipe classes for all possible requirements.

Examples of services **not** covered are:

- Chemicals (except sodium hydroxide, concentrated sulfuric acid, monoethanolamine (MEA) and CO₂ mixtures)
- Hydrogen above 425°F (alloy may be required for metallurgical stability) or over 50% by volume
- Temperatures above 750°F, which require an alloy to prevent graphitization of carbon steel
- Corrosive hydrocarbons that require an alloy for corrosion protection (for example, piping systems containing acids or high temperature H₂S)
- Low temperature services—below about 30°F (special material may be required for thick components even above 30°F)
- Piping above NPS 24 in Class 150 and Class 300 flange ratings and over NPS 16 in Class 600
- Boiler code piping above Class 600 flange rating

For these situations or other unique services, the piping engineer can develop his own pipe classes and consult with CRTC's Materials and Equipment Engineering - Technical Services.

## 132 Creating Piping Specifications for Projects

A project piping specification is created to provide a concise record of the basic piping components used in the numerous utility and hydrocarbon process services required for new facilities. Individual class sheets segregate the different services with their respective design conditions and list the selection of piping components.

The creation of a piping specification for a specific project begins with a process flow diagram (PFD), which outlines the essential operating conditions and primary equipment required to produce the process. It provides the information needed to choose of major equipment and piping, and it identifies the principal chemical characteristics of the process stream. CRTC's Materials and Equipment Engineering group uses the latter information to make material recommendations for individual piping systems, including corrosion allowance and valve trim. The recommendation is provided in a Material Selection Report.

The following are developed from the process flow diagram: (1) Piping and Instrument Diagrams (P&IDs), (2) a Plot Plan, and (3) a Project Piping Specification. The P&IDs show the instrumentation, control features, ancillary piping, and the pipe

class and line identification system. The Plot Plan establishes equipment location and pipeway routing so that distance and elevation can be determined.

The Project Piping Specification can be developed from a computer data base used for the Corporation Piping Specification. This data base is occasionally up-dated and should always be reviewed for new project applications.

Additional piping class sheets can be developed either from scratch or from a previous project that had a similar process. ASME/ANSI B31, Section 200 of this manual, and the *Fluid Flow Manual* will help you calculate the required pipe wall thickness and pipe diameter needed to satisfy the design conditions. Pressure calculations can be done manually using Standard Form Industry Source 02 Doc EF-539, Wall Thickness Calculations.

When developing a piping class you must stay within the ASME/ANSI standards for flange rating and pipe wall thickness. Otherwise, you are creating a special design with engineered items. Pipe and fittings that are not commercial mill production or valves that are not standard manufacturer's models entail additional expense and extended delivery schedules. They are not generally economical except in very large quantities. Nonstandard items also create a need for field segregation, identification, and for additional project spare parts. Future maintenance on nonstandard items can often be complicated because of long delivery schedules for parts.

For new classes, be sure to review the branch reinforcing and change of direction tables for design adequacy and component selection. Contact CRTC's Materials and Equipment Engineering - Technical Services for guidance.

## 133 Piping Item Description Database

The *Piping Item Description Database* contains material ordering descriptions for piping components referenced on the individual class sheets of the Corporation Piping Specification. Piping items that appear in other published Corporation standards are also included. The database is no longer reviewed or updated. Updates now normally occur only when current projects request that specific items be reviewed.

Corporation piping class sheets list an alphanumeric identification code (commonly referred to as an L-number) opposite each item description. These abbreviated references are intended to provide concise information for draftsmen and designers. They are not complete enough for procurement.

Piping components (pipe, valves, fittings) require lengthy descriptions for purchase orders. To save space and time on drawings, the ordering information for each component has been assigned a Industry Source 02 alphanumeric code (L-number). The L-numbers and the corresponding ordering descriptions standardize the content and notation in descriptions and provide a reliable, independently reproducible file on components. Projects can maintain a cumulative record of individual items and produce a project material list. The *Database* covers standard items that are produced routinely by manufacturers. It does not cover "engineered" items that are considered project specific.

The ordering description for each piping component includes material, process of manufacture, pressure rating, physical attributes, manufacturer, special trim or construction, etc. The full ordering description (long) is used to place an order.

The Industry Source 02 L-numbers are generated from a comprehensive classification index that segregates piping components in a systematic order. The item coding requires 5 to 9 alphanumeric characters, depending on the type of component. Each code character describes a particular feature of the component and the complete item code chronicles the significant identifying features. The heart of the coding system is the classification index found in the first section of the *Piping Item Description Database* under the tab "Index." Refer to the "Foreword" for an example of how the description is categorized.

Piping components cannot be created simply by the construction of an L-number. The items must already exist as a manufactured item conforming to one of the national or industrial standards (ASME, ANSI, API, MSS) that will satisfy the requirements of the ASME/ANSI B31 section used as the design basis. The manufacturer should be technically and commercially acceptable.

The *Piping Item Description Database* valve descriptions contain figure and/or model numbers obtained from published information provided by the manufacturers. Most valve manufacturers print a disclaimer indicating that they reserve the right to change their catalog without notice. Because of this, the full text of the item description on your purchase order is especially important.

Minimum inspection requirements are normally inherent in the purchase order if one of the national standards (e.g., ASME, ANSI, API, MSS) has been included in the ordering description. Additional inspection and nondestructive examination may be required because of process conditions. These requirements can normally be handled by one of the notes located in the "Material Ordering Description Notes" pages of the Database.

Item selections should be based on three considerations relating to process conditions (1) type of material, (2) design pressure, and (3) design temperature. Technical consulting services dealing with material selection, piping components, ASME/ANSI piping codes, acceptable manufacturers, and quality assurance are available through CRTC's Materials and Equipment Engineering group. Related commercial information is available through Industry Source 02 Purchasing Department.

During the course of a project, distributors or alternate manufacturers will offer "equal to" items. Prudent bid evaluation is highly recommended with the burden of proof for documentation placed on the bidder. A good way to limit the number of "equal to" evaluations is to request quotations from only those who represent the manufacturers already reviewed by CRTC's Materials and Equipment Engineering - Quality Assurance.

The Company uses engineering specifications for purchasing piping components and for fabrication and construction. Some of these specifications, in "Commented" format, are located in Volume II of this manual. They are:

**Fabrication and Construction Specifications**
