## C7.0 Attachment A: Vibration Analysis of Stiff Appurtenances with Multiple Valves or Fittings

For appurtenances consisting of two or more heavy high pressure valves or fittings separated by short piping nipples, calculating the natural frequency may be difficult and might not reveal a potential vibration problem. The following example provides an analysis method for this situation based on observation following plant startup.

### Example

**Problem:** Two ¾-inch, Class 1500, Y-pattern valves are to be attached at a low point of a 20-inch diameter pipe as shown in Figure C-4. The pipe contains a two-phase slug flow mixture of gas oil, and hydrogen. Will piping vibration cause the appurtenance to fail by fatigue?

![Fig. C-4 — Example of a Stiff Appurtenance](07-stress-flexibility-and-mechanical-analysis/_assets/07-stress-flexibility-and-mechanical-analysis-03/figures/07-stress-flexibility-and-mechanical-analysis-03_p0014_fig01_fig-c-4-example-of-a-stiff-appurtenance.png)

![Fig. C-5 — Mathematical Model of Figure C-4 Example](07-stress-flexibility-and-mechanical-analysis/_assets/07-stress-flexibility-and-mechanical-analysis-03/figures/07-stress-flexibility-and-mechanical-analysis-03_p0014_fig02_fig-c-5-mathematical-model-of-figure-c-4.png)

**Solution:** Two-phase slug flow will cause the pipe and appurtenance to vibrate. To determine criteria for observation after plant startup the appurtenance is modeled as shown in Figure C-5, where the appurtenance is assumed rigid and the mass of each valve is slumped at a distance from the appurtenance base corresponding to the valve center of mass. From basic vibration theory, the amplitude of a sinusoidal force required to move a lumped mass with an acceleration *a* is given by:

F = ma

(Eq. C-2)

where:

f = force

m = mass

a = acceleration

---

applying a corresponding force to each mass in Figure C-5, the moment at any location along the appurtenance can be calculated. The maximum moment, M, occurs at the base and is equal to:

$$M = \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i a_i l_i$$

(Eq. C-3)

where l_i is the distance from the center of the mass of m_i to the location where the stress is to be determined (the appurtenance base in this example). The variable a_i is the acceleration amplitude of m_i. Substituting values for this example:

M = 18 lb (7.5 in.) (386 in./sec²) a_1 +
    18 lb (14.0 in.) (386 in./sec²) a_2

M = 0.35 a_1 + 0.65 a_2

Note that the mass of a component is its weight divided by the acceleration due to gravity, 386 in./sec.² when using units of inches and seconds. The cycle stress at the base is:

$$\sigma_a = \frac{SM}{Z} = \frac{S}{Z} \sum_{i=1}^{n} m_i a_i l_i$$

(Eq. C-4)

where σ_a is the calculated stress amplitude; Z is the section modulus at the location being analyzed; and S is the stress concentration factor due to geometry at the location being analyzed, if applicable.

The section modulus for an annular cross-section is:

$$Z = \frac{\pi}{32 D_o}(D_o^4 - D_i^4)$$

(Eq. C-5)

where D_i and D_o are the inside and outside diameters, respectively. Substituting values for this example:

$$Z = \frac{\pi}{32(2 \text{ in.})}[(2 \text{ in.})^4 - (0.75 \text{ in.})^4]$$

= 0.77 in.³

(Eq. C-6)

---

From Reference [3] the stress concentration factor for the 1-inch radius at the base is approximately 1.2. From Sections C3.0 and C5.0 the maximum allowable stress amplitude is 2250 psi. The design endurance limit for carbon steel given in Figure C-1 is 9000 psi (stress range). This value must be reduced by a factor of 2.0 to increase the factor of safety to 4.0, and an additional factor of 2.0 to convert the endurance limit stress from stress range to stress amplitude.

During plant startup the vibration acceleration amplitude of each mass is measured and evaluated with Equation C-4. The calculated stress must be less than the allowable stress or remedial action should be taken. Substituting the example values for M, Z and S into Equation C-4 gives:

2250 ≥ 0.55 a₁ + 1.01 a₂

It should be noted that the cyclic stresses in the pipe, at the appurtenance base, should also be checked using the moment calculated with Equation C-3. Welding Research Council Bulletin 107 [4] and its supplement, Welding Research Council Bulletin 297 [5] provide the required formulas and data to determine the stresses in the pipe.

[... Suncor Energy logo]

## 1.0 PURPOSE & SCOPE

### 1.1 Purpose

The purpose of this standard is to define the requirements for establishing the design pressure for process piping and vessels.

### 1.2 Scope

This standard identifies the means to determine the maximum upset operating pressure and the design pressure for systems containing expansible fluids. Specifically this standard addresses the requirements for systems protected through mechanical relief (e.g. PSVs) and systems protected by mechanical design. Protection by mechanical relief shall be required for most circumstances. For systems protected by mechanical design, the maximum upset operating pressure shall be rationalized clearly identified in the design documents. Protection by mechanical design shall be utilized only where both of the conditions a) the system is defined as acceptable by this standard and b) mechanical relief is not feasible due to reliability of operation, are simultaneously present.

1.2.1 This standard applies to the following business units that are a part of Suncor Energy Inc:

- Oil Sands
- Refining and Marketing (including Pipelines)
- Natural Gas
- In Situ
- Major Projects

Use of this standard for Business Services, International and Offshore and other Business Units involved in development of technical standards is recommended.

1.2.2 This standard does not cover determination of system design basis and determination of Maximum Upset Operating Pressures for non-expansible fluids. This standard does not cover selection of pressure vessel design basis although the maximum operating pressure as defined by this Standard shall be utilized in the pressure vessel design. The requirements for testing and registering test results of mechanical relief devices is not included in this standard. The design of safeguarding of the system including design of the Safety integrity System (SIS), design of emergency isolation valves, fire protection, etc is not described by this Standard.

### 1.3 Precautions

The decision to proceed with the selection of "protection by mechanical design" should be made only when all other mechanical relief options have been discarded.

If redundant mechanical relief protection systems are provided, isolation valves between the relief and the protected system are acceptable, however one of the redundant relief isolation valves must remain in the open position with a the position locked open with a car seal, (CSO). Closing of any Car Seal Open valves shall be only executed through an approved Management of Change that addresses how the system's mechanical relief protection is maintained (usually through opening and car sealing open another redundant relief valve).

## 4.0 DEFINITIONS AND ACRONYMS

Expansible Fluids – Vapour or Gaseous fluid or a liquid under pressure and temperature that which the liquid changes to a gas when the pressure is reduced to atmospheric pressure or the temperature is raised to ambient temperature while maintaining the specified pressure.

Pressure Vessel – A vessel used for containing, storing, distributing, processing or otherwise handling an expansible fluid with a volume exceeding 42 litres.

Boiler- A vessel in which steam or other vapour may be generated from a liquid under pressure through the direct application of heat. A vessel need not contain a space for vapour to be generated to be considered a boiler.

Reactor – a vessel where chemical compositional changes occur with or without phase change

Mechanical Relief Protection – system overpressure is protected by one or more calibrated device(s) designed to pass the fluid causing overpressure to a safe disposal location at a rate sufficient to maintain pressure containment integrity of the system under review.

Maximum Operating Pressure – the maximum pressure the system can generate when operated according to it's design basis. Since a system may have pressure generators and pressure sinks, the maximum operating pressure may be different for different sections of the system

Maximum Upset Operating Pressure – the greatest pressure generated in a system component resulting from a single jeopardy event.

Single Jeopardy - an aberrant condition or event that adversely affects the system to instigate a system change

Standard 0226, Rev A, Maximum Pressure Design Basis                                                                                                  Page 6 of 16

---

of state exceeding the system design basis. Two or more simultaneous aberrant independent events are considered to be double jeopardy and are not considered in this Standard

MAWP – Maximum Allowable Working Pressure shall be the lesser of the pressure as registered for the equipment or manufacturer's data report.

## 5.0 STANDARD

Determination of Maximum Operating Upset pressure shall be based on the Maximum Operating Pressure. Design pressure shall meet or exceed Maximum Upset Operating Pressure. Design of mechanical components (vessels, equipment, and piping) shall be composed of components that meet or exceed the design pressure. Maximum Upset Operating Pressures shall be considered as short term event (maximum 10 hours per event, maximum 100 hours per year) and the increased allowable stress for piping as described in B31.3 may be utilized in the design for process piping unless noted otherwise in this Standard.

## 5.1 Determination of Maximum Operating Pressure

### 5.1.1 System Configuration Analysis

The system as designed shall be examined on an equipment by equipment basis for the maximum operating pressure through a detailed evaluation of flow rate, temperature range and upstream and downstream conditions. Flow rates for the fluids shall be determined from the system mass and energy balance. Consideration of two or three phase flow under the applicable system pressure and temperature range shall be included in the flow rate determination. Component maximum operating temperature to establish maximum operating pressure shall be based on normal flow conditions. Temperature increases from blocked-in flow conditions need not be considered in analysis of maximum operating pressure.

Maximum operating pressure shall be determined for each component of the system. Maximum operating pressure shall be based on the normal intent of the design where that is defined as the primary system design basis. Primary system design basis shall consider the range in feed conditions (flow, temperature and composition) and the variations in reactor catalyst reactivity, product selection variation in fractionating and distillation columns, and variation in gravity of fluid systems. Fluid pressure shall be determined at the operating process temperature creating the greatest pressure. If the maximum operating pressure does not occur coincident with the highest operating temperature, the pressure at maximum operating temperature shall be documented for the purposes of equipment and piping design in addition to the maximum operating pressure. If the system includes dynamic equipment for pressure generation (eg pumps, compressors, etc), the specific equipment selected for the design shall be utilized to determine operating pressure. ( e.g. the manufacturers pump curve shall be utilized to determine pressure generation in lieu of a theoretical pump curve). Inlet conditions that are most adverse to the dynamic machine's discharge pressure and maximum operating inlet pressure shall be utilized in determination of the maximum operating pressure. Dynamic equipment that reduces system pressure (e.g. turbines etc) shall utilize minimum RPM (or minimum flow passing) for determining upstream pressure. Maximum operating pressure as a minimum must be based on selected equipment but future process changes that would result in a higher maximum operating pressure such as increasing pump impeller size or pump RPM may be included if directed by the responsible Owner's Engineer.

Maximum operating pressure shall consider both normal line-up and blocked-in system configurations. Blocked-in configurations shall only consider dead head conditions and shall not incorporate upset

---

conditions that result from the blocked-in condition as those effects will be determined through the rational analysis used in section 5.2 for determining upset conditions. Conditions not to be considered for determination of maximum operating pressure for blocked-in conditions include but not limited to: thermal expansion from continuous operation of a pump against a closed discharge valve, continued firing of a boiler under fully vapourized conditions, reverse flow from leaky check valve, inadvertent loss of heat to distillation or fractionating columns acting in series, fluid crossover through leaky exchangers, suction vessel pressure at relieving condition, and transients. Conditions to be considered as a minimum for blocked-in maximum/minimum operating pressure include: fluid contraction from process cool-down, harp/blower/compressor deadhead pressure and fluid head from hydrostatic or hydro-pneumatic fluid weight from high-high liquid level plus fluid vapour pressure at maximum operating temperature, or external pressure source (e.g. well pressure with minimum fluid cap)

5.1.2 HAZOP and SIL Analysis

Prior to system-analysis, actions derived from HAZOP and SILs shall be incorporated into the design documentation. System analysis shall utilize the HAZOP review for evaluating probable operating events to establish governing Maximum Operating Pressure.

5.1.3 Documentation and review

The determination of maximum operating pressure for each system component shall be documented in design calculations prepared for the project records. Copies of those design calculations shall be uploaded to the 'Process Engineering' Discipline file folder in Livelink under the project folder. Separate system design calculations documenting each system component is not required as long as the calculations are combined with, or part of, an associated design document that is uploaded to the process discipline file folder in LiveLink.

The Suncor process project lead shall be responsible for review of the calculation basis and complete an audit to verify the maximum operation pressure conditions have been appropriately defined.

Maximum operating pressures shall be captured on all affected equipment datasheets and entered into the piping line list under the normal operating pressure. Piping line list shall record under the appropriate 'Normal' heading column, both the maximum operating pressure and the maximum operating temperature determined in the analysis whether coincident or not.

## 5.2 Determination of Maximum Upset Operating Pressure

5.2.1 General

Maximum upset pressure shall be determined based on the relieving capacity of the system. For systems provided with mechanical relief devices, the pressure shall be established at the pressure required to establish full relieving flow capacity through the mechanical relief device. For relief protection provided by rupture disks (RDs), the pressure shall be the greater of the rupture failure pressure or the pressure required to vent the full relieving capacity through the rupture disk opening.

For systems not provided with mechanical relief pressure, system relieving shall be considered as zero flow and pressure shall be determined based on increases (or decreases) of fluid volume at the upset condition.

5.2.2 Upset Conditions

5.2.2.1 External Conditions

External conditions that may result in system overpressure that shall be estimated and included

---

in the determination of the Maximum Upset Operating Pressure. Single jeopardy events need only to be considered for external conditions. External considerations shall include as a minimum; fire, loss of power (electrical and instrument air), loss of external cooling media, abnormal increase in external air temperature (e.g. loss of air refrigeration for cryogen facilities) and pressure transients from feed and discharge pipelines. Other external upset conditions to be considered are described in section 4 of Standard ANSI/API 521.

5.2.2.2 Internal Conditions

Internal conditions that may result in system overpressure shall be determined and included in the determination of the Maximum Upset Operating Pressure. Although single jeopardy events need only be considered, analysis of the event to demonstrate that the component is independent (and therefore single jeopardy) from the initiating event must be determined. Cascading events that result from a failure of a component shall be considered as double jeopardy to that component (e.g. a vessel failure results in a pool fire of a flammable fluid that generates a pool fire subjecting that vessel to increased pressure). Cascading events that result from a failure of a component shall be considered as single jeopardy to adjacent components isolated from the failed component (e.g. a vessel failure results in a pool fire and adjacent vessels are subject to the heat of the pool fire. The pool fire is single jeopardy for the adjacent independent vessels). Single valve operation and failure to operate of a single check valve shall not be considered as double jeopardy for either single events or cascading events. Provision of two check valves in series shall be considered adequate to provide single jeopardy back flow prevention with the exception of slurry conditions (exceeding 5% by weight solids) and adhesive or high viscosity conditions (fluid viscosity exceeds 50 cp at operating temperature).

a) Blocked-in Upset Conditions

Maximum pump/blower/compressor discharge upset pressure shall be determined as the combined pressure of the maximum inlet fluid elevation at maximum fluid density, the inlet pressure equal to the upstream relief pressure, and the deadhead capacity of the pump. If upstream to pump suction thermal relief is provided (and no reverse flow check valves or equivalent is provided), the upset pressure equal to sum of maximum deadhead pressure plus maximum operating suction pressure may be utilized to determine pump discharge upset conditions. If the pump deadhead with upstream relief protection is not provided, or the pump is mechanically isolated from the relief protection, the pressure resulting from the thermal expansion of the fluid or fluid phase change shall be determined and additive to the pump deadhead differential pressure. Thermal equilibrium established up to pump seizure resulting from a continuous block-in with external air or surrounding media normal average ambient temperature shall be utilized in determining thermal equilibrium. Pump seizure shall be determined by considering the expansion of the impeller resulting in closure of the annular space between the impeller and the suction ring. A thermal maximum recirculation flow of 2% of pump best efficiency point flow at design pump speed shall be used to determine fluid thermal equilibrium and the enthalpy value of 200% of manufacturer's design tolerance shall be utilized to determine maximum theoretical energy input. Check valves located upstream of pump/blower/compressor and not preventing reverse flow to an upstream relief device shall be considered as active and equivalent to the no upstream relief condition. Surge pressure shall be considered for compressors and blowers.

Boiler drum discharge valves that are utilized in shall ensure relieving capacity is equal or greater than all pressure sources supplying the boiler.

Standard 0226, Rev A, Maximum Pressure Design Basis	Page 9 of 16

---

Tower discharge block-ins shall consider uninterrupted feed to the tower plus fluid level at high-high levels. The governing condition of non-fouling reboiler heat input or loss of condensation in overhead circuit shall be considered as single jeopardy. Failure of the SIS system in combination with the events above shall be considered as double jeopardy.

b) Composition Upset Conditions

Process equipment that change the chemical composition of the process fluids shall be evaluated for operation conditions that would impact the relief pressure experienced by the vessel or piping. Changes in the chemical composition to be considered shall include loss, mal-operation or failure of a component in the process system, loss or reduction in system circulation, loss of heat or cooling, change in reactivity of catalyst and change in feed composition. Upset fluid density of mixtures resulting from a loss of one or more mixture components shall be evaluated to establish maximum hydrostatic pressures. For slurry applications, an increase in solid particulate density by 10% shall be utilized in determining maximum fluid upset density. Slurry fluids with a solid's content higher than 80% by weight need not be considered.

c) Increased/Decreased flow

Conditions that would result in increased pressure from increased or decreased flow shall be evaluated as an upset condition. Vessels receiving discharge from pumps/blowers/compressors shall consider flow rates of 105% of pump/blower/compressor rated flow for fixed speed drives and 115% for variable speed/frequency drives. Components depending on the positive removal of non-mechanical equipment shall consider loss of the downstream equipment. Equipment such as centrifugal pumps may be considered to provide pass-through flow at a rate as determined by the hydraulic resistance of the non-rotating pump but positive displacement equipment such as reciprocating compressors shall be considered as equivalent to blocked-in flow.

d) Overfilling of Storage vessels

Fluid elevation shall be determined to a height to match upset inflow condition balanced with relief capacity. Fluid pressure shall be determined at maximum upset composition density.

e) Other Conditions

Standard ANSI/API 521 section 4 shall be considered for all other upset conditions.

## 5.2.3 Determination of Relieving Capacity Requirements

For systems protected through mechanical relief devices (PSVs, PRVs, REs etc) upset conditions shall be evaluated to determine maximum relieving capacity. If the system has segments that may be blocked-in into separate discrete areas, the relieving capacity of that blocked-in segment shall be utilized to determine relieving capacity. Systems incorporating more than one mechanical relief device may consider the combined capacity of two or more devices if and only if the two or more devices may **not** be mechanically isolated from one another. Valves between relief devices that are Car Seal Opened shall be considered as adequate protection for the purposes of relief capacity protection.

### 5.2.3.1 Upset Conditions

---

Upset conditions in general shall be utilized for deriving relief valve capacity, however if a greater flow is demanded through normal operating conditions, the relief valve shall be sized accordingly. Maximum upset operating pressure shall be derived from the upset conditions at the pressure relieving flow capacity provided. The selection of relieving capacity and corresponding upset pressure necessary to achieve relieving capacity shall be based on a suitable risk, reliability, and economic analysis. The relieving rate shall be determined in accordance with recognized engineering methods based on the system configuration. The methods as defined in API 521 shall be used unless special circumstances require a more conservative approach.

### 5.2.3.2 Relief Rate Pressure Padding

For determination of mechanical relief capacity the following shall be considered:

a) The pressure difference between Maximum Operating Pressure and the pressure required to achieve full relieving rate shall not be less

   i) 10% of maximum operating pressure for Operating pressures below 3500 kPag

   ii) 175 kPa

   iii) 350 kPa for Operating pressures exceeding 3500 kPag

b) The pressure difference between Maximum Operating Pressure to achieve full relieving rate specific to equipment type shall not be less the following unless it exceeds the MAWP of the equipment. If the MAWP does not exceed the minimum pressure padding as defined in 5.2.3.2 a), the equipment MAWP shall be re-specified or system maximum operating pressure lowered (and system redesigned or design basis for system reduced accordingly) to meet required pressure padding.

   i) 15% of maximum operating pressure for reciprocating compressors

   ii) 20% of maximum operating pressure for centrifugal pumps and compressors

   iii) 10% of maximum operating pressure for vessels determined at top of vessel

### 5.2.3.3 Relief Design and Specification

Selection and specification of relief equipment shall be completed based on estimated relief capacity and relief rate pressure padding. The supplier of the relief device shall determine actual required relieving pressure at maximum relieving rate. Maximum Upset Operating Pressure shall be defined equal to the actual required relieving pressure. Relief sizing shall be based on proven practise. The requirements of API 520 shall be met or exceeded for relief valve sizing.

## 5.2.4 Determination of Maximum Upset Operating Pressure for systems with no mechanical relieving capacity provided

### 5.2.4.1 Upset Conditions

The upset conditions that would generate a volume increase in the system shall be analysed on the basis of no containment release. Compressible media on containment basis shall consider the containment pressure sufficient to compress the expansible fluid to counteract any system

---

volume increase caused by the upset conditions. Maximum Upset Operating Pressure shall be defined as the containment pressure sufficient to counteract the system volume increase.

## 5.3 Determination of Design Pressure

### 5.3.1 Vessels

Vessels containing expandable fluids shall be provided with mechanical relief. Maximum Upset Operating Pressure shall be utilized for vessel design.

### 5.3.2 Boilers and Fired Heaters

Boilers and fired heaters shall be provided with mechanical relief. Maximum Upset Operating Pressure shall be utilized for boiler/fired heater and component design. Piping connected to the boiler/fired heater and boiler/fired heater components shall be protected by the boiler/fired heater relief equipment.

### 5.3.3 Reactors

Reactors shall be provided with mechanical relief. Where multiple beds exist within a reactor, multiple mechanical relief devices shall be considered if bed collapse from differential pressure may occur. Maximum Upset Operating Pressure shall be utilized for reactor design. Piping connected to the reactor shall be protected by the reactor relief equipment.

### 5.3.4 Centrifugal Pumps, Centrifugal Compressors, and Blowers

Centrifugal Pumps, compressors, and blowers shall be protected by upstream mechanical relief or by protection by design. Pump/compressor/blower MAWP shall exceed Maximum Upset Operating Pressure. Piping connected upstream of the pump/compressor/blower shall be protected by an upstream vessel relief protection or by system design. Piping downstream of the pump/compressor/blower may be protected either by design or downstream mechanical relief. Piping between pump/compressor/blower discharge and downstream isolation valve shall be designed to pump/compressor/blower discharge Maximum Upset Operating Pressure and pressure shall be considered as continuous duty for determination of allowable stresses.

### 5.3.5 Positive Displacement Pumps and Reciprocating Compressors

Positive displacement pumps and reciprocating compressors shall be protected by mechanical relief. If relief is routed back to suction of pump or compressor, heat addition from recirculation load shall be considered in determination of Maximum Upset Operating Pressure. Piping connected upstream of the pump/compressor shall be protected by an upstream vessel relief protection or by system design. Piping downstream of the pump/compressor shall be protected by the downstream mechanical relief. Piping between pump/compressor discharge and downstream isolation valve shall be designed to pump/compressor discharge Maximum Upset Operating Pressure and pressure shall be considered as continuous duty for determination of allowable stresses.

### 5.3.6 Exchangers

Exchanger shells on shell and tube exchangers shall be provided with mechanical relief. Exchanger tubes, external pipe for pipe in pipe, plate exchangers and spiral exchangers shall be provided by mechanical relief or by mechanical design. Air Cooled exchanger tubes shall be protected by mechanical design for blocked-in conditions and by upstream and/or downstream vessel mechanical relief for normal operating conditions. Mechanical design for vacuum shall be provided where exchanger can be blocked in on inlet and outlet. Maximum Upset Operating Pressure shall be utilized for exchanger and exchanger component design. Piping connected to the exchanger

shall be protected by the upstream or downstream relief equipment or by mechanical protection design.

5.3.7 Piping

Piping with exception to piping protected by connected protected vessels shall be protected by either mechanical relief or by mechanical design. Maximum Upset Operating Pressure as determined above shall be utilized for piping design.

## 5.4 Selection of Piping Line Class and LDT Completion

Piping components shall be selected from one Suncor Standard line class between line breaks as designated on the P&IDs. The line class selected shall have design pressure and design temperature exceeding the Maximum Upset Operating Pressure for the piping under consideration. Design pressure on the LDT may be designated as any value equal or exceeding the Maximum Upset Operating. The LDT design pressure shall be equal or less than the line class MDWP. Line class components are designed to meet or exceed the pressure rating as defined in the line class. Wall thicknesses for piping and fittings designated as "Calc" shall be determined by the engineer to satisfy the appropriate piping design code (e.g. B31.1) utilizing the design pressure as designated on the LDT and the line class corrosion allowance. Design temperature shall be the coincident temperature utilized to derive the design pressure.

Testing pressure shall be established according to Standard 0205. In general, hydrotest pressure to be defined on the LTD shall be defined as the maximum pressure that the limiting mechanical component can withstand. The "Code Design test pressure" as designated on the LDT shall be defined as the Design Pressure times the applicable code multiplier. For elevated temperature conditions, Code Design test pressure shall increased to account for differences between allowable stresses at testing temperature and Maximum Upset Operating Temperature.

## 6.0 DOCUMENTATION AND DELIVERABLES

Each system pressure and relief design shall be documented and submitted as part of the project engineering records. A recommended content is listed in Appendix "A".

# 1. INTRODUCTION

## 1.1 SCOPE

This DEP specifies minimum requirements and gives recommendations for the protection of pipelines against overpressure. The following subjects are covered:

- possible pipeline pressure sources;
- requirements for determining pipeline operating and incidental pressures;
- description of possible methods and guidance on selection;
- minimum engineering, operations, maintenance and inspection requirements.

For determining allowable pipeline pressures, refer to DEP 31.40.00.10-Gen. For specific requirements relating to the classification, implementation and management of Instrumented Protective Functions, refer to DEP 32.80.10.10-Gen. and DEP 32.80.10.12-Gen.

This DEP is a revision of the DEP of the same title and number dated March 1994; a summary of the main changes from that edition is given in (1.6).

## 1.2 DISTRIBUTION, INTENDED USE AND REGULATORY CONSIDERATIONS

Unless otherwise authorised by Shell GSI and SIEP, the distribution of this DEP is confined to companies forming part of or managed by the Royal Dutch/Shell Group, and to Contractors nominated by them.

This DEP is intended for use by Functions in the Group that are involved in the design, material procurement, construction and operation of pipelines. When DEPs are applied, a Management of Change (MOC) process should be implemented. This is of particular importance when existing facilities are to be modified.

If national and/or local regulations exist in which some of the requirements may be more stringent than in this DEP, the Contractor shall determine by careful scrutiny which of the requirements are the more stringent and which combination of requirements will be acceptable as regards safety, environmental, economic and legal aspects. In all cases, the Contractor shall inform the Principal of any deviation from the requirements of this DEP which is considered to be necessary in order to comply with national and/ or local regulations. The Principal may then negotiate with the Authorities concerned with the object of obtaining agreement to follow this DEP as closely as possible.

## 1.3 DEFINITIONS

### 1.3.1 General definitions

The **Contractor** is the party that carries out all or part of the design, engineering, procurement, construction, commissioning or management of a project or operation of a facility. The Principal may undertake all or part of the duties of the Contractor.

The **Manufacturer/Supplier** is the party that manufactures or supplies equipment and services to perform the duties specified by the Contractor.

The **Principal** is the party that initiates the project and ultimately pays for its design and construction. The Principal will generally specify the technical requirements. The Principal may also include an agent or consultant authorised to act for, and on behalf of, the Principal.

The word **shall** indicates a requirement.

The word **should** indicates a recommendation.

---

DEP 31.40.10.14-Gen.
November 2003
Page 5

## 1.3.2 Specific definitions

**Pressures**

**Accumulated Pressure** - Pressure which is built up in a pipeline during the period of activation of an overpressure protection system.

**Internal Design Pressure** - The maximum internal pressure at which the pipeline is (or sections thereof are) designed in accordance with the applicable design standard.

**Incidental Pressure** - Pressure occurring in a pipeline with limited frequency and duration. Pressures due to surges or heating of blocked-in static fluid are considered incidental pressures, providing they are not regular operating occurrences.

**Maximum Allowable Incidental Pressure** - The maximum pressure that is allowed to occur in a pipeline with a limited frequency and duration, determined in accordance with the applicable design standard.

**Maximum Allowable Operating Pressure** - The maximum pressure at which a pipeline system is (or sections thereof are) allowed to operate under steady state process conditions, in accordance with the applicable design standard.

**Maximum Operating Pressure** - The maximum pressure at which a pipeline system (or sections thereof) will be operated under steady state process conditions.

**Surge Pressure** - Pressure due to mass flow velocity changes caused by operational activities, e.g. valve closures, pump shutdown, or start-up.

**Thermal Pressure** - Pressure due to thermal expansion effects on a fluid in a blocked-in pipeline or blocked-in pipeline section.

**Others**

**Instrumented Protective Function** – A function comprising one or more Initiators, a Logic Solver and one or more Final Elements whose purpose is to prevent or mitigate hazardous situations. An IPF is intended to achieve or maintain a safe state for the process, in respect of a specific hazardous event, e.g.: overpressure.

**Pressure Recorder Alarm (High)** - System for warning and registering the occurrence of pressures in excess of allowable values.

**Pressure Safety Relief Valve** - Valve for protecting a pipeline against overpressure by releasing fluid from the pipeline.

**Source** - The facility located immediately upstream of the pipeline, characterised by the type and the pressure of the produced fluid. The Source may be a well or group of wells, a treatment facility, a pump or compressor station, or a feeding pipeline.

**Specified Minimum Yield Strength** - Minimum yield strength required by the specification or standard under which the pipeline material is purchased.

| MOP | Maximum Operating Pressure |

1.6 SUMMARY OF CHANGES SINCE PREVIOUS EDITION

The previous edition of this DEP was dated March 1994. Other than editorial changes, the following are the main changes since that edition.

The prescriptive requirements for high integrity protective systems have been replaced by cross-references to newly available DEPs that specify requirements for IPFs. DEP 32.80.10.10-Gen. provides the requirements for the classification and implementation of IPFs, including risk assessment and determination of the criticality and the required level of reliability and redundancy. DEP 32.80.10.13-Gen. provides requirements and recommendations for the management of IPFs including optimisation of maintenance and inspection requirements to ensure long-term integrity.

Some definitions have been revised to align with those in ISO 13623.

In (2.4), limitations to the MAIP required for certain pipelines designed in accordance with ISO 13623 or ASME B 31.8 have been added.

## 2. PIPELINE PRESSURES

### 2.1 PRESSURE SOURCES

When operating and incidental pipeline pressures are determined, pressure sources should be categorised as:

(i) well pressure; or

(ii) pressure from pressure boosting facilities such as pumps and compressors; or

(iii) pressure from pressure controlled process vessels; or

(iv) operating pressure from a feeding pipeline; or

(v) hydrostatic head due to change in pipeline elevation; or

(vi) surges as a result of operational activities, e.g. valve closure, pump start-up/shut-down; or

(vii) thermal expansion of blocked-in fluids; or

(viii) failure of the pressure control/trip of pumps, compressors, pressure controlled process vessels or feeding pipelines; or

(ix) incidental pressures from a feeding pipeline; or

(x) accumulation pressure during the activation of the overpressure protection safety relief or isolation valves.

### 2.2 OPERATING PRESSURE

In most cases, the pipeline operating pressure, i.e., the pressure at which the pipeline operates under steady state conditions, is the pressure resulting from a category (i) to (iv) source. When no pressure limiting or overpressure protection is provided, these pressures are:

- for category (i), the closed-in tubing head pressure for pipelines conveying fluids directly from a naturally flowing well. If the pipeline is also to be used for well servicing duties like through-flowline-operations and killing, its operating pressure during such operations will be higher.
- for category (ii), the highest pressure which can be generated under steady state conditions by pumps, compressors and artificially lifted wells over the possible flow range.
- for category (iii), the upper pressure level of the range in which the pressure is controlled.
- for category (iv), the operating pressure of the feeding pipeline determined in accordance with this Section.

In the case of multiple pressure sources, the highest pressure shall be taken.

Pipeline operating pressures are normally highest where the fluid enters the pipeline and decrease along the line due to friction loss. This may, however, not be true when high-density fluids are transported in pipelines with an elevated inlet position, e.g. offshore platforms or in mountainous terrain. For these pipelines, the hydrostatic head due to changes in elevation, source (v), may cause higher pressures down the pipeline which need to be added to the source (i) to (iv) pressures when determining the MOP. The possible contribution of the hydrostatic head to the operating pressure should be checked for the complete flow range, as the effect is not necessarily highest at the maximum flowrate.

Surge pressures due to operational activities, source (vi), are normally of short duration and limited frequency and are therefore not included in the operating pressure.

Thermal pressures, source (vii), are included in the operating pressure only if blocking-in is a regular operational activity and occurs for a significant period of time.

---

DEP 31.40.10.14-Gen.
November 2003
Page 8

2.3 INCIDENTAL PRESSURE

The incidental pressure is the pressure which may occur anywhere in the pipeline at any time and is calculated from the combined effect of the operating pressure (2.2), incidental pressures of feeding pipelines determined in accordance with this Section and the other source pressures (2.1, paras vi to x).

2.4 MAXIMUM ALLOWABLE PRESSURES

The maximum allowable operating pressure (MAOP) of a pipeline system, or parts thereof, shall be determined in accordance with DEP 31.40.00.10-Gen. The MAOP relates to the design pressure and the test pressure.

The maximum allowable incidental pressure (MAIP) is 1.1 times MAOP for both liquid and gas lines except in the case of:

a) Pipelines designed in accordance with ISO 13623 conveying category C and D fluids that have been pressure tested at a reduced test pressure of 1.20 times MAOP – for such pipelines the MAIP shall be limited to 1.05 times MAOP.

b) Pipelines designed in accordance with ASME B31.8 and operating at or below 72 % of the SMYS - for such pipelines the MAIP shall also be limited to a pressure which results in a hoop stress not exceeding 75 % of SMYS.

c) Gas pipelines designed in accordance with ASME B31.8 and operating over 72 % of the SMYS – for such pipelines the MAIP shall be limited to 1.04 times MAOP.

---

## 3. METHODS FOR OVERPRESSURE PROTECTION

### 3.1 OVERVIEW AND SELECTION

Designing a pipeline for the maximum source pressures without the need for overpressure protection equipment is the simplest method for safeguarding a pipeline against overpressure. This method should be applied whenever the additional life-cycle costs, compared with the installation of overpressure protection equipment, are minor. Examples of such applications are short, small diameter pipelines where the additional pipeline material and construction costs will be offset by the life-cycle costs of overpressure protection equipment. Pipelines fed by pumps or compressors, source (ii), are other examples where matching source and allowable pipeline pressures may be obtained at low, if any, additional cost.

Overpressure protection of pipelines may be achieved by means of the following:

- mechanical devices e.g. pressure safety relief valves, etc.; or
- instrumented devices e.g. IPF.

Pressure safety relief equipment has commonly been installed to protect pipelines against pressures in excess of MAOP. This protection method may be selected instead of the above inherent safe design when the life-cycle costs are reduced. The costs for the installation, inspection and maintenance of the discharged fluid disposal facilities shall be included when comparing costs.

More recently, pipelines have also been protected against overpressure with IPFs. IPFs consist of a fail-to-close valve(s) activated to close at the set pressure by a redundant and highly reliable instrumented pressure sensing and transmitting system. This method may be applied where relief is not practical for safety or environmental reasons or the use of IPFs results in significant cost reductions. Gas transmission lines are an example where IPFs may result in a significant cost saving when compared with relief protection, due to a higher MOP as a percentage of MAOP.

Activation of the overpressure protection equipment by incidental pressure during normal operations shall be avoided by providing a sufficient margin between the MOP of the pipeline and the equipment set pressures. Besides overpressure protection, a pressure control and alarm system shall be installed for applications where the operating pressure of the source may exceed the MOP of the pipeline.

NOTE: PSV and IPF activation during normal operations should be avoided in order to maintain the integrity of the valve seals.

Pipeline entry pressures shall be monitored when overpressure protection is provided to alarm the operator for corrective action when operating pressures exceed the predicted range. Pressures in excess of MAOP shall be recorded with duration and pressure value.

Figures 1 and Figure 2 show typical schemes of pipeline overpressure protection with pressure safety relief and IPFs respectively. Typical set pressures for gas lines with minimum setpoint margins in view of the low incidental pressures are shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4. Incidental pressures can be significantly higher for lines containing liquids and consequently require lower set points for pressure control. Incidental pressures should be determined on a case-by-case basis. Incidental pressure should be determined before MOP, MAOP and the corresponding set pressures for pressure control and overpressure protection are selected.

### 3.2 COMPARISON OF METHODS

The key differences between the two overpressure protection methods are:

- with an IPF, fluids remain in the pipeline thus avoiding the need for disposal facilities and potential burden to the environment;
- with a relief protection, the pipeline remains continuously available for transport;

---

DEP 31.40.10.14-Gen.
November 2003
Page 10

- an IPF is more complex and requires more stringent control, maintenance and inspection procedures;
- pipelines protected with an IPF can operate closer to MAOP than pipelines protected by relief valves, which require typically 10 % of their set pressure for pressure accumulation; see Figure 5.

## 3.3 SURGE PRESSURES

Possible surge pressures in a pipeline system shall be estimated during the conceptual phase of a pipeline system transient flow analysis. Possible means for the control of surge pressures are:

- providing sufficient margin in the pipeline design for surge pressures;
- controlling the generation of pressure surges by reducing the rate at which mass flow velocities of the fluid can change. For example, in the case of valve closure this can be done by slowing down the valve actuator or installing a two-speed actuator reducing the valve closure speed over the last 10 % to 20 % of the valve travel movement;

NOTE: Shut-off valves installed as part of an IPF shall not be used to control surge pressures.

- the installation of a pressure relief system close to the point of surge initiation. This may consist of a vessel with a pressurised gas blanket or rapid actuation surge relief valve discharging into a surge tank, which must be ready at all times to receive the released fluid.

Operating procedures need to reflect that surge pressures should be avoided as far as practical, even if surge pressure protection equipment has been installed.

## 3.4 THERMAL PRESSURES

Unallowable thermal pressures may be avoided by the installation of thermal relief valves. These valves should be set to release thermal pressures before activation of the overpressure protection equipment.

Even if thermal relief valves are installed, operating procedures should be prepared to avoid thermal pressures where possible.

## 4. ENGINEERING REQUIREMENTS

### 4.1 LOCATION

The components of a pipeline overpressure protection system shall be installed between the source and the pipeline or included in the source facilities.

### 4.2 PRESSURE SAFETY RELIEF

#### 4.2.1 Design requirements

Pressure safety relief valves shall comply with DEP 80.45.10.10-Gen. and the additional requirements of (4.2.2) and (4.2.3).

#### 4.2.2 Number of relief valves

The PSV system may comprise one relief valve or, for higher capacities, multiple valves, always with the total relief capacity matching or exceeding the maximum possible throughput from the source.

#### 4.2.3 Set pressure requirements

The set pressures for the pressure controller, alarm and pressure safety relief valve(s) shall satisfy the following requirements:

> **Table - Set pressure requirements for pressure controller, alarm and pressure safety relief valve** - see [source crop](08-pressure-design-and-overpressure-relief/_assets/08-pressure-design-and-overpressure-relief-02/tables/08-pressure-design-and-overpressure-relief-02_p0009_tbl01_set-pressure-requirements-for-pressure-c.png)

NOTE: Spring-loaded PSVs are typically specified to require 10 % of their set pressure for accumulation and have a reseat pressure at 5 % to 7 % below the set pressure.

### 4.3 IPF

#### 4.3.1 General

IPFs shall be designed on a case-by-case basis in accordance with the requirements of DEP 32.80.10.10-Gen and DEP 32.80.10.12-Gen.

NOTE: Local regulatory authorities may either prohibit IPF systems or impose additional requirements and may have to approve the design before issuing a certificate of fitness.

---

DEP 31.40.10.14-Gen.
November 2003
Page 12

## 5. REQUIREMENTS FOR OPERATIONS

### 5.1 PRESSURE SAFETY RELIEF

An annual visual external inspection should be systematically carried out in-situ to ensure that the relief valve has no obvious defects (e.g. seal is intact and the valve is not heavily corroded). A complete inspection and test should be carried out every two to four years, dependent on service history. These inspection periods may be the subject of local statutory regulations, which shall be followed.

The last test date and set pressure should be stamped on a firmly secured tag. Relief valve exchange for testing should be arranged to coincide with inspection of the protected equipment or other shutdown, to avoid installation of twin relief valves with upstream and downstream isolation.

Where exchange of a relief valve is possible, the valve orifice size shall also be stamped on the tag.

Records shall be kept for each relief valve, showing the inspection dates, lifting pressure as found, defects, remedial action taken and location installed.

### 5.2 IPF

The operation and maintenance of IPFs shall be in accordance with the requirements of DEP 32.80.10.12-Gen.

## Summary

This document covers the Relief and Blowdown requirements for the Nanushuk Project. This covers relief valves, system depressurization and deinventory and the flare system.

The flare and relief system for the will be designed in accordance with API STD 520 Parts I and II, and API STD 521.

# 1   Overview

Atypically in the form of an automated control valve that is designed to maintain a set pressure in the system, but also pressure relief valve(s) installed on the system that will relieve pressure if the pressure reaches the Maximum Allowable Working Pressure of the system. The possible relief paths are identified below.

## 1.1   Nanushuk Processing Facility (NPF) Process Systems

All process systems within the NPF shall relieve to the flare system. All equipment with a design pressure of 100 psig and above shall be designed to relieve and blowdown to the High Pressure (HP) Flare. All other process systems shall relieve to the Low Pressure (LP) flare. To reduce the risk of over pressuring the process separation train equipment due to blocked discharge, all of the separation train equipment will be designed to a minimum 100 psig design pressure; this includes, but is not limited to:

- Inlet Separator - already above 100 psig design pressure due to operating pressure at 180 psig
- IP Separator – operates at 55 psig
- LP Separator - operates at 10 psig
- Crude Dehydrator - operates at 10 psig
- Desander Packages – operates close to separator pressure associated with it
- Produced Water Degassing Drum - operates at 10 psig
- LP Separator PW Pump and Crude Dehydrator Pumps (suction and discharge)
- IP Preheater and Crude Heater - operates close to separator pressure associated with it

Since the Flash Gas compressor is interconnected with the separation train, this will require the flash gas train to be sized for a minimum of 100 psig design pressure as well including, but not limited to:

- 1st and 2nd Stage Flash Gas Suction Cooler
- 1st and 2nd Stage Flash Gas Suction Scrubber
- 1st and 2nd Stage Flash Gas Suction Scrubber Pump
- 1st and 2nd Stage Flash Gas Suction Compressor
- 1st and 2nd Stage Flash Gas Suction Compressor Piping

With this design, nearly all the major process equipment will relieve and blowdown to the HP flare system. This leaves the LP flare available for smaller low pressure equipment such as the vents and seal gas purge from the compressors.

9/1/2018 - Issued for Use                                                                                   Page 6 of 13

NANUSHUK PROJECT
RELIEF AND BLOWDOWN PHILOSOPHY
NGE-PRPHL-000001 – REV 0

[Oil Search logo]

## 1.2 Drillsite and Flowline Process Systems

Although the Drillsites and Flowlines are outside the scope of the NPF, there will be provisions made at the NPF to allow for relief and manual blowdown from the flowlines and pipelines. The manual blowdown that will be provided at the NPF for all of the flowline systems will relieve to the HP flare. There will also be relief valves provided on the flowline for each drillsite that will relieve to the HP flare, this allows for overpressure protection of the pipeline itself, but also allows for the drillsite process equipment to relieve directly into the pipelines instead of relieving to the atmosphere. The relief system will be sized for a certain number of drillsite wells not shutting-in on demand, the number of wells use for relief sizing will be determined as a result of the Fault Tree Analysis, and is typically around 10% of wells, but will be confirmed later. It will also be sized for fire relief of heaters (or vessels); the relief load to be provided by others. Drillsite equipment will have to be designed to be able to relieve into the pipeline and have a design pressure at or above the setpoint of the flowline relief valves.

## 1.3 NPF Utility Systems

Hydrocarbon utility systems such as fuel gas shall also relieve to a flare system. High pressure fuel gas shall relieve to HP flare, and LP fuel gas shall relieve to LP flare. Liquid utility fluids shall generally relieve back to their respective storage tank, but certain combustible liquid utility fluids may relieve to the flare system if it is not practical to relieve back their respective the storage tanks; an example of this is a methanol line in the process module if the tank is located outside the module.

Non-hydrocarbon utility systems shall relieve to a safe location depending on the utility fluid. If the fluid is stored in an atmospheric tank, the fluid should relieve to the tank. An example of this is a relief valve on the fine water mist system should relieve back to the fine water mist water storage tank. Another example of this is a skid lube oil system; any lube oil relief valves should relieve back to the skid lube oil tank, crankcase, or off skid lube oil storage tank, depending on the application.

Compressed Air can relieve directly to the atmosphere, but the vent pipe shall be vented to a location where the force of relieving compressed air is not a hazard. Compressed Nitrogen can also relieve directly to the atmosphere, but it must be vented to the outside, and in a safe location where the venting cannot cause an asphyxiation hazard.

## 1.4 Atmospheric Tanks (All systems)

All atmospheric tanks shall have a relief path, regardless of the system the tank belongs to. Non-hazardous fluids such as fire water, may be stored in a tank that has a vent that is continuously open to atmosphere. These vents must be sized to handle both the max fluid inflow and outflow from the tank, and be sized for liquid overflow for the max fluid inflow case to prevent the tank from exploding or imploding.

6/1/2018 - Issued for Use                                                                                                    Page 7 of 13

---

Hazardous fluids contained in tanks are typically designed to be closed systems. These tanks must use LP fuel gas (or nitrogen in some cases) as a blanketing gas, with the feed rate of the blanket gas shall be designed to handle the max tank outflow. At the NPF, these tanks must also be connected to the vapor recovery system that is sized to handle the maximum inflow volume into the tank. In addition to these provisions, these tanks must be equipped with a pressure relief and vacuum breaker device that is sized for maximum inflow on the relieving device, and maximum outflow on the vacuum breaker device. Some tanks will also require emergency venting and will be evaluated on a case by case basis.

# 2 Relief Valves

Relief valve design and regulation shall be designed to API 520 and 521 and comply with applicable Alaska State regulations. For all process systems, relief valves shall be used as pressure relieving devices. Relief valves are preferred for all systems, but rupture discs or *other reliving devices* may be used by exception on certain auxiliary or utility systems.

Tank relief system shall be designed according to API 2000.

## 2.1 Design Pressure

Pressure containing equipment shall be designed for maximum operating pressure or expected upset, plus a safety factor, refer to NPF-PRCRT-000001 *Process Design Criteria*, "Design Pressure" section for the safety factor as well as other considerations.

The design pressure will take into consideration the required margin to prevent lifting relief valves before a high-pressure switch is triggered. Some equipment will have a design pressure much higher than the anticipated operating pressure to allow for safe integration into the flare system. See section 2.

## 2.2 Relieving Cases

All pressure containing systems shall be reviewed for the need for pressure relieving devices. Each relief valve location shall be reviewed for applicability of all of these cases.

Conservative relief load estimates will be made for each device for each of the common mode failures using short cut methods (such as by analogy with other plants or by making simplifying assumptions regarding key data such as latent heats, peak flowrates, etc.). From this the probable governing contingency for the flare/relief system is identified. More rigorous calculations will be provided for large relief loads that are identified as potential controlling case.

## 2.3 Design to Minimize Need for Relief Valves

Generally, all pressure containing systems shall have overpressure protection, typically in the form of relief valves. The requirement for overpressure protection may be minimized for a particular system if it

---

has been determined that overpressure cannot occur on the system. It should be attempted to design systems to reduce the need for relief valves when it is practical to do so.

Systems where relief valves may not be required due to overpressure not possible due to equipment capability:

- Centrifugal Pump Discharge Piping (when pump curve for the largest impeller for a given pump casing is reviewed and confirmed the line cannot overpressure, and the suction line is the same pipe spec as the discharge line.

- Interconnected Piping Systems with same design pressure – in certain cases, multiple pressure containing devices (e.g. vessels) within the same continuous system with the same design pressure, may only require a single relief valve to protect the entire system, provided there is no potential to block the relief path from all equipment in the system and the relief valve, such as an automated control valve or ESD valve. In this scenario, this single relief valve must be sized for relief of all pressure containing equipment within the system.

Systems can also be designed to remove the need for relief valves, examples of this are:

- Designing systems with the same design pressure as the upstream system design pressure, to eliminate "failed control valve" (blowby) overpressure scenario.

- Designing compressor suction and discharge piping and equipment to the same design pressure may eliminate the need for an additional relief valve on the compressor suction side (this does not eliminate the need for a relief valve on the discharge side)

- For shell and tube heat exchangers, use fluid systems with the same design pressure if possible

- Remove unnecessary obstructions to the relief path in interconnected equipment within the same pressure system. An example of this would be for a compressor train containing a scrubber vessel, a cooler, and a pulsation dampener, this equipment should be connected together without any obstruction. An obstruction could be an automated control valve, automated ESD valve, a pressure control valve (PCV), or other inline device that can stop or limit flow. In line filters should be reviewed if they are considered an obstruction. If this system was designed without obstruction, only one PSV is required for this system, but still must be sized for relief from all sources in this system.

## 2.4 Burst Discs

As an alternative to PSVs, burst discs may be used in place of a PSV if there is a design issue with locating a PSV at the particular location and/or where a PSV will not react fast enough to mitigate the pressure surge such a during a tube rupture. Burst discs are smaller and cheaper but have the significant disadvantage that once they burst, the entire system is blown down, and the burst disc must be replaced.

---

[Oil Search logo]

Burst discs are not to be used in locations where overpressure surge may occur frequently. Burst discs are only to be installed on primary process lines by approved exception by Company and/or Operations.

If a burst disc is selected for a particular location, the requirement of flowrate capacity and upstream and downstream piping requirements are identical to PSVs. The burst discs shall be sized according to API 520.

## 2.5 High Integrity Pressure Protection System (HIPPS)

There may be certain systems, where the use of a PSV or burst disc is not practicable, or the potential relief load exceeds the relief system capacity, or when the relief system is nonexistent such as on export lines tie-in location. In these systems, HIPPS methodology may be used as positive isolation to mitigate the relief scenario by making it non-existent. The use of HIPPS is to be approved by company on a case by case basis. An example of a system to use HIPPS is the export pipeline, which feeds into the KPE Oil Pipeline system. Since there are potential hazards in the KPE system that we cannot control, the export pipeline will use HIPPS systems to mitigate the hazards originating from the KPE pipeline.

# 3 Emergency Depressuring

Shutdown and Depressuring (or Blowdown) systems at the NPF will be utilized to quickly and safely isolate and de-inventory equipment in the case of leak or fire. The blowdown system will be sized to depressure high-pressure equipment and relieve to the HP Flare as determined by a "vessel survivability assessment" to mitigate jet fire scenario. A conservative approach will be taken with equipment with operating pressures of 100 psig or less, especially rotating equipment. Further investigation is necessary at a later time to determine if there will be restrictions to depressuring rates, especially with compressors. Pressure settle out studies will be done in FEED.

Blowdown of process systems will be by manual initiation from the Central Control Room (CCR) or initiated automatically per Cause and Effect (C&E) logic, for example in the case of confirmed fire. The NPF will be broken down into process segments for staged blowdown, based on fire zones as well as to accommodate vapor velocity limitations (as in packed beds). These segments will be isolated with Shutdown Valves (SDV). In concert with the isolation of process sections, Blowdown Valves (BDV) will open to the flare to initiate depressuring. SDVs will fail closed on loss of actuation and BDVs will fail open on loss of actuation (i.e. loss of electrical power, instrument air, or hydraulic fluid).

Blowdown and deinventory shall occur only after complete isolation of the affected system controlled by the Emergency Shutdown (ESD) System, for more information on the ESD system refer to NPF-PRPHL-000004 *Emergency Isolation and Shutdown Philosophy.*

---

NANUSHUK PROJECT
RELIEF AND BLOWDOWN PHILOSOPHY
NGE-PRPHL-000001 – REV 0

[... Oil Search logo]

## 3.1 Blowdown Valves

In the event the transient and emergency condition requires system depressurization, the system will open the system blowdown valves which will release hydrocarbon streams to the flare. Blowdown valves will be designed with the same considerations as emergency isolation valves described in the Emergency Isolation and Shutdown Philosophy, with additional considerations for:

1. Designed to withstand pressure drop across the valve. Considerations include:

   a. Protection against erosion and valve damage from the pressure drop

   b. Low temperature design of the valve and downstream piping

   c. Review of hydrate formation conditions

   d. Noise

2. Consider pipe stress, pressure surge, and undesired forces

Depending on the application, a restriction orifice or diffuser may be installed to control these factors.

## 3.2 System Blowdown

Considerations for the blowdown system include:

1. A blowdown valve shall be provided for all equipment or systems that are bounded with emergency isolation valves. There must be a path for every isolated system in the facility to be depressurized to flare. In some low-pressure systems where automated deinventory of the system is not necessary, such as in a low pressure system with a small contained volume, a manual depressurization valve may be used in lieu of an automated blowdown valve.

2. Opportunities for trapped pressure, such as downstream of check valves, must be reviewed in design to ensure all sections of piping can be depressurized during an emergency blowdown.

3. The blowdown system shall be designed to start blowdown after isolation is completed, such as with time delay, in order to minimize flaring.

4. The blowdown valve and piping shall be sized to provide the appropriate depressurization rate; this includes:

   a. Ensuring the isolated system is depressurized in the time per the project requirement; see section 4.3, depressurization time.

   b. Ensure depressurization rate does not exceed the acceptable depressurization rate of the equipment within the system, such as with compressors.

NANUSHUK PROJECT
RELIEF AND BLOWDOWN PHILOSOPHY
NGE-PRPHL-000001 – REV 0

[... logo Oil Search]

## 3.3 Depressurization Time

The blowdown system must be designed at a minimum to meet the required depressurization time for all individual systems. The requirement is to reduce the system pressure down to 100psig or half of design pressure, whichever is lower, in 15 minutes. The flare system shall be designed to handle this blowdown rate for the entire facility. Note that this is only a minimum requirement; a particular system may have a blowdown capacity larger to accommodate other blowdown requirements.

## 3.4 Staged Blowdown

In order to allow safe deinventory of low-pressure systems, an analysis of the system will be done to ensure the blowdown of the facility does not create problems from backflow due to backpressure generated by the blowdown. This may also be a consideration to not exceed flare system capacity.

## 3.5 Considerations for Compressors or Sensitive Equipment

Certain equipment, particularly compressors, may have a maximum depressurization rate defined by the manufacturer. If the sizing criteria for blowdown on the system requires a faster depressurization rate than that equipment manufacturer allows, the following steps should be taken:

1. Confirm with the manufacturer if any mitigations can be made to increase the allowable depressurization rate to the required blowdown rate for the system to meet the blowdown time requirement.

2. If no mitigations are possible, or practical, the blowdown system shall be sized for the maximum depressurization rate of the equipment, and system isolation valves should be moved closer to the sensitive equipment or added to split the system to minimize the contained volume within the slow depressurization system.

3. If isolation valves cannot be moved or added to minimize system size, the system shall be reviewed for all safety considerations given the system will be required to depressurize slower than the minimum blowdown requirement per the Relief and Blowdown Philosophy.

## 3.6 Liquid Deinventory

Liquid contained within process systems during an emergency isolation and blowdown will remain contained within the system, and no specific automated provisions will be made to deinventory the contained liquids. However, the blowdown system shall be designed to handle any evolved vapor from the liquids during depressurization, and for the fire case.

9/1/2018 - Issued for Use  Page 12 of 13

NANUSHUK PROJECT
RELIEF AND BLOWDOWN PHILOSOPHY
NGE-PRPHL-000001 – REV 0

[... Oil Search logo]

# 4 Flare System

## 4.1 High Pressure Flare

The HP Flare System handles the hydrocarbon reliefs from the high-pressure systems. The hydrocarbon reliefs are collected in the HP flare collection header and routed to the HP Flare KO Drum. The flare gas is then routed to the HP Flare from the KO drum. Liquid separated in the KO drum will be pumped into the slop oil tank. The HP flare stack will be equipped with a sonic flare tip with a 100% smokeless operation.

Fuel gas will be used as purge gas to keep air out of the flare stack and prevent a flammable mixture from forming. Purge gas will continuously flow into the header to maintain positive pressure on the HP flare header.

The HP Flare KO Drum shall be designed for the highest anticipated flowrate relieving event.

## 4.2 Low Pressure Flare

The LP Flare System handles the hydrocarbon reliefs from low pressure systems. The hydrocarbon reliefs are collected in the LP flare collection header and routed to the LP Flare KO Drum. The flare gas is sent to the LP Flare from the KO drum. The LP flare stack will include the associated LP Flare Assist Air Blower(s) to achieve 100% smokeless burning. Liquid separated in the KO drum will be pumped to the Slop Oil Tank. Purge gas will continuously flow into the header to maintain positive pressure on the LP flare header.

The LP Flare KO Drum shall be designed for the highest anticipated flowrate relieving event for the LP flare system.

## 4.3 Flameout

In case of flare flameout, the flare pilots will automatically re-ignite. The flare shall be designed such that, in the event that re-ignition fails, the concentration of hazardous components near personnel and equipment with spark potential will be minimized, assuming the flare is functioning as a vent only. This will be reviewed as part of the flare dispersion analyses. Considerations will be given to not only ground-level locations, but also elevated locations where personnel or ignition sources may be present.
