[TABLE: Table 3.2 Relationship between Corrosion and Flow Regimes in Wet, Sour Gas Transport]

**Table 3.2  Relationship between Corrosion and Flow Regimes in Wet, Sour Gas Transport**

| Flow regime | Detrimental effect of flow | Beneficial effect of flow |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Stratified & V$_{sl}$ < 3 m/s$^{1)}$ | Water separation and settling of solids, leading to protective scale disruption, as follows:<br>- moving solids may erode the protective scale;<br>- corrosion may occur under deposits;<br>- settled solids may prevent the inhibitor reaching the surface;<br>- settled solids may contain elemental sulphur which is itself corrosive and can lead to scale disruption;<br>- high levels of chloride in solution act as a scale disrupter; this is most severe when the water is stagnant or at low flow. | |
| Stratified & V$_{sl}$ > 3 m/s$^{1)}$ | | Solids transported through the system. Formation of protective scales and inhibitor films. |
| Intermittent slug | Protective scales disruption by increased mass transfer and/or mechanical forces and/or removal of inhibitor films. Impact of effect depends on slug characteristics (shear forces). | |
| Annular dispersed flow (or dispersed bubble flow) | | Improved scale protection |

NOTE:  1)  V$_{sl}$ > 3 m/s is used here as a temporary critical velocity above which the risk of scale breakdown due to settling of solids is considerably reduced. This criterion may be later replaced by a more appropriate rule for this transition based on actual flow velocities. The critical velocity for solids transport is V$_t$, the liquid velocity (an actual velocity, not a superficial velocity). The V$_{sl}$ value used here has been practically found to be the required gas velocity to give a high enough V$_t$ to keep the solids suspended. V$_{sl}$ is used rather than V$_t$ because it is easier to measure.

## 3.3 COMPARATIVE CORROSION MECHANISMS

There are three different corrosion domains to consider:

| Condition | Dominant Mechanism |
| :--- | :--- |
| CO₂/H₂S < 20 | H₂S corrosion dominates; |
| 20 ≤ CO₂/H₂S ≤ 500 | Mixed CO₂/H₂S corrosion; |
| CO₂/H₂S > 500 | CO₂ corrosion dominates. |

The HYDROCOR corrosion model (6, [3]) has historically covered both the CO₂ corrosion domain and the mixed CO₂/H₂S domain, though it may be more conservative in the mixed domain. The SOGACOR (6, [4]) corrosion model has been recently incorporated into HYDROCOR to cover the H₂S corrosion dominated domain. Table 3.3 summarizes the main features of CO₂ and H₂S corrosion mechanisms. This DEP is primarily focused on the region where H₂S corrosion dominates; some parts of the mitigation strategy may apply to the mixed CO₂/H₂S corrosion regime.

---

[TABLE: Table 3.3 Main Features of CO₂ and H₂S Corrosion Mechanisms]

**Table 3.3 Main Features of CO₂ and H₂S Corrosion Mechanisms**

| | **CO₂ Corrosion** | **H₂S Corrosion** | **Mixed CO₂ / H₂S Corrosion** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| CO₂/H₂S ratio, mol/mol | > 500 | < 20 | 20 to 500 |
| Dominant scale | FeCO₃ | FeS | FeS/FeCO₃ |
| Mode of failure / corrosion morphology | Rupture + Pinhole leak/ General and localized | Pinhole leak/Localized | Rupture + Pinhole leak/ General and localized |
| Top-of-line corrosion | In stratified flow under certain circumstances. Main causes: high rate of water of condensation and/or organic acids. | Not observed unless excessive methanol is injected | Not observed unless excessive methanol is injected. |
| Corrosion sensitivity to: | | | |
| - Liquid velocity | - Increasing | - Decreasing | |
| - Chloride | - Modestly increasing | - Increasing | |
| - Elemental sulphur | - N/A | - Increasing | |
| - Settled solids | - Modestly increasing | - Increasing | |
| Erosion critical gas velocity (sand free) | 20 m/s¹¹ | >> 25 m/s²¹ | Limited data available shows rates to be no worse than the CO₂ regime. |
| Galvanic coupling | Minor effect in oxygen-free environments | Coupling between different metals — minor effect, in oxygen free environments.²¹ | |
| Methanol injection induced corrosion | Not corrosive; has a beneficial effect on the corrosion rate. Injection of oxygen with the methanol has to be taken into account. | Severe; see (4.2.10) | |
| Use of HYDROCOR corrosion rate calculation | See HYDROCOR manual, (6, [3]) | See HYDROCOR manual, (6, [3]). Generally, HYDROCOR will over predict, as effect of FeS scale is difficult to predict, requiring a conservative position. | See HYDROCOR manual, (6, [3]). Corrosion rates are known to be no worse than the rates with CO₂ alone; the calculated rate may be conservative in this regime. |

## 3.4 MITIGATION MEASURES

It is important to formulate mitigation measures to suit the expected flow regimes and corrosion mechanisms. For example, if stratified flow exists, continuous-injection inhibition will not mitigate top-of-line corrosion, as the inhibitors will not be transported to the vapour-phase portion of the pipeline. Corrosion might be severe enough to require alternatives such as corrosion allowance, pigging, batching, glycol injection, or even CRA. If the corrosion is dominated by H₂S, top-of-line corrosion is usually so low that no action is needed. However, bottom-of-line corrosion in H₂S might be so severe that continuous-injection inhibitors shall be formulated to disperse well in stagnant water pools to provide protection. Table 3.4 lists the primary use of major corrosion mitigation measures for wet gas pipelines, where "X" indicates a recommended measure.

NOTES:

1) This is an inhibitor selection issue. Some inhibitors partition into the water phase under stratified flow conditions. If the inhibitor partitions into the water phase, continuous inhibition works well in stratified flow and pigging is not required to distribute the inhibitor.

2) In the CO₂ corrosion regime, for most slugging environments the shear stresses are not extreme and standard inhibitors will work. For severe slugging environments, the shear stresses may be too high for standard inhibitors. However, there are some inhibitors that work in high shear situations, so this is an inhibitor selection issue. With the correct inhibitor, continuous inhibition can work in slugging conditions.

3) Only required in rare cases where TOL corrosion is an issue. Normally, TOL corrosion is dealt with by control of the condensation rate.

4) Only of use in certain situations, notably relatively low uninhibited corrosion rates and no formation water production (condensation water only).

5) Only of use for low corrosion rates and/or short design life. Even in these cases, use of a corrosion inhibitor and lower (or no) corrosion allowance should be the primary choice.

6) According to field experience, continuous inhibition is not effective in intermittent/slug flow in the H₂S corrosion regime. This differs from CO₂ corrosion, where some inhibitors are effective in this flow regime. The sulphide scales are known to be more tenacious than the carbonate scales, so this is not thought to be related primarily to scale removal. This may be due to less effective inhibitor bonding to the sulphide scales (H₂S corrosion system) than to the carbonate scales (CO₂ corrosion system). Another possible explanation is that intermittent slugging is from the wells and the slugs contain high chlorides.

<!-- PDF2MD-ASSETS:END page=11 -->

7) In low velocity situations, any solids in the produced fluids may drop out in the pipeline. The possible effects of the solids include:

- The solids may prevent continuously injected inhibitor from reaching the pipe wall;
- The solids also absorb corrosion inhibitor, which means the inhibitor injection rate has to be increased to achieve the required concentration at the pipeline outlet;
- Flow may be sufficient to move the solids along the bottom of the line; this action can damage the protective sulphide scales;
- If elemental sulphur is present, this causes further corrosion by chemically destroying the protective sulphide scales. Operational pigging is always required if elemental sulphur is or could be present;
- Under deposit corrosion can occur.

At present, corrosion inhibitors that can provide protection in sweet systems, when solids are present in the pipeline, are being studied; this study will subsequently be extended to cover sour pipelines. Possible solids in a pipeline include construction debris, sand (from the reservoir), corrosion products and elemental sulphur.

8) Pigging is required if solids are present in the line. The frequency of pigging is assessed on a case by case basis, based on the volume of solids present, the corrosion history of the line, etc.

## 3.5 NON-STEADY STATE OPERATING CONDITIONS

Non-steady state operating conditions will often result in a different corrosion mechanism where the corrosion control program designed for the steady-state production envelope might no longer be effective. Table 3.5 lists the non-steady state operating conditions that might impact the sour gas corrosion mechanisms and corrosion control efficiency. Special enhanced corrosion mitigation programs should be formulated for these non-steady state conditions.

---

[TABLE: Table 3.5 Impacts of Non-Steady State Operating Conditions on Wet Sour Gas Corrosion]

**Table 3.5 Impacts of Non-Steady State Operating Conditions on Wet Sour Gas Corrosion**

| Operating Conditions | Typical contributors | Impacts |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Start-up; see (4.2.1) | Well bore clean-up: - higher salinity - production of solids - lower pH | - more severe effluent chemistry - adsorption of inhibitors on solids, increasing inhibitor requirements - some inhibitors do not work well in high salinity environments - high salinity environments may require different corrosion resistant alloys |
| | Mill scale conversion to loosen FeS | - adsorption of inhibitors on the mill scale increasing inhibitor requirements - potential operation problems in downstream units with scale deposits |
| Spent HCl acids (neutralized); see (4.2.9) | - much higher chlorides (up to 300,000 ppm) - production of solids - lower pH | - potential degraded inhibitor performance and FeS scale instability - adsorption of inhibitors increasing inhibitor requirements |
| Shut-in and fuel gas blanketed for long time; see (4.2.3 to 4.2.5) | Conversion of FeS to FeCO₃ | - no corrosion protection from FeS scales during restart. FeCO₃ scales not as protective as FeS scales |
| Turn around (line open to moist air); see (4.2.6) | Conversion of FeS into Fe(OH)₃ and re-conversion to greigite on start up. | - no corrosion protection from FeS scales during restart. Greigite not as protective as other types of FeS scales - potential degraded inhibitor performance |
| Methanol injection; see (4.2.10) | Methanol condensation behaviour. O₂ injected with the methanol | - potential degraded inhibitor performance - chemical reaction creates elemental sulphur which is corrosive - destroys protective scale |

## 3.6 CORROSION MONITORING CONSIDERATIONS FOR WET SOUR GAS

To be effective and efficient in a wet sour gas environment, a corrosion-monitoring device shall be capable of detecting isolated pitting, which is the most dominant form of corrosion. A single point coverage device such as a coupon will often fail to detect pitting. Recommendations for corrosion monitoring are described in (6,[5]).

## 3.7 SAMPLING PROGRAM CONSIDERATIONS

A comprehensive sampling programme is required which should include water, gas and condensate analyses. Flow rates should also be recorded. Inhibition availability

measurements (pump records, inhibitor consumption, inventory checks, etc.) for individual lines are key data for assessing day-to-day compliance with the corrosion control plan. Inhibitor residual measurements are another important part of the corrosion monitoring scheme.

The sampling frequency shall match the expected corrosion mechanisms and rates. For example, under a specific high-chloride low flow condition, the predicted corrosion rate is 10 mm/yr. For a pipeline with a remaining wall thickness of 5 mm, if corrosion proceeds unchecked, it will fail in less than 6 months. A yearly sampling program will be useless as a failure might occur before the next sample is taken; a 1 week to 4 week sampling program would be appropriate, depending on the maximum allowable loss per corrosion event.

## 3.8 INSPECTION

To validate the performance of the mitigation program, an inspection plan shall be formulated.

Any changes in the mitigation strategy shall be linked to an increased inspection strategy, to verify that the changed strategy has not resulted in increased corrosion.

## 3.9 CORROSION CONTROL DESIGN

The corrosion mitigation strategy shall be developed with the aid of the data given in (4). This is part of the corrosion control design. For each identified corrosion risk (3.1), the corrosion control design shall include:

- mitigation strategy;
- inspection requirements;
- monitoring and sampling requirements;
- special considerations (timing / remarks / recommendations).

This shall be assessed for each of the major phases of operation:

- initial pipeline start up;
- pipeline start up after well stimulation;
- pipeline start up in all possible operating modes (e.g. line pressurised, line depressurised, methanol injected etc.);
- steady state production;
- shut-ins (of all possible durations and types; see (4.2.3 through 4.2.8);
- abandonment.

## 3.10 MITIGATION STRATEGY REVIEW

The mitigation strategy should be reviewed annually. This should include:

- Check the operating envelope of the corrosion inhibitor (provided by inhibitor supplier) against the operating conditions for each pipeline segment. Flag cases where the inhibitor is being used outside its specified criteria.
- Look for cases where the current mitigation strategy is more severe than in this DEP. Review the history of these lines. Consider a relaxation of the mitigation strategy for these lines.
- Look for cases where the current mitigation is less severe than indicated in this DEP. Review the history of these lines. If it is decided that it is acceptable to do less than is indicated in this DEP, this should be agreed with and signed off by the Principal's corrosion engineer. Otherwise, the mitigation program should be revised to comply with this DEP.
- Review known corrosion problems.

---

- Review overall corrosion control system availability against the required design availability.

This review may result in a revised mitigation strategy. It should also be used as part of the selection process for pipeline inspection.

---

## 4. CORROSION MITIGATION GUIDELINES

### 4.1 SOUR GAS PIPELINE CLASSIFICATION

In a simplified combination of flow regimes and fluid corrosivity, wet, sour gas pipelines may be classified into 8 types, according to the values of the following parameters:

- flow regimes;
- chloride (Cl⁻) contents of the water;
- presence of elemental sulphur.

The flow regime profile for the pipeline is one of the outputs from HYDROCOR modelling. There may be several different flow regimes over the length of the pipeline; the mitigation strategy shall be based on the most severe regime, from the point of view of selecting line type. For example, if the line contains intermittent slug flow in some sections and annular dispersed flow in other sections, the mitigation strategy for the whole line shall be based on the intermittent slug flow regime.

If the flow regime profile for the pipeline is not known, the superficial gas velocity/critical gas velocity ratio (V_sg/V_crit) can be substituted. V_crit values are field specific and have, for example, been determined empirically for all of Shell Canada's fields (6. [6]). Application of this approach in other fields would require careful review by the Principal's corrosion engineer.

The critical chloride concentration of 10,000 ppm has been determined from field experience and laboratory testing; above a concentration of 10,000 ppm, the chloride ion can destroy the protective FeS scales. The 10,000 ppm limit has been conservatively selected.

The presence of elemental sulphur promotes corrosion in two ways: it destroys the protective FeS scale by offering a fresh steel surface for corrosion, and in addition the elemental sulphur is itself corrosive to steel. At present, any elemental sulphur is considered a problem. This may be a conservative approach when there are only low levels of elemental sulphur, but there is no data to support any alternative approach at this time. The primary risk of elemental sulphur deposition from the production fluids can be addressed by taking a bottom hole sample and analysing the fluids.

Elemental sulphur can also be caused by poor operating practices. Whenever elemental sulphur is detected, the root cause of the sulphur presence should be understood before a mitigation strategy is implemented. For example, if the sulphur deposition is caused by oxygen being injected with methanol injection, the best remedial action may be to address the oxygen being injected rather than changing the mitigation strategy.

Finally, where elemental sulphur is detected, this could also be due to poor sampling and analysis practices.

Tables 4.1(a) and 4.1(b) show the eight classes of wet sour gas pipelines.

NOTE: In classifying sour gas pipelines, the boundary values for the parameters are not absolute differentiators. Pipelines with values near those boundary limits should not be classified unthinkingly, but according to field experience. The Principal's corrosion engineer shall be consulted in such cases.

The rules given in this DEP shall be used as the basis for the mitigation strategy if no other information is known. Any changes from this mitigation strategy should be understood, documented and captured in the management of change process. An example of the type of information required is:

"Pipeline xyz is classified as a type I line. Because of past corrosion resulting in a maximum of ab % wall loss, the mitigation strategy is based on a type IA line."

Where a change is required for a specific line, the mitigation strategy for the line should be based on a different type of line, rather than changing individual elements of the strategy. For example, a line should be treated as type IA instead of type I, rather than treating it as a type I line but with a steady state pigging frequency of 4 weeks. This is to ensure that a

---

changed mitigation strategy is also adopted for the non-steady state conditions as well as the steady state conditions.

Any mitigation programme should be closely linked to changes in production and changes in the operating window for the pipeline, because this could result in a change in line classification.

## 4.2 WET SOUR GAS CORROSION MITIGATION RECOMMENDATIONS

### 4.2.1 Start-up

During initial well start-up, the well effluents might be more corrosive than the ones under steady state conditions. Intermittent production flows can further aggravate corrosion. Continuous injection inhibition alone might not be effective due to the much higher adsorption of inhibitors by competing solid particles.

As a rule of thumb, double batches (2 days to 3 days before and 2 days to 3 days after start-up) are required for most situations (Table 4.2). Increasing the continuous inhibitor injection rates to compensate for inhibitor adsorption by solids is also required for some types of sour gas clusters. Inhibitor adsorption by solids should be tested during inhibitor selection. Batch treatment programmes may have an impact on the downstream plant (large volumes of chemical arriving at the downstream plant); possible negative impacts should be reviewed prior to starting the batch programme.

For pipelines that have been shut in for more than 6 months, especially under a fuel gas blanket, these start-up procedures also apply. This is because one cannot rely on the existing iron sulphide scales and residual corrosion inhibitor films for start-up corrosion protection. During the prolonged shut-in, they might have undergone significant changes.

Other issues to be considered during start up include:

- status of line prior to start up (e.g. containing sour gas, fuel gas or nitrogen, at full pressure or at low pressure, cold or at operating temperature);
- sulphur solvent (if required) on line prior to start up;
- sampling of Total Suspended Solids to check for elemental sulphur;
- continuous inhibition (if required) on line prior to start-up;
- monitoring inhibitor residuals in produced water;
- handling spent acid fluids if the well was acidised before start up, see (4.2.9);
- monitoring pH and chloride content of produced water, see (4.2.9);
- checking impact of low flow and high flow;
- hydrate control;
- methanol injection requirements for start up, see (4.2.10);
- sand detection;
- ensuring no oxygen is left in the system prior to start-up.

---

[TABLE: Table 4.2 Corrosion mitigation for start-up]

| Type | First Batch (2 to 3 days before flowing) | Continuous Injection Inhibition over-dosage; factor, for 2 weeks | Second Batch (2 to 3 days after flowing) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| I | Required | No over-dosage | Not Required |
| IA | Required | No over-dosage | Required |
| II | Required | No over-dosage | Required |
| III | Required | No over-dosage | Required |
| IS | Required | 2 x | Required |
| IAS | Required | 2 x | Required |
| IIS | Required | 2 x | Required |
| IIIS | Required | 4 x | Required |

## 4.2.2 Normal steady state production

Based on the mitigation strategy outlined in Table 3.4, the mitigation methods (continuous injection, pigging, etc.) are recommended. The recommended frequency of pigging and batching has been determined based on current field experience and feedback from intelligent pigging. The overall corrosion mitigation methods and frequency are presented in Table 4.3.

Note: Batching frequency depends on the batch inhibitor persistency under specific operating conditions. Batch inhibitor persistency determined in the laboratory gives a lower boundary of the required batching frequency; it cannot be currently linked to the persistency achievable in the field. This depends on a combination of a number of factors, including the condition of the steel surface (bare steel, iron sulphide film), use of sulphur solvents, possibility of elemental sulphur deposition, and whether or not the inhibitor has been proven in continuous injection service in the field. If inhibitor chemicals are changed, it cannot be assumed that the batching frequency will remain the same; laboratory and field test programmes are needed to determine the required frequencies with the new chemical.

Other issues to be considered during normal steady state production include:

- defined operating window (flow regime, Cl⁻, S);
- regular sampling programme to check operating window. Change mitigation strategy if significant changes occur;
- long term trending of chlorides and water production rate to predict onset of formation water, which typically requires a change in mitigation strategy;
- compliance with batch inhibitor schedule (availability);
- compliance with inhibitor and sulphur solvent availability;
- inhibitor residual monitoring;
- intelligent pigging programme plus an inspection programme for all piping that cannot be inspected by means of intelligent pigging;
- corrosion monitoring as an indicator of potential problems;
- operational pigging and sampling of pig debris;
- impact of low flow and high flow;
- hydrates;
- methanol injection requirements for normal operation, see (4.2.10);

2) Wire brush pigging is only required in the line types indicated and in lines that are known to be corroded; it is useful in cleaning corrosion products out of pits. The wire brush pig will then replace one of the regular pigging runs; wire brushing should only be carried out with batching.

6) To determine if sulphur solvent is required, modelling should be carried out. This should look at how much sulphur is expected and how much credit can be taken for lubricants in the system that may dissolve the sulphur (solubility of sulphur in oil/condensate varies and specific testing is required). Modelling can only give an indication of quantities of elemental sulphur deposited, so a conservative approach should be taken on whether the solvent is required or not.

#### 4.2.3 Planned shut-in < 24 hours

No additional corrosion control measures are required for planned shut-ins of less than 24 hours.

#### 4.2.4 Planned shut-in ≥ 24 hours and < 1 month (turn-around)

If a sour gas pipeline is temporarily taken out of service for a period longer than 24 h, the flow regime is equivalent to the worst stratified flow. Continued protection from corrosion by the residual inhibitors (continuous injection or batch) can only last for a certain time. The aggressiveness of the corrodents can be reduced by reducing their partial pressures (line depressurisation, fuel gas blanketing). In most circumstances, the line should also be pigged to remove water and to prevent solids from settling; see Table 4.4. The requirements in these tables only relate to mitigation measures to be carried out for corrosion control: there may other reasons to carry out similar mitigation measures, e.g., a fuel gas purge may be required to prevent hydrate formation or for safety reasons.

[TABLE: Table 4.4 Corrosion Mitigation for planned shut-ins ≥ 24 hours and < 1 month (Turn-Arounds)]

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| I | Not required | | Required |
| IA | Covered by batching requirements | Required if longer than 2 weeks | Required |
| II | Not required | | Required |
| III | Covered by batching requirements | Required if longer than 2 weeks | Required |
| IS | Required if longer than 2 weeks | | Required |
| IAS | Covered by batching requirements | Required if longer than 2 weeks | Required |
| IIS | Required if longer than 2 weeks | | Required |
| IIIS | Covered by batching requirements | Required if longer than 2 weeks | Required |

#### 4.2.5 Planned shut-in ≥ 1 month

Corrosion mechanisms are similar to those described in (4.2.4). After a pipeline has been shut in for more than 6 months, even if the shut-in procedures have been followed, the start-up procedures (4.2.1) shall be used when the pipeline is re-commissioned. During the prolonged shut-in, the existing iron sulphide scales and residual corrosion inhibitor films might have undergone significant changes; hence, they cannot provide adequate protection by themselves.

| I | Required | | Required | |
| IA | Required | Required | | Required |
| II | Required | | Required | |
| III | Required | Required | | Required |
| IS | Required | Required | | Required |
| IAS | Required | Required | | Required |
| IIS | Required | Required | | Required |
| IIIS | Required | Required | | Required |

NOTE: 1) If not purged with fuel gas.

#### 4.2.6 Any planned maintenance with line intervention

If the inside of the line is exposed to the atmosphere, precautions shall be taken to minimize the conversion of iron sulphide scales to hydroxides and sulphur due to exposure to moist air. Procedural controls should be in place to minimize oxygen entry (e.g., pipeline plugs). Furthermore, if the existing pipeline steel is not resistant to HIC, upon re-start the iron hydroxide scales may be converted to greigite, which makes the steel vulnerable to HIC; see (6. [7]).

If the line is exposed during a turn-around, the corrosion mitigation measures for start-up (see Table 4.2) shall be followed when starting up the system.

#### 4.2.7 Prolonged shut-ins

For prolonged shut-ins, the line should be isolated by blind flanges or by inserting spades. Isolation by valves alone can lead to a false sense of security, because all valves leak to a greater or lesser extent.

If the shut-in lasts longer than originally planned, and the more stringent mitigation measures (pigging, de-watering, batching) could not be carried out during the turn-around, the corrosion mitigation measures for start up (see Table 4.2) shall be followed when starting up the system. In addition, it may be necessary to carry out intelligent pigging prior to restarting the line.

#### 4.2.8 Unplanned shut-ins

The actions required shall be reviewed against the expected duration of shutdown, following sections (4.2.3) through (4.2.7).

## 4.2.9 Spent acid flow back

In the spent acid flow back scenario, the effluents can contain a very high chloride brine (up to 300,000 ppm), low pH fluids and additional unknown fluid chemistry. The continuous and/or batch inhibitors in use might not be effective, due to the change in fluid properties and increasing inhibitor adsorption. This is caused by a potentially large concentration of very fine solids from the formation in the spent acid stream. The existing FeS scales on the pipeline might not be stable under this fluid chemistry.

To combat these problems, spent acid flow back fluids are not allowed to enter the pipeline until both of the following conditions are met:

- pH ≥ 4 and
- chlorides ≤ 50,000 ppm.

Temporary separation facilities shall be used, and pH and chloride measurements are required with separate disposal of liquids until the pH and chlorides targets are met.

Once the pH and chloride targets are met, the liquids can be put back in the pipeline. This should be treated as a "start-up", in line with Table 4.2. Should the flowline be batched when liquids are put back into flowlines. Extra continuous corrosion inhibitor should be added in accordance with Table 4.2, depending on flow regime, for up to 2 weeks. Weekly samples of water should be taken and analysed for chlorides, inhibitor residuals, and pH. The extra mitigation requirements given in Table 4.2 shall be maintained until stable well production is established; once this is confirmed the mitigation plan may revert to a steady state production mitigation strategy.

Any corrosion resistant alloys in the systems should be selected against this high chloride rate (300,000 ppm), because cracking due to high chloride levels can happen very quickly.

For all the 8 sour gas types, an enhanced mitigation program shall consist of the following as a minimum:

- batching of the pipeline 2 days to 3 days prior to spent acid flow back;
- daily sampling of the produced water;
- increasing inhibitor injection rates (see Table 4.2) until water chemistry returns to normal;
- weekly batching if the chloride level stays above 25,000 ppm (if normal Cl⁻ level of the fluids is less than 25,000 ppm). Batching will be discontinued when the Cl⁻ level returns to normal.

Due to the complexity of corrosion by spent acid flow back, all enhanced corrosion control programs require approval from the Principal's corrosion engineer.

## 4.2.10 Methanol injection

Experience and research have shown that excessive methanol injected for hydrate control can cause top-of-line (TOL) as well as bottom-of-line (BOL) corrosion in sour systems. According to field experience, "excessive" methanol injection occurs when the volume of injected methanol is greater than the total volume of water produced in the pipeline (water of condensation and of production). The methanol injection is thought to influence corrosion in the following ways:

- The primary effect is that oxygen injected with the methanol causes corrosion (oxygen is much more soluble in MeOH than in water) – this could lead to BOL or TOL corrosion. The oxygen reacts with H₂S to give deposits of elemental sulphur. This is not a significant change for types IS to IIIS, which already contain elemental sulphur, but would, for example, effectively change a type I gas to a type IS fine.
- The secondary effect is that methanol condensing on TOL with water, dissolving corrosion product films and carrying away corrosion products, could lead to added TOL corrosion.

---

Where this has occurred, typical corrosion rates caused by methanol injection are from 1 mm/yr to 3 mm/yr, in addition to the sour gas corrosion rates. The additional mitigation measures in Table 4.6 are recommended where excess methanol is injected, to prevent this corrosion occurring.

[TABLE: Table 4.6 Additional mitigation recommendations for excessive methanol injection]

| Type | Excessive Methanol Injection Duration | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | Less than 2 weeks | 2 to 4 weeks | More than 4 weeks<sup>1</sup> |
| I | No actions | No actions | No actions |
| IA | No actions | Pigging once | Monthly pigging |
| II | No actions | Pigging once | Monthly pigging |
| III | No actions | Batching once | Monthly pigging + quarterly batching |
| IS | No actions | No actions | Monthly pigging |
| IAS | No actions | Pigging once | Monthly pigging |
| IIS | No actions | Pigging once | Monthly pigging |
| IIIS | No actions | Batching once | Monthly pigging + quarterly batching |

NOTE 1) Only if the regular pigging/batching frequency does not meet this recommendation; otherwise, no actions.

## 4.2.11 Pipelines with known existing corrosion defects

For a given type of sour gas class (I, IA, etc.), the corresponding corrosion mitigation measures might not be effective for deep corrosion pits (believed to be approximately 8 mm). An enhanced program might be needed until it is proven conclusively that the pits are dormant. The Principal's corrosion engineer shall be consulted on the formulation and subsequent discontinuation of the enhanced corrosion mitigation plan for all pipelines with known corrosion left in place.

## 1.0 Objective

### 1.1 *Scope*

1.1.1 This specification outlines the basis for design, installation, testing and quality control procedures for the High Density Polyethylene (HDPE) pipes in underground applications.

1.1.2 Standard Detail Drawings, attached at the end of these Specifications, illustrate installation details.

### 1.2 *Terminology*

1.2.1 The '**Owner**' means Suncor Energy Inc.

1.2.2 The '**Buyer**' – means Suncor or its agent designated for that project.

1.2.3 '**Owner's Engineer**' - means the person responsible for the technical integrity of the project.

1.2.4 '**Owner's Inspector**' – means the person authorized for inspection.

1.2.5 The '**Supplier**' - means the entity, manufacturer, fabricator, vendor or contractor that supplies the material or services.

## 3.0 Design

### 3.1 General

3.1.1 HDPE does not react with most fluids being pumped. The Engineering Characteristics brochure should be reviewed to check HDPE pipe resistance to various chemicals, the operating temperature and the concentration of the chemical itself.

3.1.2 HDPE pipe should not be used in areas where significant concentrations of hydrocarbon are present in soils.

3.1.3 In considering the design Limits for a HDPE system, the interdependence of the operating pressure, temperature, safety factor and the expected life should be taken into account Special consideration should be given to surge pressures and vacuum in the system.

3.1.4 Pipe wall thickness (DR) selection should be based on earth loads, live traffic loads, soil compaction and trench design.

3.1.5 The piping system can be designed as conventional deep bury system or shallow bury insulated system.

### 3.2 *Deep Bury Installation*

3.2.1 Pipes carrying water and other fluid that have similar freezing temperature to water should be buried at a minimum depth of 10'-8" to the top of the pipe. See Drawing A1.0 in Appendix A for details.

### 3.3 *Shallow Bury Insulated Installation*

3.3.1 Where deep bury installation is not possible, practical or economical, the piping system can be installed in insulated trenches at shallow depths. The minimum depth to the top of the pipe should be 6'-0". A layer of 5" styrofoam insulation should be placed at a minimum depth of 5'-0". In special circumstances, pipe bury depth can be revised to less than 6'-0", however, the insulation thickness will have to be increased. Insulation manufacturer's instruction shall be followed to calculate the revised thickness of the insulation. See Drawing A1.1 in Appendix A for details.

3.3.2 The width of the insulation for the pipe buried at a minimum of 6'-0" shall be 12'-0". The insulation can be designed as horizontal layer or as "inverted U". The sum of the width and vertical legs of the "inverted U" insulation shall be minimum 12'-0". See Drawings A1.2 and A1.3 in Appendix A for details.

3.3.3 Styrofoam insulation is manufactured in varying compressive strengths; insulation strength should be designed for a particular application which depends on a total load calculation.

---

## 4.0 Materials

### 4.1 Pipe

HDPE pipe - PE3408 DR11, in accordance with OSG Piping Specifications "CHY", "CHZ" or "APB".

### 4.2 Fittings

HDPE fittings shall be in accordance with OSB Piping Specifications "CHY", "CHZ" or "APB" and shall be factory manufactured. Stub end adaptors to be HDPE Type, ASTM F714-DR11. Flanges to be pipe manufacturer's approved lapped joint. Gaskets shall be neoprene as per manufacturer's recommendation. Stud Bolts shall be ASTM A307 Gr. B, including washer for both sides (ASTM F606). All fittings to Suncor Energy piping specifications "CHY", "CHZ" or "APB".

### 4.3 Valves

All valves shall be as per OSB Piping Specifications "CHY", "CHZ" or "APB".

### 4.4 Insulation

Insulation shall be styrofoam min. HI-40 to CAN22CGSB-51.20-M87 (Type 4) or CAN/ULC S701 (Type 4).

### 4.5 Thrust Block

Concrete for thrust blocking shall be sulphate resistant, Type 50 developing a compressive strength of not less than 20 MPa in 28 days.

### 4.6 Bedding

Bedding material shall be well graded sand consisting of hard durable particles free from clay lumps, cementation, organic material, frozen material and other deleterious materials. The bedding sand shall meet the following gradation:

> **Table - Bedding sand gradation — Sieve size vs Percent Passing \(by weight\), first table** - see [XLSX](14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping/14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping-01_assets/tables/14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping-01_p0005_tbl01_bedding-sand-gradation-first.xlsx) and [source crop](14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping/14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping-01_assets/tables/14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping-01_p0005_tbl01_bedding-sand-gradation-first.png)

| Sieve Size 10⁻³ m (equivalent) | Percent Passing (by weight) |
| :--- | :---: |
| 12,500 (1/2") | 100 |
| 4,750 (No. 4) | 95 |
| 75 (No. 200) | 2-10 |

For trenches where the native material is fill material, the fittings shall be bedded in crush-rock bedding. The crush rock bedding shall meet ASTM C136 and ASTM C117 when tested and give a smooth curve without sharp breaks when plotted on a semi-log grading chart.

> **Table - Crush-rock bedding gradation — Sieve size vs Percent Passing \(by weight\), second table** - see [XLSX](14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping/14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping-01_assets/tables/14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping-01_p0005_tbl02_crush-rock-bedding-gradation-second.xlsx) and [source crop](14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping/14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping-01_assets/tables/14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping-01_p0005_tbl02_crush-rock-bedding-gradation-second.png)

| Sieve Size 10⁻³ m (equivalent) | Percent Passing (by weight) |
| :--- | :---: |
| 19,000 (3/4") | 100 |
| 12,500 (1/2") | 64-100 |
| 4,750 (No. 4) | 36-72 |
| 1,400 (No. 14) | 12-42 |
| 355 (No. 45) | 8-22 |
| 75 (No. 200) | 8-12 |

#### 4.7 *FILLCRETE*

Fillcrete is a cementitious fill material comprised of a sand mix with a cement bond (product of Consolidated Concrete). It shall have a minimum 7 day compressive strength of 0.5 MPa.

## 5.0 Installation

### 5.1 *TRENCHING AND BEDDING*

5.1.1 The minimum and maximum trench width below the crown of the pipe shall be not less than the nominal diameter of the pipe plus 24". The trench shall be excavated so that pipe can be laid to the alignment, grade and depth required. The subgrade shall provide a uniform and continuous support for the pipe and fittings on solid undisturbed ground.

5.1.2 Where the subgrade of the trench is unstable or where it contains ashes, cinders, refuse or organic material, such material shall be excavated and the subgrade shall be made by backfilling with stabilizing gravel compacted in 3" layers. Where the gravel subgrade can not be made to properly support the pipe, spatial foundations should be designed.

5.1.3 The pipe is to be installed in sand bedding 3" below the pipe bottom and extending at least 12" above the pipe to the full width of the trench. The bedding shall be placed in uniform layers not exceeding 6" compacted to at least 95% Standard Proctor Density. The bed shall be shaped true to grade and to provide continuous, uniform bearing surface for barrel of the pipe. Do not use blocks when bedding the pipe.

Remove all rocks and sharp protrusions from rock from the bedding material area to provide a minimum of 6" of clear bedding material on each side of the pipe. See Drawings A1.0 and A1.1 In Appendix A for details.

5.1.4 Where fittings are placed in a trench where native material is fill material, as compared to installations in bedrock, the fittings shall be bedded in crushed rock bedding for a distance of three pipe diameters in each direction from the fitting.

### 5.2 *PIPE*

5.2.1 The pipe shall be installed as per manufacturer's instructions to the alignment and grade required. Minimum depth as per drawings shall be maintained with no sags or humps and with proper bury at hydrants, monitors, valves and tie-in points. Where minor deflections in line or grade are required, the deflections shall not exceed the maximum recommended by the pipe manufacturer. Ensure barrel of the pipe is in contact with shaped bed throughout its full length. Do not lay pipe on frozen bedding.

5.2.2 Do not install any pipe sections where trench conditions are unsuitable. If the pipe must be installed below the ground water table, the pipe must be sufficiently anchored to prevent floating, such as through use of swamp weights or poured-in-place anchor blocks.

5.2.3 Keep the pipe free of dirt and water and other foreign materials. Whenever work is stopped, install a removable watertight bulkhead at open end of the last pipe laid.

5.2.4 Cut pipes in an approved manner as recommended by the pipe manufacturer, without damaging of pipe and to leave smooth end at right angles to axis of the pipe.

---

5.2.5 Follow recommendations of the pipe manufacturer regarding HDPE flanged connections. The flanged connection must be tightened initially and then allowed to creep to relieve the cold working stresses for a minimum of 8 hours, and then re-tightened.

*5.3 VALVES*

5.3.1 Place valve level to ensure the vertical stem and above grade post indicator can be placed directly above the valve in a vertical orientation.

5.3.2 All buried components, including the valve body, stem, box and below grade post indicator assembly or valve box are to be wrapped in a continuous water barrier wrapping. See Drawings A1.4 and A1.5 in Appendix A for details.

5.3.3 An annular space around the stem box is to consist only of packed gravel. The packed gravel annulus must extend a minimum of 4" radially around the valve stem box. Place a Sono-Tube to contain the gravel during backfilling.

*5.4 THRUST BLOCKING*

5.4.1 Concrete reaction blocks and supports are to be in accordance with CAN/CSA A23.1. Reinforcement shall be placed in accordance with CAN/CSA-A23.1. Place thrust blocking under valves, hydrant bowls and monitors. Do not place load upon new concrete until it is set.

5.4.2 Concrete reaction blocks shall be placed between the undisturbed ground and the fitting or valve. A layer of 12 mil polyethylene sheet is to be placed between the valve body or hydrant bowl and the concrete to prevent surface corrosion.

5.4.3 The placement of the concrete block must allow access to all flange bolts on both ends of valves.

*5.5 INSULATION*

5.5.1 Protect insulation from exposure to ultraviolet light, physical damage and contact with incompatible chemicals.

5.5.2 Place a minimum of 2" thickness of granular sand material as bedding for the insulation.

5.5.3 Install insulation with staggered joints to maintain continuity of thermal protection. Cut and trim insulation neatly to fit spaces. Butt joints tightly, offset vertical joints. Use only insulation free from chipped or broken edges. Use largest possible dimensions to reduce the number of joints. Place insulation in staggered fashion with long axis parallel to the crown of the embankment.

5.5.4 Take precautions to prevent movement of the insulation during placement of the granular cover. Immediately following placement of insulation, carefully place 10" thickness of granular material over the insulation, taking special precautions not to damage the boards. This minimum coverage of the granular material is required before the surface can be subjected to any vehicular traffic.

5.5.5 Place insulation between pipes to be crossed for shallow-bury installation. See Drawing A1.6 in Appendix A for details.

*5.6 BACKFILL*

5.6.1 Backfill shall consist of replacing the excavated material in even layers not exceeding 12" in depth and compacting each layer by mechanical means to a minimum 97% Standard Proctor Density in trenches under roads, and 95% in

---

other areas. No boulders, rock, ice, snow, organic material or debris shall be permitted in the trench. Mechanical compaction equipment should not be used until there is sufficient cover to prevent damage to the pipe and insulation.

5.6.2 In areas where 95% Standard Proctor Density compaction is required, but where such compaction could not be achieved with typical construction methods and equipment, use "Fillcrete". Follow "Fillcrete" manufacturer's recommendation for placement. Leave forms in place undisturbed for a sufficient time to ensure the matrix has cured and that settlement or subsidence of "Fillcrete" cannot occur.

## 6.0 Testing

### 6.1 *Testing*

6.1.1 Testing of HDPE pipe is to be in accordance with CSA/CAN3 B-137.1.

6.1.2 Refer to Suncor OSG Standard 0205 for details. The hydrostatic testing procedure for HDPE piping is considerably different than that for steel pipe. Where composite sections of HDPE and steel pipe are tested at one time, the procedure for HDPE pipe shall be used.

6.1.3 Test preparation, test fluid and pressure testing must be done in accordance with ANSI B31.3.

6.1.4 When the line has been filled, all the air must be expelled by high point vents, pigging or over-flushing. Time should be allowed for the water to reach a constant temperature.

6.1.5 The test pressure shall be at 1.5 times maximum design pressure of the system, but shall not exceed the pressure rating of the pipe or piping components.

6.1.6 No test shall be applied until at least 7 days after the concrete thrust reaction block has been cast, and after plugged ends have been securely braced.

6.1.7 If the test fails for any section of the water main, locate and repair the leaks. After such repairs, retesting of the repaired sections shall be conducted. Note that the testing procedure for HDPE pipe requires a "relaxing" duration between retests.

6.1.8 Test equipment shall be from an approved laboratory or manufacturer and shall be furnished with a certificate showing degree of accuracy.

6.1.9 All joints and flanged connections are to be left exposed until hydrostatic and visual inspections are completed.

### 6.2 *Corrosion Protection Testing*

6.2.1 All buried steel, cast or cast components are to be cathodically protected by an electrically bonded and properly sized anode.

6.2.2 Cathodic protection shall be installed for each hydrant assembly, monitor, and valve.

6.2.3 Cathodic protection equipment is to be installed as per manufacturer's specifications. See Drawing A1.7 in Appendix A for details.

6.2.4 Magnesium anodes are to be properly sized for the amount of buried steel.

## APPENDIX B

**FUSION BONDING OF HDPE FOR PRESSURE APPLICATION**

---

# 1.0 General

## 1.1 *Summary*

### 1.1.1 Scope of Specification

a. This specification prescribes the criteria for fusion bonding high density polyethylene piping and fittings used for pressure applications. Fusion bonding using this specification will satisfy pressure piping used for ASME B31.3 pressure piping applications and firewater piping meeting National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) requirements.

b. No deviation shall be made from this specification without written authorization from Owner's Engineer.

c. This specification may be used for shop as well as field fabrication.

### 1.1.2 Terminology

a. Shop Fabricate: Fabrication performed at a Supplier's shop, normally remote from the jobsite.

b. Field Fabricate: Fabrication performed at the jobsite, either in a field shop or at the installation site area.

c. HDPE: High density polyethylene.

d. Butt-Fusion Bonding: The use of a hot plate to heat the ends of HDPE pipe to a temperature which is conducive to allowing the ends to be fused together upon the application of pressure.

e. Sidewall-Fusion Bonding: The use of a contoured heating plate to heat the ends of a saddle face simultaneously with the surface of the pipe to a temperature which is conducive to allowing the saddle to be fused to the pipe upon application of pressure.

## 1.2 *Referenced Codes and Regulations*

### 1.2.1 The following codes and standards form an integral part of this specification. Any conflict between this specification, or referenced standard or code shall be brought to the attention of the Owner's Engineer for resolution prior to proceeding. All referenced codes and standards are to be of the latest edition or revision.

a. ASME (American Society of Mechanical Engineers)

1. B31.3 Chemical Plant and Petroleum Refinery Piping

b. ASTM (American Society for Testing and Materials)

1. D 1238 Flow Rates of Thermoplastics by Extrusion Plastometer
2. D 2657 Heat-Joining Polyolefin Pipe and Fittings
3. D 3350 Polyethylene Plastics Pipe and Fittings Materials
4. F 714 Polyethylene (PE) Plastic Pipe (SDR-PR) Based on Outside Diameter
5. F 905 Practice for Qualifications of Polyethylene Saddle Fusion Joints

c. PPI (Plastic Pipe Institute)

1. PPI-TN-13 General Guidelines for the Heat Fusion of Unlike Polyethylene Pipes and Fittings, Reaffirmed 1992

---

1.3  *Submittals*

Documents created and used by Fabricator to produce, control, and manage this Work are subject to review of approval by responsible representatives of Suncor as follows:

1.3.1  QA (Quality Assurance) Manual

QA Manual shall be submitted to Suncor for review, comment and approval. The manual shall include the procedures, instructions, and QA systems, including responsibilities, accountabilities and lines of communication to ensure that assigned field fabrication and workmanship, and other related services conform to the design engineering specifications and other contractual requirements.

1.3.2  Bonding Procedures Specification (BPS)

Bonding procedures shall be submitted to Suncor for comment and review. The procedures shall be qualified in accordance with this specification.

1.3.3  Bonder's Performance Qualifications

Bonder's performance qualification records shall be submitted to Suncor for review. The bonder shall be qualified in accordance with this specification.

1.3.4  Inspection and Test Plan

All inspection and test plans, as required by this specification, shall be submitted to Suncor for approval by QA and Engineering prior to commencement of fabrication.

1.4  *Quality Assurance*

Suncor QA shall audit the activities of the fabrication and installation to ensure that procedures are being followed to meet quality objectives.

1.4.1  The Fabricator shall be responsible for fusion bonded joint integrity. Each joint may be subject to check by Suncor.

1.4.2  The fabricator's inspection shall examine and inspect the final product to ensure that quality criteria have been met.

1.4.3  The Fabricator shall examine and inspect piping components for damage and improper manufacturing prior to beginning fabrication, in accordance with ASME 831.3, Paragraph A341. After fabrication has been completed, components shall be re-examined and re-inspected for possible damage. Repairs shall be made before installation.

1.4.4  Suncor QA may select bonds at random prior to installation, which will be removed for destructive testing to verify quality standards are being met.

## 2.0  Products

2.1  *Materials*

2.1.1  Piping materials shall be in accordance with ASTM D 2513, Class PE 3408 and ASTM D3350, Class PE3408 or PE45434. The pipe dimensions shall be in accordance with ASTM F 714. The SDR rating shall be specified on the drawings.

2.1.2  Substitutions, including thicker or thinner wall materials, are not permitted without written authorization from Suncor Engineering.

---

- 2.1.3 All HDPE materials supplied shall include material test certificates which include the test results as required by ASTM D3350. The resin manufacturer and melt index per ASTM D1238 used shall be identified in the fusion bonding procedure.

## 2.2 Material Receiving and Storage

- 2.2.1 Within the storage area, segregate pipe and fittings by material resin type, size, and SDR rating.

- 2.2.2 Upon receipt, Fabricator shall visually inspect every pipe and components. Items which contain injurious defects shall be rejected. Injurious defects are considered as misalignment in access of 10% for fabricated fittings, Internal or external surface gases, scars, scratches, blisters, or discontinuities that produce a notch effect or reduce the specified wall thickness by 5 percent or more.

## 2.3 Bonding Procedure Specification

- 2.3.1 A qualified BPS in accordance with ASME B31.3 par. A328 shall be supplied for hot plate butt fusion bonding. The qualification shall be performed on the same resin which will be used for the work.

- 2.3.2 Each qualification coupon shall be tested in accordance with ASTM D2857, par. 9.3. The testing shall be performed in accordance with Attachment A, "Butt Fusion Bonding Procedure Qualification Testing".

- 2.3.3 The BPS shall identify pre-bonding equipment inspection requirements. Attachment B, "Fusion Bonding - Work Instructions - Equipment Pre-Inspection" may be used as an example.

- 2.3.4 The BPS shall identify each step in the fusion process. The heating temperature, pressure and time as well as the fusion pressure and time shall be clearly identified for each pipe size and SDR rating. The fusion machine's hydraulic pressure shall be calculated. The use of nomographs, like those supplied by McElroy Manufacturing Inc. are, discouraged. Attachment C, "Butt Fusion Bonding Procedure Specification" may be used as an example of an acceptable procedure.

## 2.4 Fusion Bonder Performance Qualifications

- 2.4.1 Fusion bonders must pass a project qualification test prior to performing any fusion bonding. The qualifications shall be performed in accordance with ASME B31.3, par. 3282.5 with the additional essential requirement of using the heaviest SDR pipe wall that will be used during production, for the qualification testing. In lieu of the hydro testing qualification, fusion bonders may be qualified by testing in accordance with Attachment D, "Fusion Bonder's Qualification Testing".

## 2.5 Bonding Procedure Specification for Fusing Dissimilar HDPE Pipes

- 2.5.1 Butt fusing different HDPE resins require a separate BPS and must be qualified as stated in paragraph 2.3 of this specification. The guidelines of PPI-TN-13, "General Guidelines for the Heat Fusion of Unlike Polyethylene Pipes and Fittings", shall be used. The difference in heating time for each pipe must be established and identified in the procedure. This should be based on the flow characteristics (melt index) of each pipe.

---

## 3.0 Execution

### 3.1 *Field Fabrication*

#### 3.1.1 Piping

All butt fusion bonding shall be in strict accordance with the fusion bonding procedure approved for the project.

#### 3.1.2 Internal and Misalignment

a. Internal misalignment shall be less than 10% of the pipe wall thickness.

b. If the 10% misalignment is exceeded, use one of the following procedures listed in order of preference:

   1. First, rotate the pipe or fittings to reduce misalignment to the acceptable tolerances.
   2. Use the internal lineup clamps to correct moderate out-of-round condition
   3. Taper the wall of the component internally after obtaining approval from Suncor Engineering, to ensure wall thickness is not reduced below the minimum required.

#### 3.1.3 Bead (Flash) Removal

The bead or flash may interfere with slipping lap joint flanges against the stub end. Removal of part of the bead to accommodate easier removal of the flange is permitted as long as the removal does not leave any sharp notches. Use of a bead removal tool is preferred but use of a copping knife of file is also permitted. Proper safety precautions shall be used to assure method of removal does not cause injury.

#### 3.1.4 Pup-Pieces

Pup-pieces Installed to make up a length shall be a minimum of 2 pipe diameters long or 6" long, unless authorized otherwise by Suncor Engineering.

### 3.2 *Inspection and Test Prior to Installation*

#### 3.2.1 Inspection

Fabricator's Inspection shall ensure fusion bonds and completion of inspection records are in accordance with practices equal to those in Attachment E, "Fusion Bonding - Field Inspection Checklist" and Attachment F, "Fusion Bonding - Field Inspection Record".

#### 3.2.2 Records

Records, equal to those indicated in Attachment E and F, shall be maintained by the fabricator and submitted to Suncor QA no later than the next working day.

#### 3.2.3 Testing

Suncor QA may select bonds at random prior to installation, which will be removed for destructive testing to verify quality standards are being met. The type of destructive testing will be left to the discretion of Suncor. Normal testing will involve performing 180° bends in accordance with Attachment D, "Butt Fusion Bonder Qualification Testing".

---

## 4.0 Scope-But-Fusion Bonding Procedure Qualification Testing

4.1 This specification identifies the procedures used for destructive testing a thick walled Hi h Density Polyethylene pipe joint for the purpose of qualifying the fusion bonding procedure. The basis for type of tests is based on ASTM D2657, par. 9.3. The four types of tests identified are:

- 4.1.1 Tensiles
- 4.1.2 Bends
- 4.1.3 Torques
- 4.1.4 Impacts

4.2 These tests should be considered qualitative in determining the difference between a good bond and a poor bond. The quality depends on the type of failure which occurs. What may appear as a failure may not indicate a poor bond. It is important that for thick sections, all notches are removed from the coupons. This may be achieved by removing the flash from the fusion. For qualification interpretation, Suncor shall be notified if a coupon fails a test.

*4.3 TEST COUPON SIZE AND LOCATION*

4.3.1 Coupons shall be cut from each 1200 section of the bond. Four coupons shall be extracted from each 1200 section. The coupons shall be ½" thick through the thickness of the pipe wall perpendicular to the bond. Refer to Figure 1.

![Figure 1 Typical Pipe Cross Section](14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping/14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping-01_assets/figures/14-non-metallic-and-specialty-piping-01_p0023_fig01_figure-1-typical-pipe-cross-section.png)

4.4 *TENSILES*

4.4.1 Three tensile tests shall be performed. The specimens shall be machined to a size similar to ASME Section IX weld coupon requirements.

4.4.2 The specimen shall fail in a ductile manner showing a distinct amount of elongation. A specimen which fails quickly and one which indicates a shear non bonded face indicates a poor bond.

4.5 *BENDS*

4.5.1 Three 1800 inside root bends shall be performed. This shall be done by placing the specimen in a vice with the bond bead located approximately 1" above the top

---

of the vice jaws. A pipe should be used to make the bend with the edge of the pipe being located 1" from the edge of the bead.

4.5.2 If the coupon starts to buckle due to the thinness, a thicker 1" specimen may be cut and bent using a 1800 mandrel similar to that used for bending metallic weld coupons.

4.5.3 A failure which snaps in a brittle manner prior to achieving 1800 may indicate a poor bond area.

*4.0 TORQUES*

4.6.1 Three torques shall be performed. This shall be done by placing the coupon In a vice with the bond bead located approximately 1" above the top of the vice jaws. A pipe wrench shall be used to make twist the coupon a minimum of 3600, with the edge of the pipe wrench being located 1" from the edge of the bead.

4.6.2 A failure which snaps in 1800 of the twist may indicate a poor bond. Failures which occur beyond 3600 could be considered acceptable.

*4.7 IMPACTS*

4.7.1 Three impacts shall be performed. This shall be done by placing the coupon in a vice with the bond bead located approximately 1" above the top of the vice jaws. A heavy hammer or pipe can be used to "impact" the specimen.

4.7.2 A failure which occurs quickly and in a brittle manner may indicate a poor bond area. When the coupon bends and shows elongation at the bond from the force of the impacts, this can be considered acceptable.

*4.8 RE-TESTING OF PROCEDURE QUALIFICATION COUPONS*

4.8.1 If a coupon failure is indicated, upon approval from Succor's QA, two re-tests of the same coupon may be performed. If one of these coupons were to fail, the qualification needs to be redone.

## 5.0 Fusion Bonding-Work Instructions-Fusion Bonding Equipment

5.1 Fusion bonding equipment shall be inspected prior to use on the project to verify ability to perform. Once the equipment leaves the Succor site this inspection must be redone upon return at any other time to the site. Re-inspection may need to be performed if problems with fusion bond quality are encountered. The results of the inspection shall be recorded on the attached form "Attachment E - Fusion Bonding Field' Inspection Checklist". The inspection shall include as a minimum:

5.1.1 Verify heating plate has a thermostat which can control the overall heater plate surface between the temperatures of 350 to 500°F.

5.1.2 Verify heating plate has a non-stick coated surface which is free from scratches, dirt, grease, etc.

5.1.3 Verify heating plate has a calibrated built in thermometer.

5.1.4 Verify a calibrated surface pyrometer is available to check the heating surface temperature.

5.1.5 Verify the pressure gauge range and increments are suitable for the fusion pressures to be used throughout the production fusion bonding (i.e. A gauge with a maximum pressure rating of 10,000 PSI with 500 PSI pressure indicator increments would not be suitable for production bonding pressures of 100 PSI).

---

5.1.6 Verify a calibrated hydraulic pressure gauge is installed. The calibration shall have been performed within the last three months. Liquid filled gauges are preferred. Gauges shall have increments which are easily readable during the fusion bonding process.

5.1.7 Verify the hydraulic cylinder sizes and areas are clearly indicated.

5.1.8 Verify the hydraulic oil level is adequate. Add oil if necessary.

5.1.9 Verify the facing cutters are in good operating condition. Machines using sealed bearings on the cutters rather than requiring manual lubrication maintenance are recommended. Blades should project between 0.010" and 0.015" and be parallel to the face. Replace any worn or chipped cutters.

5.1.10 Verify alignment clamps, jigs and pipe pullers are in good operating condition.

## 6.0 Scope-But-Fusion Bonding Procedure Specification

### 6.1 PROCEDURE

6.1.1 The following procedure is to be used as an EXAMPLE ONLY and was developed for butt fusion bonding extra high molecular weight HMW) high density polyethylene (HDPE) piping with resins with a melt index (1902.16) of 0.09 manufactured by Union Carbide. A production fusion bonding procedure must be developed and qualified for the actual production work that will be performed.

6.1.2 Prior to performing any fusion bonding, the equipment shall be inspected by the bonder, for operability per Attachment B, "Fusion Bonding - Work Instructions - Equipment Pre-Inspection".

6.1.3 The bonder shall visually inspect the fusion bonding process and record all inspections in accordance with Attachment F, "Butt Fusion Bonding - Inspection Checklist and Record". The Fabricator's inspector shall approve all records of butt fusion bonding.

### 6.2 *EXAMPLE PROCEDURE*

The step-by-step procedure is as follows:

6.2.1 Record the ambient and pipe wall temperatures. If the ambient temperature is below 400°F, the fusion area must be hoarded and heated prior to any further work.

6.2.2 Clean the heater plate. Do not use metal tools which can scratch the coating. Set the thermostat at the temperature indicated on the Bonding Procedure Chart (normally 450°F). Plug in the heater plate and insert in protection box.

6.2.3 Identify pipe size and thickness. Select the correct heating cycle and fusion cycle pressure from the Fusion Bonding Procedure Charts. Calculate the machine pressures required using Figure 1. Record all information of the Fusion Bonding Report.

6.2.4 Set up all pipe roller supports and appropriate clamps as required.

6.2.5 Clean the inside and outside surface at the ends of the pipes to be fused using a clean dry cloth. Insert the pipe into the fusion machine so the ends extend approximately 1" past the alignment clamps. Adjust for alignment Bring the pipes together. Record the drag pressure which is required to push the pipes together as indicated on the hydraulic pressure gauge. This value must be added onto the

---

overall heating and fusion cycle pressures. As well, check for gross misalignment. Alignment may be improved by rotating one of the pipes 90° to 180°. Remember, the maximum misalignment permitted at any location is 10% of the wall thickness.

6.2.6 Position the facing tool in between pipe ends. Cut the pipe until the stops on each side of the facer are in contact with the clamp bushings. Separate the pipes and check for squareness of the cuts. DO NOT TOUCH THE PIPE SURFACE AT ANY TIME AFTER THIS STEP. Oil from the hands will contaminate the pipe and cause a poor bond.

6.2.7 Bring the two pipes together and check for misalignment. If misalignment is greater than 10% of the wall thickness at any single location, it must be corrected. Minor misalignment may be corrected by tightening the inside clamps at the high side. If the inside clamps have been adjusted or 15 minutes has elapsed since the pipe has been trimmed to when the heater plate is inserted, it will be necessary to re-trim the pipe.

6.2.8 Verify that the heater plate is at the desired fusion temperature by examining the thermometer. It is necessary to check the heater plate temperature accuracy four times daily using a contact pyrometer. The temperature shall be checked at 450 intervals around both sides of the heater plate circumference. The allowable variance is ± 10°F.

6.2.9 Separate the pipe ends and insert the heater plate, making sure that the plate does not come into contact with the pipe. Bring the two ends together against the heater. Apply, by hand or automatic actuation, the calculated heating pressure plus the drag pressure to the pipe ends. This pressure shall be applied until the appearance of a bead starts to form around the entire circumference on the outside of the pipe. Once this bead has initially formed, the pressure shall be removed, and the heating time shall start. The heating time is identified on the Fusion Bonding Procedure Chart 1. The "melt" should form an even bead around the entire circumference. Uneven melt beads are an indication that one side of the pipe is hotter than the other. This may occur during a cold sunny day, when the sun heats up the top of the cold pipe. It may be necessary to insulate the top of the pipe, to prevent this form of uneven heating. Wind and rain may also cause uneven pipe temperatures. The fusion bonding area should be protected from weather.

6.2.10 Once the heating time has elapsed, the pipes shall be separated away from the heater plate. The heater plate shall be quickly removed and the pipes brought back together with the fusion pressure, plus drag applied. The pressure shall be applied for the time indicated on the Fusion Bonding Procedure Chart 1. Upon squeezing the pipe ends together, the force applied should cause the bead to roll back onto the pipe producing an even bead around the circumference.

Note: If the bead does not "roll over" back onto the pipe in an even manner, it is an indication of a faulty fusion, and the fusion bond shall be cut out and redone. When removing the heater plate, if it comes in contact with the pipe where the melt is disturbed, the fusion shall be stopped and redone. If it takes longer than 12 seconds to remove the plate and squeeze the pipes, the fusion shall be stopped and redone.

---

6.2.11 Remove the fusion joint from the machine after the required fusion time indicated and Step 10 and when the fingernail not causes an indent into the bead. Do not apply any stress to the joint for a minimum of another 60 minutes.

| *6.3* | *Pressure Setting Calculations* |
|---|---|

6.3.1 The following formulas shall be used to calculate the pressure setting for heating and cooling of fusion bonds made with hydraulic drives:

**Formula "A":** Pipe Heating Pressure = Pipe Cross Section Area x Heating "Pressure Factor" / Total Machine Piston Area

**Formula "B":** Pipe Fusion Pressure = Pipe Cross Section Area x Fusion "Pressure Factor" / Total Machine Piston Area

1. Thermometer reading shall be stabilized prior to any heating cycle. Pyrometer reading shall be used to verify actual plate surface temperature. Templesticks shall not be used on plate surfaces.
2. Heating pressure shall be determined using formula "A", attached. This pressure shall be removed immediately upon the start of forming a melt bead. Expect a melt bead which is approximately 1/2 of the final fusion bead. Note: Add on drag pressure to these values.

4. Fusion pressure shall be determined using formula "B", attached and applied for the minimum of cool down time. Note: Add on drag pressure to these values.
5. Cool down time is minimum time for applying fusion pressure. Do not remove from machine until bond bead is checked for hardness. The finger nail should not indent the bead. Do not move excessively, lift or install in trench for a minimum of one hour after this time.

## 7.0 Scope-But-Fusion Bonder Qualification Testing - HDPE Piping

This specification Identifies the procedures used for qualifying a butt fusion bonder in general accordance with ASME B31.3, par. A328.2.5.

### 7.1 Qualification Test Coupons

**7.1.1** To each bonder shall qualify a fusion based on a 4" to 12" coupon. The test shall be performed on the maximum SDR rating intended to be used during production. Passing the qualification test permits the bonder to perform butt fusion on pipes up to 12" in diameter. The coupons shall be sufficiently long enough to fit into the fusion machine.

**7.1.2** To qualify for butt fusion bonding pipes larger than 12", each bonder must pass a qualification test on the maximum size and SDR rating intended to be fused during production.

---

7.1.3 Coupons shall be cut from each 1200 section of the bond. Four coupons shall be extracted from each 1200 section. The coupons shall be 12" thick through the thickness of the pipe wall perpendicular to the bond. Refer to Figure 1, Paragraph 4.3.

## 7.2 Visual Examination

7.2.1 The coupon shall be visually examined for soundness. The melted bead shall be uniform around the entire circumference and show complete roll over on both the internal and external side of the joint. There shall be no misalignment.

7.2.2 Melt bead width will depend on the pipe size and thickness and shall not be used as a rejection or acceptance method.

## 7.3 Destructive Tests

7.3.1 Six coupons shall be extracted from the test coupon as indicated in Figure 1. Three 1800 inside face bends and three 1800 outside face bends shall be performed. There shall be no indication of disbondment or separation during the bend test.

7.3.2 Where the thickness of the pipe prevents performing a complete 1800 bend without buckling, the coupon may be cut in half Care shall be exercised to prevent implanting notches into the coupons while performing the cutting operation (remove any suspicious notches).

7.3.3 If a failure is indicated, upon approval from Suncor, two additional coupons can be removed and tested next two the failure. Failure of any of these two coupons constitutes a failed qualification.

## 7.4 Hydro Testing

7.4.1 If requested by Suncor, the full size coupon shall be hydrotested at four times the design pressure of the pipe in accordance with ASME B31.3, par. A328.52.

## 7.5 Bonder's Re-Qualification Testing

7.5.1 Bonder's who have their fusion bonds fail the above testing, shall not be re-tested without Suncor's QA approval.

## 7.6 Records

7.6.1 The fabricator shall maintain records of all bonders who have passed the above qualification testing. The record shall include the BPS qualified, size of and SDR rating of coupon qualified and date.
