## SECTION 1: BACKGROUND

This standard establishes policies and procedures for the repair of a leak that has occurred on equipment, piping, pipe flanges, valve bonnets, or valve packing while it is in service in an operating unit at the BP Cherry Point Refinery. If the leak repair is a temporary repair, only to be in place until a permanent repair can be made, then the following procedure will be used. This procedure also applies to clamps (i.e. temporary repair enclosures) and wraps installed on thinning piping or equipment that is not yet leaking.

This procedure is NOT applicable if:

1. The repair restores the component and system to their design condition (e.g. a leaking valve is replaced with a new valve that meets the line specification).

2. The repair is a permanent repair that changes the design condition.

3. The repair involves killing a valve. Killing a valve shall be handled as an AMR.

   a) An AMR shall be created to document killing the valve.

   b) A second AMR shall be created to replace the valve and restore it to service.

   c) A TAR workorder shall be created to complete the work in the second AMR.

4. The repair consists only of the tightening of flange studs, valve packing gland bolts, or valve bonnet bolts, provided the tightening of bolts eliminates the leak. Before tightening flange studs or bonnet bolts, Reliability Engineering should be contacted to determine feasibility of tightening bolts, and to provide required torque values, if applicable.

## SECTION 2: PURPOSE

This Site Technical Practice (STP) is intended to ensure that temporary leak repairs are properly designed, installed, documented, tracked until permanent repairs may be completed at planned outages. The intent of this STP is to provide a means to mitigate the risk presented by unplanned outages by repairing leaks on equipment, piping, pipe flanges, valve bonnets or valve packing while online.

Items that have been repaired using this STP should be permanently repaired at the next planned outage, whenever possible. The next planned outage is often the next applicable turnaround, but this may not always be the case. It is the responsibility of the person filling out the leak repair form to work with necessary work groups to determine the proper time at which permanent repairs can be made. This date should be placed in the Leak Repair Form in the applicable field.

## SECTION 3: SCOPE AND APPLICATION

There are two classes of repairs. The permissions required to be obtained for each class of repair are defined by the service and the extent of the required repair method to eliminate the leak. These two classes are defined as Class 1 and Class 2 repairs:

---

## 3.1 CLASS 2 REPAIRS:

a) Installation of any clamp (i.e. temporary repair enclosures).

b) Any repair where there are signs of corrosion.

c) All repairs to hydrocarbon, chemical, steam (above 140#) and boiler feed water systems.

d) All other repairs to any system not specifically listed in section 3.2.b as a Class 1 repair.

## 3.2 CLASS 1 REPAIRS:

a) Shall not be used for the installation of clamps (i.e. temporary repair enclosures) and/or repairs where there are signs of corrosion.

b) Class 1 repairs may be used for Class 150 flange or lower systems in the following services only: steam (140 PSIG or less), condensate, air, utility water, cooling water, or firewater.

## 3.3 LEAK REPAIR DATABASE:

a) The Leak Repair Database exists as a module in the Addition and Modification Request (AMR) / Management of Change (MOC) Tracking System. The Leak Repair Form mentioned in this STP is the on-line form in the database.

b) The Leak Repair Form includes a Drawing File Path field. A folder for each leak repair shall be created in the **R:\CHPcomm\Leak Repairs** folder. The folder name shall be the Leak Repair number generated by the Leak Repair Database. All documents associated with the leak repair shall be stored in the folder and should be sufficient to verify the adequacy of the repair design as well as provide sufficient information to plan the permanent repair.

---

## SECTION 4: PROCEDURE AND RESPONSIBILITIES

### 4.1 PROCEDURE FOR REPAIR:

a) Operations (an **Operator** or the **Reliability Coordinator**) initiates the leak repair by filling out the Leak Repair Form in the Leak Repair database.

b) The **Reliability Coordinator** reviews the Leak Repair Form and informs the Fixed Equipment Engineer that there is a leak repair that requires action.

c) The **Fixed Equipment Engineer** and **Reliability Coordinator** together determine a suitable repair method and decide if it is a Class 1 or Class 2 repair. In making this determination they consult, as needed, with others, such as the **Unit Process Engineer**, **Unit Inspector**, the **Corrosion Engineer**, the **Metallurgist**, or a **Leak Repair Contractor**.

   i) For a Class 2 repair, the **Fixed Equipment Engineer** notifies the Unit Inspector and then electronically signs the Inspection Notification field on the Class 2 Repair portion of the Leak Repair Form. Upon the request of the Reliability Engineer, the Reliability Coordinator may notify Inspection and complete the sign off.

   ii) The **Inspector** directs the Inspection contractors to perform any inspections required to determine the suitability of the various repair options and forwards the results to the Fixed Equipment Engineer.

   iii) The **Fixed Equipment Engineer** reviews and approves any drawings and calculations produced by the Leak Repair Contractor.

   iv) The **Fixed Equipment Engineer** completes the engineering requirements on the Leak Repair Form, approves the repair method, and ensures that all supporting documents are filed in the Leak Repair folder described in Section 3.3.b. Supporting documents could include marked P&IDs, marked isometric drawings, clamp drawings and calculations, mill certifications, composite wrap calculations, etc.

   v) If a clamp (i.e. Temporary Repair Enclosure) is to be installed (or if a flange will wrapped and peened), the **Fixed Equipment Engineer** ensures that the requirements of Section 5 of this STP are met and then completes Appendix A of this STP and routes it to the Unit Process Superintendent for review and approval. The **Process Superintendent** then reviews and approves Appendix A.

   vi) The **Reliability Coordinator** creates Work Orders in the Maximo system as needed for the Leak Repair Contractor or BP Maintenance Shop.

d) The **Unit Control of Work Area Authority** arranges for a risk assessment appropriate for the repair method to be used and the system to be repaired.

---

i) For a Class 2 repair, the **Reliability Coordinator** will notify the Unit Supervisor and HSSE Supervisor of the upcoming repair following the applicable Control of Work risk review and sign off on those notifications on the Class 2 Repair portion of the Leak Repair Form.

ii) The **Area Authority** ensures that the Control of Work risk assessment includes a discussion of emergency response plans in the event that a leak occurs or worsens during the repair.

e) The **Reliability Coordinator** and **Area Authority** authorize the Leak Repair Contractor or BP Maintenance Shop to begin the work using the Control of Work process.

f) The **Leak Repair Contractor** or **BP Maintenance Shop** complete the leak repair.

g) The **Reliability Coordinator** updates the Details of Leakage/Repair field on the Leak Repair Form and signs the Leak Repair Form verifying that the leak repair has been completed.

h) The **Reliability Coordinator** updates the applicable repair work order as *"Maintenance Complete"* and then generates a new follow up work order for the permanent repairs needed to bring the equipment/piping back to original condition. This follow up work order shall have a clearly defined work description noting that it is to be used for the removal of the temporary repair and installation of the permanent repair. It shall be assigned with a Turnaround Routing code. The new work order for the permanent repair should be added to the Details of Leakage/Repair field.

i) The **Turnaround Planner** checks Maximo for work orders written for the permanent repair of leak repairs and adds them to the turnaround scope. The Turnaround Planner also gathers the required information needed to develop the permanent repair plan, referencing the

j) The **Turnaround Planner** informs the Reliability Coordinator post turnaround of the status of Leak Repairs that have been permanently fixed.

k) The **Reliability Coordinator** electronically signs for Permanent Repair Complete on the Leak Repair Form.

## 4.2 REWORK ON A TEMPORARY REPAIR

a) Rework of a temporary repair can include such work as: reinjection of a clamp, retorquing of clamp bolts, rewrapping of composite wrap, killing a valve, etc.

b) The **Reliability Coordinator** shall contact the **Fixed Equipment Engineer** any time rework is required on a Temporary Repair.

c) The **Fixed Equipment Engineer** and **Reliability Coordinator** together determine a suitable repair method. In making this determination they consult, as needed,

---

with others, such as the **Unit Process Engineer**, **Unit Inspector**, the **Corrosion Engineer**, the **Metallurgist**, or a **Leak Repair Contractor**.

i) The **Inspector** directs the Inspection contractors to perform any inspections required to determine the suitability of the various repair options and forwards the results to the Fixed Equipment Engineer.

ii) The **Fixed Equipment Engineer** reviews and approves any drawings and calculations produced by the Leak Repair Contractor.

iii) The **Fixed Equipment Engineer** approves the rework method, and ensures that all supporting documents are filed in the Leak Repair folder described in Section 3.3.h. Supporting documents could include marked P&IDs, marked isometric drawings, clamp drawings and calculations, mill certifications, composite wrap calculations, etc.

v) If a clamp (i.e. Temporary Repair Enclosure) is to be reworked (e.g. repumped or retonqued), the **Fixed Equipment Engineer** ensures that the requirements of Section 5 of this STP are met and then completes Appendix B and Appendix A (if required) of this STP and routes it to the Unit Process Superintendent for review and approval. The **Process Superintendent** then reviews and approves Appendix A.

vi) The **Reliability Coordinator** creates Work Orders in the Maximo system as needed for the Leak Repair Contractor or BP Maintenance Shop.

d) The **Unit Control of Work Area Authority** arranges for a risk assessment appropriate for the rework method to be used and the system to be repaired.

i) The **Area Authority** ensures that the Control of Work risk assessment includes a discussion of emergency response plans in the event that a leak occurs or worsens during the repair.

e) The **Reliability Coordinator** and **Area Authority** authorize the Leak Repair Contractor or BP Maintenance Shop to begin the work using the Control of Work process.

f) The **Leak Repair Contractor** or **BP Maintenance Shop** complete the leak repair.

g) The **Reliability Coordinator** updates the Details of Leakage/Repair field on the Leak Repair Form with the rework information.

h) If the rework changes the scope needed for the permanent repair, the **Reliability Coordinator** updates the work order for the permanent repair with the pertinent details.

---

## SECTION 5: REQUIREMENTS FOR TEMPORARY REPAIR ENCLOSURES

### 5.1 TEMPORARY REPAIR ENCLOSURE SCOPE

A temporary repair enclosure is a device such as a clamp or welded leak box that encloses a leak location. The interior of the enclosure (and the piping components it encloses) may be subject to the service fluid conditions. Wrapping and peening of flanges is also excluded in the definition of a temporary repair enclosure, as their use can result in the wetting of components (e.g. bolting) that was not designed for service fluid conditions. Requirements for clamps in this STP also apply to wrapping and peening.

### 5.2 REQUIRED EVALUATIONS AND DOCUMENTATION

a) Use of clamps requires special considerations. Some of these considerations and requirements were documented in Refining and Marketing High Value Learning (HVL 17). HVL 17 provides the basis of the requirements in Appendix A and Appendix B.

b) Before a clamp is installed the Fixed Equipment Engineer shall perform an engineering assessment using Appendix A. Approval to install the clamp must be given by the Unit Superintendent and documented on Appendix A.

c) Before rework (either reinjection or retoquing) is performed on a clamp, Appendix B must be completed by the Fixed Equipment Engineer. Before reinjecting a clamp for the fourth time, a complete re-evaluation of the clamp must be reperformed, using a new copy of Appendix A.

e) A copy of all Appendices (A and B) shall be retained in the Leak Repair Folder referenced in Section 3.3.b.

f) Articles 2.4 and 3.6 of ASME PCC-2 Repair of Pressure Equipment and Piping may be used as guidance when conducting the engineering assessments.

### 5.3 TEMPORARY REPAIR ENCLOSURES INSTALLED OVER CRACKS

If a crack is present in the damaged component, enclosures shall not be installed unless one of the following conditions has been met:

a) Conditions that lead to the crack formation and propagation have been eliminated or mitigated so that the crack will not grow during the planned life of the repair.

b) A fitness-for-service assessment determines that crack growth during the planned life is acceptable, and that the crack will not propagate across the enclosure boundary.

c) Crack circumferential has been determined and the enclosure is designed for the case of full circumferential separation of the cracked component.

---

d) Damaged components are a cracked vent or drain and the enclosure fully encapsulates the cracked vent/drain.

## 5.4 SEALANT INJECTION IN TEMPORARY REPAIR ENCLOSURES

a) The potential for damage to the enclosed component(s) due to the annulus pressure and/or uneven loading from the injected sealant shall be considered in the design and selection of enclosure type (void-filled or perimeter seal) and the injection details selected so as to minimize the likelihood of damage.

b) The possibility and consequence of sealant seeping into the damaged component shall be considered. Examples of such consequences include blocking strainers, orifice flanges and small connections; preventing the correct function of control valves; or causing a reduction in relieving capacity.

## 5.5 OTHER CONSIDERATIONS FOR TEMPORARY REPAIR ENCLOSURES

a) When equipment (including piping and piping components) that is normally not exposed to service is going to be encapsulated to eliminate a leak, it should be assumed that the service fluid can now come in contact with that equipment. Consideration should be taken to ensure that the equipment can withstand the service it is now being exposed to without failure. When equipment may not be suitable for the service, it should be upgraded or protected from the service by a suitable method. If the equipment cannot be upgraded or protected from the service, then a different repair method should be used. For example, if considering encapsulating a leaking flange or valve bonnet, the studs holding that connection together should be suitable for service. If they are not suitable, then they should be changed out with studs that can withstand the service. When it is not possible to change studs out because they are galled, or changing them out would increase exposure to personnel, then other methods of eliminating the leak should be incorporated. Such methods can include a strongback on a clamp that will hold the connection together, should the studs fail due to exposure to service. (It is important to remember that the B7 and B16 studs used in steam services can be susceptible to Stress Corrosion Cracking (SCC) if they come in contact with steam. Often times, the only way to mitigate the SCC concern is by installing strongbacks on clamps).

b) When clamps or strongbacks are being incorporated into the repair method, consideration should be given to the additional weight of the repair materials and if there is adequate support. In making this evaluation, it may be necessary to perform non-destructive examination to ensure there is adequate existing wall thickness. In some cases, additional support may be necessary to prevent excessive stress on the equipment the clamp is being installed on.

## SECTION 6: OTHER REPAIR CONSIDERATIONS AND REQUIREMENTS

---

## 6.1 GENERAL CONSIDERATIONS

Note that these considerations are only a handful of instances that may help to determine the type of repair method used to eliminate a leak. This is not a comprehensive list, as each situation can present a unique set of requirements/issues. The purpose of stating these considerations is to give the reader an idea of what unforeseen issues can arise when installing clamps or performing leak repairs. When in doubt, defer to the Reliability Engineer and Inspection Department to help give specific guidance when making repairs.

## 6.2 COMPOSITE WRAPS

a) Composite wraps may be utilized for non-leaking external repairs in all pressure classes, but shall be limited to Class 150 services for leaking defects. All repairs shall adhere to ASME PCC-2 and careful consideration shall be given to the process media and abnormal conditions such as steam out. Repairs that were leaking shall be considered temporary and shall be permanently repaired at the next turnaround. A UV topcoat should be applied to repairs that will remain in service greater than two years. The use of intumescent coatings should be considered within process areas. In many cases additional fire protection will not be necessary, as the damaged original pipe may still be adequate for a short duration fire event.

Further guidance may be found in ASME PCC-2 Articles 4.1 & 4.2, GN 36-008 and ISO 24817.

## 6.3 CLASS 1500 HYDROGEN SYSTEMS

a) Drill and taps on live process equipment is not allowed on Class 1500 hydrogen systems.

## 6.4 REPAIRS WHEN CORROSION IS PRESENT

a) When equipment is being repaired due to corrosion, regardless if there is presently a leak or not, consideration should be given to whether the corrosion is internal or external. If corrosion is external, often times the corrosion rate can be mitigated by coating the equipment before performing the repair, making the corrosion issue negligible. When the corrosion issue is internal, careful consideration should be given to the source of the corrosion and corrosion rate, then that information should be used to guide the type of repair that is made and how long that temporary repair can be kept in service. Consideration should also be given to the material compatibility with the service, should the corrosion continue far enough to cause hole through the equipment and cause exposure to the repair material. If corrosion is internal to the pipe, consideration should be given to how subsequent inspection can be performed with the repair in place to monitor the corrosion rate.

## 6.5 INJECTION SEALANT

---

a) When repairs involve the use of injection sealant, the company performing the temporary repair should be aware of possible swings in operating temperature that the equipment may be exposed to. Typically, there is a high temperature injection sealant and a low temperature injection sealant. For example, if a clamp is being installed on a warm-up line for a spare pump, the temperature of the line at the time of installing the clamp may be lower than when the spare pump is put into service. If the low temperature sealant is used because temperatures of the line at the time of installation were lower due to steady state conditions, then it may heat up and volatize when the spare pump is put into service. This can lead to gas being emitted from the clamp which is actually the injection sealant volatizing, not the process media leaking out. Typically, low temperature sealant is intended for services –300F and below, and high temperature sealant being intended for services –300F and above. It should be noted that these temperature breakdowns are only guidelines, and it is the responsibility of the person evaluating the leak repair method to work with the company installing the clamp to determine the actual temperature limitations. In some cases, temporary heat tracing and insulation may need to be installed on the clamp in order to keep it hot enough in steady state conditions for the high temperature sealant to stay set. When this is the case, consult with inspection to determine if any adverse affects will be caused by keeping stagnant service at hotter temperatures.

## 6.6 WELD REPAIRS

a) When the repair plan includes welding, consideration should be given to ensuring there is adequate existing wall thickness for the repair.

## SECTION 7: INSPECTION AND SELF AUDIT

a) Any leak repair clamp that has an intended removal date greater than 6 years from the date of installation shall have a Preventative Maintenance plan placed against the secondary work order created for the permanent repair (Section 4.1.c & 4.2.a.5) that has an inspection requirement to verify that the leak repair is suitable for continued use. The specific requirements and inspection intervals of the Preventative Maintenance plan should be determined by the Reliability Engineer and Unit Inspector.

b) A Compliance Assurance system task will be used to perform annual audits to ensure this policy is being followed.

---

### 15-hot-tapping-and-leak-repair-02

# SUNCOR ENERGY INC.

## TABLE OF CONTENTS

1.0   PURPOSE.....................................................................................................2

2.0   REFERENCED STANDARDS........................................................................3

3.0   GENERAL AND SAFETY CONSIDERATIONS .............................................3

4.0   HOT TAP DESIGN, METALLURGY, AND WELDING CONSIDERATIONS ..........4

5.0   INSPECTION AND TESTING .....................................................................11

**Attachment-I:**   Suggested Hot Tap Execution Flow Chart For Major Projects

**Appendix-I:**     Pre-Engineering Check List

**Appendix-II:**    Detail Engineering Check List

**Appendix-III:**   Hot Tap Authorization Form

**Appendix-IV:**    Hot Tap Installation Check List

**Appendix-V:**     Hot Tap Work Flow Chart

---

## 1.0 Purpose

**1.1** To provide the guidelines to design and perform online welding and hot taps.

**1.2** Compliance with this standard will ensure rigorous, systematic approach for proper identification, design, fabrication, QA/QC Control and safe installation as well as formal technical and management approval.

**1.3** This standard shall be used whenever it is proposed to make a welded attachment to piping, pressure vessels or tanks and to cut the pressure boundary while exposed to the process hazard.

**1.4** Definitions

The "Engineering" - means Suncor engineering group, or designated representative (e.g. EP / EPC / EPCM contractor) responsible for engineering of Suncor projects or jobs.

The "Design Engineer" - means engineer responsible for design of the hot tap and stamping of the design drawings.

"Inspector" – - means Suncor plant inspector assigned to specific plant and part of Suncor Maintenance and Engineering team or QA/QC inspector assigned to projects responsible for mechanical QA/QC activities.

The "Construction Coordinator (CC)" – means the Suncor construction coordinator or his designated representative responsible for field coordination of the hot tap design and installation.

The "Hot Tap Contractor" - means the contractor responsible for executing online welding and hot tapping.

## 2.0 Referenced Standards

### 2.1 Suncor Standards/Procedures

| Code | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| PMP0180A | Coffins, Hot Taps and On-line Welding |
| PGP0048A | Piping Tie-Point Identification |
| PGS0017A | Isolation of Equipment / Systems |
| 202 | Piping Material Specifications |
| 203 | Valve Specifications |
| 204 | Piping Fabrication and Installation |

---

205    Piping Pressure Tests
903    Shop And Field Welding Requirements

## 2.2 Industry Standards

API RP 2201    Safe Hot Tapping Practices in the Petroleum & Petrochemical Industries.
ASME B31.3    Chemical Plant and Petroleum Refinery Piping
ASME B31.1    Power Piping
ASME VIII    Boiler and Pressure Vessel Cod
API 510    Pressure Vessel Inspection Code
API 570    Inspection, Repair, Alteration, and Rating of In-service Piping Systems
API RP 578    Material Verification Program for New and Existing Alloy Piping Systems
API 653    Tank Inspection, Repair, Alteration and Reconstruction
API 1104    Welding on Pipelines and Related Facilities
API RP 582    Welding Guidelines for the Chemical, Oil and Gas Industries

## 3.0 General and Safety Considerations

3.1 Hot tapping is potentially hazardous and therefore should be undertaken when shown to be technically feasible and to offer a clear advantage over other alternatives.

3.2 Hot tapping is a multi-disciplinary activity, involving several departments, each carrying their own responsibilities. Coordination between departments and planning of activities is of vital importance.

3.3 Each hot tap must be evaluated individually by a Hazard and Operability review (HAZOP) in accordance with the HAZOP procedures. A copy of the report shall be included in the design package.

3.4 The operating department shall write a shutdown procedure for shutting down the subject line in case of fire or blowout. During the welding and drilling operation, the Operations department shall have a representative at site to initiate the shutdown if necessary.

3.5 The Fire department must be notified and have an opportunity to review the area and procedures. An emergency rescue plan shall be in place. If hot tap happens to be in a congested area, escape routes shall be

---

identified and marked by the appropriate personnel prior to start of hot tap activities.

3.6 A pre-job meeting shall be held at the start of each shift. Attendees shall include construction coordinator, contractor, workers executing the job, operating personnel and emergency service personnel.

3.7 A retrieved coupon shall be handed over to Inspector. Any coupon that is not retrieved from the system during the extraction of the hot tap machine shall be considered as a potentially serious problem. Any such problem shall be immediately reported to Operations to review the risks associated and to plan further action.

3.8 Before starting the hot tapping, the machine, cutter, and pilot shall be carefully inspected that all components are in satisfactory condition. The seals must be pressure tested.

## 4.0 Hot Tap Design, Restrictions, and Welding Considerations:

### 4.1 Hot Tap Design

4.1.1 The design engineer shall be responsible for hot tap design per applicable codes (i.e., B31.1, B31.3, or ASME BPV Code) and regulations. A registered professional engineer shall stamp the design calculations and drawings.

4.1.2 Hot tap design and the required thickness calculations shall take the following into account.

- 4.1.2.1 Design and operating temperature and pressures.
- 4.1.2.2 Actual wall thickness and required corrosion allowance.
- 4.1.2.3 External pressure to be applied to the existing pipe/equipment during testing of the hot tap connection weld.
- 4.1.2.4 The loads applied by the hot tap machine.
- 4.1.2.5 Where required per Suncor standards and/or in the opinion of the engineer, pipe stress analysis of the tie-in point shall be performed to ensure flexibility and integrity during and after installation of tie-in. Finite Element Analysis (FEA) shall be performed as required.
- 4.1.2.6 Carbon equivalent of the pipe material.

---

4.1.2.7 Limitations of the services and metallurgy of the run pipe.

4.1.3 For hot tap connections, external pressure calculations shall be prepared for the carrier pipe based on the hot tap hydrostatic test pressure minus the pipe operating pressure, to verify the carrier pipe strength against the external load.

4.1.4 In consultation with the hot tap contractor, nozzle length shall be determined for particular tapping machine that will be used in order to ensure a complete cut through the piping wall. For flanged nozzles, length shall be adequate to permit removal of flanged bolts.

4.1.5 The hot tap machine shall be checked for suitability of use at low ambient temperatures. When the ambient temperature is less than -45°C (-50°F), hot tapping or on-line welding is not permitted. Under all circumstances hot tapping shall be limited to the pressure and temperature rating of the machine.

4.1.6 Maximum allowable pressure during hot-tap welding:

4.1.6.1 Shall be calculated based on temperature de-rating which allows for reduction in pipe strength at predicted pipe temperature during online welding as per the applicable code. Predicted temperatures may be calculated by log mean temperature (LMT) formula given below

LMT = (T2-T1) / Ln (T2/T1)

T1 = Operating temperature of the pipe, Deg C
T2 = Temperature at base of Heat Affected Zone (HAZ), Deg C

*Note1: It should be recognized that stresses and temperature will be higher in the reduced strength zone during welding operation than in the normal operation of the pipeline. Sufficient thickness shall be ensured so that the stresses within it are below the temperature corrected design stress.*

*Note-2: Present studies indicate that a burnthrough will not occur if the inside surface temperature is below 1800° F when using low-hydrogen electrodes and the wall thickness is 0.25" or greater.*

---

4.1.6.2 A pressure reduction may be justified to prevent from rupturing during the installation of a full encirclement sleeve on the basis of protecting the welding / installation crew.

4.1.6.3 Reduced wall thickness shall be calculated based on actual thickness minus the reduction in wall thickness during welding, representing the weld pool penetration. Conservative assumption of weld pool penetration may be 0.1".

4.1.6.4 For metal thickness greater than ½", the effect of flow on both weld cooling rates and the risk of burn-through may be negligible.

4.1.7 Hot tap connections shall be one of the following:

4.1.7.1 Integrally reinforced outlet branch connections shall be per Suncor standard 0202.

4.1.7.2 Reinforcing pad (stub-in with reinforcing pad) connections shall be per Suncor standard 0202.

- When branch/run ratio exceeds 50%, in addition to area replacement considerations, analysis of ASME VIII div1 App 1-7 shall also be applied.

- When branch/run ratio exceeds 70% in addition to ASME VIII div 1 App 1-7, a finite element analysis shall be performed, following ASME VIII div 2 approach.

4.1.7.3 Other branch (such as reducing tee) connections shall be using the *Full Encirclement Sleeves* (weld-on sleeves). The weld details shall be per Fig.328.5.4D of ASME B31.3. The diameter of the branch should be at least one standard pipe size smaller than diameter of the run pipe. It should be recognized that the hole drilled into the run pipe will be smaller than the internal diameter of the branch.

4.1.7.4 Pre-formed split tees (TD Williams or equal) shall be considered only after thoroughly evaluating the other design options and requires owner's approval. Split tees shall be designed to withstand full pipeline pressure. Split tees shall

---

not be used in corrosive and steam service where the corrosion rate will be accelerated due to existing crevice.

*Note-1. Split Tees shall be considered as temporary fittings and they shall be replaced by standard fittings at the first available opportunity. ABSA approval shall be obtained for use of split tees and this item shall be properly tagged and noted as an action item for plant maintenance. After execution of hot tap, a work request shall be initiated in the Maintenance Management System to track until the split tee is replaced.*

*Note-2. All hot tap fittings (welded branch fitting or split tee) may be considered as permanent for piping systems conveying non-expansible fluids. However, design engineer shall consult the area maintenance engineer for permanent tappings. Refer to Alberta Regulation 293/94, para 1(2)(c) for definition of expansible fluids. Further, also see ASME B31.3, para 300.1.3 for code exemptions.*

4.1.7.5 A hot tap, less than 70% of run diameter, may be performed under Suncor's quality control program provided it is designed in accordance with the applicable piping code, taking into account the need for reinforcement of the branch connection, and that a detailed hot tap procedure exists.

A hot tap on a boiler and pressure vessel shall be submitted to ABSA for review and approval prior to implementation.

4.1.8 Valves, packing, gaskets, and other piping components shall be in accordance with the piping material specifications per Suncor standard 0202.

4.1.9 Full-port gate valve with the same NPS and rating as branch connection shall be specified per Suncor standards.

4.1.10 The seals and materials of the construction of the hot tapping machine shall be compatible with the contents of the piping or equipment.

4.1.11 Vessels or lines to be welded or hot tapped shall be inspected for adequate wall thickness and absence of laminations and/or other

---

imperfections. The base thickness shall provide support for new connection and hot tap machine.

4.1.12 The carbon equivalent of the material on which hot tap is proposed shall be determined. The formula to be used is:

$$CE = \%C + \%Mn / 6 + (\%Cu+\%Ni) / 15 + (\%Cr+\%Mo+\%V) / 5$$

Relationship between CE and cooling rate that produces HAZ (Heat Affected Zone) should be recognized. As a guideline, a CE of up to 0.4 may be used. However if the CE is greater than 0.4, metallurgical engineer shall be consulted to review the CE, cooling rates and welding procedure for a specific hot tap

4.1.13 All pressure hot tap fitting shall be registered with ABSA and have CRN numbers.

## 4.2 Restrictions on Hot Tap Applications

### 4.2.1 Process Fluids

**4.2.1.1** Hot tapping should not be performed on equipment/piping containing the following materials: If required, a detailed engineering evaluation and risk assessment shall be performed.

- Toxic chemicals such as concentrated hydrogen sulfide, chlorine, sodium hydroxide, ammonia and acids.

- Vapor/air or vapor/oxygen near or within their flammable explosive range.

- Oxygen or oxygen enriched atmospheres.

- Compressed air systems.

- Temperature-sensitive, chemically reactive materials which may undergo reaction or decomposition leading to dangerous increase in pressure, explosion or attack on metal.

- Caustic service and amine service where concentration and temperature require PWHT.

---

- Hazardous substances such as Acetylene, Butadiene, Chlorine, Ethylene, Ethylene oxide, Rich/Lean DEA/MEA, Hydrofluoric acid, Sulphuric acid etc.

## 4.2.2 Materials

**4.2.2.1** Hot tapping is usually not permitted where for process or metallurgical reasons PWHT is required unless determined by Suncor engineering review to be acceptable. The area metallurgical engineer shall be consulted in such cases. In such cases, a pre-approved on-line welding procedure specification is required.

**4.2.2.2** Hot tapping on pressure vessels is not recommended. If required, a detail engineering review shall be carried out to check the feasibility of hot tapping.

**4.2.2.3** Hot tapping shall not be performed on piping and storage tanks that are jacketed, cladded or lined.

**4.2.2.4** Minimum wall thickness shall be 1/4" unless approved by the responsible Suncor engineer. Lower thickness may be permitted with the approval of Suncor Engineer after detail review of design and welding specifications.

## 4.2.3 Process Conditions

**4.2.3.1** Welding on a line under no-flow conditions is not permitted. Minimum flow velocity of 1.3 ft/sec should be maintained. A high flow condition in gases is permitted subject to attainment of acceptable interpass temperatures. High liquid flow will usually cause rapid cooling which can cause excessive hardness. A suggested maximum velocity for liquid flow during welding is 4.0 ft/sec. In case of high velocities and rapid cooling, special interpass heating techniques may be needed or the welding procedures amended.

**4.2.3.2** Because of insufficient flow or unstable operating conditions, hot -tap welding on flare lines is feasible only with special precautions such as flushing of the

---

flare line with steam or an inert gas during welding operations creating a minimum velocity of 1.3 ft/sec and application of a quick-acting warning system.

4.2.3.3 Any conditions exceptional to the above shall be reviewed and approved by Suncor Engineer.

4.2.3.4 Hot Tapping on Tanks:

4.2.3.4.1 Do not pump into or out of tank during hot tapping or online welding. Avoid operation of any valve including gas-blanketing valve.

4.2.3.4.2 Do not operate heating coils during hot tapping / welding.

4.2.3.4.3 Do not hot tap if the tank liquid level is below 3 feet above the area where the welding or hot tapping is being done.

4.2.3.4.4 Hot tapping is not permitted on the deck of a floating roof tank that is in service.

4.2.3.5 Hot tapping shall be avoided on piping systems that are in vibrating service.

4.2.3.6 Downstream equipment, rotating machinery, control valves, orifices etc. must be considered to ensure that cuttings from the hot tap machine, or loss of coupon will not create dangerous or detrimental conditions.

## 4.3 Welding

4.3.1 Proper flow through the pipeline shall be maintained during welding to prevent overheating or burn-through, excessive cooling rate and the risk of cracking.

4.3.2 The hot tap contractor shall submit an on-line Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) and associated Procedure Qualification Record (PQR) for approval.

4.3.3 Storage and handling of electrodes shall be in accordance with Suncor procedures and manufacturer recommendations.

---

4.3.4 Only the welder shall be allowed to change the settings of the welding machine during online welding. All welding equipment shall be maintained in good working order and shall comply with site safety regulations.

4.3.5 Run-pipe shall be prepared by removal of coating, surface cleaning, ovality check and other defect checks. Ovality checks may done in advance to properly design encirclement sleeves

4.3.6 AWS Class EXX16 and /or EXX18 basic coated low-hydrogen electrodes shall be specified in the approved WPS and used throughout.

4.3.7 The run pipe and branch should be preheated to avoid weld cracking and high hardness. Preheat temperatures should be determined based on CE and weld thickness. Preheat temperatures of approx. 200 Deg F is usually required when CE>0.4 and thickness is over 0.75". However, preheat temperature shall be maintained as specified on WPS.

4.3.8 To minimize the risk of burn through, the first weld pass to piping should be made with 3/32" diameter welding rods to limit the heat input.

4.3.9 Welding including reinforcement pads (if required) or hot tapping shall not be permitted closer than 18 inches to a flange or threaded connection, or approx. 3 inches to a weld seam (including longitudinal seam of welded piping) unless determined by engineering review to be acceptable.

4.3.10 For longitudinal butt welds of full encirclement sleeves and split tees, the joints should be fitted with a back-up strip to prevent penetration of weld into the carrier pipe.

4.3.11 The longitudinal seams on full encirclement sleeve and split tees should be completed prior to circumferential seams. These seams shall be welded simultaneously so that contraction strain will improve the fit-up between fitting and run pipe. However, circumferential welds shall not be welded simultaneously. Use API-1104 for welding sequence guidelines.

## 5.0 Inspection and Testing

5.1 NDE personnel for inspection shall be qualified to CGSB Level II or Level I under the direct supervision of a Level II.

---

5.2 The weld area plus 3" on either side shall be fully examined by magnetic particle inspection (liquid penetrant for non-magnetic materials) and ultrasonic examination to locate any defects and/or laminations prior to welding.

5.3 Visual inspection of all attachment welds shall be performed after welding the hot tap fitting and before attaching the hot tap machine. Ensure that weld root is not excessive as shown on the hot-tap engineering drawing.

5.4 Magnetic particle inspection (liquid penetrant inspection for non-magnetic materials) shall be performed on 100% of root and cap welds.

5.5 Ultrasonic inspection shall be performed on 100% of the finished welds, 48 hours after the completion of welds. Alternatively, MPI or LPI shall be performed on the root pass before welding the 2nd pass and MPI shall also be performed on the weld, 48 hours after completion of the weld. However, area metallurgical engineer may vary the delayed inspection time depending upon the factors such as cooling rates, restraints, carbon equivalence, hydrogen contamination from moisture or surface contaminants etc.

5.6 Hardness testing shall be performed on welding and HAZ and the results shall be reviewed by inspector.

5.7 The valve to be installed at the hot tap location shall be leak tested in accordance with API 598 or as shown on the engineered drawing prior to installation in the field.

5.8 Valve to be inspected for sufficient clearance of cutter prior to tapping. Valves must have clear, full round openings at least 1/8" greater in diameter than the specified drill or cutter OD.

5.9 The branch connection shall be hydrostatically or pneumatically tested prior to cutting the pipe or equipment. Hydrostatic testing is limited to a skin temperature of 200° F (93°C). For temperatures above 200° F, pneumatic test must be performed with the use of inert gas (Nitrogen) or Helium. Inspector to verify the test. Caution to be exercised during the pneumatic testing of the branch connection. Online welding or hot tap contractor shall submit the pneumatic procedure to Suncor field engineering for review and approval.

In case of pneumatic testing, extreme caution shall be exercised to ensure that pressure is increased in very small steps and allow stabilization of pressure at elevated temperature experienced in the branch. In no case, the

---

pressure shall be permitted to exceed the test pressure required by governing standard. Suncor field engineer shall determine the need for a safety relief valve (minimum ¾" size) that is set at the test pressure to prevent overpressure.

5.10 The test pressure shall be as follows:

The maximum value of the test pressure shall be calculated in accordance with the particular design code. However, following shall be also taken into account in determining the test pressures:

Test pressure for pre-formed split tees and full encirclement sleeves shall be summation of actual operating pressure in the run-pipe and maximum allowable pressure differential with respect to buckling of the run pipe calculated as defined in ASME Section VIII, Division 1, and Section UG-28.

In any case, the test pressure shall not be greater than the designed code test pressure of the branch pipe.

*Note: Design Engineer may use Williamson Industries published guide titled "Approximate Guide for Maximum External Testing Pressure on Run Piping" to determine the maximum differential pressure and test pressures. However, in no case shall the test pressure exceed the design code test pressure of the branch pipe.*

5.11 The general testing procedure to be followed shall be:

5.11.1 Shop leak testing of the hot-tap valve, preferably with the valve not installed on the branch, for duration of at least 5 minutes.

5.11.2 Testing of the branch connection, with the valve installed and in the open position, to demonstrate leak tightness and strength. Duration shall be at least 30 minutes.

5.11.3 Leak testing of the drilling machine mounted on the valve (with valve closed), for a duration of at least 5 minutes. Leak test pressure shall be equal to the highest operating pressure in the run pipe during the hot-tap operation.

Note: Testing sequence and testing combinations may be modified depending upon the field or contractor's practice. However, any modified procedure shall be reviewed by Suncor field engineer.

5.12 The saddle or reinforcing pad shall be pneumatically tested at 15 PSIG. The Inspector shall verify this test.

---

## ATTACHMENT-1

### SUGGESTED HOT TAP EXECUTION FLOW CHART FOR MAJOR PROJECTS

---

In this section hot tap execution methodology is outlined by providing the hot tap execution sequence and responsibilities of the engineering and construction. A flow chart is also attached. However, this flow chart is based on the current organization set-up within MCU Project and may be modified to suit a particular organization / Silo.

## 1.0 Sequence and Responsibilities

### 1.1 Sequence of Events

1.1.1 Engineering shall identify the location of hot tap after evaluating that the hot tap is appropriate in coordination with operations. API-2201 guidelines shall be used to determine this.

1.1.2 Once the location of the hot tap installation is determined, Engineering shall initiate Appendix-I with preliminary HT package containing PFD, P&ID, and other available information on HT location, pipe size, coordinates, photos, etc. Construction Coordinator shall coordinate with Area Operations, Inspector and HT contractor to complete the "Pre-Engineering Checklist" Appendix-I and obtain the approval for location. The checklist shall be forwarded to Engineering for detailed design of the hot tap.

1.1.3 After hot tap location is approved, Construction Coordinator shall tag the hot tap location per procedure, PGP0049A, in coordination with operations.

1.1.4 Engineering shall finalize the detail engineering in accordance with applicable codes and Suncor standards and complete the "Detail Engineering Checklist" per Appendix-II. An Engineering Work Package (EWP) shall be prepared and issued to Construction Management Team (CMT). The package shall contain:

- Tie-in List
- Process Flow Diagram (PFD) – Optional
- Appendix-I with available results
- P&ID
- Design Check List (Appendix-II) with carbon equivalent and copy of welding procedure
- Design Calculations
- Tie-in location drawing , Pictures (if available)
- Line Designation Table (LDT)
- Isometrics
- Other documents as necessary

---

1.1.5 Upon finalizing the installation time and schedule, construction coordinator shall convene a meeting consisting of representatives from Operations, Maintenance & Engineering (if required), Safety and Fire Department to finalize the work plan specific for each hot tap.

1.1.6 Construction Coordinator shall obtain the required approvals on "Hot Tap Authorization Form" per Appendix-III.

1.1.7 After final approval, but before any fieldwork (except scaffolding and site preparation), Construction Coordinator shall hold a "Kick-Off" meeting for each stage of the job.

1.1.8 The hot tap is executed as per the work plan, complete with final inspection, sign-off, site clean up and filing of documentation.

Note: Refer to the suggested 'Hot Tap Execution' flow chart at Appendix-V.

## 1.2 Responsibilities:

### 1.2.1 Area Operations Manager

#### 1.2.1.1
Reviews the process and inspection data on Pre-Engineering Design Checklist (Appendix-I) and provides the location approval on Appendix-I.

#### 1.2.1.2
Reviews the work plan and other hot tap Documents; verify that qualified people have completed the checklists and gives approval to proceed by signing on Authorization form (Appendix-III).

### 1.2.2 Construction Coordinator

#### 1.2.2.1
Investigates feasibility along with Suncor Operations and Inspection by field verification, noting exact location and other potential hazards in the area and sign-off Appendix-I after obtaining the signatures from Inspection and operations.

#### 1.2.2.2
Provides the approved Appendix-I to Engineering in order to complete the detail engineering activities.

---

1.2.2.3 Shall coordinate with Suncor field engineering or QA/QC to review and approve the online welding procedures (WPS/PQR).

1.2.2.4 Shall coordinate with all the concerned parties, mentioned herein, to execute the hot tap. Prepare an execution work plan including hot tap drawings (execution plan may be prepared by contractor for installation of hot tap), contingency plans, inspection and check lists and the operating condition at the time of hot tap. The execution plan shall also consist of standby equipment for safety and fire fighting, and any other requirement for such execution on a case-basis. Shall also obtain the hot tap authorization from Operations on Appendix-III.

1.2.2.5 Ensure that 'Safety Plan' is in place for each hot tapping operation and shall be agreed beforehand with relevant departments. The suggested topics to be included are:

- Site accessibility for personnel and equipment
- Roles and responsibilities of the personnel at site
- Monitoring of operating conditions (flow rate, pressure & temperature) and gas levels
- Communications on site
- Warning system and emergency shutdown
- Foreseeable hazards and contingency actions
- Fire fighting equipment and personnel
- Safety equipment and services
- First-aid facilities
- Means of escape

1.2.2.6 After final approval but before any field work (except scaffolding & site preparation), Construction Coordinator shall hold a "Kick-off" meeting with welders & pipe fitters, hot machine operator, permit issuer and other members as deemed necessary for each stage of the job. Shall also review the Appendix-IV with the concerned persons and obtain the necessary signatures.

1.2.2.7 Shall be responsible to coordinate the execution of hot tap including obtaining the permits, supervision during

---

hot tap, QA/QC inspections, hydrostatic testing, closeouts and filing of final documentation.

### 1.2.3 Inspector

**1.2.3.1** Shall be responsible for completing the initial inspection of proposed hot tap location, checking and reviewing to make judgement whether a proposed location is acceptable. Necessary inspection data shall be recorded on Appendix-I.

**1.2.3.2** During preparation and fabrication work, the inspector or designate shall monitor the installation and welding. Prior to welding of the nozzle or fitting, the inspector shall verify the nozzle fit-up location against the location of UT measurements taken.

### 1.2.4 Design Engineer

**1.2.4.1** Shall initiate the Appendix-I by completing the required information and shall forward to Construction Coordinator for hot tap location approval.

**1.2.4.2** Shall ensure that the design is in accordance with applicable design codes and Suncor engineering standards.

**1.2.4.3** Shall complete the design checklist (Appendix-II) and prepare necessary drawings showing the fit-up / welding details, hydrostatic test pressures, NDE requirements, MAWP calculations, nozzle flange-pipe tolerances, stress analysis and Finite Element Analysis (if required).

### 1.2.5 Welding Contractor / Welding Operator

**1.2.5.1** Shall submit qualified on-line weld procedure specification and Procedure Qualification Record (PQR) for each specific on-line welding operation to Construction Coordinator and Design Engineer.

**1.2.5.2** Shall submit welding personnel qualification to the Suncor Inspector for approval.

---

1.2.5.3 Shall perform the on-line welding.

### 1.2.6 Hot Tap Contractor

1.2.6.1 Shall verify that the selected machine has the required pressure and temperature ratings for the job.

1.2.6.2 Complete the hot tap operator checklist (part of Appendix-IV).

1.2.6.3 After installation of machine, check the alignment and clearance between the cutter and valve seat rings and do a pressure test of the machine and of the assembly as specified on drawings.

1.2.6.4 Execute the hot tap, recover the coupon and hand over the coupon to the Inspector.

![Appendix V — Suggested Hot Tap Work Flow Chart](15-hot-tapping-and-leak-repair/15-hot-tapping-and-leak-repair-02_assets/figures/15-hot-tapping-and-leak-repair-02_p0029_fig01_appendix-v-suggested-hot-tap-work-flow-c.png)

The flow chart covers two organizational swim lanes — **ENGINEERING** and **OPERATIONS, MAINTENANCE & CONSTRUCTION** — and traces the full hot tap authorization and execution sequence from initial task list through close-out.

Key process steps shown in the chart (left to right, top to bottom):

**Engineering lane:**
1. Engineering Task List with preliminary package reviewed by Engineering and Operations and HT Contractor
2. Decision: Hot Tap (HT) or Cold Tap (CT)?
3. Engineering to study the feasibility of HT and initiate Appendix I in coordination with Design and Construction
4. Engineering starts detailed design
5. Prepare engineering package and EWP including completed P&ID and Process Piping
6. Decision: ABSA approval required?
7. ABSA approved?
8. Apply for ABSA approval

**Operations, Maintenance & Construction lane:**
1. Appendix I sent to Construction Coordinator (CC) to coordinate with Inspection and HT Contractor

3. Area Operations approval on Appendix I
4. Tag HT line-in by CC in coordination with Operations
5. Send approved Appendix I to Engineering
6. CC is to ensure final plans for Emergency Shutdown, Emergency Response (ER) or FSS (risk management) etc. are in place
7. Obtain Operators approval for Appendix III
8. CC convenes meeting of Operations & Maintenance (O&M), Fire & Maintenance, Construction Head/prior review
9. CC to prepare EWP and schedule the work
10. Appendix IV to be reviewed and completed by QA/QC Inspector and HT Machine Operator
11. CC signs off Appendix IV
12. Welder to weld the connector torque under supervision of Inspector
13. Complete QA/QC of welds
14. Install valve
15. Hydrated (Hydrotest)
16. Execute the hot tapping
17. Close-out

**Final step:** Final Docs by CC

# 1. INTRODUCTION

## 1.1 SCOPE

This DEP specifies requirements and gives recommendations for the planning and execution of "hot-tap" branch connections onto piping systems and pipelines containing hydrocarbons under operating conditions. It has been developed to reflect current understanding of the technology and to improve safe practices in the field. It is intended to cover hot-tapping on carbon, carbon-manganese and high-strength low-alloy steels (e.g. ISO 3183 L-245 to L485 or API 5L grades B to X70), though many aspects may be relevant for other applications. Hot-tapping on other materials requires special consideration.

This DEP is not intended to cover subsea hot-tapping but many aspects are still relevant for such applications.

Due to the distinction made in the relevant standards between on-plot piping and off-plot pipelines or flowlines, a similar distinction is sometimes made within this DEP, but this has been avoided wherever possible. Additionally, it is assumed that the piping systems are designed and operated in accordance with ASME B31.3 and pipeline systems are designed and operated in accordance with ISO 13623 (or other recognised pipeline design code e.g. ASME B31.4, B31.8), or a combination thereof. The use of alternative standards is not expected to conflict with any of the principles adopted in this DEP or most of the specific requirements. However, see (1.2) below.

It is assumed that all hot-tap branch connections will be welded.

NOTE: Where in accordance with the requirements of this DEP, or for other reasons, welding is not permitted, consideration may be given to the use of a non-welded system. Such systems are becoming increasingly available but require special considerations, including long-term integrity aspects.

This DEP mainly considers hot tapping on pipes but it is possible to perform hot-taps on tanks and other equipment as outlined in (7).

It should also be noted that hot-tapping often requires the approval of the relevant statutory authorities.

This DEP is relevant to the hot-tapping aspects of "stoppling" operations; although the specific stoppling activities are excluded from the scope of this DEP, they should be subject to similar procedural detail as the hot-tapping activities described herein.

This DEP is a revision of the previous publication of the same number dated December 1998; see (1.5) regarding the changes.

## 1.2 DISTRIBUTION, INTENDED USE AND REGULATORY CONSIDERATIONS

Unless otherwise authorised by Shell GSI, the distribution of this DEP is confined to Shell companies and, where necessary, to Contractors and Manufacturers/Suppliers nominated by them.

This DEP is intended primarily for use in exploration/production facilities and oil refineries, but it may also be useful in chemical plants, gas plants and liquid/gas pumping installations.

When DEPs are applied, a Management of Change (MOC) process should be implemented; this is of particular importance when existing facilities are to be modified.

If national and/or local regulations exist in which some of the requirements may be more stringent than in this DEP, the Contractor shall determine by careful scrutiny which of the requirements are the more stringent and which combination of requirements will be acceptable as regards safety, environmental, economic and legal aspects. In all cases the Contractor shall inform the Principal of any deviation from the requirements of this DEP which is considered to be necessary in order to comply with national and/or local regulations. The Principal may then negotiate with the authorities concerned with the object of obtaining agreement to follow this DEP as closely as possible.

---

## 1.3 DEFINITIONS

### 1.3.1 General definitions

The **Contractor** is the party which carries out all or part of the design, engineering, procurement, construction, commissioning or management of a project or operation of a facility. The Principal may undertake all or part of the duties of the Contractor.

The **Manufacturer/Supplier** is the party which manufactures or supplies equipment and services to perform the duties specified by the Contractor.

The **Principal** is the party which initiates the project and ultimately pays for its design and construction. The Principal will generally specify the technical requirements. The Principal may also include an agent or consultant authorised to act for, and on behalf of, the Principal.

The word **shall** indicates a requirement.

The word **should** indicates a recommendation.

### 1.3.2 Specific definitions and abbreviations

| Term | Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Asset operator** | The individual within the Principal's organisation who is responsible for the operation of the pipeline, piping or equipment to be hot-tapped. |
| **Branch pipe** | The pipe which is to be connected to the run-pipe by means of the hot-tap. |
| **Coupon** | Section of pipe cut out during the hot-tap cutting operation. |
| **HAZ** | Heat Affected Zone |
| **HFW linepipe** | High-frequency welded linepipe |
| **Hot-tapping** | A method of making connections to piping (or other equipment) by attaching a fitting to the system, usually by welding, followed by cutting through the pipe wall at the point of attachment utilising an appropriate ("hot-tapping") machine. This operation is generally carried out on a live ("hot") system without decommissioning or interrupting flow. |
| **Lock-O-Ring flange** | Flange with internal segments which can be moved from the outside to lock into the circumferential recess of a Lock-O-Ring plug. |
| **Lock-O-Ring plug** | Plug which can be set into position inside a hot-tap connection flange in order to retain internal pressure. |
| **DN** | Nominal Pipe Diameter |
| **Off-plot Pipeline** | Pipeline designed in accordance with a recognized pipeline design standard e.g. ISO 13623, ASME B31.4 or B31.8 (see Note below). |
| **On-plot Piping** | Piping system designed in accordance with ASME B31.3 (see Note below). |

NOTE: Some parts of a pipeline system, although physically located "off-plot", may be designed in accordance with ASME B31.3. For the purposes of this DEP, such piping shall be considered to be on-plot. Similarly, some refinery piping, although physically located "on-plot", may be designed in accordance with ISO 13623, ASME B31.4 or B31.8. For the purposes of this DEP, such piping shall be considered to be off-plot.

---

**Operating conditions** All conditions of piping and equipment when containing hydrocarbons under a positive internal pressure.

**Run pipe** The pipe into which a hot-tap is to be made.

**SAW linepipe** Submerged arc-welded linepipe

**Stoppling** A hot-tapping operation which includes the insertion and setting of a sealing plug in the pipe in order to stop flow and withstand a certain fluid pressure.

**WPS** Welding procedure specification
