## 1335 Accidental Releases

Federal law (CERCLA) requires that the release to the environment of hazardous substances such as chlorine be immediately reported to allow necessary emergency response to protect the public and environment. Any chlorine release of 10 pounds (1.2 gallons, 49.9 SCF) or more within a 24-hour period must be reported to the National Response Center (NRC) in Washington, D.C. (telephone 1-800-424-8802) and, if exposure occurs to persons outside of the facility, to the state and local emergency response agencies required by Federal Law SARA—Title III. Additional state and local agencies may also require notification.

## 1336 Materials Considerations

Materials selection must take into account the possibility of mechanical damage as well as service conditions. Dry chlorine at room temperature is noncorrosive to carbon steel, copper and the nickel alloys. However, the frequent changing of chlorine containers exposes the piping internals to atmospheric moisture. The corrosion products resulting from the use of carbon steel piping will foul the downstream chlorination equipment.

Chlorine can be handled in Monel piping, tubing, and valves. Container "pigtails" can be cadmium plated copper tubing and should be rated at least 500 psig minimum working pressure. Container "pigtails" should be capped or plugged when out of service to mitigate the intrusion of moisture.

Few alloys can continuously resist wet chlorine. PVC may be considered for the parts of a chlorination system that are continuously wet with, for instance, chlorinated water.

Lead gaskets are used for the container isolating valves. A good practice is to use new lead gaskets when placing a container into service.

Be sure all packing, seals, and gasketing are compatible with chlorine service. Teflon and Viton are acceptable materials.

Consult with your materials engineer for guidance if the recommendations provided in this practice are not suitable for your application.

## 1337 Chlorine Storage

Chlorine containers should be stored outside in a secure, well ventilated area. Provide suitable platforms and supports to hold the containers, and keep them free of standing water. Platforms should be large enough for inspection and emergency repairs.

One-ton containers may require a monorail or crane with a special lifting beam. The containers can be set on roller trunnions to provide support, maintain fixed spacing, and facilitate container rotation in the event of a leak. All 150-lb cylinders should be secured with safety straps or chains and one-ton containers with positive hold-down clamps to prevent inadvertent movement during servicing or in an earthquake.

Minimize the number of chlorine containers that are distributed to the sites where chlorine is used. Spare containers with their associated valves tend to increase the possibility of a chlorine leak. Full and empty containers should be separated from each other as well as segregated from other compressed gas containers and hydrocarbon chemicals.

Usually a four-week supply at a consolidated storage area will be adequate; consult with purchasing regarding optimum delivery schedule to hold storage to a minimum. Chlorine containers should be used on a first-in, first-out basis.

# 1340 Design and Construction Requirements

## 1341 Dispersion Modeling and Risk Assessment

Dispersion modeling may be performed to determine potential chlorine concentrations in air in the event of an accidental release. Modeling results and risk assessment may be used to develop guidelines on design criteria needed to mitigate potential exposure to the community or plant personnel. Possible design criteria affected by the risk assessment are the quantity of chlorine stored and where the chlorine user should be located within the plant. Modeling results may also be used to develop emergency response plans for responding to accidental releases.

Concentrations resulting from a release are highly specific to release rates and meteorological conditions. Furthermore, releases of liquid chlorine forms fine liquid droplets (an aerosol) as well as vapor. The presence of the aerosol makes the chlorine cloud denser than air, which permits the cloud to travel a substantial distance downwind. Each situation should be modeled on a case-by-case basis. The Health, Environment and Safety Group at CRTC has a license to use a model developed by Energy Analysts Inc. called the Energy Analysts Hazards Analysis Package (EAHAP) which is specifically designed to predict concentrations from releases of hazardous chemicals. EAHAP can predict concentrations as a function of distance from the source.

Contact the Health, Environment and Safety Group at CRTC for assistance in dispersion modeling and CRTC Materials and Equipment Engineering for

assistance in risk assessment. A wide variety of chemical releases can be modeled. Releases can be either gaseous or liquid.

## 1342 Container Location

Chlorine containers should be located at least 50 feet from flammable materials and structures, such as wooden cooling towers. Radiated or direct sources of heat should also be avoided.

Additional design considerations should include ample area lighting, fire protection, drainage, and the possibility of mechanical damage. Locate the containers so that drainage from hydrocarbon sources will not expose them to a fire risk.

Containers located close to roads should be guarded and be far enough from the road to provide safety from vehicular traffic while still retaining good access for service and emergencies. Standard Drawing GA-S99975, Standard Details for Removable and Stationary Guard Posts, provides a typical design.

Location relative to hydrocarbons, hot lines, occupied buildings, ventilation intakes, roads, personnel gates, and safety equipment is extremely important and must be evaluated with facility safety personnel.

Refer to Section 1370 for other applicable requirements in locating containers at the chlorine user's site.

## 1343 Piping

Piping downstream of Chlorine Institute standard container valves should be ANSI Class 300, Schedule 40 for Monel pipe sized NPS 1½ and smaller, and installed per ANSI/ASME B31.3 as a minimum requirement. Socket-welded construction is preferred for NPS 1½ and smaller. Do not use unions in straight chlorine service.

Seal-weld all threaded joints, excluding the container isolating valves, pigtails and connections to instruments. Nonmetallic pipe and unions, such as PVC, are acceptable in chlorinated water service.

Piping should be located aboveground and be as simple as possible. Isolating valves should be readily accessible. Minimize the number of threaded joints and flanges that cannot be seal welded. Provide adequate support and protection from mechanical damage. Steel angle, channel or equal should be used to protect nonmetallic piping.

Avoid trapping liquid chlorine. Slope piping so that it is self-draining. Liquid chlorine has a high coefficient of thermal expansion and will produce high pressure and, possibly, piping failure when trapped and heated. Good practice will limit the system to a pair of isolation valves located at each container.

Do not use hydrocarbons, nonchlorinated solvents, alcohols, cutting oil, sealants, or grease in the fabrication or cleanup of chlorine piping systems. Chlorinated solvents such as trichloroethylene may be used to clean the piping before placing the system

into service, but these solvents must be used in accordance with their MSDS and the manufacturer's safety recommendations.

Chlorine piping systems should be pressure-tested when new and prior to being placed in service after repairs or alterations. Piping sections operating under vacuum (between the container valve and chlorinator) may be pressure-tested using N₂ gas and soap-tested for leaks. Safe testing practices using a compressed gas should be adhered to. A 150-pug test pressure is recommended for metallic piping systems, but may need to be lowered for nonmetallic piping materials.

Piping for pressurized chlorine feed systems should be hydrostatically tested in accordance with ANSI/ASME B31.3 requirements. Chlorine Institute Pamphlet 6, Piping Systems for Dry Chlorine, should be used for guidance in preparing a hydrostatic test procedure. It is important to thoroughly clean and dry the piping system after testing and prior to the introduction of chlorine. A dryness to a minus 40°F dewpoint is recommended.

☞ **Caution** *Never attempt to repair leaks until all chlorine has been purged from the system. See Associated Piping Leaks in Section 1334.*

Chlorination system P&IDs (Figure 1300-2 and Figure 1300-3 at the end of Section 1300) for cooling water treatment using 150-lb and one-ton containers are included as guidelines. These P&IDs are reproduced with the permission of CPDS, Richmond Refinery.

## 1344 Vendor-Supplied Systems

All chlorination systems and their proposed site locations shall be reviewed, evaluated, and approved by facility management.

Vacuum-operated chlorinator systems with vacuum regulators attached at the containers offer the safest operation. Applications with chlorine requirements above 20 lb/hr may require a pressure-vacuum system. The pressurized portion of a system should be minimized to reduce the possibility of a leak. Manufacturers of chlorine gas feed equipment can supply their standard system design for evaluation by engineering and safety personnel. They also can provide system setup, maintenance, and periodic service.

Liquid chlorine usually damages the chlorinator components. The following methods may be used to prevent liquid chlorine from entering the chlorinator:

- Install a pressure reducing valve to flash residual liquid.
- Install an electric heater in the chlorinator (most can be factory equipped).
- Heat trace the piping between the containers and chlorinator.
- Install a liquid trap in the piping upstream of the chlorinator.

Chlorinators should be installed in weatherproof enclosures suitable for both the environment and electrical area classification. The enclosure should permit viewing the chlorinator safely through a suitable window.

## 1345 Sizing Criteria

The dependable continuous discharge rate of chlorine gas from a single one-ton container without frosting under normal conditions (70°F) is about 15 lb/hr against a 35 psig backpressure. The rate for a single 150-lb cylinder is about 1.75 lb/hr under similar conditions.

If the gas discharge rate from a single container will not meet usage requirements, alternate arrangements may be considered, such as manifolding more than one container to a common chlorinator or installing an evaporator. Operability and safety of these alternatives require review and approval by the facility management.

If two or more containers are manifolded together, they must be at the same temperature to prevent the transfer of chlorine from a warm container to a cool container. If a container becomes completely filled with liquid and the container valve is then closed, subsequent pressure buildup as the container warms may cause it to burst.

## 1350 Vapor Control and Fire Protection

### 1351 Vapor Control

Vapor control should be done only by personnel specifically trained in handling hazardous materials and experienced in using the appropriate protective equipment.

Alert designated emergency response personnel and downwind facilities regarding any leak. A liquid chlorine leak is appreciably more hazardous than a gaseous leak. Isolate the containers from a piping leak by using the isolating valves at the containers. If the container body is leaking, orient the cylinder or one-ton container so that gas, rather than liquid, is released. This will reduce the rate of release by a factor of fifteen.

To protect internal building environments and the occupants, immediately close doors, windows and air conditioning inlets and vents, and turn off the air ventilation system.

If a chlorine leak should occur, use water to knock down and safely direct the gas away from personnel. Do not apply water directly into the leak, and do not immerse the container in water or alkaline solution. Mixing water with chlorine produces hydrochloric acid, whose corrosive action can increase the size of the initial opening.

Contain drainage water if possible and route to a neutralizing reservoir. Liquid chlorine must be kept out of the sewer system. Soda ash may be used to contain the puddle.

### 1352 Fire Protection

Under fire conditions keep the chlorine containers cool to avoid releasing chlorine through their fusible metal plugs. If possible, remove containers from the fire zone and relocate to a remote area that will not endanger facility access or public safety.

If the container integrity is uncertain, contact CHEMTREC (800-424-9300) or your local CHLOREP (chlorine emergency plan) team for assistance before trying to move the container.

Providing additional spacing away from fire exposure; and using a radiant heat barrier, a water spray, fire monitors or hose stations may be considered.

## 1360  Facility Identification and Guarding

Equipment and lines handling chlorine should have paint stenciled identification, and signs should be posted in compliance with the Company's *Safety in Designs Manual*.

Guard posts, and "caution" and "no parking" signs should be installed at the perimeter of the chlorine storage area and each location where chlorine is used.

## 1370  Inspection

### 1371 Frequency

Due to the potential hazard that can result from equipment and/or piping failure, an effective semiannual facility inspection should be conducted. A typical inspection checklist is included in Section 1372. The inspection should be primarily visual. Nondestructive examination (NDE) may be used on piping as appropriate. Local facility inspection practices should be followed.

Some of the checklist items are suitable for more frequent inspection. Checking for leaks should be a daily routine. Emergency repair kits should be restocked after each use as well as inventoried at the semiannual inspections. It is suggested that inspection and testing be done weekly for safety equipment, including respiratory units, shower/eyewash and protective clothing.

### 1372 Typical Checklist

#### Housekeeping/Design

1. Number of containers and size? Vertical or horizontal? Are there more than the normal number of containers? If so, why?

2. Are guard posts installed?

3. Are positive hold-down clamps in position? Are safety chains in place?

4. Is the area free of combustible material?

5. Are "caution" and "no parking" signs in place?

6. Is the discharge line connected to the one-ton container gas valve in the 12 o'clock position? Is liquid valve in the 6 o'clock position capped?

7. Do empty and spare containers have protective domes installed?

8. Check DOT hydrotest date for each container. Are they current? DOT requires retesting every five years—return noncurrent containers to the supplier.

9. Are there any leaks?

10. Is a chlorine container valve wrench available?

11. Are emergency repair kits available and complete?

12. Are respiratory units properly located and functional?

13. Is the safety shower/eyewash operable?

14. Is the piping in good condition?

15. Does the system meet the design standards? Use this engineering guideline and Attachments I and II at the end of Section 1300 to prepare a detailed checklist.

#### Operation/Operator Awareness

1. Are operating standards and emergency response procedures adequate and readily available to those who use the facility?

2. Is MSDS 646 for chlorine readily available?

3. Are all personnel trained on the hazards, first aid and operation of the chlorine facility?

4. Are Operating Standards/Instructions followed?

5. Do operators use breathing air when changing cylinders?

6. Do operators/supervisors know what to do when a leak occurs?

# 1 Introduction

Safety critical element (SCE) is identified for the purpose of assuring availability and functionality of equipment that provides the greatest contribution to risk reduction for major accident hazards. The intent of identifying SCE is to facilitate prioritization of inspection, testing, maintenance and performance standards by the operating company.

The intent of this philosophy is not to identify SCE, but rather give a guideline on:

1. What constitutes safety critical, pertinent to the work;

2. What studies, relevant to the Project, will define SCE and;

3. What purpose the resulting SCE list will serve.

## 2 Safety Critical Element Designation

SCE is classified as an equipment or system, whose failure could cause or contribute to a major accident, or whose purpose is to prevent or mitigate the effect of a major accident.

### 2.1 Purpose

SCE is identified for the purpose of assuring reliability, availability and functionality of the equipment that prevents and/or mitigates 'major accident hazards'. Major accident hazard is a term defined by the operating company's risk criteria.

SCE will have prioritized inspection, testing, and maintenance tasks, thus providing the greatest relative contribution to risk reduction for potential major accident events. SCE is an integral component of integrity management. The SCE list generated will be provided to the operating company for incorporation into asset and operations integrity management systems (Maintenance Management Systems, Management of Change, Procedures) to enable items to be flagged, prioritized, tracked and managed appropriately.

### 2.2 Definition of Safety Critical

Safety-critical, as will be considered by the Project, is defined by the following:

4. Pieces of equipment where the consequences of failure could cause or contribute substantially to a major accident event.

    a. Examples of this include a control valve failing closed or a pump failing to operate, resulting in an overpressure condition in upstream equipment. It should be noted that the control valve or the pump will only qualify as an SCE if the extent of the overpressure consequence is defined as a 'major accident' (see section 2.3.1).

5. Equipment that prevents, detects, controls and mitigates a major accident (see section 2.4 for examples).

## 2.3 Hazard Assessments

For the scope of work, SCE will be identified through the Hazard Identification (HAZID) Study and Hazard and Operability Study/Layer of Protection Analysis (HAZOP/LOPA). Other equipment may be considered SCE by the operating company, as determined through other criticality assessment methodologies implemented external to the Project scope of work.

### 2.3.1 Qualifying events for SCE consideration

For an item to be considered for SCE designation, all credible failure events will be evaluated. Based on these failure events, any that are categorized as a health and safety related ‘major accident’, a term defined by the operating company’s risk criteria, will be considered safety-critical.

## 2.4 SCE Evaluation and Categorization

For events determined to be safety-critical by the Project, per section 2.3, equipment will be evaluated and designated as a SCE based on the two categories that follow:

### 2.4.1 Isolation and Prevention

1. Equipment under this category, often referred to as Independent Protection Layer (IPL), is defined as the ultimate safety-critical device that by engineered design, provides managed control for avoiding a hazardous event leading to a hazardous release of hydrocarbons/ chemicals. The systematic loop analyses of these SCE components should be based on HAZOP/LOPA data.

   a. IPLs are generally specified in the HAZOP/LOPA study, include all equipment from sensing devices to ending devices, and are required to be independent of the initiating event or the action of any other protection layer associated with the scenario.

   b. Examples of IPLs include, but are not limited to: Pressure safety valves (PSVs), safety-instrumented systems (SIS), key control valve loops, critical alarms that require operator intervention, combination IPLs such as a limiting element (restriction orifice/spools, check valves or control valve that limits flow) and a PSV sized for full capacity of restricted flow.

### 2.4.2 Control, Detect and Mitigate

1. This equipment will provide detection, mitigation, and control functions in the event of an uncontrolled release of hydrocarbons/chemicals. The primary intent for these SCEs is to prevent and/or control a catastrophic release of hydrocarbons (which generally reduces severity of event).

   a. Equipment in this category are generally listed in the HAZOP/LOPA study as Safeguards.

b. Examples of these equipment types include, but are not limited to: Active fire and gas systems, ventilation systems with detection/mitigation/control equipment, manually initiated ESD and blowdown systems.

## 2.5 SCE Exclusions

Although they may be discussed during the HAZOP/LOPA, following is a list of equipment categories that are generally not considered SCE:

- Passive mitigation and evacuation systems (i.e., fire and blast walls, egress structures)

- Electrical Systems (i.e., junction boxes)

- Fixed hydrocarbon-containing equipment

  - These equipment types do not actively mitigate or prevent a catastrophic release by their function, and are not designed to alert personnel of an impending or occurred release

  - Their pressure-containment function is only passive in nature; therefore, as a rule, these equipment types not to be classified as SCE include vessels, tanks, piping, and flow lines. Pumps, compressors, and turbines are also included in this category unless they are part of a protective system.

- Occupational Personal Safety Equipment (PPE, SCBA, fall protection gear, eye wash)

It should be noted the above mentioned categories will have maintenance activities through their associated regulatory requirements and/or facility maintenance strategies.

## 2.6 SCE List

A SCE list will be generated by the project upon completion of the HAZOP/LOPA that will identify:

- A description of the equipment/instrument classified as SCE, including type and function;

- Equipment/instrument tag number;

- Corresponding HAZOP/LOPA scenario reference number;

- P&ID reference number;

- Safety Integrity Level (SIL) Requirement for Safety Instrumented Functions (SIF).

## 2.6.1 Integrity Management of SCE

The SCE list will be turned over to the operating company for assignment of required inspection, testing and maintenance tasks and frequencies, as well as definition of performance standards, in line with the company's standards and criteria. Testing and inspection frequencies and methodologies are generally established through consideration of the following:

- Codes and standards such as the National Board Inspection Code, American Society for Testing and Materials, American Petroleum Institute, National Fire Protection Association, American National Standards Institute, American Society of Mechanical Engineers;
- Factors such as magnitude of risk from malfunction/failure of equipment, intensity of use, operating environment and variety of operations that the equipment is exposed to;
- Failure rate of equipment (published values such as those available in OREDA, as well as historical data once available) which in turn influences inspection and testing frequency;
- For SIFs, testing and inspection frequency is established in accordance with ISA-84.00.01.

Equipment/systems identified in the SCE list should be incorporated into asset and operations integrity management systems, including maintenance management systems, procedures and Management of Change. This facilitates identification of SCE, provides a means to track and ensure completion of required tasks at the required intervals, and provides administrative controls of SCE items to ensure changes to the SCE are not made that would defeat its intended function as a protective device.

# 1 Objective

The objective of this document is to describe the minimum process requirements for the measurement of produced fluids, oil, gas, water, and other components at the Nanushuk Processing Facility (NPF).

Many metering requirements are regulated by a regulatory agency, and compliance with the regulations is required, even if in excess of the requirements specified in this document.

# 2 General Requirements

Many metering locations are regulated by agency and shall meet all of the requirements specified by the governing body. In addition, the metering equipment shall be designed to be compliant with the requirements of the Project.

Typical considerations required by governing body and/or Project requirements for metering equipment are:

- Metering accuracy during normal conditions
- Metering accuracy at varying conditions, as applicable, including:
  - Varying flow
  - Varying temperatures and pressures
  - Varying composition
  - Over the usable life of the device
- Accuracy for both instantaneous flow rate as well as accuracy of totalized value
- Size of metering equipment
- Serviceability
- Pressure drop
- Interface with Process Control System
- Protection from unintentional modification of flow computer
- Meter provers installed for LACT meters

## 3 Metering Types

### 3.1 Custody Transfer Meters

Custody Transfer Meters establish the quantity of product transferred between two legal entities. These types of meters will be added when an importing or exporting of a product occurs. This will include:

- Sales Oil
- Imported Makeup Gas
- Imported Makeup Water

The sales oil line shall be LACT type meter with meter proving system installed.

### 3.2 Leak Detection Meters

Leak detection metering is used for the purposes of detecting leaks, typically in pipelines, by comparing the flow measurements on the export side of a pipeline to the import side of the pipeline. Leak Detection Meters to be designed to API 1130. The leak detection system for the Sales Oil shall be integrated with the LACT system.

### 3.3 Flare and Vent Gas

Regulatory Agencies require the metering of flared and vented gases, and as such, all flare and vented gas shall be metered, and for flare meters shall be non-intrusive to avoid obstructions in the relief path.

## 3.4 Well Fluid Meters

Produced well fluids from the drill sites shall be metered, but this scope is by others, and will not be part of the Nanushuk Processing Facility (NPF).

## 3.5 Fuel Gas Meters

Regulatory agencies require the metering of fuel gas consumed within the plant. These meters will be associated with fuel gas powered equipment such as engines, turbines, fired heaters, incinerators, etc. Fuel gas meters may not be required in equipment that returns unburned fuel gas back to the process, such as equipment that uses fuel gas as a stripping gas.

If fuel gas meters are not required by regulatory agency, fuel gas metering may be eliminated if not otherwise required, but is typically added to major fuel gas consumers for performance testing if not already included as part of the vendor package.

## 3.6 Injection Meters

Injection lines are to be metered, including gas injection, process water injection, graywater injection, any disposal wells, miscible injectant wells, etc. If different fluids are combined into one stream, only one meter is required for the stream. For example, if graywater and process water are injected into the same wells, only one meter is required for this combined stream. Each drill site shall be separately metered.

## 3.7 Rotating Equipment Flow Meters

Rotating equipment, especially centrifugal pumps and compressors require flow metering for surge and minimum flow control. Typically the requirements for these meters are defined by the vendor, but at a minimum, shall monitor the flowrate of the fluid for the purposes of controlling the rotating equipment to maintain it within its minimum to maximum operating range (such as to prevent compressor surge).

## 3.8 Chemical Injection

Small quantity injection chemicals shall be locally metered to quantify injection rate. It is not required for the metering technology to be electronic or interface with the process control system for these purposes.

## 3.9 Utility Fluids

Utility fluids such as diesel fuel, gasoline, methanol, glycol, lube oil, etc. shall be metered to monitor consumption, but are not required to be electronic or interface with the process control system.

## 3.10 Sand Metering

Metering of produced sand may be elected to be added if quantification of sand input into the process is desired. Sand detectors enable Operations to be aware of the amount of sand produced from the well,

which can be used for estimating erosion on the process equipment over time, and to potentially prevent failure due to an unknown high production of sand. Sand meters do not require high accuracy compared to other types of meters.

## 4 Accuracy Requirements

The accuracy requirement for metering varies in the type of fluid, and the purpose. The table below lists the recommended accuracy requirements. The meters shall be rated for the below max inaccuracy, or better, through the entire required flow range for the meter, including all turndown requirements.

## 5 Additional Considerations

### 5.1 Flow Conditions Over the Life of the Facility

Certain processes may change significantly throughout the life of the Facility. These changes may include changes in the condition of the stream such as a change in flow, temperature, or pressure, to

significant changes such as the composition or ratio of Gas, Oil, and Water in the stream. This change over time needs to be considered when selecting the flowmeter technology for the service. This may be in the form of selecting a flowmeter that is usable over the entire expected range, or use of software to compensate. If the change in flow conditions over time is significant where flowmeter technology is not capable of covering the entire range, provisions to replace the flow device over time shall be designed.

This may include:

1. For flow changes over the long term (months or years), a device that can be easily exchanged with a brief shutdown may be acceptable. An example of this is exchanging an orifice plate from one orifice size or another to keep the readings accurate within the new flow calibration range. Alternatively a flow device can be installed with a manual bypass or a parallel meter to be installed so a shutdown is not required for exchanges.

2. For out of range flow changes over the short term (months or less than a month), or in services where breaking containment is not practical or desired, other flow technologies may be required. These alternates may include:

   a. Use of flowmeters with high turndown capacity

   b. Devices that can be exchanged with different flow elements without breaking containment.

   c. Non-intrusive flow devices may be used with multiple elements installed to include the required calibration range

   d. Multiple flow meters with different calibrated flow ranges may be added in parallel to each other. Installed with isolation valves around each meter so the desired flow range/condition can selected for the current operating condition.

## 5.2 Flow Computers

Flow computers can be used to compensate for variability in the flow conditions for certain meters. The flow computers use analyzers to compensate for changes in composition or other conditions. Advanced flow computers can reduce or eliminate the need to exchange out flow devices over varying process conditions that would normally be required with conventional flow devices.

## 5.3 Multiphase Meters

Multiphase meters are typically located at the drill sites to measure oil production, and are thus out of the scope of the NPF; however, this section describes the general requirements for Multiphase meters if any are required within the NPF limits.

The use of Multiphase Meters to measure oil production presents unique measurement challenges. In addition to flow rate changes over the life of a well or facility, the proportion of gas, oil and water may vary greatly and these are in turn affected by pressure and temperature of the stream. When considering

the uncertainty limits of such a meter for a specific application it is frequently found that over the facility lifetime, the accuracy may be adequate for most of the time, while the measurement may be completely erroneous for some small proportion. These meters are similarly impacted by very high and low water fractions and by high Gas Volume Fractions (GVFs).

When establishing the performance of a Multiphase Meter, it is necessary to establish the predicted lifetime of the facility/well and to predict the characteristic production rates for each product. This is typically done on a year-by-year basis. The accuracy requirements from Section 4 is the worst case uncertainty for production rates not exceeding the meter's stated limitations for GVF, flow rates, water fractions, etc. (the operational window). As a guideline, in addition to meeting the stated uncertainty, the meter is expected to be within its operational window for 100 percent of the first 3 years of operations at least, and during 85 percent of the oil production or more, for the life of the measurement equipment. Specific reservoir management, contractual or regulatory obligations may dictate different terms of functionality and will ultimately define minimum expectations.

Meters used to measure multiphase gas production streams fall into two categories--full wellstream meters, and wet gas meters. Wet gas meters are generally conventional gas meters with correction factors applied to compensate for errors caused by the presence of liquids. Additional calculated factors may be used to determine liquid quantities. Full wellstream meters are Multiphase Meters intended to simultaneously measure and calculate the quantity of each phase in the fluid. In some cases, the meters may not distinguish between different liquid phases (e.g., they don't provide separate water and condensate measurements). The uncertainties referred to in Table 1 refer to either type of measurement system, although it should be noted that the expected uncertainties may vary greatly depending on the measurement system used, the location of the meter (surface or subsea), water fraction, liquid fraction, and other variables.

# 1 Objective

The purpose of this document is to identify the minimum design requirements for Emergency Isolation and Shutdown of the Industry Source 03 Processing Facility. The ability to progressively shutdown energy sources, isolate hydrocarbon inventory, and depressure the process system is the preferred method of protecting hydrocarbon processing facilities.

The hierarchy for system control and loss prevention is:

1. Process Control System (PCS)

2. This system is designed to keep the system operating in its normal operating conditions and set-points. During transient conditions, it is designed to control the system back into normal operating state.

3. Safety Instrumented System (SIS)

4. This system is designed to respond to instrumentation in the process equipment, typically when process conditions exceed certain setpoints, such as high-high pressure, or low-low level. If the process control system is not able to respond to the transient condition, and the process reaches high-high or low-low levels, the SIS will shutdown certain equipment, systems, or the entire process, until a safe condition is met.

5. Mechanical Relieving Devices

6. If the PCS and SIS are not able to respond or contain a transient condition, particularly high pressure, mechanical relief devices are provided as an additional level of protection.

7. Fire & Gas Systems

8. If there is a mechanical failure in the system, leading to a leak and/or fire, the fire and gas systems will trigger alarms, and ultimately lead to a confirmed fire or confirmed gas signal. A confirmed gas or confirmed fire signal from the Fire & Gas system will trigger a shutdown and depressurization of affected systems through the SIS. In applicable modules, the fine water mist system may be started through the Fire & Gas system, or the SIS, or both.

9. Manual Operator Shutdown

10. Operations can initiate a shutdown and/or depressure of individual systems or of the entire facility. This occurs when the previous 4 safeguards do not completely contain or shutdown the systems as

required. This shutdown is typically pushbuttons located in the control room and in strategic locations within modules.

The scope of this document is limited to items 2, 4 and 5 above.

The SIS in conjunction with the PCS is also the primary protection against the escalation of materials release and propagation of fire. In the event of a fire, the SIS is engineered to isolate and depressurize the affected areas and systems to reduce the stress on equipment to maintain containment of flammable process fluids within the systems, or safely evacuate the flammable materials through the flare stack.

Further information about the blowdown system is included in document Industry Source 03 Doc PRPHL-000001 *Relief and Blowdown Philosophy*.

# 2 Design and Application

The SIS designed for this facility shall be designed to be fail-safe, with included redundancies as necessary for the application. The primary requirements for the SIS are:

1. Safely stop the flow in an emergency condition.

2. Isolate systems, vessels, equipment, pipelines, etc. as necessary

3. Provide safe shutdown of equipment

4. Initiate blowdown/depressurization as necessary

In the event of Process or Plant Shutdown, the SIS system will communicate with all affected outside systems such as Drillsites, Campsite, etc. for notification or appropriate actions as needed.

# 3 Emergency Isolation

## 3.1 Shutdown Valves

Emergency Isolation of the Process Systems shall be achieved with automatic shutdown valves. These valves shall be designed with appropriate fail-safe considerations, and designed to withstand an upset and emergency condition, including:

1. Process pressures and temperatures during the upset condition

2. Fire (fire safe); explosion, chemical exposure from release of hydrocarbons or other hazardous fluids from nearby equipment or process lines

3. Valve to move to, or remain in, the safe position (fail safe) upon emergency isolation condition and upon removal of electricity, control signal, instrument air, hydraulic lines, etc.

4. Valve should also open/close in a time frame appropriate for the system, the valve shall actuate quick enough to safety isolate the system in time to minimize damage, but delayed enough to avoid equipment damage due to pressure surge.

Isolation valves should also remain in safe position following an emergency isolation until locally reset and repositioned. Local reset or a reset from the DCS which should be programed to allow resetting of Shutdown and Isolation valves in a specific sequence without software override. If done out of sequence, password protected override should be used.

There may be additional requirements or exceptions, such as the need for certain shutdown valves requiring the ability to perform partial stroke test online, but all these will need to be reviewed case-by-case.

## 3.2 System and Equipment Isolation

Emergency isolation valves shall be provided at the inlet and/or outlet process equipment at the following locations:

1. Upstream of any Equipment (Vessels, Pumps, Compressor, etc.) that has upstream equipment that has a higher design pressure or temperature.

2. On the liquid outlet downstream of vessels containing significant amounts of liquid hydrocarbons

3. At the Suction and Discharge of every compressor train, or pump trains, processing hydrocarbons or other hazardous fluids.

4. If the compressor/pump train includes dedicated: scrubber vessel(s), cooler(s), pulsation dampener(s), or other equipment, only one set of shutdown valves are required and are placed upstream of the first piece of equipment in the train, and downstream of the last piece of equipment in the train.

5. If the compressor/pump train includes multiple stages, interstage emergency isolation valves are required if the piping and equipment design pressure changes between stages, or if the normal operating liquid level within the stage is a significant volume.

6. Fuel feed to users, including gas turbines, fired heaters, power generators, etc.

## 3.3 Industry Source 03 Processing Facility (NPF) Battery Limit Isolations

Isolation valves must be provided for the overall plant feed and export lines at or near the battery limits. Isolation valves will need to be provided for any imported hydrocarbon streams such as fuel gas, makeup gas, etc. Isolation valves will need to be provided at hydrocarbon export lines, including the crude sales line, and any fuel gas export lines, and lift gas and injection gas lines, in addition to any pump or compressor discharge valves that may exist. Compliance with EIS requirements is required, such as the need to add ESD valves at major river crossings on export crude lines.

# 4 Shutdown

During an emergency or transient condition, in addition to system isolation, the SIS will also trigger equipment shutdown, depending on the emergency or transient condition. Within a system the equipment will generally be triggered to shutdown, which may involve an instantaneous removal of power, or a controlled slow down to stop, or in the case of critical utility or safety related equipment, may still fully operate even during an emergency shutdown, such as electric generators, fire and gas systems, etc.

## 4.1 Shutdown Levels

These shutdowns are listed below in order of smallest shutdown with least impact, to most significant shutdown involving total shutdown of the facility. Each higher shutdown level will trigger the shutdown the respective lower level shutdowns. For example, a particular Unit Shutdown signal will trigger multiple Local Shutdown signals associated with that Unit Shutdown, such as a compressor system shutdown (Unit Shutdown) will trigger the shutdown of the scrubber pump and compressor lube oil pumps (Local Shutdowns) associate with that system.

### 4.1.1 Local Shutdown (SD)

Local Shutdown is designed to isolate and protect as single piece of equipment or section of the system. It is applied in cases where shutdown of a single piece of equipment does not necessitate a larger shutdown. An example of a single equipment shutdown is for a pump motor winding high temperature shutdown when a spare pump is present and can be turned on.

### 4.1.2 Unit Shutdown (USD)

The USD is an Automatic or Manual shutdown of a group of equipment or a process system. The USD is designed to isolate a group of equipment or process systems due to an unsafe operating condition, such as an over-the-limit operating pressure, temperature, flow, or level, which will trigger an automatic unit shutdown. The NPF will be divided into process systems that allow for safe shutdown of the individual unit, while allowing other systems to maintain operation, possibly at a lower capacity. An example is

shutdown of a compressor station (all Flash Gas, or all Lift Gas, or all Injection Compressors as a group). Another example is a shutdown of the HP or LP fuel gas system. This shutdown trips the next lower hierarchy or local shutdown.

### 4.1.3 Process Shut Down (PSD)

The PSD is an Automatic or Manual shutdown of the entire NPF Process System, while maintaining operation of utilities and electrical generation capabilities. An example of a condition that might trigger a manual shutdown could be a leak or loss of pressure containment that is detected during a field walkdown. The PSD will not automatically trigger a blowdown, but provisions are provided in the control room to manually blowdown after a PSD if required.

### 4.1.4 Emergency Shutdown (ESD)

Emergency Shutdown is triggered by manual ESD pushbutton at the module exits and in the control room, or by confirmed fire or gas detection. This will trigger isolation and shutdown of the entire NPF and well pads. Confirmed fire or gas will trigger automatic blowdown, however the ESD pushbutton by Operator will not automatically trigger a blowdown, but provisions will be provided in the control room to blowdown the affected areas as required.

### 4.1.5 Total Plant Shutdown (TPS)

Manually initiated shutdown located in the control room triggers an automated shutdown entire NPF process systems, utilities, and power generation systems. The TPS does not automatically trigger a blowdown of the facility, but provisions will be provided in the control room to blowdown the affected areas if required.

## 4.2 Critical Equipment

Within a system, non-essential rotating equipment are typically shutdown during an emergency isolation to deenergize the system. The shutdown method depends on the equipment and the manufacturer's recommendations.

Some essential equipment may remain energized despite a system or total plant shutdown, if the equipment is critical for emergency operation. The two common examples of this is a firewater or fine water mist pump, standby generator sets, and instrument air, which will be designed to remain operable despite a shutdown.

## 4.3 Minimization of Shutdowns

The shutdown system and hierarchy shall be designed to minimize the number of equipment shutdown during a particular event. During a shutdown event, the shutdown shall be minimized to the smallest

shutdown listed in Section 4.1 that would contain the event. If a local equipment shutdown would be sufficient to contain the fault, this shutdown should be used, and maintain the remainder of the plant in normal operation, potentially at reduced throughput. The design of the SIS in conjunction with the PCS should consider the effects of shutdown on the affected system and any potentially affected systems to ensure one isolated shutdown does not cause cascading shutdowns of other systems unnecessarily. For example a trip of one the gas lift compressor will result in high pressure in the inlet separator. The PCS will open the back pressure valve to HP Flare while the SIS will send a signal to the well choke valves and the gas lift valve to step down production so inlet separator flaring is no longer required.

# 5 Depressurization

During some shutdowns, it may be required to depressurize the equipment, system, or entire facility. The intent of depressurization is to relieve stress on the system by reducing the pressure, as well as safety deinventorying the system in order to reduce the impact of a leak, fire, or other emergency. The depressurization is enabled by blowdown valves that will actuate open to release the contained volume to the flare for all hydrocarbon gas systems. For most compressors, some degree of automated blowdown will be required to handle settle out pressure and protect integrity of gas seals. For process vessels, automated blowdown may not be required, rather would be a result of an Operator input. There could be certain process conditions that would drive an automated blowdown of certain process vessels or systems and this should be determined as part of the HAZOP/LOPA studies. This depressurization system is described in more detail in document Industry Source 03 Doc PRPHL-000001 *Relief and Blowdown Philosophy*.

- Safety Instrumented System Hierarchy

## 3.0 DEFINITIONS

### 3.1

Additional Notes - Designations which identify additional attributes of a piping system, see REP 5-1-1.

### 3.2

Insulation Condition - Designation which identifies attributes of the insulation system:

1. H-heat conservation
2. C-cold insulation
3. PP-personnel protection
4. ET-electric tracing
5. ST-steam tracing

### 3.3

Line Number Sequence - A number assigned to each line starting with Number 1 for each fluid symbol.

### 3.4

Line Service Symbol - The fluid service in each line is identified by a letter symbol. One, two, or three letters may be used for a fluid symbol, see Table 1.

### 3.5

Owner - Phillips 66.

### 3.6

Owner's Engineer - A Phillips 66 appointed engineer.

### 3.7

Pipe Size - More than one pipe size may be required for a line. Each line size is shown along with its physical data. Normally, only one line of a Line Rating Sheet is used for each line size listed. However, for additions, a second size can be included if an unused space is not available. There is one exception - pipe sizes in material classes which require wall calculations must have each size listed independently.

#### 3.8

Piping Material Specification - Specific designation based on pressure class, piping material, service, and temperature. Permissible designations are described in REP 5-2-3. Normally only one material class is assigned for piping covered by a single line number. This requires a piping system to carry two line numbers when a class-break occurs. However, two classes may be included under one number where there is a limited amount of pipe or piping components in the second class.

#### 3.9

Unit Identifier - An abbreviated string of Alpha-Numeric characters used to identify the Plant unit or area to which the line number corresponds.

# 1. INTRODUCTION

## 1.1 SCOPE

This new DEP specifies requirements and gives recommendations for the application of Human Factors Engineering (HFE) principles in project design. It identifies best practice HFE procedures to enable project teams to identify what level of HFE input is required and where in a project it would be most beneficial.

This DEP adopts many of the principles and recommendations of human-centred design established in ISO/DIS 6385 and ISO 13407.

## 1.2 DISTRIBUTION, INTENDED USE AND REGULATORY CONSIDERATIONS

Unless otherwise authorised by Shell GSI and SIEP, the distribution of this DEP is restricted to companies forming part of the Royal Dutch/Shell Group, and to Contractors nominated by them.

This DEP is intended for use in oil refineries, chemical plants, gas plants and, where applicable, exploration and production facilities and supply/marketing installations. When DEPs are applied, a Management of Change (MOC) process should be implemented. This is of particular importance when existing facilities are to be modified.

If national and/or local regulations exist in which some of the requirements may be more stringent than in this DEP the Contractor shall determine by careful scrutiny which of the requirements are the more stringent and which combination of requirements will be acceptable as regards safety, economic and legal aspects. In all cases the Contractor shall inform the Principal of any deviation from the requirements of this DEP which is considered to be necessary in order to comply with national and/or local regulations. The Principal may then negotiate with the Authorities concerned with the object of obtaining agreement to follow this DEP as closely as possible.

## 1.3 DEFINITIONS

### 1.3.1 General definitions

The **Contractor** is the party that carries out all or part of the design, engineering, procurement, construction, commissioning or management of a project or operation of facility. The Principal may undertake all or part of the duties of the Contractor.

The **Manufacturer/Supplier/Vendor** is the party that manufactures or supplies equipment and services to perform the duties specified by the Contractor.

The **Principal** is the party that initiates, and ultimately pays for, the project. The Principal will generally specify the technical requirements. The Principal may also include an agent or consultant, authorised to act for the Principal.

The **Purchaser** is the party that buys the equipment and services for its own use or as agent for the owner. The Purchaser may be either the Principal or the Contractor.

The word **shall** indicates a requirement.

The word **should** indicates a recommendation.

The word **may** indicates a possible course of action.

## 2. MANAGEMENT SUMMARY

### 2.1 GENERAL

The Royal Dutch/Shell Group's diverse activities require projects to be designed to allow a wide range of end users to reliably use the end product in an effective, efficient, safe, healthy and productive manner. In some cases, the end users may also be members of the public who must interface with certain facilities and products, which requires additional design measures to ensure their health, safety and satisfaction.

Industry today is even more conscious about how people work and recognises that the design of the working environment plays a critical role in the effective functioning of a work system and the productivity a working population can achieve. Any limiting factors that hinder an efficient and effective design, and hence overall system performance, should therefore be properly identified early in the design stages and minimised by a user-centred, participative design approach as outlined in this procedure.

The Royal/Dutch Shell Group's Committee of Managing Directors (CMD) has endorsed a set of Minimum Health Management Standards (MHMS). These are the *minimum* requirements for the implementation of Health standards where Shell has operational control. At the same time, compliance with the national statutory requirements of each country where the Group operates is mandatory for all aspects of health management.

This DEP is one of several HFE-related DEPs which support the MHMS *Human Factors Engineering (HFE) in New Facilities Projects*, and are designed to support a wide range of projects.

***Human Factors Engineering principles shall be considered and applied during early design stage of new facilities projects where design can have a critical impact on equipment usability and user safety or health.***

### 2.2 GOALS AND OBJECTIVES

The primary goal of this DEP is to help Project Teams with the implementation of HFE principles and to assist Shell OUs to become compliant with the MHMS *Human Factors Engineering (HFE) in new facilities projects*.

This DEP will ensure that HFE principles are properly considered and applied in the early design stages of new projects where design can have a critical impact on project success.

This DEP also provides a best practice methodology for OUs to meet the mandatory achievement criteria. The process presented and the accompanying appendices provide further guidance to assist in meeting these mandatory criteria; see (3.4).

### 2.3 TARGET READERSHIP

The target readership for this DEP is primarily the Project Team of new projects. However, Process Engineers, Discipline Engineers, IT designers, Retail station designers and Operations and Maintenance personnel should also refer to this DEP throughout the design of new facilities. This DEP is aimed at the promotion of health, safety, efficiency and usability.

When work systems are changed or new projects are developed there may also be changes in the organisational structure/procedures/practices. As described in (3), HFE considers the organisational elements of projects as well, recognising that the system as a whole must be properly designed. Therefore, Human Resources, Organisational Design and Resource Planners should also make use of this DEP.

### 2.4 RELATIONSHIP WITH OTHER DOCUMENTS

The Royal/Dutch Shell Group has a hierarchy of documents dealing with Health, Safety and Environmental issues starting with the *Statement of General Business Principles*. These

were issued in March 1997, along with *Group Procedures for an HSE Management System*.

The *Group HSE Management System* (February, 2002) describes how mandatory Group requirements are managed at Group level. Each Group Business Organisation has an HSE-MS.

This DEP should be read independently of all other MHMS governing documents. Following the procedures and achieving the criteria set out in (3.3) constitutes compliance with the Minimum Health Management Standard, *Human Factors Engineering in New Projects*.

# 3. HUMAN FACTORS ENGINEERING (HFE)

## 3.1 BENEFITS

NOTE: The term "ergonomics" is used by many organisations and can be considered synonymous with HFE. Shell has adopted the term "Human Factors Engineering" and this term will be used throughout this DEP.

A driving philosophy behind the application of HFE is that strong operational performance starts with good design and that an understanding of what constitutes good design requires a detailed knowledge of how humans interact within the work system.

As a formal definition, HFE is a multidisciplinary field that considers the integrated knowledge of human capabilities, limitations and needs in the interaction between humans, technology and the working environment. HFE is applied to the design of work systems, workplaces and products, with the following objectives:

1. To increase the operational performance, safety, health and comfort of the work system (through attention to safety, operability, maintainability and constructability in design).
2. To reduce the likelihood of or prevent human errors and/or limit the consequences (through attention to human and systems reliability in design).
3. To enhance the productivity of human efforts (through attention to efficiency in design)
4. To enhance overall system performance by improving the ease and efficiency of use (through attention to usability issues in design).
5. To incorporate user knowledge in the design of the system/product (through attention to user acceptability and marketability).

These objectives will form the philosophy of this procedure and be the key drivers in the process outlined in the following sections.

HFE includes the design of user centred products, workstations and work systems. This science also addresses organisational issues and looks at how the job and tasks are structured and designed within a wider context so that all human efforts are optimised.

Some potential benefits of HFE in projects include:

- CAPEX reduction.
- Engineering hours reduction.
- Operational and maintenance life cycle costs reduction.
- Reduced re-work during construction.
- Overall improvement of HSE performance.
- Improved usability of designed products, information technology and buildings
- Enhanced client commitment ('buy in') often resulting in a reduction of approval cycles in the design phase.
- Improvement of knowledge of operations and maintenance tasks during design and engineering leading to improved life cycle cost awareness and cost reduction measures in design.

## 3.2 HFE IN PROJECTS

Human Factor Engineering shall be applied in the following projects:

- New plants/facilities (onshore and offshore),
- Revamp of existing plant/facility (unless there is no change to the work system, e.g. like-for-like change out, and no benefits from design improvements can be justified).
- Buildings and workstations design (e.g. retail stations, central control rooms, offices, workshops, laboratories);

- IT software/hardware, instrumentation.

An important principle in the approach to meeting the HFE MHMS is that the process of identifying, understanding and specifying the detailed HFE design requirements should be started at an appropriately early stage in the design process, so that these 'requirements' (technical design specifications and/or HFE scopes of work to be executed to derive/check design specifications) are incorporated in the Basic Design and Engineering Package (BDEP) / Project Specification (PS) documents. While further refinement activities may be required at later stages (e.g., in detailed design), this avoids the need to change design at a late stage, when to do so may not be cost effective.

Application of the principle is based on the premise that strong operational performance begins with good design. The operational performance requirements/expectations need to be actively considered in order to specify design requirements that will serve as a platform for desired performance levels.

## 3.3 HFE IN DESIGN

At a high level, the key design principles that should be considered include the need for a user-centred, integrated, proactive and participative approach to design. HFE principles have been developed for a range of work contexts and are all aimed at guiding the designer in the achievement of fit for purpose work systems.

The user-centred design approach should be initiated at the development phase. While HFE efforts are initiated at the development stage, the overall HFE input may well span the entire development and implementation phases.

Design activities shall be addressed from an HFE standpoint and shall not only cover hardware and software, but also consider other critical issues and design interfaces that arise from a project such as organisational design, work cycles, locations, job/task design, and operational and manning philosophy.

The following aspects shall be addressed:

1. Critical impact - This is where poor design can have a negative impact on task and system performance.

2. Equipment usability - This describes the ease with which people interface with machines or technology.

3. User safety and health - Human performance during work is optimised by a user centred design approach, leading to a safe, comfortable and healthy working environment that minimises the likelihood of human error and work related injuries or ill health. Safety refers to occupational health and safety and also major hazard safety.

The HFE design analysis process is detailed in Appendix 4.

## 3.4 ACHIEVEMENT CRITERIA

The Minimum Health Management Standard is achieved when:

1. All new facilities projects are reviewed for minimum HFE requirements.

2. Where the screening indicates that HFE input is necessary, the location or business applies the correct processes, tools and competencies at the correct stages of the project.

3. The HFE recommendations have been discussed with management and action parties and target dates agreed.

## 4.2.2 Project Development (Figure 2)

### 4.2.2.1 Basic Design

1. *Assemble Project Ergonomics Team (PET)*

The PET meets at the beginning of the Basis of Design Phase, and shall include the:
- Project Manager, Project Engineer;
- Process Engineer;
- Operations/Maintenance representative.

2. *Apply HFE in Project*

The Project Manager shall address this question in order to assure that the project complies with MHMS (3.3).

3. *Identify Design Hotspots and Performance issues*

This is achieved by means of the HFE Focusing Tool (Appendix 1), and the Work Systems Analysis Tool (Appendix 2). These tools are used to help identify relevant Performance Factors in the project that may require more detailed thought and HFE attention.

The PET shall consider the 10 Performance Factors in the HFE Focusing Tool through discussion of past experiences from similar projects and knowledge of the current project. Such discussions shall be open with participation from all relevant team members. Where specific past experience is not known or clearly understood, it should be captured and evaluated for the purposes of the current project, e.g. by identifying end users with the required experience and competence, and by analysing the data and root causes of any accidents and incidents (e.g. from Tripod Beta databases, HFE relevant general failure types, and the associated organisation and procedures).

Once it has been established which specific design aspects would benefit from attention, those hotspots and associated performance issues shall be recorded within the project Work Systems Analysis Tool.

The Work Systems Analysis Tool is used by the PET to identify the work systems of the project that will benefit from HFE efforts with respect to the performance factors identified by means of the HFE Focusing Tool.

4. *Identify HFE Scope of Work*

Figure 4 (Appendix 2) assists in determining the appropriate level of HFE activity in order to achieve the desired design and performance outcome. Table 5 (Appendix 2) outlines the criteria for the three levels of HFE effort that may be applied.

Any Level 1 HFE input required (application of HFE specs alone) must adhere to the criteria laid out in Table 5. Activities for this level will not require the involvement of additional HFE competence (other than the awareness training that the team has already undertaken).

Identified Level 2 activities are carried out by a competent individual (6) and are incorporated as part of the regular review procedures of the project (e.g. at 30 %, 60 % and 90 % completion). This individual shall perform required reviews from the necessary HFE perspective.

For Level 3 activities, it will have been decided by the PET that either additional scrutiny of a particular project aspect is required (using a more formal front end HFE requirements identification tool) in order to identify key issues and requirements, or/and particular actions have been identified that will require specific targeted scopes of work to achieve the end result. For either of these, Human Factors Engineer (i.e. a skilled or mastery level HFE professional (6)) will be required to assist.

If any Level 3 HFE activities are identified as being required for the project, then the Project Team must utilise the support of a Human Factors Engineer. Level 3 inputs therefore require the addition of a Human Factors Engineer to the PET.

With Level 3 HFE activities identified, depending on the project scope, the PET should include, as appropriate, the following disciplines, e.g.:

- Operations;
- Process Engineering;
- Maintenance and/or shutdown;
- Piping and layout specialists;
- Discipline engineers, e.g., mechanical, instrumentation, running/static equipment;
- Human Factors Engineer;
- IT Developers;
- Retail Station Designers.

If Level 3 HFE activities are required for the project, the Human Factors Engineer should lead or facilitate them.

### 5. *Develop HFE Plan*

After the required levels of HFE input (or actions for further scrutiny) have been decided, conclusions shall documented and included in the overall project report for audit purposes.

By using the two Tools described here, the PET starts the process of considering how design will interact with specified future end-users, and what steps must be taken to ensure and confirm that task demands will be fully supported by design features. Design should obviously reflect operational conditions and the requirements of all end users, taking account of their mental and physical capacities and limitations. This process is likely to continue into subsequent stages of the design.

### 6. *Incorporate HFE Plan into PEP*

All actions required in the development phase shall be tracked throughout subsequent design phases.

## 4.2.2.2 Basic Design and Engineering /Project Specification

### 7. *Conduct HFE Analysis (when specified)*

At this stage either formal HFE scope of work will be ready to execute, and/or a front end HFE review session will have been requested. Appendix 4 provides an HFE design analysis tool specifically designed to identify end user requirements for a new project.

The PET supports the Human Factors Engineer in all HFE analysis activities throughout this stage of the project. Such support could come by way of regular design meetings, information gathering or the provision and development of human centred policies (e.g. manning philosophy).

The Human Factors Engineer is responsible for the required Level 3 analyses identified at the Work System Analysis Tool stage. The type of project will dictate how the analysis is carried out and which tools are appropriate.

The PT shall engage a Human Factors Engineer to carry out all level 3 HFE activities; see (Appendix 3) for a competence screening tool.

The Human Factors Engineer shall produce an HFE design report as part of the normal Level 3 analysis activities. The Project Manager shall consider each recommendation provided by the Human Factors Engineer and decide to accept or reject the recommendation.

Most PTs will have a process for accepting design recommendations and should include HFE design recommendations in that process.

### 8. *HFE Specifications and scopes of work accepted by Project Manager*

In case of dilemmas the Investment Justification Tool in DEP 30.00.60.12-Gen. should be applied to test the economics of HFE recommendations.

Both the Project Manager and the Human Factors Engineer should use this DEP.

9. *Include HFE requirements in the Project Specifications Document*

The approved recommendations shall form the basis for the Human Factors Engineering specifications in the Project Specifications Document.

## 4.2.2 PROJECT IMPLEMENTATION PHASE (Figure 3)

### 4.2.3.1 Detailed Design and Engineering

10. *Determine HFE Implementation Plan*

A project specific HFE implementation plan is produced, specifying all activities required (drawing on the results from the Work Systems Analysis tool and any subsequent analyses undertaken by the Human Factors Engineer etc.). The plan details what actions shall be executed in the subsequent project phases, and explains how these are to be executed. Again, the 3 levels of HFE activity should be represented in the plan, as appropriate, and as indicated from the Work Systems Analysis Tool. The plan should also indicate what additional activities are required in the Project Specification phase to confirm/further specify requirements, as a result of any additional information. An example of such a plan is given in (Appendix 5).

11. *Project Manager Approval of Plan*

Should the HFE Implementation Plan not be approved, a feedback loop is required to adjust the plan. The Human Factors Engineer should address points of contention and misinterpretation, possibly in the HFE Implementation Plan.

12. *Include HFE Implementation Plan into the Project Implementation Plan*

When the HFE Implementation Plan has been finalised it should be included in the final Project Implementation Plan (PIP) by the Project Manager (or his delegate).

### 4.2.3.2 Construction Phase

13. *Execute HFE Activities*

This step is to be carried out for all Level 2 and 3 HFE activities that were identified in Step 7 (4.2.2.2). HFE reviews and other required activities should be carried out during the same period when overall project design reviews are carried out, and should be executed as part of the overall design activities to ensure proper co-ordination and communication. Reviews shall be carried out by the Human Factors Engineer or alternatively can be carried out by the HFE focal point provided the individual has a working knowledge level; see (6)

The process for the reviews is:

- Identification of the objective of the review.
- Identify the appropriate design specifications for the work system under review.
- Carry out the review/verification process (i.e. does the design meet the required standards).

14. *Determine Construction Plan*

The Human Factors Engineer and representatives from the construction management team shall develop the construction plan inclusive of the HFE requirements outlined in the PS document.

15. *Construction Plan Approval*

Should the Construction Plan not be approved, a feedback loop is required to adjust the plan. Points of contention and misinterpretation should be addressed by the HFE Engineer in order for the project to move forward into the construction phase.

## 16. Implement Construction Plan

The purpose of the HFE construction plan is to guide the construction contractor with respect to installing equipment not usually shown in the 3D CAD model. This concerns mainly 'field run' installed equipment (e.g. small bore piping, lighting fixtures, secondary cable trays etc.). This will ensure that the HFE specifications are assured throughout the construction phase and are not compromised inadvertently.

It may be necessary to insert relevant requirements into the installation contractors' work scope, as well as monitoring and verifying that needs have been met. This process can be met through:

- Awareness sessions with on-site contractors.
- Execution of HFE verification rounds.
- A procedure which advises the contractor how to deal with a situation, diagnosed as ergonomically undesirable.

### 4.2.3.3 Post Implementation

#### 17. Evaluate the success of the Application of HFE in the Project

The Human Factors Engineer may, together with the Project Manager and/or client/owner, decide to evaluate the HFE undertaken on the project. This evaluation may include:

- Ergonomics evaluations during operations (to verify that ergonomics hazards have been properly controlled in design and to identify other possible issues that were not predicted adequately or dealt with).
- Organisational design issues (to verify that organisational demands were adequately predicted and dealt with during the design phase).
- Costs and benefits of HFE involvement in the project, etc.

This feedback process, together with other sources of data (e.g. from Tripod Beta analyses considering HFE related general failure types (GFTs) such as design, organisation and procedures), can generate an important source of data on opportunities for improving in designs in future projects. It can also be used to assess and/or improve the HFE methods and tools employed to ensure that required performance standards are achieved. Such data should be actively captured and made available as input to new project design specifications.

# 6 COMPETENCES

The Group HSE Management System states that "Competence stems from a combination of factors such as innate ability, experience, training and capacity to learn; it involves the ability to deal with routine as well as non-routine situations." Human Factors Engineering competence is no different. Training cannot be the sole source of competence development for all levels. The four levels of competence are defined in Table 2:

> **Table - Table 2 Competence Definitions for HFE in New Projects** - see [XLSX](19-project-engineering-and-documentation/_assets/19-project-engineering-and-documentation-02/tables/19-project-engineering-and-documentation-02_p0019_tbl01_competence-definitions-for-hfe-in-new-pr.xlsx) and [source crop](19-project-engineering-and-documentation/_assets/19-project-engineering-and-documentation-02/tables/19-project-engineering-and-documentation-02_p0019_tbl01_competence-definitions-for-hfe-in-new-pr.png)

| Competence level | Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| Awareness (A): | (Can discuss) The individual is familiar with the HFE process and understands the principals, concepts and language. The individual knows when and how the HFE design process applies to projects and is familiar with the different project phases and timing. |
| Working Knowledge (WK): | (Can do) The individual has undergone the Working Knowledge training course. This individual can carry out the Human Factors Engineering tools in this DEP (Focusing and Work Systems Analysis Tools). This individual has a number of years of project experience and is familiar with the principles of Human Factors Engineering. |
| Skilled (S): | (Can Lead) The individual can apply and adapt Human Factors Engineering principles and tools to a variety of project settings. This person can think analytically and produce new solutions to existing problems, and can lead and coach a design team. |
| Mastery (M): | (Can Design) The individual can design Human Factors Engineering Tools and teach their use to individuals of other engineering disciplines. |
